IT & infrastructure · my level: ■■■□□ working · proof
Active Directory is the phone book and the keyring of a Windows network. Learn domains, OUs, users, groups and how permissions really flow, then find the account that's secretly a Domain Admin.
simple // the idea in plain words

In a company, hundreds of Windows machines and users need to trust the same logins. Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is the central database that makes that work. A server running it is a Domain Controller (DC). When you log into a work PC, the DC checks your password and tells the PC who you are.
The building blocks:
Domain: the security boundary, like corp.local
Users and computers: objects in the directory
Groups: collections of users, used to grant access ("Finance Share Readers")
OUs (organizational units): folders to organize objects and to target Group Policy
$ cat ~/ad/structure.txt
$ cat ~/ad/users.csv
Grant access to groups, not to individual users. When someone changes jobs, you move them between groups instead of hunting down every permission.

Domain: a company's directory, such as corp.example.com. Everything inside trusts the same authority.
Domain controller (DC): the server that holds the directory and answers logins. Usually two or more.
Object: a user, computer, group or printer. Each has attributes (name, password hash, group membership).
OU (organizational unit): a folder you use to organize objects and to attach policy.
Forest and trust: a forest is one or more domains that share a schema; trusts let users from one domain use resources in another.
SID: the unique ID Windows actually uses to identify an account. Names are just labels.
When someone logs into a work PC with their company account, the PC asks a domain controller to verify the password, and the DC replies with proof of who they are and which groups they are in.

Groups can contain other groups (nesting). The recommended Microsoft pattern is AGDLP: put Accounts into Global groups (by role, like "Finance Staff"), put global groups into Domain Local groups (by resource, like "Finance Share RW"), and assign Permissions to the domain local group.
Nesting is powerful and easy to lose track of: a user's real access is the sum of every group they're in, directly or through nesting.
$ cat ~/ad/groups.txt
$ grep "Domain Admins" ~/ad/groups.txt

Domain logins use Kerberos: the DC gives you a ticket-granting ticket (TGT) at logon, and you trade it for service tickets to reach file shares, SQL servers and so on. Older NTLM still shows up as a fallback and is weaker.

Resetting a password, unlocking an account, adding a user to a group, moving a laptop to the right OU, and disabling an account for a leaver are 90% of help-desk AD work. In Active Directory Users and Computers you do these with a right-click; in PowerShell they are one-liners (see the reference). Always disable and move a leaver rather than deleting, so you can recover the account and its SID.

DNS: AD depends on it. If a PC cannot find the DC through DNS, logins fail. Most AD outages are DNS problems.
LDAP (389/636): how clients query the directory.
Kerberos (88): ticket-based authentication; a user gets a ticket-granting ticket (TGT) at login, then service tickets as needed.
NTLM: the older challenge-response fallback, still around and still abused.
SMB (445): file shares and the SYSVOL folder that distributes Group Policy.

Locked out (too many bad passwords, clears itself or an admin unlocks it), disabled (admin switched it off), expired (password or account date), and "must change password at next logon". Event IDs: 4624 logon, 4625 failed logon, 4740 lockout, 4720 account created, 4728/4732 added to a privileged group.

Owning AD means owning every machine that trusts it. Common paths, all of which are misconfigurations a defender can find first:
Nested group membership that quietly grants admin rights (BloodHound maps these paths as a graph)
Kerberoasting: service accounts with SPNs and weak passwords
AS-REP roasting: accounts with "Do not require Kerberos preauthentication"
Stale privileged accounts, shared admin passwords, and admins logging into workstations (leaving credentials in memory)

Keep Domain Admins tiny and used only on DCs (the tiered admin model)
Separate admin accounts from daily-use accounts (nate vs adm.nate)
Audit privileged group membership recursively, on a schedule, and alert on changes (event IDs 4728/4732/4756 = member added to a security group)
Use LAPS for local admin passwords, gMSAs for service accounts, and disable NTLM where you can
$ grep -E "4728|4732|4756" ~/ad/security.evtx.txt
Attack paths worth being able to describe

Password spraying: one common password tried against many accounts, staying under the lockout threshold.
Kerberoasting: any user can request a service ticket for an account with an SPN, then crack it offline. Defense: long random passwords on service accounts, or managed service accounts.
Pass-the-hash: NTLM hashes can be used as passwords without cracking them. Defense: no local admin reuse (LAPS), restricted admin logons, credential guard.
DCSync: an account with replication rights asks a DC for everyone's hashes. Defense: tightly limit and alert on replication rights.
Golden ticket: stolen krbtgt hash lets an attacker forge tickets. Defense: reset krbtgt twice after a compromise.
Delegation and ACL abuse: a user with write access over a group or an account can take it over. Tools like BloodHound map these paths.

Keep three tiers: domain controllers and identity (tier 0), servers (tier 1), workstations (tier 2). Admins for a higher tier never log into a lower one, because their credentials would be left in memory on a machine that is easier to compromise.

Audit says Domain Admins should have exactly two human members: adm.nate and adm.jrivera.
A direct look at the group shows just those two. But group nesting counts, and one other user ends up with Domain Admin rights through a chain of nested groups.
Resolve the ticket with that user's username.
This one is a ticket in the queue. Open the attachments, investigate in the console under the ticket (every ▶ run above works there), then resolve it with your answer. Hints cost 15 points, wrong answers 5.

linux · my level: ■■□□□ familiar
Stop typing the same five commands. Variables, loops, conditions and scripts, run for real in the sandbox, then write a tiny scanner that finds a planted backdoor.
simple // the idea in plain words

A bash script is just the commands you'd type, saved in a file and run top to bottom. Before scripts, learn the two building blocks: variables and command substitution.
A variable stores text. Set it with NAME=value (no spaces around =) and read it with $NAME:
$ TARGET=10.0.0.5; echo "scanning $TARGET"
$(command) runs a command and drops its output into the line:
$ echo "I am $(whoami) on $(hostname)"
$ echo "there are $(ls ~/sites | wc -l) site files"
Single quotes keep everything literal: echo '$TARGET' prints the dollar sign. Double quotes still expand variables. That one rule explains half of all bash bugs.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
name="${1:-world}"
echo "hello, $name"
The first line (shebang) says which program runs it. set -euo pipefail makes the script stop on errors (-e), on undefined variables (-u) and when any part of a pipe fails. $1 is the first argument and ${1:-world} gives it a default. Save it, make it executable with chmod +x script.sh, and run it with ./script.sh nate.

x=5 (no spaces around =), read with $x or ${x}. Always quote expansions ("$x"), because unquoted values break on spaces and glob characters. $(command) captures output. $? is the last exit code, $# is the number of arguments, $@ is all of them.

Scripts get useful when they repeat and decide.
A for loop runs the same commands once per item:
$ for f in ~/sites/*.conf; do echo "checking $f"; done
if runs a command and checks whether it succeeded (exit code 0). grep -q is perfect for this: it prints nothing and just succeeds or fails.
$ if grep -q "ssl on" ~/sites/shop.conf; then echo "shop: tls"; else echo "shop: NO TLS"; fi
$((...)) does integer math, which is handy for counters:
$ N=0; for f in ~/sites/*.conf; do N=$((N + 1)); done; echo "$N configs"
Put lines like these in a file and run it with bash file.sh. $1, $2... are the arguments you pass:
$ cat ~/bin/audit.sh
$ bash ~/bin/audit.sh ~/sites

if [[ -f "$file" && -r "$file" ]]; then echo ok; elif [[ -d "$file" ]]; then echo dir; else echo missing; fi
for host in web1 web2 db1; do ping -c1 -W1 "$host" >/dev/null && echo "$host up"; done
while read -r line; do echo "$line"; done < hosts.txt
case "$1" in start) echo go;; stop) echo halt;; *) echo "usage";; esac
Test flags: -f file, -d directory, -e exists, -z empty string, -n non-empty, -eq -ne -lt -gt for numbers, == and != for strings.

log() { printf '%s %s\n' "$(date +%T)" "$*" >&2; }
hosts=(web1 web2 db1)
for h in "${hosts[@]}"; do log "checking $h"; done
getopts handles -v -f file style flags. Return values come from return N (an exit code) or from echoing a result and capturing it with $(...).

Loop over files (for f in *.log), rename in bulk (mv "$f" "${f%.log}.txt"), parse CSV columns with cut or awk, run commands on many hosts with ssh host cmd, and schedule with cron. Print errors to stderr (>&2) and exit non-zero on failure.
1. Exit codes are the real booleans

Every command returns a number: 0 means success, anything else is failure. $? holds the last one. && runs the next command only on success, || only on failure:
$ grep -q root /etc/passwd && echo "found root" || echo "no root"
$ ls /nope; echo "exit code: $?"

while read line; do ...; done < file walks a file one line at a time, which is how most log and inventory scripts work:
$ while read h; do echo "would ping $h"; done < ~/hosts.txt
3. Write scripts that don't hurt you

Start real scripts with #!/usr/bin/env bash and set -euo pipefail (stop on errors, unset variables and failed pipes)
Always quote variables: "$f", or a filename with a space becomes two arguments
Never build commands out of untrusted input. eval "$user_input" is command injection waiting to happen
Prefer [[ ]] over [ ] in bash, and $(...) over backticks
The sandbox supports one-line for, while read and if blocks plus bash script.sh, which covers most of what security scripts do.

Quote everything. Use -- before filenames that might start with -.
Use mktemp for temporary files and trap 'rm -f "$tmp"' EXIT to clean up.
Never build commands from untrusted input (eval and unquoted variables lead to command injection).
Validate input with patterns before using it; check that required tools exist (command -v jq).
Use shellcheck script.sh to catch bugs automatically. It is the single best habit.
Avoid parsing ls output; use globs or find -print0 with xargs -0.

bash -x script.sh prints every command as it runs, set -x and set +x turn tracing on and off inside, and echo to stderr at decision points helps. If it works in your terminal but not in cron, suspect the PATH and the working directory.

Someone planted a backdoor in one of the web server's site configs: an extra proxy_pass line that forwards traffic to an outside address.
There are a lot of configs in ~/sites. Write a loop (or finish ~/bin/hunt.sh) that checks every .conf file and prints the ones containing proxy_pass to an address outside 10.0.0.0/8.
Submit the file name of the backdoored config, e.g. submit blog.conf.
Solve it in the sandbox. Every ▶ run above works on the same lab files, so the examples are your toolbox. Type hint when stuck and submit <answer> when you have it.

offense & RE · my level: ■■□□□ familiar
Binary exploitation is turning a memory bug into control of a program. Learn how the stack works, why gets() is dangerous, and step through a buffer overflow until you control the return address.
simple // the idea in plain words

When a function runs, it gets a slice of memory called a stack frame. Its local variables live there, and so does the return address: where the CPU should jump back to when the function finishes.
A buffer overflow happens when a program copies more data into a variable than it has room for. The extra bytes don't vanish, they spill into whatever sits next to the variable in memory. On the stack, the return address sits just past the local variables.
vuln.c in the lab has a 64-byte name buffer and reads it with gets(), which never checks length. It's loaded in a debugger with an 80-byte input. Start it and watch:
$ start
$ step
$ info locals
The fix is boring and total: never use gets, and use length-checked functions (fgets(name, sizeof name, stdin)).

A vulnerability is a bug that lets an attacker do something unintended; an exploit is code that uses it; a payload is what runs afterward (a shell, for example). Memory corruption bugs happen in languages without bounds checking (C, C++): the program writes or reads outside the memory it owns. Memory-safe languages (Rust, Go, Java, Python) remove most of them.

Practice on your own VMs, deliberately vulnerable programs (the lab in this guide, picoCTF, pwnable.kr, ROP Emporium, pwn.college) and CTFs. Binary exploitation against systems you do not own is illegal.

At the moment greet() is running, its frame looks like this, from lower to higher addresses:
name[64] (the buffer), starting at &name
padding the compiler may add (here: none)
the saved RBP (8 bytes): the caller's frame pointer
the saved RIP (8 bytes): the return address into main
Writing past name overwrites saved RBP first, then saved RIP. Step to just after gets() and look at what happened to them:
$ break 12
$ continue
$ print saved_rbp
$ print saved_rip
0x41 is the byte for "A" and 0x42 for "B", so the saved registers are now made of your input.
$ continue

Stack buffer overflow: copying input into a fixed buffer without checking length (gets, strcpy, scanf("%s")).
Format string: printf(user_input) lets %x read the stack and %n write to memory.
Integer overflow: a size computed with wrapping arithmetic becomes small, so too little memory is allocated.
Heap overflow and use-after-free: corrupting heap metadata or using memory after it was freed.
Off-by-one: one byte beyond the buffer, often enough to change a saved pointer.

Check protections: checksec ./prog.
Find the crash: feed a long pattern (cyclic 200 from pwntools), see which bytes land in rip or the saved return address, and compute the offset (cyclic -l value).
Decide the goal: overwrite the return address to jump to a function that already exists (like win()), to your own shellcode, or to a ROP chain.
Write it in Python with pwntools and test under gdb.
Then fix the bug and see the exploit fail, which is the point of learning it.

A crash at 0x4242424242424242 means the CPU tried to return to an address you chose. Replace the B's with a real address and the function "returns" wherever you want. In this binary, win() is at 0x401196, so the classic payload is:
72 bytes of padding + 0x401196 as 8 little-endian bytes (\x96\x11\x40\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00)
Finding the offset is usually done with a cyclic pattern (pwntools cyclic 100, or pattern_create in Metasploit): every 8-byte chunk is unique, so the value in RIP at the crash tells you exactly where it lies. Or compute it from addresses, &saved_rip - &name.
$ print &name
$ print &saved_rip
Mitigations, and how each is attacked

Stack canaries: a random value before saved RIP that's checked on return. Bypassed by leaking it
NX / DEP: the stack isn't executable, so injected shellcode won't run. Bypassed with ROP (chaining existing code snippets ending in ret)
ASLR / PIE: addresses are random each run. Bypassed by leaking one address and computing the rest
checksec shows which are on. This lab binary was built with all of them off (-fno-stack-protector -no-pie -z execstack)
Modern mitigations and what they stop

NX/DEP makes the stack non-executable, so injected shellcode will not run (answer: return-oriented programming, reusing existing code snippets called gadgets). ASLR randomizes addresses (answer: information leaks, or brute force on 32-bit). Stack canaries detect overwrites before a function returns (answer: leak the canary or avoid it). PIE randomizes the binary itself. RELRO protects the GOT. CFI and shadow stacks check control flow in hardware or software. Each raises the cost; chains of bugs still win.

Compile with -fstack-protector-strong -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2 -fPIE -pie -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now, run fuzzers (AFL++, libFuzzer) and sanitizers (-fsanitize=address,undefined), replace unsafe functions (fgets, snprintf, strncpy with care), prefer memory-safe languages for new code, and keep software patched.

from pwn import *
p = process("./vuln")
payload = b"A" * 72 + p64(0x401196)
p.sendline(payload)
p.interactive()
The offset (72 here) comes from the crash analysis and the address from objdump or nm.

To aim at win() you need the offset: how many bytes of input fill the buffer and everything else before the saved return address.
Step through the overflow and work it out from the addresses the debugger shows.
Submit the offset in bytes (a decimal number), e.g. submit 40.

languages · my level: ■■□□□ familiar · proof
Assembly is what the CPU actually runs, and what you read when there's no source code. Learn registers, the stack, flags and calling conventions, then single-step a license check and pull the valid key out of a register.
simple // the idea in plain words

A CPU only understands machine code: numbers. Assembly is the human-readable version, one instruction per line. C compiles down to it, and reverse engineers read it in Ghidra, IDA or gdb.
Registers are the CPU's tiny, super-fast variables. On x86-64: rax, rbx, rcx, rdx, rsi, rdi, rsp (stack pointer), rbp (frame base), rip (next instruction). eax is the lower 32 bits of rax.
Basic instructions (Intel syntax, destination first):
mov ecx, 5 put 5 in ecx
add ecx, 2 / sub / imul / xor / shl (shift left = multiply by 2 each step)
push / pop the stack, call / ret functions
The debugger on the right is stopped in a disassembled function:
$ start
$ step
$ info registers

Every program ends up as machine instructions. Reading them lets you understand malware, crashes, exploits and compiler behavior when no source exists. You do not need to write much of it; you need to read it calmly.

General-purpose registers hold values: rax (return value), rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9 (the first six arguments on Linux), rbx, rbp (frame base), rsp (stack top) and r10-r15. rip is the next instruction. eax is the lower 32 bits of rax, ax the lower 16, al the lower 8. Flags (ZF, SF, CF, OF) record the result of the last comparison or arithmetic.

cmp a, b subtracts b from a, throws away the result, and sets flags: ZF (zero flag, set when they're equal), SF (sign), CF (carry). A conditional jump reads them: je/jz jump if equal, jne if not, jg/jl signed greater/less, ja/jb unsigned. That's how every if in C looks after compiling.
$ break 10
$ continue
$ print ecx
$ print edi

Arguments go in rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9; the return value comes back in rax. (Windows x64 uses rcx, rdx, r8, r9.) So in check_key(int key), the key is in edi, and eax = 1 at the end means "return 1".
The instructions that do most of the work

Data: mov dst, src copies; lea dst, [expr] computes an address without loading; push/pop use the stack.
Math: add, sub, imul, inc, dec, xor eax, eax (the idiom for zero).
Logic: and, or, xor, not, shl, shr.
Compare: cmp a, b (subtract, set flags only), test a, b (AND, set flags only).
Branch: jmp, je/jz, jne/jnz, jg, jl, ja, jb, then call and ret.
Memory operands use brackets: mov eax, [rbp-4] loads the 4 bytes at that address. In Intel syntax the destination comes first; AT&T syntax (used by gcc -S and objdump by default) reverses it and adds % and $.

if (x > 5) y = 1; else y = 2;
becomes roughly cmp [x], 5 / jle else / mov [y], 1 / jmp done / else: mov [y], 2 / done:. Loops are a label, a body, a cmp and a conditional jump back. A function call places arguments in registers, executes call, and reads the result from rax.

push rbp; mov rbp, rsp (the prologue) starts a frame; local variables live below rbp, and the return address that call pushed sits just above it. Overwriting that return address is a buffer overflow. pop rbp; ret (the epilogue) undoes it and jumps back.

This function is really:
int check_key(int key) { int k = ((500 << 3) + 42) ^ 15; return key == k; }
Constant math like this is common in simple crackmes and malware string decoding. You can solve it two ways: statically (do the math by hand) or dynamically (let it run and read the register right before the cmp).
$ continue
$ print eax
$ back
$ print ZF
x86 is little-endian: the value 0x0fc5 is stored in memory as bytes c5 0f 00 00. You'll see this every time you read a hex dump or build an exploit payload.

On entry a function typically runs push rbp; mov rbp, rsp; sub rsp, N (making room for locals), and exits with leave; ret (which restores rsp and rbp and pops the return address into rip). Locals sit at negative offsets from rbp, saved rbp and the return address sit above them. A buffer overflow that writes past a local reaches the saved rbp and then the return address, which is why that single field decides who controls the program.

gcc -S -masm=intel file.c shows what the compiler generated, objdump -d -M intel binary disassembles, gdb (with pwndbg or gef) steps through, radare2 and Ghidra decompile, and Compiler Explorer (godbolt.org) lets you type C and watch the assembly. Compare -O0 and -O2 output to see how optimizers rewrite code.

Skim for call targets (what library functions are used), strings referenced by lea, and comparisons that guard branches. Name what you learn. Look for the pattern cmp then jne fail: that is almost always the check you are interested in.

licensed.bin calls check_key(key) with the number you type. It was run with 1234 and said "invalid license".
The function computes the valid key in a register and compares it to yours. Step to the cmp and read it.
Submit the valid key as a decimal number.

Every attack and every defense travels over a network. Learn the OSI and TCP/IP layers, how DNS, ARP and the TCP handshake really work, then read a capture to catch ARP spoofing on a LAN.
simple // the idea in plain words

A network is devices agreeing on rules (protocols) to send data to each other. The idea everything else builds on is layers: each layer does one job and hands off to the next.
The OSI model has 7 layers. Remember them bottom-up with "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away":
Physical: cables, radio, bits
Data link: MAC addresses, switches, Ethernet, Wi-Fi frames
Network: IP addresses, routers
Transport: TCP (reliable) and UDP (fast), ports
Session, 6. Presentation, 7. Application: HTTP, DNS, SSH, SMTP
$ cat ~/notes/ports.txt
$ grep -w 53 ~/notes/ports.txt
When something "doesn't work", troubleshoot bottom-up: link light, IP address, gateway ping, DNS, then the app.

When you open a web page: the browser asks DNS for the IP (application), opens a TCP connection (transport), wraps data in IP packets with source and destination (network), puts them in frames for the next device using MAC addresses (data link), and sends bits over Wi-Fi or Ethernet (physical). Each layer wraps the one above in its own header, called encapsulation, and the receiver peels them off in reverse.
Remember the OSI layers: Physical, Data link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application ("Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away"). TCP/IP squeezes them into four: link, internet, transport, application.

MAC (layer 2): burned into the NIC, only meaningful on the local network
IP (layer 3): logical, routable across networks
Port (layer 4): which program on that host (443 = HTTPS)
ARP connects layer 3 to layer 2: "who has 10.0.10.1? tell 10.0.10.44", and the owner replies with its MAC. DNS turns names into IPs (A, AAAA, MX, CNAME, TXT records).
$ cat ~/notes/arp-table.txt
$ dig +short updates.corp.example

TCP opens a connection with the three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), numbers every byte and resends what's lost. UDP just sends: DNS queries, VoIP, video, games. A TCP RST slams a connection shut, which is also what a closed port answers to a SYN.
$ grep -E "Flags \[S\]|Flags \[S\.\]" ~/caps/handshake.txt
Devices and what layer they work at

Hub (1, repeats everything), switch (2, forwards by MAC), router (3, forwards by IP between networks), firewall (3 to 7), load balancer (4 or 7), access point (1 and 2). A collision domain is where devices share a wire; a broadcast domain is everyone who hears a broadcast, which VLANs and routers split up.

A (name to IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail server), NS (name server), TXT (free text, used for SPF and verification), PTR (reverse lookup), SOA (zone info), SRV (service location). Resolution: the stub resolver asks a recursive resolver, which walks root, TLD, then the authoritative server and caches the answer for the TTL.
HTTP and TLS in a minute

HTTP is request and response: method (GET, POST), path, headers, optional body, then status code and body back. TLS wraps it: the client says hello and the server name, the server presents a certificate, they agree on keys, then everything is encrypted. Status codes: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.

Switches and ARP were designed to trust everyone on the LAN:
ARP spoofing / poisoning: an attacker sends unsolicited ARP replies saying "the gateway's IP is at *my* MAC". Victims send their traffic to the attacker, who forwards it (on-path / man-in-the-middle). Sign: one MAC claiming several IPs, or the gateway's MAC suddenly changing
MAC flooding: overflow the switch's CAM table so it floods frames to every port
VLAN hopping, rogue DHCP servers, rogue access points
Defenses: Dynamic ARP Inspection and DHCP snooping on managed switches, port security (limit MACs per port), 802.1X network access control, and encryption everywhere (TLS, SSH) so an on-path attacker sees nothing useful.
$ grep "is-at" ~/caps/lan.txt
$ grep "is-at" ~/caps/lan.txt | awk '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c
Cache poisoning, DNS tunneling (data hidden in long subdomains), and hijacked records. Watch for very long or random-looking query names and a host making thousands of TXT queries.

2.4 GHz reaches farther and is crowded, 5 and 6 GHz are faster at shorter range. WPA2-Personal uses a shared passphrase that can be attacked offline from a captured handshake, so use a long one; WPA3 resists that. WPA-Enterprise (802.1X/RADIUS) gives each user their own credentials. Disable WPS, and put guests and IoT on separate networks.
Network attacks to be able to explain

ARP spoofing (man-in-the-middle on a LAN), DHCP starvation and rogue DHCP, DNS spoofing and cache poisoning, VLAN hopping, SYN flood, MAC flooding, and smurf-style amplification. For each, know the layer, what the attacker gains, and the defense (dynamic ARP inspection, DHCP snooping, DNSSEC, port security, rate limiting, 802.1X).
ping and traceroute (3), arp -a (2/3), dig (7 DNS), curl -v (7 HTTP/TLS), nc -vz host port (4 connectivity test), ss/netstat (4 sockets), Wireshark/tcpdump (all layers).

Users on VLAN 10 say pages load slowly and they got a browser certificate warning. The gateway is 10.0.10.1.

offense & RE · my level: ■■□□□ familiar · proof
Crypto is everywhere you look in security, usually misnamed. Learn encoding vs hashing vs encryption, how keys and certificates fit together, then verify which download is genuine.
simple // the idea in plain words

Three things get mixed up all the time:
Encoding (base64, hex) changes the format so data travels safely. No key, anyone can reverse it. It's not security
Hashing (SHA-256) makes a fixed-size fingerprint of data. One way: you can't get the data back. Used for integrity (did it change?) and password storage
Encryption (AES, RSA) scrambles data with a key. Only someone with the right key can reverse it. Used for confidentiality
$ echo -n "0xday" | base64
$ echo -n "MHhkYXk=" | base64 -d
$ echo -n "0xday" | sha256sum
$ echo -n "0xdaz" | sha256sum
If someone says a password is "encrypted with base64", it isn't protected at all.

Encoding (base64, hex, URL encoding) changes the form of data so it travels safely. Anyone can reverse it, there is no key. It is not security.
Hashing (SHA-256) turns data into a fixed-size fingerprint. It is one way. Used for integrity and password storage.
Encryption (AES, RSA) hides data using a key and can be reversed by someone with the right key.
Also: signatures prove who wrote something and that it was not changed; MACs (HMAC) prove integrity with a shared secret; KDFs turn a password into a key slowly.

Symmetric (AES): one shared key encrypts and decrypts. Fast, used for bulk data. Problem: how do both sides get the key?
Asymmetric (RSA, ECC): a public key anyone can have and a private key you keep. Encrypt with someone's public key and only their private key can decrypt. Sign with your private key and anyone can verify with your public key
Real protocols (TLS, SSH, Signal) use both: asymmetric crypto to agree on a key, then symmetric AES for the actual data.

Software sites publish the SHA-256 of each download. Hash what you downloaded and compare. If even one byte differs, the hash is completely different:
$ cat ~/downloads/SHA256SUMS
$ sha256sum ~/downloads/*.iso
A hash on the same website as the download only proves the file wasn't corrupted. A signature (GPG, code signing) proves who published it.
Key sizes and choices that are fine today

AES-128 or AES-256 (use an authenticated mode: GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305), RSA 2048 or larger or, better, elliptic curves (Ed25519 for signatures, X25519 for key exchange), SHA-256 or SHA-3 for hashing, Argon2id or bcrypt for passwords. Avoid MD5, SHA-1, DES, 3DES, RC4, ECB mode and RSA with PKCS#1 v1.5 padding for new designs.

Asymmetric crypto is slow, so real protocols use it only to agree on a session key (key exchange) or to sign, then encrypt the bulk data with fast symmetric crypto. HTTPS does exactly this. Forward secrecy (ephemeral keys per session) means that stealing the server's long-term key later does not decrypt old recordings.
Where you meet it every day

TLS on websites, SSH, disk encryption (BitLocker, LUKS, FileVault), VPNs, password managers, signed software updates, git commit signing, email (S/MIME, PGP), Wi-Fi (WPA2/WPA3), and certificates in your browser.

A certificate binds a public key to a name (like www.example.com), signed by a Certificate Authority. Your browser trusts a set of root CAs; a site's cert is valid if it chains up to one of them, hasn't expired, matches the hostname, and hasn't been revoked (CRL / OCSP).

ECB mode: encrypts identical blocks identically, so patterns show through. Use GCM or another authenticated mode
Reusing a nonce/IV with the same key in stream modes (CTR, GCM) leaks plaintext
XOR with a short repeating key isn't encryption: known plaintext reveals the key
Rolling your own crypto. Use vetted libraries
$ echo -n "uryyb jbeyq" | tr 'a-z' 'n-za-m'
That's ROT13, a Caesar shift by 13. It shows up in CTFs and malware strings because it hides text from a quick glance, nothing more.

Hard-coded keys in source code, reused nonces or IVs (catastrophic with GCM), unsalted or fast password hashes, rolling your own algorithm, comparing MACs with == (timing leaks), weak randomness (rand() instead of a cryptographically secure generator such as /dev/urandom, secrets in Python or crypto.randomBytes in Node), skipping certificate validation "just for testing", and storing the key next to the data it protects.
Key management is the hard part

Generate keys with a secure source, store them in a vault, HSM or KMS (not in git or env files on disk), rotate them, limit who can use them and log use. Plan for loss (backups of keys, escrow for recovery) and for compromise (revocation, re-encryption procedure).

Quantum computers would break RSA and elliptic curves (Shor's algorithm) but only weaken symmetric crypto, so AES-256 stays fine. NIST has standardized post-quantum algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA), and organizations are starting to inventory where they use public-key crypto ("crypto agility").

The right data structure turns a slow, buggy check into a fast, correct one. Learn Big-O, arrays, hash tables, trees and graphs, then debug a binary search that lets a blocked attacker through.
simple // the idea in plain words

A data structure is a way to organize data; an algorithm is a recipe that works on it. The basics:
Array: items side by side in memory, instant access by index (a[5])
Linked list: each item points to the next; easy inserts, slow lookups
Stack (last in, first out: undo, the call stack) and queue (first in, first out: print jobs, packet buffers)
Hash table (dictionary, map): key to value in about one step
Tree and graph: items connected by links (folders, networks, social graphs)
Big-O describes how the work grows with input size *n*: O(1) constant, O(log n) halving each time, O(n) look at everything once, O(n²) compare everything with everything.
The debugger on the right runs is_blocked(), a binary search over a sorted firewall blocklist:
$ start
$ step
$ step
$ info locals
What a data structure is for

Choose a structure by what you do most. Array/list: fast access by position. Hash table (dict, set): fast lookup by key. Stack: last in, first out (undo, call stack). Queue: first in, first out (job processing, BFS). Linked list: cheap insert in the middle, slow to search. Tree: hierarchical data and sorted lookup. Heap: always gives the smallest or largest next. Graph: networks and relationships (hosts, users, attack paths).
Big-O describes how work grows with input size: O(1) constant, O(log n) halving, O(n) one pass, O(n log n) good sorting, O(n²) nested loops, O(2ⁿ) trying everything.

On a sorted array, look at the middle: if it's too small, throw away the left half, if too big, the right half. Each step halves what's left, so a million entries take about 20 steps: O(log n). Linear search would take up to a million.
$ break 12
$ continue
$ print mid
$ print lo
$ continue
$ print mid
Merge sort and quicksort are O(n log n); bubble sort is O(n²). You usually call the language's built-in sort, but you need to know that binary search only works on sorted data.

A hash function turns the key into a bucket number. Average O(1) lookup, which is why blocklists, caches and password-cracking wordlists use them. Collisions (two keys, same bucket) are handled with chaining or probing.

Array index O(1), array search O(n), sorted array binary search O(log n), hash lookup average O(1), insert into a balanced tree O(log n), sort O(n log n), nested loops over the same list O(n²). Space matters as well as time: a hash set trades memory for speed.

Hash map for counting and lookup: count occurrences, find duplicates, two-sum.
Two pointers / sliding window: pairs in sorted data, longest substring without repeats.
Stack: matching brackets, parsing, undo.
BFS (queue): shortest path in an unweighted graph, nearest neighbor.
DFS (stack or recursion): explore everything, find connected components, detect cycles.
Sorting first: many problems get easy once the data is ordered.
Binary search: not just arrays, any monotonic yes/no question.

A recursive function needs a base case and a step toward it. Each call uses stack space, so deep recursion overflows; convert to a loop when depth is large. Memoization (cache results) turns exponential recursion like Fibonacci into linear.

The most common algorithm bug. Binary search has three places to get it wrong: the initial hi (n or n - 1), the loop condition (< or <=), and the updates (mid or mid ± 1). They must agree. With hi = n - 1 (inclusive), the loop must be while (lo <= hi), otherwise the last remaining candidate is never checked.
$ delete
$ break 16
$ continue
$ print lo
$ print hi

Hash flooding DoS: send keys that all collide, turning O(1) lookups into O(n). Languages now use randomized (keyed) hash functions like SipHash
Regex DoS (ReDoS): badly written patterns take exponential time on crafted input
Graphs: BloodHound models Active Directory as a graph and runs shortest path to find the quickest route from a normal user to Domain Admin
Bloom filters: tiny probabilistic sets, used to check "is this password in a breach list?" without storing the list
Tries and Aho-Corasick: match thousands of IDS signatures in one pass

When a problem breaks into overlapping subproblems (shortest edit distance, knapsack, longest common subsequence), store each subproblem's answer in a table so it is computed once. Define the state, the transition, the base case and the order of filling.

Hosts and connections form a graph: BFS finds the shortest path an attacker could take, BloodHound is a graph of Active Directory permissions, dependency trees are graphs (supply chain), and firewall rule analysis is reachability. Trie and bloom filters power fast blocklist lookups, hashing powers integrity checks, and rate limiting uses queues and sliding windows.

Hash collision attacks degrade a hash table to O(n) per lookup (a denial of service), catastrophic regex backtracking (ReDoS) takes exponential time on crafted input, and unbounded recursion or allocation exhausts memory. Know the worst case, not just the average case, for anything that handles untrusted input.

Databases are where the valuable data lives. Learn tables, keys, normalization, transactions and indexes, then run real SQLite in your browser to find the account whose balance was tampered with.
simple // the idea in plain words

A relational database stores data in tables: rows (records) and columns (fields). Each table has a primary key that uniquely identifies a row, and a foreign key in one table points at the primary key of another, which is how tables relate.
SQL is how you ask questions. The sandbox runs real SQLite (the first run downloads it once):
$ sqlite3 bank.db ".tables"
$ sqlite3 bank.db "SELECT * FROM accounts;"
The four basic operations are CRUD: Create (INSERT), Read (SELECT), Update (UPDATE), Delete (DELETE).
Other databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server) use the same SQL with small differences. MongoDB and Redis are NoSQL: documents or key-value pairs instead of tables.
Picking the right kind of database

Relational (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server) stores structured data with relationships and strong consistency. Document (MongoDB) stores JSON-like objects, flexible. Key-value (Redis) is a fast cache. Graph (Neo4j) is for relationships. Time-series and search (Elasticsearch, which is the engine behind Security Onion) are for logs and metrics. Most apps start well with a relational database.

Identify the things (tables), give each a primary key, connect them with foreign keys, and avoid duplicating data. A table of orders should store customer_id, not the customer's name and address on every row.

One customer has many transactions: a one-to-many relationship. A JOIN combines tables on the key that links them, and GROUP BY + SUM / COUNT turns many rows into one per group:
$ sqlite3 bank.db "SELECT a.owner, COUNT(*) FROM accounts a JOIN txns t ON t.account_id = a.id GROUP BY a.owner;"

Store each fact once. If the owner's name is copied into every transaction row, changing it means updating hundreds of rows, and some will be missed. Normal forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF) are rules for splitting tables so data can't contradict itself.
A transaction groups changes so they all happen or none do (moving money: subtract here, add there). ACID = Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable.

1NF: one value per cell, no repeating groups. 2NF: every column depends on the whole key. 3NF: columns depend on the key and nothing else. If changing one fact means editing many rows, you need to split a table. Denormalize on purpose only for read performance, and document why.

Take regular full backups plus transaction log or point-in-time recovery, store copies off the host, encrypt them, and test restores. Know the two numbers: RPO (how much data you can afford to lose) and RTO (how long you can be down).
Export with pg_dump or mysqldump, import with psql < file.sql, check running queries with pg_stat_activity or SHOW PROCESSLIST, and find slow ones with the slow query log and EXPLAIN.

The I in the CIA triad. Databases protect it with constraints (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK (balance >= 0), foreign keys), transactions, and audit trails. A classic check: does a stored total match the sum of the records it's supposed to summarize? If not, someone changed one without the other.
$ sqlite3 bank.db "SELECT account_id, SUM(amount) FROM txns GROUP BY account_id;"

An index is a sorted lookup structure (usually a B-tree) on a column, turning a full table scan into a quick search. It speeds up reads and slows down writes. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows whether a query uses one.

SQL injection: always parameterized queries (? placeholders), never string concatenation
Least privilege: the web app's DB user can't DROP TABLE or read the HR schema
Encryption at rest (TDE) and in transit (TLS), tokenization or masking for card numbers
Backups tested by actually restoring them, and database activity monitoring

Do not expose it to the internet; bind to localhost or a private network and firewall it. Remove default accounts and sample databases. Separate accounts for the application (limited rights), migrations (schema changes) and admins. Enable TLS, encrypt at rest, turn on audit logging, patch regularly, and never store passwords in plain text (hash with Argon2id or bcrypt). Mask or encrypt sensitive columns, and restrict who can run ad hoc queries on production.

ACID: Atomic (all or nothing), Consistent (rules hold), Isolated (concurrent work does not interfere), Durable (committed means saved). Isolation levels trade speed for safety; the anomalies to know are dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantom reads. Race conditions in application code (check balance, then withdraw) need a transaction with locking or a constraint.

Forensics is proving what happened on a machine, in a way that holds up later. Learn evidence handling, file signatures, timelines and hidden data, then find the file someone tried to disguise.
simple // the idea in plain words

Digital forensics is collecting and examining digital evidence so you can say, with proof, what happened: which files existed, who touched them, and when.
Two rules come before any analysis:
Don't change the evidence. Work on a copy (an *image*) made through a write blocker, never the original drive
Prove it's unchanged. Hash the image when you make it and again when you're done. Same hash, same data
$ cat ~/case/chain-of-custody.txt
$ sha256sum ~/case/evidence/notes.txt
The chain of custody records every person who handled the evidence, when, and why. Without it, evidence can be thrown out.

Preserve: never work on the original. Make a forensic image with a write blocker, hash it (SHA-256), and work from a copy.
Document: record every step, tool and time. Another examiner should be able to repeat your work and get the same result.
Analyze: look at files, deleted data, logs, browser history, USB history, user activity and memory.
Report: state facts, separate them from opinion, and say what you could not determine.
Digital evidence is easy to change by accident (just booting a disk alters timestamps), so the process matters as much as the findings.
File names lie, file signatures don't

A file's extension is just part of its name. What it actually is lives in its first few bytes, the magic number (file signature):
FF D8 FF JPEG, 89 50 4E 47 (.PNG) PNG, 25 50 44 46 (%PDF) PDF
50 4B 03 04 (PK..) ZIP, which is also DOCX, XLSX and APK
4D 5A (MZ) Windows executable
Look at the first bytes with xxd:
$ ls -l ~/case/evidence/photos
$ head -c 16 ~/case/evidence/photos/beach.jpg | xxd

Even binary files carry readable text: paths, URLs, usernames, metadata. strings pulls out every run of printable characters:
$ strings ~/case/evidence/photos/beach.jpg | head

Registry hives (NTUSER.DAT, SYSTEM, SOFTWARE, SAM): user activity, USB devices, installed programs, autostart keys.
Prefetch (C:\Windows\Prefetch): which programs ran and when.
Event logs (.evtx): logons, service installs, PowerShell activity.
Recycle Bin, LNK files and Jump Lists: files a user opened or deleted.
Browser profiles: history, downloads, cookies, cache.
$MFT, $UsnJrnl: the file system's own record of creation, modification and deletion.
hiberfil.sys, pagefile.sys: slices of memory saved to disk.

/var/log/ logs, ~/.bash_history, /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow, cron entries, ~/.ssh/ (known_hosts shows where someone connected), /tmp and /dev/shm for dropped tools, package manager logs and the systemd journal.

Deleting a file usually removes only the directory entry; the data stays until overwritten. File carving recovers files from raw bytes using header and footer signatures (foremost, photorec, scalpel). SSDs with TRIM and encrypted disks reduce what you can recover.

Filesystems record MAC times for every file: Modified (content changed), Accessed, Changed (metadata changed, on NTFS: $MFT entry), plus Born/created on many systems. Sorting every timestamp on the disk into one super timeline (tools: fls + mactime from The Sleuth Kit, plaso/log2timeline) shows the sequence of events:
$ sort ~/case/timeline.csv | tail -6
Attackers timestomp (fake the timestamps) to hide. On NTFS that leaves the $FILE_NAME timestamps different from $STANDARD_INFORMATION, and a creation time later than the modification time is a classic giveaway.

Deleted files: deleting removes the pointer, not the data, until it's overwritten. Carving tools (PhotoRec, foremost, Autopsy) find files by their signatures in unallocated space
Slack space at the end of clusters, alternate data streams on NTFS, volume shadow copies
Memory: running processes, network connections and decrypted keys exist only in RAM. Capture it before pulling the plug (order of volatility: registers/cache, RAM, network state, disk, logs, backups) and analyze with Volatility
Windows artifacts: Prefetch (what ran), LNK files and Jump Lists (what was opened), Registry (USB devices, recent docs), browser history
$ grep -i usb ~/case/timeline.csv

RAM holds what disk never shows: running processes, network connections, injected code, decrypted data and encryption keys. Capture it first (WinPmem, LiME on Linux, or a VM snapshot's memory file), then analyze with Volatility: list processes (windows.pslist, windows.pstree), compare with windows.psscan to spot hidden ones, check windows.netscan for connections, windows.malfind for injected code, and windows.cmdline for arguments.

Autopsy / Sleuth Kit (disk analysis, timelines), FTK Imager (imaging), Volatility 3 (memory), Plaso / log2timeline (super-timelines), exiftool (metadata), Wireshark (network), Eric Zimmerman's tools (registry, prefetch, MFT parsers), KAPE (fast triage collection).

Merge timestamps from every source into one ordered list, then ask what happened just before and after the key event. Be careful with time zones, clock skew and the difference between created, modified and accessed times. Anti-forensics (timestomping, log clearing, secure delete) shows up as gaps and contradictions.

Disk forensics starts with a perfect copy and a hash, and ends with a timeline. Learn FTK Imager for acquisition and Autopsy for analysis, then find a deleted file by its hash.
simple // the idea in plain words

Disk forensics is examining a drive's contents without changing them. Two jobs, two tools:
FTK Imager acquires: it makes a bit-for-bit image of a drive (.E01 or raw .dd) and records its hash.
Autopsy analyzes: it opens the image read-only, lists files (including deleted ones), builds timelines and runs keyword and hash searches.
The rule that everything else follows: never work on the original. Image it, hash it, store the original, examine a copy.
$ sha256sum case/disk.dd
$ cat case/acquisition.txt

Image: an exact copy of a drive or partition, including free space and deleted data
Hash: SHA-256 (or MD5) of the image. If it matches at acquisition and again later, nothing changed
Write blocker: hardware or software that stops the examiner's machine writing to the evidence drive
Chain of custody: the log of who held the evidence, when, and why
Unallocated space: disk area no file currently owns; deleted data often survives there

Attach the source through a write blocker (or use a read-only mount)
File > Create Disk Image > pick Physical Drive > format E01 (compressed, stores case info) or raw

FTK Imager can also add an image as evidence, browse its file tree read-only, export files, and capture memory or protected registry files from a live system.

Deleting removes the directory entry or flags it free, but the data stays until overwritten. Where it hides: deleted entries still in the file table, unallocated space (carve it by file signature), the recycle bin ($Recycle.Bin), shadow copies, and slack space. SSDs with TRIM can really erase it, so say so in a report.
NTUSER.DAT (recent files, run keys), $MFT (file records, timestamps), Prefetch (programs run), UsrClass.dat, browser profiles, setupapi.dev.log and USBSTOR (plugged-in USB drives), event logs.

Timestamps lie in two ways: clocks are wrong, and the filesystem updates some times on copy and move. Note the machine's timezone, then compare several sources before claiming a time. A file copied to a USB drive keeps its modified time but gets a new created time on the destination: created later than modified is a copy signature.

Wiping tools, timestomping (altered times: compare $STANDARD_INFORMATION with $FILE_NAME in the MFT), renamed extensions (check the file signature, not the name), encrypted containers, and data in alternate data streams. Extension mismatch ingest catches the second one.

A known-good set (NSRL) filters out the operating system so you read what is left. A known-bad set flags files you already care about, like the stolen document's hash. Matching a hash proves content, even if the filename changed.

IT & infrastructure · my level: ■■■□□ working · proof
A firewall is a list of rules read top to bottom, and the first match wins. Learn how pfSense filters traffic between interfaces, how NAT and aliases fit in, then figure out which rule actually lets traffic through.
simple // the idea in plain words

A firewall decides which network traffic is allowed between zones. pfSense is a free firewall/router OS (based on FreeBSD) that runs on a small box or a VM, and it's the edge of my homelab.
Each rule matches traffic by: interface, direction, protocol, source, destination and port, then takes an action: pass, block (silently drop) or reject (drop and tell the sender).
Two ideas cover most of it:
Default deny: anything not explicitly allowed is blocked
First match wins: rules on an interface are checked top to bottom and the first one that matches decides
$ cat ~/pfsense/rules-LAN.txt

Think of pfSense as a building's security desk with a clipboard of rules. Every packet is a visitor. The guard checks the list from the top; the first line that describes the visitor decides whether they get in. No line matches means no entry.

WAN the side facing the internet or my ISP router. Untrusted.
LAN my normal devices. Trusted, but still filtered.
SERVERS / LAB / IOT separate networks (usually VLANs). Isolating them means a hacked smart plug or a malware test VM cannot talk to everything else.
The web interface lives at the LAN address of the firewall (for example https://10.0.0.1), and there is a special anti-lockout rule that keeps you from blocking your own access to it.

pfSense filters traffic as it enters an interface. A rule on the LAN tab controls traffic *from* LAN hosts going anywhere. Out of the box: WAN blocks everything inbound, LAN allows everything outbound. You add rules on each internal interface (LAN, SERVERS, LAB, IOT VLANs) to control what each can reach.

Instead of typing the same IPs and ports into ten rules, define aliases (ADMIN_PCS, WEB_PORTS) and reference them. Change the alias once, every rule updates:
$ cat ~/pfsense/aliases.txt
pfSense tracks connections, so a pass rule for the request automatically allows the reply. You only write rules for the side that starts the connection.

Block LAB from reaching LAN: on the LAB tab, put a block rule at the top with source LAB net and destination LAN net, then a pass rule below it for internet access. Order is the whole trick.
Allow only DNS to the firewall: pass UDP/TCP 53 from LAB net to the LAB address, block the rest of that address.
Let one admin PC reach a management page: pass from the alias ADMIN_PCS to NAS_ADMIN on the alias port, above a general block.

Block drops silently, which slows a scanner down. Reject replies with an error, which is friendlier on an internal network because things fail fast instead of hanging. On WAN, block. On internal interfaces, reject is often nicer when you are troubleshooting.

pfSense usually runs the DHCP server (leases, static mappings so servers keep one address) and the DNS resolver (Unbound) for each interface. A VLAN is a tagged slice of a physical network; you create it under Interfaces → Assignments → VLANs, assign it, give it an address, enable DHCP, then write its rules. Nothing is allowed on a new interface until you add a pass rule.

Because the first match wins, a broad pass rule near the top makes every block rule below it meaningless. Order rules from specific to general: anti-lockout, specific blocks (e.g. LAB → LAN), specific passes, then a general rule or nothing (default deny).

Outbound NAT hides internal hosts behind the WAN IP automatically. Exposing a service needs a port forward (WAN:443 → 10.0.0.30:443) plus a matching WAN pass rule, which pfSense can add for you. Every forward is attack surface; a VPN is usually the better way in.

Turn on logging for block rules and for sensitive pass rules. Each log line names the rule that matched, which is how you debug "why can/can't this host reach that":
$ grep "10.0.30.20" ~/pfsense/filter.log
pfSense adds features through packages: Suricata/Snort (IDS/IPS on the interface), pfBlockerNG (IP and DNS blocklists), WireGuard/OpenVPN (remote access).
Floating rules, states and the order of evaluation

Rules are evaluated in this order: floating rules first (they can match any interface or direction), then the interface group tabs, then the specific interface tab. The first match wins in each case, except floating rules without "quick" which let later rules override. Keep floating rules to a minimum, they are the hardest to reason about.
Every allowed connection creates an entry in the state table. Changing a rule does not always kill an existing state, so after tightening a rule, clear states (Diagnostics → States) before testing, or you will think the old rule still works.

Is the rule on the right interface? Traffic is matched where it enters.
Is there an earlier rule that already matched? Check the rule counters and the firewall log.
Are the source, destination and port aliases what you think they are?
Is the destination actually listening, and does it have its own host firewall?
Does the reply have a route back? Asymmetric routing breaks stateful filtering.

Disable the web UI on WAN, use HTTPS only, change the default admin password, restrict the UI to an admin alias, turn on two-factor if you have it, keep pfSense updated, and back up config.xml (Diagnostics → Backup) before big changes. Treat the config like a secret, it contains VPN keys and password hashes.

Find the rule that's actually letting it through. Remember: first match wins.

computer science · my level: ■■□□□ familiar · proof
A web app is a browser, an API and a database passing JSON back and forth. Learn HTTP, REST, React and MongoDB from a security angle, then decode session tokens to catch a forged admin request.
simple // the idea in plain words

A modern web app has three parts:
Frontend: runs in the browser (React, TypeScript). Draws the page, sends requests
Backend / API: runs on a server (Node.js + Express). Checks who you are, applies the rules, talks to the database
Database: stores the data (MongoDB keeps JSON-like documents)
They talk over HTTP. A request has a method (GET read, POST create, PUT/PATCH update, DELETE), a path, headers and maybe a body. The response has a status code: 2xx OK, 3xx redirect, 4xx your fault (401 not logged in, 403 not allowed, 404 not found), 5xx server's fault.
$ cat ~/api/request.http
$ curl -s https://api.shop.local/products/7
Never trust the frontend. Anyone can skip your React app and send requests straight to the API with curl.

React builds the user interface in the browser out of components. The browser calls an API (usually JSON over HTTPS) served by Node.js with a framework like Express. The API reads and writes MongoDB, a database of JSON-like documents. TypeScript can cover all three layers. This is the "MERN" stack.
A request's journey: user clicks → React handler → fetch("/api/orders") → Express route → middleware (auth, validation) → database query → JSON response → React state updates → screen redraws. When something breaks, find which hop failed using the Network tab in the browser (status code, payload) and the server logs.
A REST API maps resources to URLs: GET /api/orders lists, GET /api/orders/12 reads one, POST /api/orders creates. Data travels as JSON.

After login, the API gives the client a token to send with every request (Authorization: Bearer <token>). A JWT is three base64url parts joined by dots: header.payload.signature. The payload is readable by anyone, only the signature protects it from being changed:
$ cat ~/api/token.txt
$ cut -d. -f2 ~/api/token.txt | base64 -d

React escapes values you render, which blocks most XSS by default. It's bypassed by dangerouslySetInnerHTML, by putting user input into href (javascript: URLs), and by server-side templates that don't escape.

Components are functions that return markup (JSX). Props pass data in, state (useState) holds data that changes, useEffect runs side effects like fetching, and lists need a stable key. React escapes values in JSX by default; dangerouslySetInnerHTML turns that protection off.

Collections of documents; find, insertOne, updateOne, deleteOne, aggregate. Mongoose adds schemas and validation. Index fields you query on. NoSQL injection exists too: passing req.body.username straight into a query lets an attacker send { "$ne": null }, so validate that inputs are strings.
The OWASP Top 10, as it shows up in this stack

Broken access control: the API checks you're logged in but not that order 12 is *yours* (IDOR). Every endpoint must check ownership and role on the server
Injection: MongoDB has NoSQL injection: sending {"password": {"$ne": null}} instead of a string makes the query match any password. Validate types (zod, joi) and never pass raw request bodies into queries
Cryptographic failures / broken auth: JWTs signed with a weak secret, or a server that accepts "alg": "none" (no signature at all)
Security misconfiguration: verbose error stack traces, open CORS (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with credentials), MongoDB exposed to the internet without auth
$ cut -d. -f1 ~/api/token.txt | base64 -d
$ cat ~/api/login-attempts.log
Server-side validation, parameterized queries, HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookies, a Content Security Policy, rate limiting on login, and logging of every authorization failure.

Session cookies (server remembers you; cookie flags HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite) or JWTs (self-contained signed tokens; hard to revoke, so keep them short-lived and use refresh tokens). Hash passwords with Argon2id or bcrypt, add rate limiting and MFA, and never roll your own crypto. Authorization is separate: check *every* request against what that user may do, on the server.

Environment variables for secrets (never committed), HTTPS everywhere, CORS limited to your real front-end origin, security headers (helmet), logging that never prints passwords or tokens, dependency updates (npm audit), a reverse proxy like nginx, containers (Docker), and backups for the database. Add automated tests and a CI pipeline that fails on lint, type or test errors.

Is it a front-end bug (console errors, wrong state), a network bug (wrong URL, CORS, status code), a server bug (stack trace in logs), or a data bug (document shape differs from what the code expects)? Reproduce it with curl, then trace inward one hop at a time.

Ghidra and IDA Pro turn a binary back into something you can read. Learn the workflow that works in either tool: strings, imports, cross-references, renaming, then find the function that does the interesting thing.
simple // the idea in plain words

A disassembler turns machine code back into assembly instructions. A decompiler goes one step further and shows C-like code. Ghidra (free, from the NSA) and IDA Pro (commercial, long the industry standard) both do the analysis on a program you never run, which is called static analysis.
You don't read the whole program. You use the tool to answer one question, like "where does it contact the network?", by following clues.
$ cat ~/ghidra/strings.txt
$ cat ~/ghidra/xrefs.txt

Listing / disassembly: the instructions, with addresses
Decompiler: C-like pseudocode for the selected function
Functions window: every function the tool found (named, or FUN_00401a30 when unnamed)
Strings: text found in the file
Imports / symbol tree: the Windows API calls the program uses
Start from something that stands out (a string, an API call) and ask the tool who uses it. That's a cross-reference (xref): press X in IDA, or right-click > References in Ghidra.

Triage outside the tool: hashes, file type, PE headers, strings. Is it packed? Unpack first
Create the project and import the file; accept the analyzer defaults
Open Strings and Imports, note anything useful (URLs, file paths, registry keys, CreateRemoteThread)
For each, jump to where it's used with xrefs and read that function in the decompiler

Ghidra is free, scriptable in Java and Python, supports collaboration through a server, and has a strong decompiler for many CPUs. Git remembers everything, including the secret you deleted. Learn commits, branches and pull requests, then dig a leaked API key out of a repository's history.
simple // the idea in plain words

Git tracks changes to files over time. Each commit is a snapshot with a message, an author and a unique ID (a SHA hash). You can see who changed what, when, and go back to any version. GitHub hosts Git repositories online and adds pull requests, issues and CI.
The everyday loop:
$ git status
$ git log --oneline
git add file stages a change, git commit -m "message" saves the snapshot
git push sends commits to GitHub, git pull gets others' commits
A branch is a separate line of work; merge it back when it's done
Write commit messages that say *why*, not just *what*. Future you will read them during an outage.

Git saves snapshots (commits) of your project, each with a message, an author and a pointer to its parent. A repository is the folder plus its history. A branch is a movable label on a commit. GitHub hosts a remote copy so you can back up, share and collaborate. Three places hold your files: the working directory (what you see), the staging area (what will go in the next commit) and the repository (committed history).

git status
git add file.txt
git commit -m "Explain why, not just what"
git push
Commit small, commit often, write messages in the imperative ("Fix login redirect"). git pull brings in other people's work first.

Teams don't commit straight to main. You make a branch, push it, and open a pull request (PR): a request to merge, where others review the diff and CI runs the tests. Branch protection can require reviews and passing checks before merging.
$ git branch -a
$ git show --stat a41c9e2
git diff shows uncommitted changes; git show <sha> shows exactly what one commit changed; git log -p file shows a file's whole history, change by change.

git switch -c fix/login-bug
git commit -am "Fix login redirect"
git switch main
git merge fix/login-bug
Merge keeps history as it happened; rebase replays your commits on top of the latest main for a straight line (never rebase commits other people already have). Conflicts appear when two branches edit the same lines: open the file, keep the right text between the <<<<<<< markers, remove the markers, then git add and commit.

git restore file discards unstaged edits, git restore --staged file unstages, git commit --amend fixes the last commit message, git revert <commit> makes a new commit that undoes another (safe for shared branches), git reset --hard <commit> throws away work (dangerous), and git reflog shows where HEAD has been, which rescues "lost" commits.

A PR proposes merging a branch. Good ones are small, explain the reason, link the issue, and pass automated checks. Reviewers look for correctness, security and clarity. Protect main with required reviews and checks.

Deleting a secret in a new commit doesn't remove it: the old commit still contains it, and anyone who clones the repo gets the whole history. Bots scan public GitHub for leaked keys within minutes of a push.
$ git log --oneline --all -- config/settings.py
$ git log -p --all -S "API_KEY" --oneline
-S "text" (the "pickaxe") finds commits that added or removed that text.

Rotate it immediately. Assume it's compromised the moment it was pushed
Then clean history if needed (git filter-repo, BFG) and force-push, knowing forks and clones may still have it
Prevent it: .gitignore for .env files, pre-commit secret scanning (gitleaks), GitHub push protection, and secrets in a vault or CI secrets, never in code
Signed commits, protected branches, required reviews and pinned dependency versions all exist because a malicious commit or package can reach production through Git.

git log --oneline --graph --all, git blame file (who changed each line), git log -S"password" (when a string appeared or vanished), git diff main..feature, git show <commit>, and git bisect (binary search for the commit that introduced a bug).

If a secret is committed, rotate it first; rewriting history (git filter-repo) is cleanup, not a fix.

Trunk-based development (small changes straight to main with feature flags) suits fast CI; GitHub Flow (short branches plus PRs) is the common default; Git Flow (develop, release, hotfix branches) suits versioned releases. Pick one and write it down.

Group Policy is how one admin configures ten thousand Windows machines. Learn where GPOs link, the LSDOU order that decides who wins, and how to troubleshoot with gpresult, then find why a security setting isn't applying.
simple // the idea in plain words

A Group Policy Object (GPO) is a bundle of settings (password rules, firewall, drive mappings, software, desktop restrictions) that Active Directory pushes to computers and users. You create a GPO once and link it to a site, the domain, or an OU, and every machine or user in that scope gets it.
Computer Configuration applies at boot to the machine, whoever logs in
User Configuration applies at logon to the user, wherever they log in
Machines refresh policy about every 90 minutes; gpupdate /force does it now
$ cat ~/gpo/links.txt

A Group Policy Object (GPO) is a bundle of settings. You link it to a domain, a site or an OU, and every computer or user inside that container receives the settings automatically at startup, logon and every 90 minutes or so. Settings are split into Computer Configuration (applies to the machine) and User Configuration (follows the person).
Typical things GPOs do: map network drives, set the password policy, install software, push printers, block USB storage, set the desktop wallpaper, turn on the firewall, and configure Windows Update.

When GPOs conflict, they're applied in order Local, Site, Domain, OU (parent OU first, then child OU). Each later one overwrites earlier ones, so the closest OU wins. Two exceptions:
Enforced on a link makes that GPO win over everything below it
Block Inheritance on an OU stops parent GPOs from applying (except enforced ones)
Within one container, GPOs with a lower link order number win.
$ grep -i "lockout\|password" ~/gpo/settings.txt

gpresult /r (summary) or gpresult /h report.html shows which GPOs applied, which were filtered out and why (security filtering, WMI filters, disabled links):
$ gpresult /r

Group Policy Management Console (GPMC): create, link, back up and review GPOs.
gpupdate /force on a client to refresh now; gpresult /r or gpresult /h report.html to see what applied and why.
Group Policy Modeling and Results inside GPMC to predict or confirm effects.
Event Viewer → Applications and Services → Microsoft → Windows → GroupPolicy for errors.

Security filtering decides which users or computers a GPO applies to (default: Authenticated Users). WMI filters restrict by hardware or OS. Loopback processing applies user settings based on the computer, useful for kiosks and labs. Enforced stops lower levels from overriding and Block Inheritance stops higher ones, use both sparingly because they make troubleshooting painful.

Policies are enforced and grayed out for the user; Preferences set a value once and let the user change it (drive maps, shortcuts, registry values). Preferences used to store passwords in XML in SYSVOL, encrypted with a key Microsoft published, which is why that feature was removed and why old cpassword entries are a finding.

Most Windows hardening is GPO: account lockout and password length, disabling LLMNR and NetBIOS, SMB signing, restricting who can log on locally, Windows Firewall rules, LAPS, AppLocker/WDAC, PowerShell logging (script block logging, event 4104). Microsoft's Security Compliance Toolkit ships ready-made baseline GPOs.
One important exception: domain password and lockout policy only works from a GPO linked at the domain level (for domain accounts). The same settings in an OU GPO only affect local accounts on those machines. Different policies per group need Fine-Grained Password Policies.

GPOs are also an attack path: anyone who can edit a GPO linked to an OU can run code on every machine in it. Old Group Policy Preferences stored passwords (cpassword) in SYSVOL with a published key, which is why that feature was removed and why SYSVOL is worth auditing.
$ grep -ri "cpassword" ~/gpo/sysvol

Never edit the Default Domain Policy beyond password and Kerberos settings. Create new, well-named GPOs (SEC - Workstation Baseline, USR - Drive Maps). Test on a pilot OU first, back up before changes (Backup-GPO), and document each GPO's purpose. Keep the number of GPOs applied to a machine small, since every one adds logon time.

Most "the computer is broken" tickets are one failing part. Learn a repeatable troubleshooting method and how to read drive, memory and thermal diagnostics, then find the drive that's about to die.
simple // the idea in plain words

Hardware troubleshooting follows the same steps every time (CompTIA's method):
Identify the problem (ask what changed, reproduce it)
Establish a theory of probable cause (start simple: power, cables, seating)
Test the theory
Plan and implement the fix
Verify full functionality
Document it
Symptoms point to parts. Clicking or slow file access: storage. Random crashes and blue screens: RAM or heat. Shutting off under load: power or cooling. No display but fans spin: RAM, GPU or display cable.
$ cat ~/bench/intake.txt
Back up the user's data before you change anything on a machine with a suspect drive.

Start with the cheapest, most likely cause and work toward the expensive one. Ask what changed, reproduce the problem, check power and connections first (a surprising number of "dead" machines are an unplugged cable or a dead outlet), then isolate: swap one known-good part at a time. The beep codes and LED patterns on a motherboard are a language, look them up in the vendor manual.
The parts and what failing looks like

PSU: random shutdowns, no power at all, clicking at boot.
RAM: blue screens with different errors, failure to boot, beeps.
Storage (HDD/SSD): slow, freezing, clicking drive, file corruption, missing boot device.
CPU/cooling: thermal throttling, shutdowns under load, loud fans.
GPU: artifacts on screen, black screen with fans running.
Battery/charger on laptops: swelling battery, not charging, shuts off at "50%".

Drives track their own health in SMART attributes. The ones that predict failure:
Reallocated Sector Count (5): bad sectors already swapped out. Any growth is bad
Current Pending Sector (197): sectors waiting to be reallocated
Offline Uncorrectable (198), UDMA CRC errors (199, usually a bad cable)
NVMe: Percentage Used, Media and Data Integrity Errors, Available Spare
$ smartctl -a /dev/sda

MemTest86 runs patterns through RAM; any error means a bad stick (test one at a time to find which). For heat, check temps under load and look for dust, dried thermal paste and dead fans.
$ cat ~/bench/memtest.log
$ sensors
Order of checks on a PC that will not boot

Power: outlet, PSU switch, cable, power button, a different charger for laptops.
Display: is it the monitor or cable? Try another port.
POST: beeps or error LEDs? Reseat RAM, try one stick at a time.
Boot device: is the drive detected in BIOS/UEFI? Boot order correct?
Peripherals: unplug everything except keyboard and monitor.
Clear CMOS (battery out for a minute) if settings look corrupt.
Minimal build: CPU, one RAM, PSU, board, and see if it posts.

Screwdriver set, anti-static strap, compressed air, thermal paste, a PSU tester, a multimeter, a USB boot stick with diagnostics (MemTest86, vendor tools, a live Linux), a known-good spare of common parts, and a drive-to-USB adapter for data recovery.
Before repairs that risk the disk, ask whether the data matters and whether there is a backup. If a drive is failing, stop using it, image it (ddrescue) to a healthy disk, and repair the copy.

One number rarely decides it. A drive with 2 reallocated sectors that hasn't changed in a year is stable; one that went from 0 to 400 this month is failing. Compare against the last report, and correlate with OS logs (disk I/O errors in Event Viewer / dmesg):
$ grep -i "error\|reset" ~/bench/dmesg.txt

For refurbished laptops the call depends on part cost vs unit value, and on whether the failure could recur (a swollen battery is always a replace). Document the serial numbers of anything you swap, because warranty and asset tracking depend on them.
Ground yourself (wrist strap or touch bare chassis metal), unplug and remove the battery before opening a laptop, and never open a power supply.

Reallocated sectors, current pending sectors and offline uncorrectable counts above zero on a spinning disk mean it is dying: copy data and replace. Media wearout and percentage used matter on SSDs. smartctl -H gives a pass/fail, -a the details, and -t short runs a self-test. A PASSED health flag with bad attributes is still a warning.

Run MemTest86 for at least one full pass (several is better); any error means replace the module. Watch temperatures with HWMonitor or sensors: idle in the 30s to 40s °C, load under about 85°C for most CPUs. Dust, dried thermal paste and a failed fan are the usual causes of heat issues.

Record serial number, symptom, tests run and results on the ticket. Check warranty status before opening a device (some warranties void with opened seals) and keep removed parts in labeled, anti-static bags.
