languages · my level: ■■■□□ working
Python is the security field's glue language. Learn it from variables to parsing logs with real Python running in your browser, then write a script that finds a brute-force attacker.
simple // the idea in plain words

Python reads almost like English, which is why it's the first language for most security people. The sandbox runs real Python (Pyodide, the first run downloads it once).
Values go in variables, print shows them, and f-strings drop variables into text:
$ python3 -c 'name = "0xDay"; print(f"hello, {name}")'
$ python3 -c 'print(7 * 6, type(42), type("42"))'
A list holds items in order, and a for loop walks through them:
$ python3 -c 'for p in [22, 80, 443]: print("checking", p)'
Indentation is syntax in Python. The body of a loop or if is whatever is indented under it.

Most security scripts do the same thing: open a file, go line by line, split the line, keep counts. A dictionary maps keys to values, perfect for counting.
$ cat ~/scripts/count_status.py
$ python3 ~/scripts/count_status.py
Useful string methods: line.split() (split on spaces), .strip(), .startswith(), "x" in line. And collections.Counter counts anything in one line:
$ python3 -c 'from collections import Counter; print(Counter("mississippi").most_common(2))'
Core data types and when to pick them

list is an ordered, changeable sequence; tuple is fixed; dict maps keys to values (fast lookup); set holds unique items (fast membership test and set math). Strings are immutable. Comprehensions build collections in one line: [x.upper() for x in names if x], {k: v for k, v in pairs}, {ip for ip in ips}.
Modules you will use all the time

os and pathlib (paths), sys (arguments), re (regex), json, csv, datetime, collections.Counter (count things), argparse (command line options), subprocess (run other programs), hashlib, socket, and third-party requests, scapy, pandas.
Regular expressions and the standard library

re finds patterns (IPs, emails, hashes), ipaddress understands networks, hashlib hashes, base64 and json decode the formats you see everywhere, datetime parses timestamps:
$ python3 -c 'import ipaddress; print(ipaddress.ip_address("10.0.20.44") in ipaddress.ip_network("10.0.0.0/8"))'
$ python3 -c 'import hashlib; print(hashlib.sha256(b"0xday").hexdigest())'

wrap the logic in functions and use if __name__ == "__main__":
take inputs from sys.argv or argparse instead of hard-coding paths
handle bad lines with try/except instead of crashing on line 40,000
for real work: requests (HTTP), scapy (packets), pandas (big tables), pwntools (CTFs)

You can't attack or defend what you haven't mapped. Learn host discovery, port and version scanning with Nmap, how Metasploit turns a finding into access, then find the one vulnerable box on a lab network.
simple // the idea in plain words

Reconnaissance is mapping a target before touching it hard: which hosts are alive, which ports are open, and what software is listening. Nmap is the standard tool for this.
Only scan networks you own or have written permission to test. Here, 10.10.10.0/24 is a lab network built for practice.
The first question is simply *who's there?* A ping sweep (-sn) finds live hosts without port scanning them:
$ nmap -sn 10.10.10.0/24
Then ask one host which ports are open:
$ nmap 10.10.10.5
An open port has a program listening. Closed means the host answered but nothing's there. Filtered means a firewall ate the probe.

Only scan systems you own or have written permission to test. In a homelab that means your own VMs and a lab network (Metasploitable, DVWA, TryHackMe or Hack The Box machines). A scan against someone else's network can be a crime, and even on your own it can crash fragile devices. Write down the scope before you type a command.

Discover which hosts are alive (nmap -sn).
Enumerate ports and services on each (-sV).
Dig deeper into interesting services (web directories, SMB shares, banners).
Match versions to known vulnerabilities.
Validate safely and record evidence.
Report what you found and how to fix it.

Knowing port 21 is open is a start; knowing it's vsftpd 2.3.4 is a finding. -sV probes each open port to identify the service and version, and -sC runs the default safe scripts (banners, titles, anonymous login checks):
$ nmap -sV -sC 10.10.10.5

-sS SYN scan (default as root): sends SYN, reads the reply, never completes the handshake
-sT full TCP connect (no root needed, noisier)
-sU UDP (slow, but finds DNS, SNMP, TFTP)
-p- all 65,535 ports, --top-ports 100 the most common ones
-T4 faster timing, -oA name save output in every format
$ nmap -p- --min-rate 1000 10.10.10.7

PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION: the state is open, closed, filtered (a firewall dropped it) or open|filtered (cannot tell, common with UDP). The version column tells you what to research. Add -oA scan to save normal, grepable and XML output together, which you can feed to other tools or diff against a later scan.

-Pn skip host discovery when ICMP is blocked, -n skip DNS lookups for speed
-iL hosts.txt read targets from a file, --exclude 10.0.0.1 skip a host
--open show only open ports, -v show results as they arrive
-sC default scripts, --script vuln known-vulnerability checks (read what a script does before running it)
-O guess the OS, -A is -sV -sC -O plus traceroute

Web (80/443): browse it, check robots.txt, run gobuster dir -u URL -w wordlist for hidden paths, nikto -h URL for known issues.
SMB (445): smbclient -L //host -N lists shares, enum4linux collects users and shares.
FTP (21): try anonymous login. SSH (22): note the version and whether passwords are allowed.
DNS (53): dig axfr @server domain tests for zone transfer.
SNMP (161/UDP): snmpwalk -v2c -c public host if the community string is default.

Once you have a product and version, look it up: CVE databases, vendor advisories, and searchsploit (an offline copy of Exploit-DB):
$ searchsploit vsftpd 2.3.4

Metasploit organizes attacks as modules: auxiliary (scanners), exploits, payloads (what runs after: a shell or Meterpreter) and post modules. The workflow is always the same: search, use, show options, set RHOSTS, run.
$ msfconsole -q -x "search vsftpd"

Every scan you just ran is visible: a SYN scan is a burst of SYNs to many ports from one IP, and IDS rules (Snort's scan detection, Zeek's Scan::Port_Scan) catch it. Reduce what recon finds by closing unused ports, keeping software current, and hiding version banners.

msfconsole
search vsftpd
use exploit/unix/ftp/vsftpd_234_backdoor
show options
set RHOSTS 10.10.10.5
check
run
Modules are exploits, auxiliary scanners, payloads and post-exploitation. show options lists required settings (RHOSTS is the target, LHOST your address). Use check when a module supports it. db_nmap stores scan results in the Metasploit database so hosts and services list them. A meterpreter session gives you commands like sysinfo, getuid and shell.

Take notes as you go: command, time, output, screenshot. A finding needs a title, affected host, evidence, impact in plain words, severity (CVSS helps) and a fix. A tester who cannot explain the fix has done half the job.
Detecting this from the defender's side

A SYN scan appears as many connections from one source to many ports with no completed handshakes. Look for it in firewall logs, Zeek conn_state of S0 and REJ, and IDS scan rules. Rate-limit, segment, and alert on internal hosts that scan, because that usually means a compromised machine.

You're on an authorized internal pentest of 10.10.10.0/24. The client wants to know if any host is running software with a known public exploit that gives a remote shell.

computer science · my level: ■■□□□ familiar · proof
A REST API is how apps talk over HTTP, and Spring Boot is how a Java backend serves one. Learn methods, status codes, JSON and the Spring layers, then find the endpoint that forgot an ownership check.
simple // the idea in plain words

An API (application programming interface) is a menu of requests a program accepts. A REST API uses plain HTTP: a URL names a thing, a method says what to do with it, and the reply is usually JSON.
GET /api/posts list posts
GET /api/posts/7 one post
POST /api/posts create a post (data in the body)
PUT /api/posts/7 replace/update it
DELETE /api/posts/7 remove it
The reply starts with a status code: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request (your fault, bad input), 401 Unauthorized (not logged in), 403 Forbidden (logged in but not allowed), 404 Not Found, 500 Server Error (their fault).
Spring Boot is a Java framework that starts a web server with very little setup. A class marked @RestController maps URLs to Java methods, and Spring turns objects into JSON for you.
$ cat ~/api/PostController.java
$ cat ~/api/requests.http

Endpoint: a URL plus method (DELETE /api/posts/7)
Request / response: what the client sends and what comes back, both with headers and an optional body
Stateless: the server keeps no session between calls; each request carries its own credentials (a token)

Controller: handles HTTP (@GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PathVariable, @RequestBody)
Service: business rules (@Service), where checks like "only the owner may delete" belong
Repository: talks to the database (MongoRepository<Post, String> or JpaRepository)
Model / entity / DTO: the data shapes; use a DTO (a shape made for the API) rather than exposing the entity directly
Spring wires them together by dependency injection: a controller declares the service it needs in its constructor and Spring supplies it.

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/posts -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -d '{"text":"hello"}'. The -i shows the status line and headers. Postman or the VS Code REST Client do the same with a GUI.
Errors and status codes in Spring
Throw a ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND) or write an @ControllerAdvice that turns exceptions into consistent JSON errors. Never return a stack trace to the client.

Authentication: who are you? (a login that returns a JWT or session). Authorization: what may you do? Spring Security checks the token on every request, and rules like @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") guard methods.
Broken access control (the top API bug)

Authentication isn't enough. For DELETE /api/posts/{id} the server must check that the post belongs to the caller (or the caller is an admin). If it only checks "is logged in", anyone can delete anyone's post by guessing ids. This is an IDOR (insecure direct object reference), and OWASP ranks broken access control #1. Put the ownership check in the service, return 403 (or 404 to hide existence), and write a test for "user B cannot delete user A's post".
Other API flaws to design out

Mass assignment: binding a request straight onto an entity lets a client set role=admin; use DTOs with only the allowed fields
Excessive data exposure: returning password hashes or internal ids; return only what the screen needs
No rate limiting: allows brute-forcing logins or scraping
**Verbose errors, CORS set to *, secrets in the repo**, and unauthenticated actuator endpoints (/actuator/env)

Nouns in URLs, verbs as methods. Be idempotent where you can (PUT and DELETE repeated give the same result). Version the API (/api/v1/). Paginate lists (?page=0&size=20). Document it with OpenAPI/Swagger (springdoc-openapi) and test with MockMvc or @SpringBootTest.

application.properties (or .yml) holds the port and database URL; put secrets in environment variables, not the repo. Profiles (dev, prod) swap settings. Build with ./mvnw package or ./gradlew build, run with java -jar target/app.jar. A React or React Native client then calls the API with fetch.
Access logs show the method, path, status and caller. Many 403/404 across sequential ids is someone enumerating. A 200 on a DELETE for ids that don't belong to the caller is an IDOR being exploited.

The posts API defines four handlers in PostController.java. The ones that change an existing post should check that the caller owns it (or is an admin). One of them doesn't, so any logged-in user can modify any post by guessing its id. The review is for fictional training code.

Reverse engineering is reading a program you don't have the source for. Learn how compiled code maps back to logic, then step through a crackme in a debugger and pull the password out of memory.
simple // the idea in plain words

When you compile a program, the readable source code is gone. What ships is machine code: bytes the CPU executes. Reverse engineering (RE) is working backwards from that to understand what the program does, without the source.
Two kinds of tools do the work:
A disassembler/decompiler (Ghidra, IDA) turns the bytes back into assembly and rough C, so you can *read* it (static analysis)
A debugger (gdb, x64dbg) runs the program one instruction or line at a time, so you can *watch* it (dynamic analysis)
The lab on this page is a debugger. Try it: start the program, step one line, and look at the variables.
$ start
$ step
$ info locals
The highlighted line in the source pane is the line about to run, and the panel on the right shows variables right now. Values that just changed turn amber.

Reverse engineering is working out what a program does from the program itself. You use it to understand malware, check a vendor's claims, find vulnerabilities, recover lost source, and solve crackme and CTF challenges. Two approaches that work together: static (read the code without running it) and dynamic (run it in a debugger and watch).

file prog for the type and architecture, strings prog for messages and hints (often "Wrong password!" gives away where the check is), ltrace or strace to see library and system calls, and objdump -d prog or Ghidra to read the logic. Start from an interesting string, find where it is used, and read backward to the comparison that decides which message is printed.

You rarely step through a whole program. You find the interesting spot, put a breakpoint there, and let the program run until it hits it.
Here the interesting spot is the loop in check() that builds buf. Break on line 12, run to it, then inspect:
$ break 12
$ continue
$ print i
$ print secret[i]
continue again jumps to the next time line 12 runs (the next loop iteration). back steps backwards, which real gdb can do with record / reverse-step.
$ continue
$ print secret[i]
$ back
Reading the decompiled code first tells you where to break. Then the debugger tells you the actual values, which is often faster than doing the math by hand.

Create a project, import the binary, run auto-analysis, open the Symbol Tree and find main (stripped binaries lack names: look at entry, then the first argument of __libc_start_main). The Decompiler window shows C-like code. Rename variables (L), retype them (Ctrl+L), follow cross-references (X), and read the Defined Strings window for text to anchor on. Treat decompiler output as a strong hint, not truth.

A loop over bytes with xor and a constant is simple encryption or obfuscation.
strcmp or memcmp against a literal is a hard-coded password.
A table of 256 values suggests a lookup-based cipher (RC4, AES S-box constants).
Calls to socket, connect, CreateProcess, RegSetValue reveal capabilities.
A large switch on a number is a command dispatcher.

Set a breakpoint at the comparison, run, look at registers and memory to see what is compared with what, and change a register or a jump to see another path. Watch system calls with strace, files with Process Monitor, and network with Wireshark.

Decompiled code is a reconstruction. Variable names are gone (Ghidra calls them local_28, param_1), loops become do/while with gotos, and constants show up as raw hex. Renaming things as you understand them is most of the job. This crackme's names were added by hand.

x ^ KEY in a loop over bytes is XOR encoding: the secret is stored scrambled so strings won't show it
strcmp(input, buf) means buf must hold the real password by the time it's called, fully decoded
The return value of a function ends up in the rax register on x86-64, so "did the check pass?" is $rax after the call
3. Static vs dynamic, and why both

You can solve this statically: XOR each secret byte with 0x6b yourself. Or dynamically: stop at the strcmp and read buf. Malware authors know this, so real samples add anti-debugging (checking for a debugger, timing checks, VM detection) to make the dynamic route harder. That's the point of patching anti-VM checks, like in my anti-VM patching post.
$ list
$ break 15

Programs may detect debuggers (IsDebuggerPresent, ptrace self-attach, timing checks), run only in certain environments, encrypt strings until needed, pack the real code, use control flow flattening or opaque predicates, and generate code at runtime. Counters: patch the check, use a debugger hiding plugin, dump memory after unpacking, and emulate small functions (angr, Unicorn, Frida) to avoid running everything.

Frida injects JavaScript into a running process to hook functions, print arguments and return values, and change behavior without editing the binary, on desktop and mobile. It is the quickest way to see what an app sends before it encrypts it.

Keep notes of every renamed function and address, work from the outside in, write small scripts to replicate algorithms you find, and verify understanding by writing a keygen or a decoder. Reading compiler output for your own C code is the best training for recognizing patterns in other people's.

IT & infrastructure · my level: ■■■■□ strong · proof
Deleting a file doesn't erase it, and the wrong wipe can leave a whole drive readable. Learn NIST 800-88's clear, purge and destroy, which method fits which media, then catch the drive that was handled wrong.
simple // the idea in plain words

When you delete a file, the OS just marks its space as free. The data stays until something overwrites it, which is how forensic tools recover deleted files. Sanitization means making data unrecoverable before a device is reused, sold or thrown out.
The standard is NIST SP 800-88, which defines three levels:
Clear: overwrite with standard tools so normal recovery fails (fine for reuse inside the company)
Purge: methods that defeat even lab-level recovery: firmware secure erase / sanitize, cryptographic erase, degaussing (magnetic only)
Destroy: shred, disintegrate, pulverize, incinerate
$ cat ~/attachments/sanitization-matrix.txt

Old laptops, phones, copiers and USB sticks carry business secrets and personal data. Bad disposal is a breach: stolen or resold drives with readable data have caused real fines and lawsuits. A written process, applied every time, proves you did the right thing.

Clear: overwrite with standard tools. Defeats ordinary recovery. Good when the device stays inside your organization.
Purge: stronger methods that resist lab recovery, such as cryptographic erase, ATA Secure Erase or Sanitize, or degaussing for magnetic media.
Destroy: physical destruction, shredding, disintegration or incineration. Used when media is too sensitive or broken.

HDDs (magnetic platters): overwriting works; degaussing works (and destroys the drive)
SSDs and NVMe: wear leveling and spare blocks mean overwriting the visible drive misses data. Use the drive's own ATA Secure Erase, NVMe Sanitize/Format or crypto erase. Degaussers do nothing to flash
Self-encrypting drives: crypto erase throws away the key, making all data unreadable in seconds
$ grep -i "nvme\|ssd" ~/attachments/sanitization-matrix.txt

Every wipe needs a record: asset tag, serial, method, tool, operator, date and verification result. Vendors that destroy drives give a certificate of destruction. Without the record, you can't prove it happened.

HDD: a single overwrite pass is enough with modern drives; degauss is an alternative; shred for the highest sensitivity.
SSD / NVMe / flash: overwriting is unreliable because of wear-leveling and spare blocks. Use the drive's Secure Erase / Sanitize or cryptographic erase (destroy the encryption key of a self-encrypting drive or fully encrypted disk), and destroy if that is not available.
Phones and tablets: encrypt, then factory reset, remove accounts first (Activation Lock, FRP) and the SIM and SD card.
Printers and copiers: have internal storage, wipe through the manufacturer menu.
Optical and tape: shred or disintegrate.
Cloud: delete data and keys, check retention and backups, request provider attestation.

A sanitization record shows: asset tag, serial number, media type, method and tool, date, operator, verification result and the destination (reuse, resale, recycle). A certificate of destruction from a vendor lists the serials destroyed. Check legal holds first: never destroy anything subject to litigation or an investigation.

Sanitization isn't done until it's verified: sample the drive (or read it fully) and confirm no original data remains. Tools like Blancco produce signed reports. A secure-erase command that returns "success" on a drive with a buggy firmware is a known failure mode, so verification matters.

Planning for sanitization from day one

Full-disk encryption on every laptop makes disposal easy: destroy the key and the data is unreadable. Keep an asset inventory so nothing leaves unrecorded, store removed drives in a locked container, and make destruction vendors sign a contract that covers chain of custody and liability. Treat remote wipe (MDM) as a loss-response tool, not a disposal procedure.

A SIEM is where every log in the network ends up so one analyst can see everything. Learn how Security Onion collects, alerts and hunts, then find a beacon that no alert caught.
simple // the idea in plain words

Every device makes logs: firewalls, servers, laptops, the IDS. Looking at them one box at a time is hopeless. A SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) collects them all in one place, makes them searchable, and raises alerts when something matches a rule.
Security Onion is a free SIEM/NSM (network security monitoring) platform, and the one in my homelab. It bundles:
Suricata: an IDS that alerts on known-bad traffic (signatures)
Zeek: writes a log line for every connection, DNS query, HTTP request and file it sees, alert or not
Elasticsearch + Kibana / SOC console: storage and search over all of it
In the sandbox, ~/so/alerts.log is a Suricata alert export and ~/so/conn.log is a Zeek connection log.
$ head -5 ~/so/alerts.log
$ grep -c "sev=medium" ~/so/alerts.log
Alerts are the starting point, not the answer. Most are noise, and the worst attacks often don't trigger one at all.

Group alerts by signature to see what's noisy and what's rare. Rare is interesting:
$ grep -o 'msg="[^"]*"' ~/so/alerts.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
Then pivot from an alert to the hosts behind it. This one is a host pulling an executable over SMB, which is how ransomware and lateral movement tools spread:
$ grep "SMB2" ~/so/alerts.log | grep -o "src=[0-9.]*" | sort | uniq -c

Zeek logs are tab-separated with a #fields header that names each column. cut -f picks columns by number: here 2 is the client, 4 the server, 5 the port, 9 and 10 the bytes sent and received.
$ head -1 ~/so/conn.log
$ cut -f2,4,5 ~/so/conn.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
In Security Onion's hunt console the same pivot is a click: group by source.ip, then by destination.ip.
The Security Onion pieces, in one paragraph

Sensors watch the wire (Suricata for signature alerts, Zeek for rich connection logs, Stenographer for full packet capture). Elastic stores and indexes everything. Kibana-style dashboards and the Hunt and Alerts pages in the Security Onion Console are how you look at it. A grid is the set of nodes (manager, search, sensors) working together, and a single standalone box can do all of it in a lab.
An alert is a question, not an answer

Every alert deserves the same four questions: what fired (rule and category), who is involved (source, destination, user), is it expected for this host, and what else did that host do around the same time. Pivot from the alert to the Zeek conn, dns, http and ssl logs for the same IPs and time window, and to the PCAP if you need the bytes.
Hunting: finding what no rule caught

Threat hunting starts from a hypothesis ("malware is checking in with a C2 server") and looks for its fingerprint in the data, alert or not. Beaconing has a clear fingerprint:
the same internal host to the same external IP, over and over
at a regular interval (every 60 s, maybe with a little jitter)
with small, nearly identical byte counts
often on an unusual port, with no recognized service
Count connections per (client, server, port) and look for the outlier, then check whether its byte counts are identical:
$ awk '{print $2, $4, $5}' ~/so/conn.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
$ awk '$5 == 443 {print $9}' ~/so/conn.log | sort -n | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3

"Stacking" is counting how often each value appears across the whole environment and looking at the rarest ones: rare user agents, rare destination ports, a process name that runs on only one machine. Attackers hide in the long tail.

Once you've found something by hand, turn it into a rule so the SIEM catches it next time: a Suricata signature, a Sigma rule, or an Elastic query over Zeek fields. Then tune it until it's quiet enough that people actually read it.
Writing a detection that is worth keeping

A good rule has a clear hypothesis ("a workstation should not run powershell -enc from Office"), a log source that really contains the field, a test (generate the behavior in the lab and confirm it fires), a known false-positive list, and a note on what to do when it fires. Map it to an ATT&CK technique so gaps are visible. Sigma is a portable format that converts to Elastic queries, and Suricata rules cover the network side. Track each rule's alerts per week and retire or tune the noisy ones.

Keep an eye on disk (PCAP fills it fast), set retention, watch the sensor's dropped-packet counters (a sensor that drops packets is blind), and make sure the SPAN or TAP really sends both directions. Time sync (NTP) matters, because correlating across sources with skewed clocks gives nonsense timelines.

Threat intel says a new Cobalt Strike variant is evading our Suricata rules. The alert queue in ~/so/alerts.log shows nothing about it.

languages · my level: ■■■□□ working · proof
SQL is how you ask a database questions. Learn SELECT, WHERE, JOIN and GROUP BY on a real SQLite database running in your browser, then use them to find a compromised account.
simple // the idea in plain words

A database table is like a spreadsheet: rows are records, columns are fields. SQL (Structured Query Language) is how you ask it questions. The most important statement is SELECT: pick columns FROM a table, and filter rows with WHERE.
The sandbox has a real SQLite database, hr.db, with an employees table and a logins table. Look around first:
$ sqlite3 hr.db ".tables"
$ sqlite3 hr.db "SELECT * FROM employees;"
$ sqlite3 hr.db "SELECT name, title FROM employees WHERE dept = 'Finance';"
Text goes in single quotes ('Finance'). Numbers don't. Every statement ends with a semicolon.
You can also type sqlite3 hr.db on its own to get an interactive sqlite> prompt. Type .quit to leave it.

Data in tables: rows (records) and columns (fields). A primary key uniquely identifies a row. A foreign key points at another table's primary key, which is how tables relate (an orders.customer_id points to customers.id). SQL is the language to ask questions of that data and to change it.
The four verbs: SELECT (read), INSERT (add), UPDATE (change), DELETE (remove). Always run a SELECT with the same WHERE first to see which rows an UPDATE or DELETE will touch.

Real questions need four more tools:
ORDER BY col DESC sorts, LIMIT n keeps the top n
COUNT(*), SUM(), MIN(), MAX() are aggregates: they collapse many rows into one number
GROUP BY col runs the aggregate once per distinct value of col
LIKE matches patterns: % means "anything", so '10.%' is "starts with 10."
How many failed logins (success = 0) does each source IP have?
$ sqlite3 hr.db "SELECT src_ip, COUNT(*) AS fails FROM logins WHERE success = 0 GROUP BY src_ip ORDER BY fails DESC;"
The logins table only stores employee_id, not names. A JOIN stitches two tables together on a shared key, so you can read results as people instead of numbers:
$ sqlite3 hr.db "SELECT e.name, COUNT(*) AS fails FROM logins l JOIN employees e ON e.id = l.employee_id WHERE l.success = 0 GROUP BY e.name ORDER BY fails DESC;"
logins l and employees e are aliases, so you can write l.success instead of logins.success.

SELECT columns FROM table WHERE row-filter GROUP BY column HAVING group-filter ORDER BY column LIMIT n. The database evaluates them in a different order (FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT), which explains why you cannot use a column alias in WHERE and why WHERE filters rows while HAVING filters groups.

INNER JOIN keeps rows that match on both sides. LEFT JOIN keeps every left row and fills NULL where there is no match, which is how you find things that have no counterpart (customers without orders: LEFT JOIN ... WHERE o.id IS NULL). UNION stacks two results with the same columns.
COUNT(*), SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. NULL means unknown, so = NULL is never true; use IS NULL. COUNT(column) ignores NULLs while COUNT(*) does not. COALESCE(a, b) returns the first non-null value.
Two things separate a quick query from a correct one.

"Who has the most failed logins?" and "who is being attacked?" are different questions. The top name in the last query is someone fat-fingering their password from their own desk. Filter on what actually matters (here, sources outside the 10.0.10.0/24 office network), and keep the filters in WHERE (before grouping) vs HAVING (after grouping) straight:
$ sqlite3 hr.db "SELECT e.name, l.src_ip, COUNT(*) AS fails FROM logins l JOIN employees e ON e.id = l.employee_id WHERE l.success = 0 AND l.src_ip NOT LIKE '10.%' GROUP BY e.name, l.src_ip HAVING fails >= 3 ORDER BY fails DESC;"

A subquery is a query inside a query. "Which employees never logged in from outside?" is NOT IN (SELECT ...). And remember NULL is not a value: col = NULL is never true, you must write col IS NULL.
$ sqlite3 hr.db "SELECT name FROM employees WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT employee_id FROM logins WHERE src_ip NOT LIKE '10.%');"
3. Why this is a security skill

Most SIEMs and log tools speak SQL or something close to it (Splunk SPL, KQL, Elastic ES|QL)
SQL injection happens when an app glues user input into a query string. ' OR '1'='1 turns WHERE pass = '...' into a condition that's always true. The fix is parameterized queries (WHERE pass = ?), never string concatenation

WITH recent AS (
 SELECT user_id, ts FROM logins WHERE ts > date('now','-7 day')
)
SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS n,
 RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) AS rnk
FROM recent GROUP BY user_id;
A CTE (WITH) names a subquery so the main query reads top to bottom. Window functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, SUM() OVER) calculate across rows without collapsing them, handy for "latest login per user" or "time since the previous event".

If an application builds a query by gluing user text into a string, input like ' OR '1'='1 changes the meaning of the query. The fix is always the same: parameterized queries (prepared statements), where the database treats input strictly as data. Add least-privilege database accounts, input validation and no verbose errors shown to users.

Index the columns you filter and join on, avoid SELECT * on wide tables, use EXPLAIN to see whether an index is used, and remember that a function on an indexed column (WHERE lower(name)=...) can stop the index from helping.

The help desk got an alert: an outside attacker sprayed passwords at employee accounts overnight, and one of them worked.
hr.db has every login attempt. Find the employee whose account was successfully logged into from outside the office network (10.0.10.0/24) after the spraying.

Hardening means removing everything an attacker could use before they show up. Learn baselines, least privilege and the usual misconfigurations on Linux and Windows, then audit a server and find its backdoor account.
simple // the idea in plain words

A fresh install is built to *work*, not to be *safe*: default passwords, extra services, broad permissions. Hardening is shrinking the attack surface:
remove or disable what you don't need (services, software, ports, accounts)
change every default password, and enforce strong ones
patch, and keep patching
give every user and service only the access it needs (least privilege)
turn on logging and a host firewall
Start by seeing what the box exposes. Which services are listening?
$ cat ~/audit/listening.txt
The CIS Benchmarks and DISA STIGs are free, detailed hardening checklists for almost every OS and app. Hardening is mostly working through one.

Inventory: what is on this machine (software, services, ports, accounts)?
Baseline: what should it look like? Use a published benchmark (CIS Benchmarks, DISA STIGs, Microsoft security baselines) instead of inventing your own.
Apply: change settings, ideally through automation (Group Policy, Ansible, scripts) so every machine matches.
Verify: scan with a tool (Lynis, OpenSCAP, CIS-CAT, Microsoft Security Compliance Toolkit) and read what failed.
Repeat: configurations drift, and new patches arrive every month.
Hardening is a trade: every control costs some convenience. Document exceptions rather than silently skipping them.

/etc/passwd has one line per account: name:x:UID:GID:comment:home:shell. Only root should have UID 0. Service accounts should have a nologin shell. Pull the fields you care about with awk -F::
$ awk -F: '{print $1, $3, $7}' ~/audit/etc/passwd
SSH is the front door. Check the settings that matter: no root login, no passwords (keys only), no empty passwords:
$ grep -E "^(PermitRootLogin|PasswordAuthentication|PermitEmptyPasswords)" ~/audit/etc/ssh/sshd_config
Windows: the same ideas, different tools

Group Policy enforces baselines across a domain. Typical wins: disable SMBv1 and LLMNR, enforce account lockout, turn on Windows Defender and the firewall, deploy LAPS (a unique local admin password per machine), and remove users from the local Administrators group.
$ cat ~/audit/windows-baseline.txt

Patches: apt update && apt upgrade, turn on unattended security updates.
Accounts: no empty passwords (awk -F: '($2=="")' /etc/shadow), only root has UID 0, lock unused accounts, use sudo with named users.
SSH: PermitRootLogin no, PasswordAuthentication no once keys work, AllowUsers list, maybe a non-default port to cut log noise (not a real defense).
Services: systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled, disable what you do not use. ss -tulpn should show only what you expect.
Firewall: default deny incoming with ufw or nftables, open only needed ports.
Files: world-writable files and SUID binaries reviewed, /tmp mounted noexec,nosuid where possible.
Logging: auditd or journald with remote forwarding, time sync on.
Extras: fail2ban, AppArmor or SELinux left on, kernel parameters (sysctl) such as disabling IP forwarding when not routing.

Patches through Windows Update or WSUS, third-party software included.
Local admin: rename or disable the built-in Administrator, use LAPS so every machine has a unique admin password.
Accounts: standard users for daily work, strong password and lockout policy, MFA for admins.
Defender on, with tamper protection, ASR rules and cloud protection; BitLocker on laptops.
Firewall on for all profiles, inbound default block.
Remove SMBv1, disable LLMNR/NetBIOS if not needed, restrict RDP to a VPN or gateway with NLA.
PowerShell: script block logging and transcription, constrained language mode where practical.
Audit policy and Sysmon forward to the SIEM.
Privilege escalation is a hardening checklist in reverse

Attackers who land as a normal user look for exactly the misconfigurations hardening removes:
SUID binaries that let anyone run something as root (find / -perm -4000)
sudo rules that are too broad ((ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL, or sudo on editors and interpreters that can spawn a shell)
world-writable files run by root (cron scripts, services)
extra UID 0 accounts, weak file permissions on /etc/shadow
$ cat ~/audit/suid.txt
$ grep -v "^#" ~/audit/etc/sudoers | grep -v "^$"
GTFOBins lists how almost every common binary can be abused when it's SUID or allowed via sudo. If find, vim or python3 is on that list, it's a root shell.

Harden once, then keep it that way: define a baseline (CIS level 1), apply it with automation (Ansible, GPO, Intune), and scan for drift regularly (OpenSCAP, Lynis, Microsoft Security Compliance Toolkit).

CIS Benchmarks come in Level 1 (sensible, little breakage) and Level 2 (stricter, may affect function). Apply Level 1 widely, Level 2 to sensitive systems after testing. Keep a register of exceptions with owner, reason and review date. A finding you decided to accept is fine, an undocumented one is a gap.

World-writable service paths, unquoted service paths with spaces, scheduled tasks running as SYSTEM with editable scripts, NOPASSWD entries in sudoers, SUID copies of find, vim or python, readable backups and .bash_history, passwords in scripts, shares open to Everyone, and old protocols such as telnet, FTP and SMBv1. Compare with GTFOBins (Linux) and LOLBAS (Windows) to see why each is dangerous.

The strongest posture is to stop hand-editing servers. Build from a template or an Ansible role, rebuild when something drifts, keep the config in git, and treat any manual change as an incident to be explained.

languages · my level: ■■□□□ familiar · proof
The language of the browser, and of a lot of malware droppers. Learn JavaScript from first values to closures, run real code in the sandbox, then decode an obfuscated payload.
simple // the idea in plain words

JavaScript runs in every browser and, through Node.js, on servers. A program is a list of statements. You store values in variables with const (can't be reassigned) or let (can), and print them with console.log.
The sandbox runs real JavaScript with node -e '<code>':
$ node -e 'const name = "0xDay"; console.log("hello, " + name)'
$ node -e 'console.log(7 * 6, typeof 42, typeof "42")'
A function is a reusable block that takes inputs and returns an output:
$ node -e 'function double(n) { return n * 2 } console.log(double(21))'
TypeScript is JavaScript plus type labels (function double(n: number): number). The compiler checks the types and then strips them out, so what actually runs is plain JavaScript.

JavaScript runs in browsers and on servers (Node.js). let and const declare variables (use const unless it changes), functions can be written as function f(a) {} or const f = a => a * 2, and objects { name: "nate", role: "analyst" } and arrays [1, 2, 3] carry most data. Strings can use template literals (backticks around the text, with ${name} placeholders). JavaScript is loosely typed and coerces: "5" + 1 is "51" but "5" - 1 is 4, and == converts types while === does not, so always use ===.

Most real JavaScript is moving data around: arrays (lists), objects (key/value records) and JSON (objects as text, the format every web API speaks).
The three array methods you'll see everywhere:
map transforms every item
filter keeps items that pass a test
reduce folds the list into one value
ports.js in the sandbox holds a fake scan result. Read it, then run it:
$ cat ports.js
$ node ports.js
Arrow functions (p => p.open) are just short functions. Template strings use backticks and ${}:
$ node -e 'const hosts = ["10.0.0.5", "10.0.0.9"]; hosts.map((h, i) => console.log(`${i}: ${h}`))'
$ node -e 'console.log(JSON.stringify({ user: "nathan", admin: false }))'
Arrays and objects you use daily

map, filter, reduce, find, some, includes, spread ([...a, ...b], {...obj, x: 1}), destructuring (const { id, name } = user), optional chaining (user?.profile?.email) and nullish coalescing (value ?? "default").

document.querySelector, addEventListener, textContent (safe) versus innerHTML (can execute attacker markup), localStorage, and the Network tab in developer tools. View Source and DevTools are how you read what any page is really doing.

Every character has a numeric code. "A".charCodeAt(0) is 65, and String.fromCharCode(65) is "A". That's the basis of almost every obfuscation trick: shift, XOR or encode the codes so the text doesn't look like a URL anymore.
$ node -e 'console.log([..."hi"].map(c => c.charCodeAt(0)))'
$ node -e 'console.log(String.fromCharCode(104, 105))'

XOR (^) flips bits with a key, and XOR-ing twice with the same key gives you the original back: (c ^ k) ^ k === c. Base64 (btoa / atob) turns bytes into safe printable text. Droppers often stack them: XOR the URL, then base64 it.
$ node -e 'const k = 0x2a; const x = 104 ^ k; console.log(x, x ^ k)'
$ node -e 'console.log(btoa("hi"), atob("aGk="))'
3. Closures, async and why attackers love eval

A closure is a function that remembers variables from where it was created, the trick behind private state and module patterns
async/await lets code wait on network calls without freezing the page
eval(string) runs a string as code, so a dropper only needs to *decode* a string and eval it. As an analyst you do the opposite: swap eval for console.log and read what it would have run
Never run an unknown script to "see what it does". Copy only the decoding logic, and print instead of executing.

npm init, npm install pkg, npm audit, npx tool. package.json lists dependencies and scripts; package-lock.json pins exact versions and should be committed. Supply chain attacks hit npm often (typosquatting, malicious updates, install scripts), so review new dependencies, prefer fewer of them, and use npm ci in builds.

XSS (escape output, never put untrusted data in innerHTML, use a Content-Security-Policy), prototype pollution (be careful merging untrusted objects), eval and new Function on input, regex denial of service, insecure Math.random for tokens (use crypto.getRandomValues), and trusting client-side checks (always re-validate on the server).

Malicious scripts hide strings with String.fromCharCode, base64 (atob), hex escapes and XOR loops, then run the result with eval. Replace the final eval with console.log in a safe environment (Node in a VM) to see the real code, or run a beautifier first. The lab in this guide walks through that idea.

IT & infrastructure · my level: ■■■■□ strong · proof
One physical box can be a whole company network. Learn hypervisors, VMs vs containers, Proxmox storage, bridges and snapshots, then find the VM plugged into the wrong network.
simple // the idea in plain words

Virtualization lets one physical computer run many virtual machines (VMs), each with its own OS, as if they were separate computers. The software that does it is a hypervisor:
Type 1 (bare metal) runs directly on the hardware: Proxmox VE, VMware ESXi, Hyper-V
Type 2 runs as an app on a normal OS: VirtualBox, VMware Workstation
Proxmox VE is a free type 1 hypervisor built on Debian, KVM (for VMs) and LXC (for containers), managed in a web UI on port 8006 or with the qm and pct commands. It runs my whole homelab.
$ qm list
$ pct list
A homelab on Proxmox is the cheapest way to practice enterprise IT and security: a DC, a firewall, a SIEM and attack VMs on one box.

Hypervisor: software that lets one physical machine run many virtual ones. Proxmox VE is a hypervisor built on Debian Linux with a web UI.
Node: one Proxmox server. Several nodes can be joined into a cluster.
VM (virtual machine): a full pretend computer with its own kernel. CT (container, LXC): shares the host's kernel, so it starts in seconds and uses less memory.
ISO: an installer image you upload once and boot VMs from. Template: a prepared VM you clone instead of reinstalling.
Guest: any VM or container running on the node.
Each guest gets an ID number (100, 101, ...) which is what the command-line tools use.

A VM emulates a whole computer and runs its own kernel. Strong isolation, any OS (Windows included)
An LXC container shares the host's Linux kernel. Much lighter and faster to start, Linux only, weaker isolation

A Linux bridge (vmbr0, vmbr1) is a virtual switch. Each VM's virtual NIC plugs into a bridge, and the bridge may connect to a physical port or nothing at all. A typical lab: vmbr0 = the physical uplink (WAN side of pfSense), vmbr1 = internal LAN behind pfSense, plus VLAN tags for separate segments.
$ cat ~/pve/interfaces
$ qm config 101

local holds ISOs and templates, local-lvm (or ZFS) holds VM disks. pvesm status shows how full each is.
$ pvesm status
Creating a VM, in the order that matters

Upload an ISO to a storage that allows ISO images.
Create VM: give it a name and ID, pick the ISO, set the OS type.
Disk: use VirtIO SCSI on local-lvm or similar. CPU: type host unless you plan to migrate across different CPUs. Memory: set what it really needs.
Network: attach to a bridge (vmbr0), with a VLAN tag if your network uses them.
Install, then install the QEMU guest agent inside so Proxmox can see its IP and shut it down cleanly.

Do not give a guest more vCPUs than it will use, because idle vCPUs still need scheduling. RAM is the usual limit in a homelab, so budget it. Use thin provisioning for disks but keep an eye on the pool filling, because a full thin pool freezes every guest on it.

Keep three copies, on two kinds of media, one off-site. In Proxmox that means scheduled vzdump jobs to a different disk or a NAS (Datacenter → Backup), plus an occasional copy off the box. A snapshot is not a backup, because it lives on the same disk as the VM.

Snapshot: point-in-time state of a VM on the same storage. Perfect before a risky change or before detonating malware. Not a backup
Backup (vzdump, Proxmox Backup Server): a separate copy that survives losing the disk
Template: a golden VM you clone from (cloud-init can set hostname/IP/SSH keys on first boot)

Whoever controls the hypervisor controls every VM on it. Keep the management interface (8006) on an admin-only network, use 2FA on the Proxmox UI, patch the host, and never put a vulnerable lab VM on the bridge that reaches your real LAN. VM escape bugs exist, so the riskiest labs (live malware) belong on an isolated bridge with no uplink.
$ grep -A4 "vmbr2" ~/pve/interfaces

A Linux bridge (vmbr0) behaves like a virtual switch. Make it VLAN-aware and tag each guest NIC to put guests on different networks over one cable; the upstream switch port must be a trunk. For a fully isolated lab, create a bridge with no physical port and let only the pfSense VM connect to both it and the outside, so the lab can only reach the world through the firewall.

Clusters need an odd number of voters for quorum; a two-node cluster loses quorum when one node dies unless you add a QDevice. Live migration needs shared or replicated storage. For a single-box homelab, skip clustering entirely, it adds failure modes you do not need.

Put the web UI (port 8006) behind the VPN, never on the open internet.
Use named admin users with realm pve or PAM, enable two-factor, avoid daily use of root@pam.
Turn on the Proxmox firewall at datacenter, node and guest level, with the datacenter default policy set to drop for input.
Pass-through of PCI devices or disks to a guest weakens isolation, so do it only for guests you trust.
Apply updates through apt update && apt full-upgrade, then reboot if the kernel changed. Remove the enterprise repository if you have no subscription, or updates will error.

Lab rule: VMs running malware or vulnerable services must be attached only to vmbr2, the isolated bridge with no physical uplink.
Check every VM's config. One malware-analysis VM is attached to a bridge that has a route to the real network.

IT & infrastructure · my level: ■■□□□ familiar · proof
A VPN lets you be "on" a network you're not physically on. Learn tunnels, IPsec vs TLS vs WireGuard, how Tailscale builds a mesh with ACLs, then work out who can reach the homelab's Proxmox UI.
simple // the idea in plain words

A VPN (virtual private network) builds an encrypted tunnel across the internet, so your laptop at a coffee shop acts as if it's plugged into the office (or your homelab). Everything inside the tunnel is encrypted, so the coffee shop's Wi-Fi only sees scrambled traffic to the VPN server.
Two common shapes:
Remote access: one device into a network (the laptop to the office)
Site-to-site: two networks joined permanently (branch office to HQ)
Tailscale builds on WireGuard and gives every device a stable 100.x.y.z address on a private mesh (a "tailnet"), with no ports to open on your router.
$ tailscale status
$ ipcalc 100.101.7.12/10

Your homelab sits behind your home router. Opening ports on that router so you can reach it from outside exposes services to the whole internet, where scanners find them within hours. A VPN flips that: the lab opens no inbound ports, and you prove who you are to get in.

Tunnel: an encrypted path between two points.
Peer / node: a device in the VPN.
Public key: WireGuard and Tailscale identify devices by key pairs, not passwords. The private key never leaves the device.
NAT traversal: tricks that let two devices behind home routers connect directly without port forwarding. If that fails, traffic relays through a server (DERP in Tailscale) and stays end-to-end encrypted.

IPsec: the standard for site-to-site, works at the network layer (IKE to negotiate keys, ESP to encrypt)
TLS/SSL VPNs (OpenVPN, many vendor clients): runs over TCP/UDP 443, easy through firewalls
WireGuard: modern, tiny codebase, fast, public keys per peer, UDP

Full tunnel sends all traffic through the VPN (more control and inspection, more load). Split tunnel sends only corporate subnets through it and the rest directly (faster, but the device is on two networks at once).

A device on the tailnet can advertise a whole subnet (--advertise-routes=10.0.10.0/24) so other tailnet devices can reach machines that don't run Tailscale, like a Proxmox host or a printer.
$ tailscale status --json | grep -i route

Install Tailscale on each device, run tailscale up and sign in. Each device gets a stable 100.x.y.z address and a MagicDNS name (proxmox.tailnet-name.ts.net). From then on ssh nate@proxmox works from anywhere, without any open port at home.
Useful options: --ssh lets Tailscale handle SSH authentication with your identity, --advertise-routes=10.0.0.0/24 turns a node into a subnet router, --advertise-exit-node makes it an exit node (all your internet traffic leaves through it), and --accept-routes lets a client use routes others advertise. Routes and exit nodes must be approved in the admin console.

Servers should be tagged (tag:server) rather than owned by a person, so they do not disappear when someone leaves. Keys expire (180 days by default); for servers you disable expiry deliberately and note it. Use device approval and MFA on your identity provider, because the identity account is now the key to the whole network.
Access control is the real security

A VPN that lets every device reach everything just moves the flat network somewhere else. Tailscale uses an ACL policy (a JSON file) to say which users, groups or tags can reach which destinations and ports. Like a firewall, anything not allowed is denied.
$ cat ~/tailnet/acl.json

Zero trust says don't trust a device just because it's "on the VPN". Check identity (SSO + MFA), device posture (patched, disk encrypted) and grant the smallest access. Mesh VPNs with per-device ACLs and short key expiry are a step in that direction; ZTNA products go further with per-app access.
Leaked or never-expiring auth keys, old devices that still have access, exit nodes that let a device browse "from" your network, and split tunnels on unmanaged devices.

Tailscale's default policy lets every device talk to every device. Replace it with least privilege: groups for people, tags for machines, and rules that allow exactly what is needed.
{ "groups": {"group:admins": ["nate@example.com"]},
 "tagOwners": {"tag:lab": ["group:admins"]},
 "acls": [ {"action":"accept","src":["group:admins"],"dst":["tag:lab:22,8006"]} ] }
Run the ACL tests in the policy file (tests) so a typo cannot silently open everything. Read tailscale status and the admin console's last-seen times to spot devices you forgot.

WireGuard (fast, small, you manage keys and config), Tailscale (WireGuard plus identity, coordination and ACLs), OpenVPN (older, flexible, TLS-based), IPsec/IKEv2 (built into many OSs and routers). For a homelab with a handful of devices, Tailscale or plain WireGuard on pfSense are both sound. Keep a break-glass path (console access) in case the VPN itself is down.

The Proxmox web UI (10.0.40.11:8006) is reachable through a Tailscale subnet router. It should only be reachable by admin devices.
Read the tailnet's ACL policy and device list. Exactly one device that is not an admin's can still reach port 8006, because of how the ACL is written.

offense & RE · my level: ■■□□□ familiar · proof
Metasploitable 2, DVWA and WebGoat are machines and apps built to be broken, so you can practice safely. Learn how to run them without exposing them, what each one teaches, and how to read the vulnerable code.
simple // the idea in plain words

A vulnerable-by-design target is software with known holes, made for practice. Attacking something you own, in an isolated lab, is legal and the best way to learn. Attacking anyone else's system is not.
The three in the homelab:
Metasploitable 2: a whole Linux VM full of old services (FTP, SMB, Tomcat, a backdoored vsftpd). Practice: scanning, service exploits, Metasploit
DVWA (Damn Vulnerable Web App): a PHP/MySQL site with SQL injection, XSS, command injection, file upload and more, with security levels low, medium, high and impossible
WebGoat: a Java teaching app that walks you through lessons (injection, broken access control, JWT, XXE) with hints and a check for each one
$ cat ~/targets/README.txt
$ ls ~/targets/dvwa

These machines are meant to be compromised. Put them on an isolated lab subnet (a pfSense interface with no route to your home network, no port forwarding, no bridged adapter). Never expose them to the internet: scanners will own them within hours and use your IP.

Metasploitable 2: import the VM into Proxmox/VirtualBox, give it a host-only or isolated lab network, log in with the credentials printed on its banner, and snapshot it before you start
DVWA: run it in Docker (docker run -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 vulnerables/web-dvwa) or on a Linux VM; open /setup.php, click create database, log in, then set DVWA Security from the menu
WebGoat: java -jar webgoat-*.jar or the Docker image; browse to port 8080 /WebGoat, register a local account (nothing leaves your machine)
Always bind to localhost or the lab network only. Take a snapshot so you can reset in a minute.

Metasploitable: nmap -sV the host, search each version in searchsploit, try Metasploit modules (vsftpd 2.3.4, Samba usermap, distcc), read the resulting logs from the defender's side in Security Onion
DVWA: SQL injection (' OR '1'='1), reflected and stored XSS, command injection (; id), file inclusion and upload. Use Burp Suite or the browser dev tools to see the requests
WebGoat: follow the lessons in order; they teach the idea, then make you exploit it
Read the source at every level

DVWA lets you view the source of each page. Compare low (no checks), medium (a weak filter that can be bypassed), high (stronger but quirky) and impossible (parameterized queries, tokens). Seeing why impossible is safe is worth more than the exploit.

Every attack you run leaves a trail. After each success, look at what the web server log, the pfSense log and Security Onion saw. A good lab note says: what I did, what the log showed, and the control that would have stopped it.

Separate VLAN/subnet per purpose: attacker (Kali), targets, monitoring, management; allow attacker to targets only
pfSense default-deny with explicit rules; log blocked traffic, since a blocked attempt is a lesson too
Snapshots before and after each exercise; revert to a clean state

PowerShell is how Windows admins and attackers both get work done. Learn cmdlets, objects and the pipeline, then use exported service data to find malware disguised as a Windows service.
simple // the idea in plain words

PowerShell is Windows' shell and scripting language. Its commands are cmdlets named Verb-Noun: Get-Process, Get-Service, Stop-Service, Get-ADUser. Get-Help <cmdlet> explains any of them, and Get-Command *service* finds them.
$ Get-Service
$ Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5
The big difference from bash: PowerShell pipes objects, not text. Get-Process sends process objects with properties (Name, Id, CPU), so the next cmdlet can filter on a property instead of parsing columns.

PowerShell commands (cmdlets) are named Verb-Noun: Get-Process, Stop-Service, New-Item. The pipeline passes objects, not text, so you can sort or filter by a property name without cutting columns. Get-Command *service* finds commands, Get-Help Get-Service -Examples shows examples, and Get-Member lists the properties of whatever is flowing through.
Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 Name, CPU
Aliases like ls, cat, ps and ? exist for speed; use full names in scripts so they stay readable.

Where-Object keeps objects matching a condition: Where-Object Status -eq 'Running'

$ Get-LocalUser | Where-Object Enabled

$ head -3 ~/exports/services.csv

Get-ChildItem -Recurse -Filter *.log, Get-Content file -Tail 50 -Wait, Select-String -Path *.log -Pattern "failed" (grep for Windows), Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run for autostart entries. Set-ExecutionPolicy only stops accidental script runs; anyone can bypass it with -ExecutionPolicy Bypass. Treat it as a seatbelt, not a lock. Real control comes from code signing, AppLocker or WDAC, and constrained language mode.

Malware loves to hide as a service: it survives reboots and runs as SYSTEM. Real Windows services run from C:\Windows\System32 (or Program Files for apps), are signed by Microsoft or a known vendor, and have sensible names. Red flags: a binary in C:\Users\...\AppData, C:\ProgramData or Temp, a name that's *almost* a real one, an unsigned binary.
$ Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object Name, PathName, StartMode
$ grep -viE "C:\\\\Windows\\\\|Program Files" ~/exports/services.csv

Attackers use PowerShell too (downloading payloads, running in memory, -EncodedCommand to hide scripts). Defend with Script Block Logging (event 4104 records the decoded script), Constrained Language Mode and AMSI, and by alerting on -enc, IEX and DownloadString.

IT & infrastructure · my level: ■■■■□ strong · proof
Imaging hundreds of laptops means drivers, images and logs. Learn how Windows deployment works, how drivers are matched to hardware by ID, then fix the device that came up with no driver.
simple // the idea in plain words

Deploying Windows means getting a clean, configured OS onto a machine. At scale you don't click through setup: you boot from a USB or the network (PXE), apply a prepared image (a .wim file), and let an answer file (unattend.xml) handle the setup questions.
After the OS is on, every piece of hardware needs a driver: the software that lets Windows talk to it. Device Manager shows a yellow warning on anything without one.
$ cat ~/deploy/device-manager.txt
Error Code 28 means "the drivers for this device are not installed". Code 10 means the device can't start, Code 43 means Windows stopped it after it reported a problem.

Installing Windows by hand on 200 laptops is slow and each ends up different. A golden image is one prepared machine with the OS, drivers, apps and settings captured, then applied to many. Better today is modern deployment: Windows Autopilot or Intune configure a fresh, factory-installed device when the user signs in, so no image is needed at all.

WIM/ESD files hold Windows images. DISM mounts and edits them. Sysprep generalizes an installed system so each clone gets a unique SID and identity. MDT and SCCM/Intune automate task sequences. Windows ADK/WinPE is the tiny boot environment that applies the image.

Windows doesn't match drivers by name. Every device reports a Hardware ID like PCI\VEN_8086&DEV_A0F0, where VEN is the vendor (8086 = Intel, 10EC = Realtek, 14E4 = Broadcom) and DEV is the specific device. A driver's .inf file lists the IDs it supports.
$ grep -i "VEN_" ~/deploy/device-manager.txt
$ grep -il "DEV_A0F0" ~/deploy/drivers/*.inf

In MDT / SCCM / WDS you import driver packs per model so the right ones get injected during deployment. On one machine: pnputil /add-driver <file>.inf /install. Offline images: DISM /Image:C:\mount /Add-Driver /Driver:<folder> /Recurse.

Build a reference machine in a VM (not on hardware, so no hardware-specific drivers sneak in).
Install updates and standard apps, configure policy, and remove temporary files.
Run sysprep /generalize /oobe /shutdown.
Capture the disk to a WIM (dism /Capture-Image).
Boot target machines from WinPE or the network (PXE), apply the image, then inject or install the right drivers.
Join the domain, run Windows Update, test a sample machine, and record the version in your image log.

Organize drivers by make and model. Use the manufacturer's driver pack or enterprise tool (Dell Command, HP Image Assistant, Lenovo System Update). Unknown device in Device Manager? Open Properties → Details → Hardware Ids, search the VEN and DEV values, and install the matching driver. Missing storage or network drivers need injecting into WinPE or the image up front, because you cannot download them if the NIC does not work.

Build a reference image, generalize it with sysprep /generalize /oobe /shutdown (removes the machine SID and hardware specifics), capture it with DISM
Keep it thin: OS + updates, and let the task sequence add apps and drivers per model
When deployment fails, the answers are in logs: setupact.log / setuperr.log (Panther), setupapi.dev.log (every driver install attempt), smsts.log (SCCM task sequences)
$ grep -i "fail\|error" ~/deploy/setupapi.dev.log

Only use drivers from the OEM or Windows Update (malicious or vulnerable drivers are a real attack path, "BYOVD"), enable Secure Boot and BitLocker as part of the task sequence, and never bake passwords into a plain-text unattend file.

The key logs are C:\Windows\Panther\setupact.log and setuperr.log, C:\Windows\INF\setupapi.dev.log for driver installs, C:\Windows\Logs\DISM\dism.log, and X:\Windows\Panther inside WinPE. Common failures: missing storage driver ("no drives found"), TPM or Secure Boot requirements, a sysprep that fails because of a Store app, bad answer file syntax, and wrong partition style (GPT versus MBR with UEFI versus legacy).

Enable Secure Boot and TPM, use BitLocker with keys escrowed to AD or Entra ID, remove the built-in admin or randomize it with LAPS, keep the image patched (stale images are a quiet risk), restrict who can edit task sequences and the deployment share, and never bake credentials into an image or unattend file.

stage 2 · shell · practice with: bash guide · bash dojo · linux guide
One-liners, loops and small scripts that turn a pile of logs into an answer. Practice with the grep, sort and uniq pipeline every analyst ends up using.
simple // the idea in plain words

The shell lets you chain small tools: each does one job and passes its output to the next with a pipe (|). Most log questions are the same four stages:
Select the rows you care about: grep
Extract the field: awk '{print $1}' or cut
Count how often each value appears: sort | uniq -c
Rank them: sort -rn | head
$ cut -d' ' -f1 logs/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3
$ grep " 404 " logs/access.log | wc -l
uniq only collapses neighbours, so it needs sort first. Forgetting that is the most common wrong answer from this pipeline.

"Take column 1 of the log, sort it, count the duplicates, sort by count high to low, show the top 3." If you can say it, you can build it one stage at a time. Run the first stage alone, check the output, then add the next.

$ awk '{print $1, $7}' logs/access.log | head -3
$ awk '$9 == 404 {print $1}' logs/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
$ grep -c "curl/" logs/access.log
In a combined-format web log, $1 is the client IP, $7 the path, $9 the HTTP status. grep -c counts matching lines, -v inverts a match, -E allows a|b alternatives.

Counting requests per IP is one question. Counting different paths per IP is another, and it is the one that finds scanners: a person browses a few pages many times, a scanner hits many pages once. sort -u removes duplicate lines, so unique (ip, path) pairs come first:
$ awk '{print $1, $7}' logs/access.log | sort -u | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3

for f in logs/*.log; do
 echo "$f: $(grep -c ' 404 ' "$f") not-found"
done
Put it in a file with #!/usr/bin/env bash on the first line, chmod +x, run with ./script.sh arg. $1 is the first argument, $# the count, $(...) captures output.

Start every non-trivial script with:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
-e stops at the first failing command instead of ploughing on
-u makes an unset variable an error (so rm -rf "$DIR/" with an empty DIR does not become rm -rf /)
-o pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any stage failed, not just the last
Other habits that matter: quote your variables ("$f"), check arguments ([ $# -eq 1 ] || { echo "usage: $0 <log>"; exit 2; }), use mktemp instead of fixed /tmp names, and trap 'rm -f "$tmp"' EXIT to clean up.

cron: 0 2 * * * /home/ops/bin/scan_report.sh /var/log/nginx/access.log > /var/log/scan_report.txt 2>&1 runs it at 02:00 and keeps the output. Cron has a tiny PATH, so use absolute paths.
systemd timers are the modern alternative: they log to the journal and can retry
Exit codes: exit 1 when the report finds something, so a wrapper can alert
shellcheck catches quoting and portability mistakes before they reach production
Know when to stop: past about 50 lines, or once you need a real data structure, move to Python (see the Python chapter)

sort is O(n log n), so sort | uniq -c is dominated by the sort, while a one-pass counter in a dictionary (what Python's Counter does) is O(n). For a few hundred megabytes of log either is fine. More reps in the Bash dojo, and see Big-O for the cost model.

stage 6 · structures · practice with: data structures guide · big-o · python dojo
Dictionaries, sets, stacks, queues and heaps are the tools you reach for in security scripts. See each one solve a real detection problem. Practice with a sliding-window brute-force detector.
simple // the idea in plain words

A data structure is a way of holding data so a certain question is cheap to answer. Choosing the right one is most of the skill. The five worth knowing cold, with a security use for each:
List / array: ordered, indexed. The lines of a log in order.
Dictionary (hash map): key to value, near-instant lookup. IP address to failure count.
Set: unique items, near-instant "is it in here?". The blocklist, or the IPs already seen.
Stack: last in, first out. Undo history, nested brackets, a call stack.
Queue: first in, first out. Jobs waiting for a worker, events in arrival order.
$ python3 -c "ips=['a','b','a','c','a']; print(len(set(ips)), 'unique', ips.count('a'), 'times')"
"Is this IP on the blocklist?" in a list means checking every entry. In a set it is one step. With 500,000 entries and a million log lines, that choice is the difference between a second and an afternoon.
Need order and position: list. Need to count or group by a key: dictionary. Need uniqueness or membership: set. Need the most recent first: stack. Need the oldest first, or a moving window: queue.

from collections import Counter, defaultdict
fails = Counter(ip for ip in ips) # ip -> count
by_user = defaultdict(set) # ip -> set of usernames tried
for ip, user in pairs: by_user[ip].add(user)
spray = [ip for ip, us in by_user.items() if len(us) >= 4]
defaultdict(set) creates the empty set for a new key automatically. A scanner that tries many usernames is a spray; one that tries many passwords on one user is a brute force. Different data structure question, different alert.
a & b (in both), a | b (either), a - b (in a, not in b). "IPs that failed and later succeeded" is failed_ips & success_ips, one line, and it is the shape of most correlation rules.

Detection usually means "N things within T seconds". Keep a deque of recent timestamps per key: add the new one on the right, drop old ones from the left, and check the length.
from collections import deque
window = deque()
for ts in times:
 window.append(ts)
 while window and ts - window[0] > 30: # older than 30 s
 window.popleft()
 if len(window) >= 5:
 print("alert at", ts)
deque.popleft() is O(1). list.pop(0) is O(n), because it shifts every element, which is why you do not use a plain list as a queue.
The call stack, an undo list, matching ( with ): append to push, pop to take the last. A stack is also how a depth-first search over a directory tree or an attack graph works.

| Structure | Lookup | Add | Remove | Note
 | list | O(n) | O(1) at end | O(n) | index by position O(1)
 | dict / set | O(1) avg | O(1) avg | O(1) avg | unordered keys, O(n) worst case
 | deque | O(n) | O(1) both ends | O(1) both ends | the right tool for windows
 | heap | min O(1) | O(log n) | O(log n) | top-k, "what is next"
 | sorted list + bisect | O(log n) | O(n) | O(n) | range queries on timestamps
More detail and a visualizer on the Big-O page.

Dedup a stream: seen = set(); if x in seen: continue; seen.add(x). Memory grows with distinct items, so cap it or use a Bloom filter when it will not fit
Top-k: heapq.nlargest(10, counts.items(), key=...) is O(n log k), better than sorting everything when k is small
Rate limiting / detection: the per-key deque above, or a token bucket: a counter that refills over time
Graphs: hosts and connections are nodes and edges. A dict of sets ({host: {neighbours}}) plus breadth-first search answers "how far can an attacker get from this machine", the lateral-movement question
Trie / prefix tree: match a log line against thousands of indicator prefixes at once
Memory versus time: a bigger dict can answer faster. Streaming a log with fixed-size state is how you handle logs larger than RAM
The honest rule of thumb: reach for dict, set and deque first. They cover most of it, and the katas in the Python dojo drill each one.

Careful: one IP fails far more often overall, but slowly. Only one IP actually trips the rule. Submit that IP address.

stage 5 · history · practice with: git guide
Your scripts are code. Put them in git so you can see who changed what, undo a bad change, and keep secrets out of history. Practice with the cron job that ate the log directory.
simple // the idea in plain words

A script you wrote once and never touched is fine. A script that runs from cron every night, that three people edit, is a liability unless you can answer: what changed, who changed it, and how do I go back? That is what git is for.
A commit is a labelled snapshot of the whole folder
git log is the list of snapshots, newest first
git diff shows exactly which lines changed
git blame file shows who last touched each line
$ git log --oneline
$ git blame rotate-logs.sh
If a script deletes or sends things, change it on a branch and test it before it reaches the machine that runs it. The nightly job is not the test environment.

The scripts, a short README with how to run them, and sample input
Not API keys, passwords, tokens, real logs or exports with customer data. Put those names in .gitignore before the first commit.

git switch -c fix-rotation # branch for the change
# edit, test with --dry-run
git add rotate-logs.sh
git commit -m "Keep 30 days of logs, not 0"
git switch main && git merge fix-rotation
Commit messages say why. "Speed up rotation" tells you nothing at 3 a.m.; "Delete logs older than 30 days only" tells you what the code was meant to do, which is the thing you need when it does not.
Finding the commit that broke it

git log -p -- rotate-logs.sh shows every change to one file, with the diff
git log -S"mtime +0" --oneline finds the commits that added or removed that exact text
git blame -L 12,14 rotate-logs.sh shows who changed lines 12 to 14, and in which commit
git show <sha> prints one commit in full
$ git log -S"mtime +0" --oneline
$ git show 77f3a0e

Git remembers everything, including the key you deleted in the next commit. Use .gitignore for files that hold secrets, read them from environment variables in the script, and if one leaks, rotate the key. Rewriting history does not un-leak a key that was ever pushed.
Bisect: let git do the search

When you do not know which commit broke the behavior, git bisect binary-searches the history. Mark one good and one bad commit; git checks out the middle, you test, you say good or bad, and it halves the range. Fifty commits take about six steps. That is O(log n) applied to your own history, same as binary search on the Big-O page.
git bisect start
git bisect bad HEAD
git bisect good 1a05f9b
# test, then: git bisect good | git bisect bad
git bisect run ./test.sh # fully automatic if the test exits 0/1
git bisect reset

Pre-commit hook (.git/hooks/pre-commit) runs a secret scanner such as gitleaks before the commit is created, so the key never enters history
Protected branch + review on the shared repo: a second pair of eyes on anything that deletes or sends
Tags (git tag v1.4) mark what is deployed, so git diff v1.4 HEAD is exactly what a release changes
Signed commits prove who made a change on repositories where that matters
**git revert <sha>** undoes a commit by adding a new one; safe on shared branches. reset --hard rewrites history and loses work, so keep it off anything pushed
Deploy from a tag, not from someone's laptop: cron should run a checked-out tagged version
The same moves as the git guide, pointed at your own automation.

stage 3 · windows · practice with: powershell guide · powershell dojo
PowerShell passes objects, not text, so pulling failed logons out of the Windows event log takes four short stages. Practice with Get-WinEvent, Group-Object and Invoke-RestMethod.
simple // the idea in plain words

In bash a pipe passes text. In PowerShell a pipe passes objects with properties, so you filter on .Status instead of cutting column 7. That makes admin chores short:
Get-Service returns service objects
Where-Object keeps the ones you want
Select-Object picks properties
Sort-Object, Group-Object and Measure-Object order and count
$ Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5
Commands are named Verb-Noun (Get-, Set-, New-, Remove-). Get-Command *event* finds commands by keyword and Get-Help Get-WinEvent -Examples shows how to use one. Get-Member shows what properties an object has, which is the key to every pipeline.
A $_ inside a script block means "the object currently in the pipeline". Where-Object { $_.Id -eq 4625 } reads "keep objects whose Id is 4625".
Windows logs everything as structured events. Event ID 4625 is a failed logon, 4624 a successful one, 4688 a new process. PowerShell reads them as objects, so you never parse text.

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4625; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-24)}
The -FilterHashtable form filters inside the log service, which is far faster than pulling everything and using Where-Object afterwards. Filter early, shape late.
The event's useful fields (account, source address) sit in the message. Many people export to CSV first, or use Import-Csv on an export, and then everything is a property:
$ Import-Csv .\4625.csv | Group-Object TargetUserName | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 Name,Count
$ Import-Csv .\4625.csv | Where-Object TargetUserName -eq 'svc-backup' | Group-Object IpAddress | Sort-Object Count -Descending
Output you can hand to someone

Export-Csv -NoTypeInformation out.csv for a spreadsheet
ConvertTo-Json and ConvertFrom-Json for APIs and configs
Format-Table -AutoSize for the screen only (it produces formatting objects, so do not pipe it onward)

Invoke-RestMethod does the request and parses the JSON in one step:
$key = $env:VT_API_KEY
$r = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "https://www.virustotal.com/api/v3/ip_addresses/203.0.113.77" `
 -Headers @{ "x-apikey" = $key } -TimeoutSec 10
$r.data.attributes.last_analysis_stats.malicious
Same rules as Python: the key comes from an environment variable, there is a timeout, and results are cached.

function Get-FailedLogons {
 [CmdletBinding()]
 param([int]$Hours = 24, [int]$Threshold = 10)
 $since = (Get-Date).AddHours(-$Hours)
 Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{ LogName='Security'; Id=4625; StartTime=$since } |
 Group-Object { $_.Properties[5].Value } |
 Where-Object Count -ge $Threshold |
 Select-Object Name, Count
}
Parameters with types and defaults make a function safe to reuse. [CmdletBinding()] adds -Verbose, -ErrorAction and friends for free
Return objects, not formatted strings, so the caller can pipe the result
Error handling: try { ... } catch { ... } only catches terminating errors; add -ErrorAction Stop to turn a cmdlet's non-terminating errors into catchable ones
Remoting: Invoke-Command -ComputerName srv01,srv02 -ScriptBlock { ... } runs it on many machines at once (needs WinRM and permission)

Scheduling: Register-ScheduledTask runs a script on a timer; run it as a least-privileged service account, never your admin account
Execution policy is a guardrail against accidents, not a security boundary. Sign scripts that others will run, and review any script before -ExecutionPolicy Bypass
Logging: turn on Script Block Logging (event 4104); it is how defenders see what PowerShell actually ran, and why attackers' obfuscated scripts show up in the log anyway
Complexity: Group-Object builds a hash table (O(n)); calling Where-Object once per item inside another loop is O(n times m). Build the lookup once
