Android apps run in a per-app sandbox, ask for permissions in a manifest, and ship as APK files you can unpack and read. That makes both defending and testing them very hands-on.
simple // the idea in plain words

Each Android app runs as its own Linux user in a sandbox, so one app cannot read another's files. What an app may do beyond that is declared in its AndroidManifest.xml and granted as permissions (camera, location, contacts, internet).
An app ships as an APK (a zip file) holding the manifest, compiled code (classes.dex), resources and a signature. Anyone can unzip one, which is why you must assume attackers can read your client code and any secret inside it.
The main risk areas (from the OWASP Mobile Top 10 and MASVS):
Insecure storage: secrets left in plain files, SharedPreferences, SQLite or logs.
Insecure communication: no TLS, or TLS with certificate checks turned off.
Weak authentication and authorization: checks done only in the app; the server must enforce them.
Exported components: activities, services and receivers other apps can call.
Hard-coded secrets: API keys and passwords inside the APK.
Weak crypto and poor code quality: ECB, static keys, debuggable builds.

Look for:
android:exported="true" on components without a permission requirement: any app can start them.
android:debuggable="true": lets anyone attach a debugger. Never in release builds.
android:allowBackup="true": app data can be pulled with adb backup on older versions; set false for sensitive apps.
android:usesCleartextTraffic="true" or a network security config allowing HTTP.
Dangerous permissions the app does not need.

Private app files are in /data/data/<package>/ and are protected by the sandbox on an unrooted device. But external storage is shared, and a rooted device or a backup exposes everything. Use the Android Keystore for keys (hardware-backed where available) and EncryptedSharedPreferences / Jetpack Security for small secrets. Do not log tokens.
Use TLS everywhere. Android's Network Security Config can block cleartext and pin certificates. Do not ship a TrustManager that accepts everything.

apktool decodes resources and the manifest, jadx decompiles to readable Java, adb talks to a device or emulator, Frida hooks functions at runtime, MobSF automates static and dynamic analysis, and Burp or mitmproxy intercept traffic from a test device. Practice on intentionally vulnerable apps (DIVA, InsecureBankv2) and on devices you own.

SELinux confines processes, verified boot protects the OS image, Play Protect scans apps, and app signing ties updates to the original developer. Scoped storage limits file access, and runtime permissions let users revoke access. Newer releases tighten background launches and clipboard access.

Intents: an exported component that trusts intent extras can be tricked into performing actions (intent redirection). Validate inputs and prefer explicit intents and non-exported components.
WebViews: JavaScript enabled with untrusted content, or addJavascriptInterface exposed to remote pages, can lead to code execution. Load only trusted content and restrict file access.
Deep links: handlers that skip authentication checks.
Content providers: SQL injection or path traversal through exported providers.
Root and tamper detection: obfuscation (R8/ProGuard), integrity checks and runtime protection raise the cost but never replace server-side enforcement.

Static: unpack, read manifest, search for URLs, keys and risky APIs. Dynamic: proxy traffic, exercise every screen, test authorization by replaying requests with another user's IDs. Report findings against MASVS control IDs with evidence.

iOS locks down apps tightly and gives developers hardware-backed key storage, so the mistakes are usually about what the app chooses to store, trust and send.
simple // the idea in plain words

iOS apps run in a sandbox, are code-signed, and are distributed through Apple's review process (or enterprise/TestFlight). The system provides strong tools, and most vulnerabilities come from not using them.
The pieces to know:
Keychain: the place for passwords, tokens and keys. Items can be locked to the device, require a passcode or biometrics, and be excluded from backups.
Secure Enclave: a separate hardware processor that holds private keys and performs signing without ever exposing the key.
Data Protection: files are encrypted with keys tied to the device passcode; classes decide when they are readable (for example only while unlocked).
App Transport Security (ATS): by default the app must use HTTPS with modern TLS. Exceptions are declared in Info.plist.
Entitlements and permissions: what an app may access, shown to the user as prompts.
The same big risks as Android apply: secrets stored in plain UserDefaults or files, TLS verification disabled, authorization enforced only in the client.

Tokens and keys: Keychain with an accessibility level like whenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly.
Never in UserDefaults, plain files, Info.plist, logs, or the pasteboard.
Sensitive screens: hide content in app-switcher snapshots; clear the clipboard.

Use platform libraries (CryptoKit, Android Keystore / Tink). Do not write your own.
Keys generated on the device and kept in hardware-backed storage; non-extractable if possible.
AEAD modes (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) with fresh nonces. No ECB, no static IVs, no keys in the binary.
Use biometrics as a local unlock for a key, not as the only proof sent to the server.

Pinning makes the app accept only specific certificates or public keys, which blocks a rogue CA or an intercepting proxy. Pin to a key plus a backup, plan for rotation, and have a safe update path. Testers bypass it with Frida or objection on devices they own, so pinning raises effort and does not replace server-side checks.

Common tools: a jailbroken test device (or the Xcode simulator), frida, objection, class-dump / Ghidra for the binary, Burp or mitmproxy with the proxy certificate installed, and MobSF. Keep to your own apps and test builds.

A jailbreak removes sandbox and signing protections, giving a tester (or malware) full file access. Detection checks (known files, writable system paths, forking) are easy to bypass, so treat the client as hostile and design the server accordingly: rate limits, device attestation (App Attest on iOS, Play Integrity on Android), and server-side authorization.

OAuth 2.0 with PKCE through the system browser (ASWebAuthenticationSession / Custom Tabs), not an embedded web view that sees the password. Short-lived access tokens, refresh tokens in the Keychain, revocation on logout and on device loss. Passkeys (FIDO2) remove passwords altogether.
Data at rest and in transit end to end

Combine ATS or Network Security Config, pinning (where justified), field-level encryption for the most sensitive data, and server-side logging of anomalies such as token use from two countries. Plan for lost devices: remote wipe, short sessions, and no long-lived secrets on the device.
Storage, Crypto, Auth, Network, Platform interaction, Code quality, Resilience, Privacy. MASTG is the matching testing guide. Report findings with these IDs so teams can track fixes.

Compliance is proving to customers, regulators and auditors that you follow the rules. Learn the difference between compliance and security, SOC 2, PCI DSS and HIPAA, how an audit runs and how to collect evidence.
simple // the idea in plain words

Compliance means meeting the requirements of a law, regulation, contract or standard. An audit is an independent check that you did. Security is about actually being safe. Compliance is about being able to prove you follow a defined set of rules. They overlap but they are not the same: you can pass an audit and still get breached, and you can be secure and fail an audit for missing paperwork.

Laws and regulations: HIPAA (health), GLBA (financial), SOX (public company financial reporting), GDPR (EU personal data), FERPA (student records)
Industry standards with contractual force: PCI DSS (payment cards)
Voluntary frameworks and attestations: ISO 27001 certification, SOC 2 report
Customer contracts: security questionnaires and addenda

$ cat ~/audit/sample.txt

A report by an independent CPA firm on a service provider's controls, based on the AICPA Trust Services Criteria: Security (required), Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy.
Type I: controls are designed properly at a point in time
Type II: controls operated effectively over a period (usually 6 to 12 months). This is what customers usually want
Reports are shared under NDA; they are not a pass/fail certificate. The auditor gives an opinion and lists exceptions.

The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard, for anyone who stores, processes or transmits cardholder data. Version 4.x has 12 principal requirements, including secure network, no vendor default passwords, protecting stored account data, encrypting data in transit, anti-malware, secure systems and software, restricting access by need to know, authentication, physical access, logging and monitoring, regular testing and an information security policy. Shrink the scope (tokenization, hosted payment pages) to reduce the work. Merchants are grouped by volume into levels and may do a self-assessment questionnaire (SAQ) or an on-site assessment by a QSA.

US law protecting health information (PHI). The Privacy Rule limits use and disclosure, the Security Rule requires administrative, physical and technical safeguards for electronic PHI (risk analysis is mandatory), and the Breach Notification Rule requires notice to affected people and regulators. Business associates (vendors who handle PHI) are covered too and sign a BAA.

Scoping and planning: what systems, what period, which controls
Request list: the auditor asks for policies, screenshots, configs, tickets, logs, lists of users
Fieldwork: sampling and testing (for example, 25 of last quarter's 400 new hires: was access approved before it was granted?)
Findings: exceptions and observations, with time for management to respond
Report: opinion or result
Remediation and follow-up

Evidence must be dated, attributable, complete and from the system of record. A screenshot of a settings page with the date visible is good; a statement "we do this" is not. Good evidence is collected continuously, not in panic before the audit.

Auditors test design (is the control appropriate?) and operating effectiveness (did it work every time?). Methods: inquiry, observation, inspection of documents, and reperformance. Samples are chosen by the auditor, not by you. One failed sample is an exception, a pattern is a finding.

Tools (Vanta, Drata and similar) and cloud-native services (AWS Config, Azure Policy) pull evidence straight from systems and flag drift. Benefits: continuous assurance and less scrambling. Caveat: tools check configuration, not whether the control is right, so a human still decides scope and risk.

Joiner-mover-leaver gaps (access not removed on termination), missing quarterly access reviews, unpatched critical vulnerabilities past the policy deadline, backups never test-restored, policies not reviewed annually, no evidence of training completion, and vendors with no assessment on file.
Use compliance as the floor and risk as the ceiling. Unique risks (your biggest customer, your riskiest app) may need controls no standard requires. Report both.

GRC analyst, compliance analyst, IT auditor (CISA certification), privacy analyst, third-party risk analyst. Security+ gives the vocabulary; CISA, CISSP, CRISC and ISO 27001 Lead Implementer/Auditor are the common next steps. See ~/careers.
Auditors must be independent and objective, keep what they see confidential, and not alter evidence. If you are audited, never fabricate or backdate evidence. That turns a finding into fraud.

Security work gives you access that other people never will. Learn professional codes of ethics, what authorization really means, how responsible disclosure works, and the legal lines every researcher should know.
simple // the idea in plain words
Security people can read things, break things and see things that ordinary users cannot. That power is why the field runs on ethics: doing the right thing when nobody is checking.

Authorization first. Only access systems you own or have clear permission to test. "It was unprotected" is not permission
Minimize harm. Prove the problem with the least access and the least data. Don't read the whole database to show you could
Confidentiality. What you learn on a job stays on the job
Honesty. Report what you found accurately, including your own mistakes. Never fabricate or hide results
Competence. Don't claim skills or do work you can't do safely
Duty to the public. When your work shows serious risk to people, there are limits to silence

Most organizations publish one: the ACM Code of Ethics, the (ISC)² Code of Ethics (protect society, act honorably, provide diligent service, advance the profession), ISACA and SANS. Break them and you can lose certifications as well as jobs. They are also frequent exam questions.
The legal line, in plain words

Laws such as the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) make it a crime to access a computer without authorization or beyond the authorization you were given. Other countries have similar laws. Good intentions don't remove the crime. That is why scope documents and written permission matter (PEN300).
If you find a vulnerability on a site you don't have permission to test, stop. Don't poke further to "confirm". You can still report it, carefully.
$ cat ~/ethics/case.txt

What to do when you find a flaw in someone else's product:
Stop at the minimum evidence. Don't access other users' data
Find the right contact: security.txt (/.well-known/security.txt), a vulnerability disclosure policy (VDP), a bug bounty program, or the vendor's security email. A CERT such as CERT/CC can mediate
Report privately: what, where, how to reproduce, impact, your contact details
Give time: the common norm is around 90 days to fix (Google Project Zero uses 90, plus a grace period if a patch is imminent), shorter for actively exploited bugs
Coordinate publication: agree on a date, a CVE ID, and credit
Don't extort: asking for money in return for silence is not bounty, it is blackmail
Full disclosure (publishing everything at once) pressures vendors but exposes users. Non-disclosure keeps users unaware. Most of the industry prefers coordinated disclosure with a deadline.

A bug bounty pays for valid reports within a stated scope. A VDP invites reports but doesn't pay. Read the policy: scope, banned tests (DoS, social engineering), safe harbor language, and rules on data. Programs that promise "safe harbor" state that they won't pursue legal action for good-faith research that follows the rules.

You find customer data exposed in a public bucket. Right: report it and don't download it
A client asks you to soften a finding to avoid embarrassing the CEO. Right: report accurately; discuss wording, not truth
You discover your friend's unauthorized access to a company system. Right: follow the incident or whistleblower process
A tool you wrote is misused. Think about dual-use risk before release and how you describe and license it
Admins, developers and analysts have privileged access; good controls (separation of duties, logging, least privilege, review) protect both the company and the honest employee.

CFAA: "exceeds authorized access" was narrowed by the Supreme Court in *Van Buren v. United States* (2021): it covers entering areas of a system you are barred from, not misusing data you may legitimately access
DOJ charging policy (2022): federal prosecutors are told not to charge good-faith security research, though state laws and civil suits can still apply
DMCA section 1201 bans circumventing copy protection, with exemptions for security research that are reviewed every three years
Contracts and terms of service can create civil liability even when no crime occurs
Other countries: the UK Computer Misuse Act, EU directives, local laws with different or no research exemptions
Before researching on a system you don't own, read the policy, consider the jurisdiction and, for anything risky, consult a lawyer. Organizations like the EFF publish researcher guidance.

If you stumble onto sensitive data during legitimate work: stop viewing it, preserve only what's needed as evidence (with hashes), tell the right person immediately, secure the copy, and follow the data-handling terms. Privacy law (see privacy law) may apply to you as well.

Teaching and publishing exploit code is a long-standing debate. Responsible practice: publish proof-of-concept after a fix is available, avoid ready-to-run weaponized tools for unpatched bugs, describe defenses along with attacks and obey platform rules. This site does the same: labs are fictional and the guides stress defense and detection.

Security knowledge can be used to protect or to surveil and manipulate. Consider the people affected by what you build: facial recognition, stalkerware, monitoring tools and AI systems have real harms. Ethical review is part of professional judgment, not an obstacle.

When you see unlawful or dangerous conduct, use internal channels first where they are safe; know your protections (SOX, Dodd-Frank, the EU Whistleblower Directive, and state laws) and keep records. This is the hardest part of the job.
Write down your own rules of engagement before you need them. Keep a log of decisions. Ask: Would I be comfortable if this appeared in the report, in the news, or in front of the person affected?

Frameworks are shared checklists and structures for running a security program. Learn what NIST CSF, NIST SP 800-53, ISO 27001 and CIS Controls are for, how they differ, and how to choose and map between them.
simple // the idea in plain words

GRC stands for governance, risk and compliance. Governance is who decides and how. Risk is what could go wrong and how likely. Compliance is proving you follow the rules (laws, contracts, standards). A framework is a ready-made structure so a company does not invent its security program from scratch.

| Framework | What it is | Typical user
 | NIST CSF 2.0 | A high-level model of what a security program does, in six functions | Any organization; common US starting point
 | NIST SP 800-53 | A large catalog of detailed security and privacy controls | US federal agencies and contractors
 | ISO/IEC 27001 | An international standard for an information security management system (ISMS) you can be certified against | Global companies, service providers
 | CIS Controls | 18 prioritized practical safeguards | Small and medium organizations
 | NIST RMF | A step-by-step process for managing risk to systems (SP 800-37) | Federal systems

Govern: strategy, roles, policy, risk appetite, supply chain
Identify: know your assets, risks and weaknesses
Protect: safeguards (access control, training, data security, hardening)
Detect: find attacks and anomalies (monitoring)
Respond: act on an incident (plan, analysis, containment, communication)
Recover: restore operations and learn
The earlier 1.1 version had five functions. Govern was added in 2.0 (2024). Memorize the six in order.

A control is one specific safeguard ("require MFA for remote access"). A framework groups controls and says when each is needed. You pick the framework, then implement and prove the controls.
$ cat ~/frameworks/controls.txt

Controls are grouped into 20 families with two-letter IDs, for example:
 | ID | Family
 | AC | Access Control
 | AT | Awareness and Training
 | AU | Audit and Accountability
 | CA | Assessment, Authorization, Monitoring
 | CM | Configuration Management
 | CP | Contingency Planning
 | IA | Identification and Authentication
 | IR | Incident Response
 | RA | Risk Assessment
 | SC | System and Communications Protection
 | SI | System and Information Integrity
 | SR | Supply Chain Risk Management
(others: MA, MP, PE, PL, PM, PS, PT, SA). A control has an ID like AC-2 (account management), text, and optional "enhancements" like AC-2(1). Baselines (low, moderate, high) say which controls apply to a system based on its impact.

Clauses 4 to 10 describe the ISMS: context, leadership, planning (risk assessment), support, operation, performance evaluation, improvement. It follows plan-do-check-act
Annex A lists 93 controls in four themes: Organizational (37), People (8), Physical (14), Technological (34)
A Statement of Applicability (SoA) says which Annex A controls apply and why
You can be certified by an accredited auditor: stage 1 (document review), stage 2 (implementation), then yearly surveillance audits and a recertification every three years
ISO 27002 gives implementation guidance for the controls

18 controls ordered roughly by value: inventory of assets, inventory of software, data protection, secure configuration, account management, access control, vulnerability management, audit logs, email and browser protection, malware defenses, data recovery, network infrastructure, monitoring, awareness training, service providers, application software, incident response, penetration testing. Implementation Groups (IG1 to IG3) say how much a small versus large organization should do.

Selling to the US government: NIST 800-53 / FedRAMP
Customers abroad ask for "ISO 27001" or "SOC 2"
Small team with limited budget: CIS IG1 plus CSF as the language
Frameworks overlap heavily. A crosswalk (mapping) lets one control satisfy several: "MFA" covers NIST IA-2, ISO A.8.5 and CIS 6. Build one control set and map outward instead of three separate programs.
Seven steps: Prepare, Categorize (impact of the system), Select controls, Implement, Assess, Authorize (an official accepts the residual risk: the ATO), Monitor continuously.

CSF Implementation Tiers (Partial, Risk Informed, Repeatable, Adaptive) describe how mature the process is. A profile records the Current state and the Target state and the gap between them is the roadmap. Other maturity models: CMMI levels, C2M2.

COBIT: IT governance
ITIL: IT service management
FedRAMP: US cloud authorization built on 800-53
CMMC: US defense contractors, built on 800-171
MITRE ATT&CK: describes attacker behavior, used to test whether controls cover real techniques
Cloud Security Alliance CCM: cloud controls
HITRUST: healthcare-flavored combined framework

By function: preventive, detective, corrective, deterrent, compensating, directive. By category: technical, managerial, operational, physical. Security+ domain 5 tests these terms. Example: a badge reader is physical + preventive; a log review is operational + detective.

Scope the program (systems, data, locations)
Assess the current state against the framework (gap assessment)
Rank gaps by risk, not by how easy they are
Build a roadmap with owners and dates
Collect evidence as you go, not the week before an audit
Report to leadership with a few measures that matter (patch latency, MFA coverage, mean time to detect)
Primary sources are free: NIST CSF, SP 800-53 catalog, CIS Controls. Read the real documents, since this chapter is a map, not a replacement.

Policies turn security goals into rules people can follow and auditors can check. Learn the policy, standard, procedure and guideline hierarchy, how to write a clear requirement, and the policies every company needs.
simple // the idea in plain words

A policy is a short statement from leadership of what the organization requires. Without one, security is a pile of good intentions. With a bad one, it is a document nobody reads. A good policy is clear, enforceable and brief.

| Layer | What it is | Example | Changes
 | Policy | High-level rule and why; approved by leadership | "All laptops must be encrypted." | rarely
 | Standard | Specific mandatory requirement | "Use AES-256 full-disk encryption with centrally escrowed keys." | sometimes
 | Procedure | Step-by-step how | "How to enable BitLocker and escrow the key." | often
 | Guideline | Advice, not required | "Prefer a passphrase of 4+ words." | often
Policy says what and why, standard says how much, procedure says how exactly, guideline says what we recommend.

Must / shall / required: mandatory
Should: expected unless you have a good reason (an exception)
May: optional
Vague phrases ("appropriate measures", "as soon as practical") cannot be checked. Prefer: "within 30 days", "all production systems", "at least 14 characters".

Information security (the umbrella), acceptable use, access control, password/authentication, data classification and handling, incident response, backup and recovery, remote work, change management, vendor management, BYOD, and retention.
$ cat ~/policy/draft.txt

Title, owner, version, date, next review
Purpose: why it exists, in one or two sentences
Scope: who and what it covers (all employees, contractors, all company systems)
Policy statements: the numbered requirements
Roles and responsibilities: who does what
Exceptions: how to request one, who approves, how long it lasts
Enforcement: consequences of violating it
Related documents and definitions
Revision history
Writing a requirement people can follow

Bad: "Passwords must be strong." Better: "User passwords must be at least 14 characters and must not appear in a breached-password list. MFA is required for all remote access." Test each line: can an auditor check this yes or no? Can an employee tell whether they are following it?

Plain language at about a ninth-grade reading level; short sentences; active voice; one requirement per statement so it can be numbered and tested; no unexplained jargon. A two-page policy people follow beats a twenty-page policy they skip.

Involve the people who will have to comply in the draft
Get executive sign-off, since it is what makes the policy binding
Train and attest (employees acknowledge they read it)
Make the safe way the easy way (a password manager removes the excuse)
Measure compliance and report it

Acceptable use: what company systems may be used for, personal use limits, monitoring notice. Data classification: levels such as Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted, each with handling rules for storage, sharing, encryption and disposal (see privacy law). Incident response: how to report, who leads, severity levels, communication. Change management: request, review, test, approve, schedule, roll back.
Draft, review (legal, HR, IT, business), approve, publish, train, enforce, review at least annually, retire. Keep version history; auditors ask for last year's version to see what applied when.
Exceptions are normal, but they must be recorded in the risk register: who, what, compensating controls, expiry date. A pile of permanent exceptions means the policy is wrong or unenforced.

Automate enforcement where you can: MDM enforces disk encryption, conditional access enforces MFA, DLP enforces handling rules, config baselines enforce standards. Policy as code tools can test cloud configuration against the written rule every day, which is stronger evidence than a PDF.

Map each policy statement to a framework control (NIST, ISO 27001 A.5.1) and to evidence
Keep a policy register: document, owner, approver, version, review date
Avoid duplication and contradiction by having one owner for the whole set

Policies must be applied consistently. Selective enforcement undermines trust and exposes the company legally. Work with HR and legal on the language for discipline and on employee monitoring notices, which are regulated differently by region.

Policy writing is a real job skill: GRC analyst roles ask for it. Keep samples you wrote for your own lab or club (never a client's). A one-page acceptable use policy and an incident response plan make strong portfolio items alongside a risk worksheet result.

Privacy law decides what you may collect, how long you may keep it, who must be told when it leaks, and what it costs when you get it wrong. Learn GDPR, CCPA/CPRA, HIPAA and FERPA, plus data classification and breach clocks.
simple // the idea in plain words

Privacy is about people's rights over data about them. Security protects data from the wrong people. You need both: you can have perfect security and still break privacy law by collecting data you had no reason to hold.

PII: personally identifiable information (name, ID number, address, email, IP address in some laws)
Sensitive data: health, biometrics, financial accounts, race, religion, precise location, children's data. It gets stricter rules
Data subject: the person the data is about
Controller: decides why and how data is processed. Processor: handles it on the controller's behalf (your cloud provider, your payroll vendor)
Data minimization: collect only what you need, keep it only as long as you need
The laws you will hear about

| Law | Covers | Notable points
 | GDPR (EU, 2018) | Personal data of people in the EU, wherever the company is | Lawful basis needed, data subject rights, 72 hour breach notice, fines up to the greater of 20 million euros or 4% of global revenue
 | CCPA / CPRA (California) | Residents' personal information held by larger businesses | Right to know, delete, correct, opt out of sale or sharing
 | HIPAA (US) | Health information held by providers, plans and their vendors | Privacy, Security and Breach Notification Rules
 | FERPA (US) | Student education records at schools that receive federal funds | Parents or eligible students control access
 | GLBA (US) | Customer financial information at financial institutions | Safeguards Rule
 | COPPA (US) | Online collection from children under 13 | Parental consent
This is education, not legal advice. Laws change and have exceptions. A company asks its lawyer; a security person knows when to ask.
$ cat ~/privacy/incidents.txt

Lawful bases for processing: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, legitimate interests. Data subject rights: be informed, access, rectify, erase ("right to be forgotten"), restrict, port, object, and not be subject to purely automated decisions. Requests must generally be answered within one month. Other duties: privacy by design and by default, a record of processing, a DPIA (data protection impact assessment) for high-risk processing, a DPO (data protection officer) in some cases, a contract with each processor, and safeguards for transfers outside the EU (adequacy decisions, standard contractual clauses). Breach notice: tell the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware, unless the breach is unlikely to risk people's rights. Tell the individuals without undue delay if the risk is high.

There is no single federal privacy law. Instead there are sector laws (HIPAA, GLBA, FERPA, COPPA), the FTC's authority over unfair or deceptive practices, and a growing set of state laws (California, Virginia, Colorado, Texas and many others). Every US state has its own breach notification law; deadlines and triggers differ (often 30 to 60 days, some "without unreasonable delay").

Covered entities must notify affected individuals within 60 days of discovery. Breaches affecting 500 or more people also go to the HHS and the media promptly; smaller ones are reported to HHS annually. Properly encrypted data is generally a "safe harbor": loss of an encrypted laptop is not a reportable breach.

Label data so handling follows the label. A typical scheme: Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted. Each level states where it may be stored, whether it must be encrypted, who may see it, how it is shared, and how it is destroyed. Match classification to policy.

Encryption at rest and in transit, access control and logging, pseudonymization and anonymization (true anonymization is hard), retention schedules with deletion, vendor assessments, and training. Retention matters: data you deleted cannot be breached.

Moving personal data across borders is regulated. The EU-US Data Privacy Framework, standard contractual clauses and binding corporate rules are the usual mechanisms. Some countries require data to stay inside them (data localization). Cloud architecture must account for this: region choice is a legal decision.

Build the clocks into your incident response plan: who decides if personal data was involved, who calls legal, who contacts regulators, where the contact list is. Time starts at *awareness*, so document when and how you became aware. Contracts with customers may add shorter deadlines (24 or 48 hours is common) than the law.

Privacy by design: data flow maps, default settings protect the user, collect least
DPIA / PIA as a gate in development for new features
Consent management: record what the user agreed to, honor withdrawal, respect browser signals like Global Privacy Control where required
Subject access request (DSAR) process: verify identity, find data across systems, return it within the deadline
Deletion across backups, analytics and partners
Tools: data discovery and classification scanners, DLP

Regulators fine for unlawful processing, inadequate security and late notification. Examples are large: GDPR fines in the hundreds of millions of euros for big tech companies; HIPAA settlements in the millions; class-action suits after breaches. Executives can be personally accountable in some regimes.

Training data can contain personal data; models may memorize it; automated decisions have special GDPR rights. Check ~/ai for the security side and ask legal before sending personal data to an outside AI service.
Know what personal data your systems hold and where it flows; keep the data inventory current; classify; encrypt; restrict; log access; delete on schedule; know the clocks and whom to call.

Risk management is how a company decides what to protect and how much to spend. Learn assets, threats and vulnerabilities, qualitative and quantitative scoring, the ALE formula, treatment options and the risk register.
simple // the idea in plain words

Risk is the chance that something bad happens and how much it would hurt. Security cannot remove all risk, so the job is to find the biggest risks and decide what to do about them with a limited budget.

Asset: something worth protecting (customer database, laptops, reputation, a website)
Threat: something that can cause harm (ransomware gang, flood, careless employee)
Vulnerability: a weakness the threat can use (unpatched server, no backup)
Likelihood: how probable
Impact: how bad (money, downtime, legal trouble, safety)
Risk = Likelihood x Impact. A big impact that almost never happens and a small impact that happens daily can both matter.

Mitigate: reduce it with a control (patch, MFA, backup)
Transfer: shift the cost (cyber insurance, outsourcing to a provider; responsibility still stays with you)
Accept: knowingly live with it because the cost of fixing is higher than the loss
Avoid: stop doing the risky thing (retire the service)
What remains after your controls is residual risk. What exists before any controls is inherent risk.

Rate likelihood 1 to 5 and impact 1 to 5, multiply. 1-5 low, 6-12 medium, 13-25 high. Simple, fast, and good enough to rank a list. Use the risk worksheet to try it.
$ cat ~/risk/asset.txt

Identify assets and their value and owner
Identify threats and vulnerabilities (scans, interviews, past incidents, threat intelligence)
Analyze likelihood and impact
Evaluate against the organization's risk appetite (how much risk leadership will take) and risk tolerance (the acceptable variation around it)
Treat with one of the four responses
Monitor and review: risks change when systems, threats or business change

| Term | Meaning | Formula
 | AV | Asset value | dollars
 | EF | Exposure factor: percent of the asset lost in one event | 0 to 1
 | SLE | Single loss expectancy | AV x EF
 | ARO | Annualized rate of occurrence | events per year
 | ALE | Annualized loss expectancy | SLE x ARO
Example: a server worth $200,000, a flood destroys 25% of it per event (SLE = $50,000), and a flood is expected once every 4 years (ARO 0.25). ALE = $12,500 a year.
Control justification: a control is worth buying if the drop in ALE is greater than its yearly cost. If the ALE falls from $12,500 to $2,500 and the control costs $4,000 a year, the net benefit is $6,000.

Quantitative gives numbers executives like, but the inputs are often guesses. Qualitative is faster and honest about uncertainty. Many teams use a heat map (likelihood across, impact down) and add dollar figures only for the top risks. FAIR is a structured quantitative model.

A table of every known risk: ID, description, asset, threat, vulnerability, likelihood, impact, score, owner, treatment, status, review date. Each risk has one owner who can make decisions about it. The register is a living document reviewed at least quarterly.

BIA (business impact analysis) finds critical processes and how long they can be down: RTO (recovery time objective), RPO (recovery point objective, how much data loss is acceptable), MTTR, MTBF. Third-party risk covers vendors; supply chain risk covers what they depend on.

A good statement is specific: "Because the payments API lacks rate limiting (vulnerability), an attacker could run credential stuffing (threat) and take over customer accounts, causing fraud losses and notification costs (impact)." Vague entries like "hackers" cannot be owned or fixed.

Use ranges, not single numbers (low, likely, high) and a Monte Carlo simulation if you can
Anchor estimates on data: incident history, industry reports (Verizon DBIR, IBM Cost of a Data Breach), insurance quotes
Document assumptions so the estimate can be challenged and improved
Beware precision theatre: ALE of $12,483 is not more accurate than "about $12k"

Acceptance is a business decision: written, with an owner at the right level, a time limit and a review date. "We never got to it" is not acceptance, it is neglect. Exceptions to policy should have the same discipline.

Leadership sets thresholds: for example, no risk scored High stays open more than 30 days without an approved plan; no single event may exceed $1M. Reports to the board use a few key risk indicators, such as time to patch critical vulnerabilities, percent of systems with MFA, and number of overdue risks.

Counting only technical risk and missing process, people and vendor risk. Rating by gut and never revisiting. Treating compliance as risk management (passing an audit does not mean you are safe). Hiding risks to avoid blame, which guarantees the surprise comes later.
Pentests, vulnerability scans and threat modeling feed the register. A finding from PEN300 becomes a risk entry with an owner and a treatment. Frameworks supply the control choices: see frameworks.

Most modern apps are a front end talking to an API. Learn REST, JSON, how requests are authenticated, and the one authorization mistake that shows up in almost every API review.
simple // the idea in plain words

An API (application programming interface) is a door a program uses to ask another program for something. On the web, most APIs are HTTP APIs: you send a request to a URL and get JSON back. Your phone app, the page you are looking at, and other companies' systems all use them.
JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the text format. It has objects {}, arrays [], strings, numbers, true/false and null:
{"id": 1001, "customer": "alice", "items": [{"sku": "CAB-7", "qty": 2}], "paid": true}
REST is a style of API design: URLs name things (nouns) and HTTP methods say what to do to them.
 | Request | Meaning
 | GET /v1/orders | list orders
 | GET /v1/orders/1001 | read one order
 | POST /v1/orders | create an order (body is JSON)
 | PATCH /v1/orders/1001 | change part of it
 | DELETE /v1/orders/1001 | delete it
The reply uses a status code (see HTTP and the web): 200, 201 created, 400 you sent junk, 401 who are you, 403 not allowed, 404 not found, 429 slow down.
An API is just a website with the pretty part removed. Anything the page can do, an attacker with curl can try to do directly, so the server has to enforce the rules, not the front end.
Authentication: how the API knows who you are

API key: a long secret in a header (X-API-Key) or query string. Simple, identifies an *application*. Keep it out of URLs and public repos.
Bearer token: Authorization: Bearer <token>. You log in once, get a token, send it on every call. Anyone holding it is you, so treat it like a password.
JWT (JSON Web Token): a token with three base64url parts, header.payload.signature. The payload is readable by anyone (it is encoded, not encrypted), the signature proves it was not altered. Check exp (expiry), iss/aud, and pin the allowed algorithm on the server.
OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect: "log in with Google" style delegation. The app gets a limited token instead of your password. Scopes say what the token may do.
Mutual TLS and signed requests are used between services.
Authorization: what you are allowed to do

Authentication is *who*. Authorization is *what they may touch*. The classic failure is broken object level authorization (also called IDOR, insecure direct object reference): the API checks you are logged in but never checks that order 1002 belongs to you.
GET /v1/orders/1001 (alice) -> 200, her order
GET /v1/orders/1002 (alice) -> 200, bob's order <- the bug
The fix is on the server: every object lookup also checks ownership or role (WHERE id = ? AND owner_id = ?), or returns 404. Unguessable ids help a little but are not a control.

Excessive data exposure: the API returns the whole database row (password_hash, is_admin, internal notes) and trusts the front end to hide it. Return only the fields needed.
Mass assignment: the server copies every JSON field you send onto the object, so {"is_admin": true} sneaks through. Allow-list the fields.
No rate limiting: credential stuffing, scraping, enumeration. Answer with 429 and Retry-After.
Verbose errors: stack traces and SQL errors help attackers. Log them, return a short generic message.
Old versions: /v1 still runs with no auth fixes after /v3 shipped. Keep an inventory (shadow and zombie APIs).
Working with APIs from the terminal

$ curl -s https://api.shop.example/v1/orders/1001 -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
$ curl -s -X POST https://api.shop.example/v1/orders -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"sku":"CAB-7","qty":1}'
$ curl -s URL | jq '.items[].sku'
$ echo "$JWT" | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d
jq filters JSON: .field, .[0], .items[], select(.paid==true). In a browser, the Network tab shows every API call the page makes; "copy as cURL" turns one into a command.
Designing it so it holds up

Deny by default. A new endpoint is closed until someone writes the rule for it. Centralize checks in middleware so a developer cannot forget one.
Schema validation (OpenAPI/JSON Schema): reject unknown fields, wrong types, oversized bodies. It stops mass assignment and a lot of injection at the door.
Least privilege tokens: short expiry, narrow scopes, refresh tokens that can be revoked. Rotate keys. Never log tokens.
Idempotency keys on POSTs that move money, so a retry does not charge twice.
Pagination caps: limit has a maximum, otherwise ?limit=10000000 is a free denial of service.
GraphQL variant: one endpoint, the client picks the fields. Watch depth and cost limits, disable introspection in production, and still authorize every field and object.
CORS is a browser rule, not API security. Server-to-server calls ignore it entirely.
Testing an API you are authorized to test

Use Burp Suite or OWASP ZAP as an intercepting proxy, and Postman/curl for hand-built calls. Methodology (OWASP API Security Top 10): map every endpoint, log in as two ordinary users and an admin, then replay user A's requests with user B's ids and tokens, try methods the docs do not list, and read what comes back, not just the status code. Only against systems you own, a signed scope, or a training app such as Juice Shop or crAPI.
Detecting trouble from the blue side

In API logs, an IDOR sweep looks like one account walking sequential ids (/orders/1001, 1002, 1003...) with a run of 200s. Credential stuffing looks like many 401s across many usernames from few IPs. Alert on both, and add per-user and per-IP rate limits.

Scenario (fictional, training only): the Shopwell API has an authorization bug. You have its access log and the order table (made-up data, ~/api). Each log line shows which user made the call and which order they asked for. A user is only allowed to read their own orders.
Find the one user who successfully (200) read an order that belongs to somebody else. Submit their username.
Solve it in the sandbox. Type hint when stuck and submit <answer> when you have it.

The three goals of security and the handful of cryptographic tools that deliver them: hashing, symmetric and asymmetric encryption, signatures and TLS.
simple // the idea in plain words

The CIA triad is the checklist for what security protects:
Confidentiality: only authorized people can read it. Tools: encryption, access control, MFA. Breach example: a leaked customer database.
Integrity: it hasn't been changed without authorization. Tools: hashing, digital signatures, file permissions, version control. Breach example: tampered financial records.
Availability: it works when needed. Tools: backups, redundancy, patching, DDoS protection. Breach example: ransomware locks the files.
Extras: non-repudiation (you can't deny what you did; signatures and logs), and AAA: authentication (who are you), authorization (what may you do), accounting (what did you do).
Encryption in one paragraph: plaintext goes through an algorithm with a key and becomes ciphertext. Strong systems stay secure even if everyone knows the algorithm; only the key is secret.
 | Tool | Keys | Speed | Goal | Examples
 | Hash | none | fast | integrity | SHA-256, SHA-3
 | Symmetric | one shared key | fast | confidentiality | AES-128/256
 | Asymmetric | public + private pair | slow | key exchange, signatures | RSA, ECC

A hash turns any input into a fixed-size fingerprint. One-way (can't reverse), deterministic, and a tiny change flips the whole output. Used for file integrity (sha256sum), storing passwords (with a unique salt and a slow function like bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2), and inside signatures. MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for security (collisions); use SHA-256 or better. A collision means two inputs share a hash.
$ echo -n hello | sha256sum
$ sha256sum file.iso

Same key encrypts and decrypts. AES is the standard (128, 192, 256 bit). Block modes matter: ECB leaks patterns, so use GCM (also checks integrity) or CBC with a random IV. The hard problem is sharing the key safely.

Two linked keys: what one encrypts only the other decrypts. Anyone can have the public key; only the owner holds the private key.
To send a secret: encrypt with the recipient's public key.
To sign: sign with your private key, others verify with your public key (proves origin and integrity, gives non-repudiation).
RSA (2048+ bit) and ECC (smaller keys, same strength) are the main families. Diffie-Hellman lets two parties agree on a shared secret over an open line.

Client says hello with supported ciphers; server sends its certificate (public key plus identity, signed by a certificate authority).
Client checks the signature chain, the hostname and the dates.
Both sides derive a shared session key using key exchange (ephemeral Diffie-Hellman gives forward secrecy).
Everything after that is fast symmetric encryption (AES-GCM).
So asymmetric crypto is used briefly to agree on keys, then symmetric does the work.
CA issues certificates; CSR is the request; CRL and OCSP report revoked certificates; root of trust is the CA certificates preinstalled on your device; self-signed means no outside CA vouches for it.

Brute force / dictionary / rainbow table: guess keys or passwords; salts defeat rainbow tables, long random keys defeat brute force.
Birthday attack: finds hash collisions faster than expected, which is why short hashes are weak.
Downgrade / SSL strip: force a weaker protocol or plain HTTP. Defense: HSTS, disable old TLS (SSL, TLS 1.0/1.1).
Man-in-the-middle: defeated by certificate validation, so never click through certificate warnings.
Key management failures are the most common real break: keys in code repos, reused keys, no rotation. Use an HSM or a secrets manager, and rotate.
Weak randomness breaks everything; use the OS cryptographic random source.
Side channels leak keys through timing or power use.
Quantum: a large quantum computer would break RSA and ECC (Shor's algorithm) and weaken symmetric keys (Grover), so AES-256 stays fine. NIST has standardized post-quantum algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA); "harvest now, decrypt later" is why migration planning has started.
Data states and where encryption fits

At rest: disks and databases (BitLocker, LUKS, TDE).
In transit: TLS, VPN (IPsec, WireGuard), SSH.
In use: confidential computing and enclaves; the hard one, because data must be decrypted to be processed.

Obfuscation (hiding), encoding (Base64: format only, no secrecy) and encryption are three different things. Base64 is not security.
Steganography hides data inside other files; tokenization and masking replace sensitive values.
Digital signature flow: hash the document, encrypt the hash with the private key; the verifier hashes the document and compares it with the decrypted signature.
MAC / HMAC gives integrity and authenticity with a shared key; AEAD modes like AES-GCM combine encryption and authentication.

Password storage: salted slow hash. File integrity: SHA-256. Bulk data: AES-256-GCM. Key exchange or identity: ECC or RSA 2048+ inside TLS 1.2/1.3. Never invent your own algorithm.

Follow one click from the browser to the database and back: DNS, TCP, TLS, proxies, the app, the data store. Then learn the browser dev tools that let you watch it happen.
simple // the idea in plain words

When you type https://shop.example/cart and press Enter, a lot happens in about a tenth of a second:
DNS: the browser asks for the IP address of shop.example (cached if it asked recently).
TCP: it opens a connection to that IP on port 443 (the three-way handshake).
TLS: both sides agree on encryption and the server proves its identity with a certificate.
HTTP: the browser sends GET /cart with its cookies.
The server side: a reverse proxy or load balancer receives it, passes it to an application server, which runs your code, which asks a database for the cart rows, builds a response and sends it back.
Rendering: the browser reads the HTML, then fetches the CSS, JavaScript, images and API calls it mentions, and draws the page.
The pieces:
 | Piece | Job | Examples
 | Browser (client) | shows pages, runs JavaScript | Firefox, Chrome
 | DNS | name to IP | 1.1.1.1, your router
simple // the idea in plain words

| CDN | caches static files near the user | Cloudflare, Fastly
 | Reverse proxy / load balancer | TLS termination, routing, spreading load | nginx, HAProxy
 | WAF | filters known-bad requests | ModSecurity, cloud WAF
 | App server | business logic | Node, Django, Spring, PHP
 | Database | stores the data | PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite
 | Cache / queue | speed and background jobs | Redis, RabbitMQ
Never trust the browser. Everything on the client side (form limits, hidden fields, disabled buttons, JavaScript checks) can be changed by the person using it. The server must validate and authorize every request.

Front end: HTML (structure), CSS (looks), JavaScript (behavior). Runs in the user's browser, so the user can read and change all of it.
Back end: the code and data on servers you control. This is where authentication, authorization, validation and business rules belong.
Static site: files served as-is (this site is one). Tiny attack surface.
Server-rendered app: the server builds the HTML for each request from templates and data (PHP, Rails, Django).
Single-page app (SPA): the browser loads one JS bundle (React, Vue) that calls a JSON API and draws the page itself. The API becomes the real attack surface (see APIs, REST and JSON).
Typical stack names: LAMP (Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP), MERN (MongoDB, Express, React, Node). Deeper on the full stack: full-stack guide.

The browser holds cookies, localStorage, and the page itself. The server holds sessions, the database, and uploaded files. Each place has different rules about who can read or change it. Questions that find bugs: *which of these did the client choose, and did the server check it?*

| Tab | Use
 | Elements | the live DOM and CSS; edit anything to test layouts, see hidden fields
 | Console | JavaScript errors and warnings (mixed content, CSP and CORS blocks show here) and a prompt to run JS on the page
 | Network | every request: URL, method, status, size, timing, headers, payload, response. The most useful tab
 | Application (Storage) | cookies and their flags, localStorage, sessionStorage, service workers
 | Sources | the page's JavaScript, with breakpoints
 | Security | certificate details
Network tab habits: tick *Preserve log* so a redirect doesn't wipe it, filter by Fetch/XHR to see only API calls, click a request and read Headers, Payload, Response, Timing. Right-click a request, *Copy as cURL*, and replay it in a terminal. *Export HAR* saves the whole session as JSON for a colleague or a ticket (remove cookies and tokens first, a HAR contains your session).
Reading a failure like a pro

| Symptom | Likely cause
 | page loads, button does nothing | check Console for a JS error, Network for a failed API call
 | 502 Bad Gateway | proxy reached no healthy app server, look at the upstream
 | 504 Gateway Timeout | upstream too slow
 | 403 on one file only | permissions or WAF rule
 | padlock warning / blocked scripts | mixed content: an http:// resource on an https:// page
 | works for you, fails for them | cache, CDN, DNS, or a cookie difference
 | CORS error in console | the API did not allow this origin
Where each layer can fail or be attacked

| Layer | Failure or attack | Defense
 | DNS | poisoning, hijack, expired domain | DNSSEC, registrar lock, monitor records
 | TLS | expired cert, weak ciphers, downgrade | auto-renew, TLS 1.2+, HSTS
 | Proxy / CDN | origin IP exposed, request smuggling, cache poisoning | restrict origin to proxy, keep software patched
 | WAF | bypassed or too loud | tune rules, but fix the bug, a WAF is not a patch
 | App | injection, broken access control, logic bugs | validation, parameterized queries, authz middleware
 | Session | theft, fixation | see HTTP and the web
 | Database | exposed port, default credentials, excess privileges | private network, least-privilege DB user (see relational databases)
 | Dependencies | known-vulnerable libraries | inventory, scanning, updates
 | Secrets | keys in repos, .env served publicly | secret scanning, vaults

Load balancers spread requests over several app servers, so the app must keep state in shared stores (database, Redis), not in one machine's memory.
Caching layers: browser, CDN, proxy, app, database. A cache that ignores Vary or cookies can serve one user's page to another.
Logs and metrics: access logs at the proxy, application logs, database slow query log. Put them in a SIEM (siem guide); correlate by request id.
Containers and CI/CD: apps typically ship as container images through a pipeline. Pipeline credentials and base images are part of the attack surface.
Environments: development, staging, production. Staging with real data and weak auth is a classic breach.
A methodical walkthrough (own app or lab)

Open the Network tab and use the app normally. List the hosts and endpoints.
Note what the client sends that the server should not trust: ids, prices, roles, hidden form fields.
In Application, check cookie flags and what is stored in localStorage.
Read the response headers for version leaks and missing security headers.
Write down findings with the request, response and a one-line fix. That write-up is the deliverable.

Scenario (fictional): for some users of Shopwell the login button does nothing since the deploy. A tester saved the browser's Network tab as network.txt and the Console as console.txt from a failing attempt. The load balancer adds an X-Upstream header naming which backend answered each request.
Read both attachments in the console. Resolve the ticket with the name of the backend host that is returning the error on the login call.
Open the attachments, investigate in the console, then resolve the ticket with your answer.

HTTP is the conversation every browser, app and API has with a server. Learn the request, the response, the status codes, the headers, and how cookies turn a stateless protocol into a login.
simple // the idea in plain words

HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is a plain request/response protocol. The client (browser, curl, a phone app) sends a request. The server sends back one response. That is the whole idea. HTTPS is the same thing wrapped in TLS so nobody on the path can read or change it (see crypto basics). Web servers listen on 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS).
A request is text: a request line (method, path, version), headers, and an optional body.
GET /products?id=7 HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example
User-Agent: curl/8.5.0
Accept: application/json
The response has a status line, headers and a body:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 41
{"id":7,"name":"USB-C cable","price":9}
The method says what you want to do. The status code says how it went. Remember the families:
 | Code | Family | Examples
 | 1xx | informational | 101 switching protocols (WebSockets)
simple // the idea in plain words

| 2xx | success | 200 OK, 201 created, 204 no content
 | 3xx | redirect | 301 moved permanently, 302 found, 304 not modified
 | 4xx | client error | 400 bad request, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 429 too many requests
 | 5xx | server error | 500 internal error, 502 bad gateway, 503 unavailable, 504 gateway timeout
HTTP is stateless: the server does not remember you between requests. Logins work because the browser sends a cookie with every request, and the cookie holds (or points to) your session.

| Method | Meaning | Safe | Idempotent
 | GET | read a resource | yes | yes
 | HEAD | like GET, headers only | yes | yes
 | POST | create or submit something | no | no
 | PUT | replace a resource | no | yes
 | PATCH | change part of a resource | no | no
 | DELETE | remove a resource | no | yes
 | OPTIONS | ask what is allowed (CORS preflight) | yes | yes
Safe means it should not change anything. Idempotent means doing it twice has the same effect as once. A GET that deletes something is a bug and a security problem, because browsers, crawlers and link previews fire GETs freely.

Host: which site on this IP (one server hosts many).
User-Agent, Referer (sic), Accept, Accept-Language: what the client is and wants.
Content-Type and Content-Length: what the body is (application/json, application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data) and how big.
Authorization: Bearer <token>: API credentials.
Cookie (request) and Set-Cookie (response).
Location: where a 3xx sends you.
Cache-Control, ETag: caching. Server, X-Powered-By: often leak software and version, which helps an attacker fingerprint you.
X-Forwarded-For: the original client IP when a proxy or load balancer sits in front. Clients can forge it, so never trust it for security decisions unless your own proxy sets it.

The server answers a login with Set-Cookie: sid=9f2c...; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax. From then on the browser sends Cookie: sid=9f2c.... The server looks the value up in its session store and knows who you are. Whoever holds the value is you, so a stolen session cookie is a login without a password.
 | Attribute | What it does
 | Secure | only sent over HTTPS
 | HttpOnly | JavaScript cannot read it, which blunts XSS cookie theft
 | SameSite=Lax/Strict | not sent on most cross-site requests, which blunts CSRF
 | Domain, Path | which hosts and paths receive it
 | Max-Age / Expires | lifetime. No value means a session cookie that dies with the browser
Other state mechanisms: server-side sessions (cookie holds a random id), signed tokens such as JWTs (the cookie or header holds the data itself plus a signature), and localStorage (readable by any script on the page, so a poor place for secrets).

$ curl -I https://shop.example
$ curl -v https://shop.example/login
$ curl -s -H "Accept: application/json" https://shop.example/products/7
$ curl -i -X POST -d "user=demo&pass=demo" https://shop.example/login
-I is headers only, -i includes headers with the body, -v shows the whole request and response, -X sets the method, -d sends a body, -H adds a header, -L follows redirects, -k skips cert checks (never as a habit).

HTTP/1.1: text, one request at a time per connection (browsers open several). Connection: keep-alive reuses it.
HTTP/2: binary, many requests multiplexed over one connection, header compression. Same methods and status codes.
HTTP/3: HTTP/2 semantics over QUIC (UDP 443), which avoids TCP head-of-line blocking.
Request smuggling attacks exist because a front-end proxy and a back-end server can disagree about where one request ends (Content-Length vs Transfer-Encoding). Concept only: it is a reason to keep proxies and servers patched and consistent.
Security headers (the server tells the browser how strict to be)

| Header | Purpose
 | Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) | browser must use HTTPS for this host from now on
 | Content-Security-Policy | which sources may load scripts, styles, frames. The main defense in depth against XSS
 | X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff | don't guess MIME types
 | X-Frame-Options / frame-ancestors | stop other sites framing yours (clickjacking)
 | Referrer-Policy | how much URL leaks to other sites
 | Permissions-Policy | switch off camera, mic, geolocation etc.

An origin is scheme + host + port. By default a script on https://a.example cannot read responses from https://b.example. CORS (cross-origin resource sharing) lets a server opt in with Access-Control-Allow-Origin. Misconfigurations: reflecting any Origin back, or Allow-Origin: * together with credentials. CORS protects *reading* responses in the browser; it does not stop the request from being sent, which is why CSRF needs its own defenses.

Session ids are long, random and unguessable (128 bits or more from a CSPRNG), never sequential.
Regenerate the id on login (stops session fixation, where an attacker plants a known id before you authenticate) and invalidate it on logout, server-side.
Set Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite. Use short idle and absolute timeouts. Bind sensitive actions to a recent re-authentication.
Never put session ids in URLs; they end up in logs, history and Referer.
Cache: responses that carry personal data need Cache-Control: no-store.

Web server logs are in the combined log format: ip - user [time] "METHOD /path HTTP/1.1" status bytes "referer" "user-agent". Reading them is a core SOC skill: a burst of 404s is scanning, a burst of 401/403 is guessing or probing, one IP with thousands of requests is a bot, and 500s right after odd input is a bug being poked. Pair with log analysis.

Scenario (fictional, training only): the dev team at Shopwell, a made-up store, saved one captured login exchange from their own test server into ~/capture. A reviewer asks one question: which cookie is the session cookie, and what is it missing? Read the exchange with cat ~/capture/login.txt and the notes in README.txt.
The session cookie is the one the server uses to recognise a logged-in user. Submit its name followed by the flags it lacks, in the order Secure then HttpOnly, e.g. submit foo Secure. If it lacks only one, submit just that one.
Solve it in the sandbox. Type hint when stuck and submit <answer> when you have it.

Enough Linux and Windows to move around, read logs, check permissions, and know where things live. The commands are on this page and on the cheatsheets.
simple // the idea in plain words
Nearly every security and IT task happens on one of two operating systems, so be comfortable on both.

Everything is a file, and the file system is one tree starting at /.
/etc config, /var/log logs, /home user files, /root root's home, /tmp temporary, /usr/bin programs, /dev devices, /proc live process info.
Paths: ~ is your home, . is here, .. is up one.
$ pwd
$ ls -la
$ cd /var/log
$ cat auth.log
$ grep "Failed" auth.log
$ whoami
$ man ls
Rule of thumb: man <command> and <command> --help always work.

Drives and folders: C:\Windows (the OS), C:\Users (profiles), C:\Program Files (apps), C:\ProgramData (shared app data). Two shells: cmd and PowerShell (objects, not text; the one to learn).
$ dir
$ cd C:\Users
$ whoami /all
$ ipconfig /all
$ Get-Process

Permissions -rwxr-xr--: type, then owner / group / others, each r(4) w(2) x(1). chmod 640 file means owner rw, group r, others none. chown user:group file changes owners. Extra bits: setuid (runs as the file's owner, a classic privilege escalation target), sticky bit on /tmp.
$ ls -l /etc/passwd /etc/shadow
$ chmod 600 secret.txt
$ find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
$ sudo -l
Users: /etc/passwd lists accounts, /etc/shadow holds password hashes (root only), /etc/sudoers controls sudo. Processes and services: ps aux, top, kill <pid>, systemctl status|start|stop|enable <svc>, journalctl -u <svc>. Packages: apt update && apt upgrade (Debian/Ubuntu), dnf (Fedora/RHEL). Networking: ip a, ip route, ss -tulnp, ping, curl. Text tools: grep, sed, awk, sort | uniq -c, head, tail -f, wc -l, pipes | and redirects > >>. Logs: /var/log/auth.log (or secure), syslog, journalctl. Persistence spots: cron (crontab -l), systemd units, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, shell profiles.

Permissions use NTFS ACLs: icacls file, plus share permissions on top (the stricter wins). Users and groups: net user, net localgroup administrators, UAC prompts before admin actions. Services: services.msc, Get-Service, sc query. Processes: Task Manager, Get-Process, tasklist, taskkill /PID. Registry: regedit; hives HKLM (machine) and HKCU (user); autoruns live in Run keys. Task Scheduler and startup folders are persistence spots. Networking: ipconfig /all, netstat -ano, nslookup, ping, tracert. Updates: Windows Update, WSUS. Tools: Event Viewer, Resource Monitor, Sysinternals (Process Explorer, Autoruns).

Linux: /var/log/*, journalctl.
Windows: Event Viewer, Security log. Key event IDs: 4624 logon success, 4625 logon failure, 4672 admin logon, 4720 account created, 4688 process created, 1102 audit log cleared.

Patch the OS and apps; remove unused software and services; close unused ports.
Least privilege: no daily use of root or Administrator; limit sudoers and local admins; unique admin passwords (Windows LAPS).
Strong auth: SSH keys with password login off (PasswordAuthentication no), MFA, account lockout.
Encrypt disks (LUKS, BitLocker); firewall on (ufw, iptables/nftables, Windows Defender Firewall).
Central logging, time sync, and file integrity monitoring (AIDE, Tripwire; Windows audit policy).
Baselines: CIS Benchmarks and DISA STIGs define the settings to check.

Boot to login: firmware, bootloader (GRUB), kernel, init/systemd, services, login. dmesg shows kernel messages.
Standard streams: stdin 0, stdout 1, stderr 2. cmd 2>/dev/null drops errors, cmd > out 2>&1 merges.
Mounts and disks: lsblk, df -h, du -sh *, mount, /etc/fstab.
Privilege escalation hunting (defensive review): SUID binaries, sudo rules, writable cron scripts, world-writable files, credentials in history and configs.
Quick incident triage: last, w, ps auxf, ss -tulnp, crontab -l, ls -lat /tmp, grep -i "accepted\|failed" /var/log/auth.log.

Active Directory adds domains, groups and Group Policy; Kerberos (88) and LDAP (389) do the work. See the AD and Group Policy guides.
PowerShell triage: Get-LocalUser, Get-NetTCPConnection, Get-ScheduledTask, Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security';Id=4625}, Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run.
Execution policy is a safety rail, not a security boundary. Constrained language mode, script block logging and AMSI are the real controls.
Pass-the-hash and credential dumping target LSASS memory; Credential Guard and removing local admin reuse blunt them.

| Task | Linux | Windows
 | list files | ls -la | dir / Get-ChildItem
 | show IP | ip a | ipconfig /all
 | open ports | ss -tulnp | netstat -ano
 | processes | ps aux | Get-Process
 | find text | grep -r word . | Select-String -Path * -Pattern word
 | who am I | id | whoami /all
 | services | systemctl status x | Get-Service x
 | edit/permissions | chmod, chown | icacls

Binary, decimal, hex and octal, converting between them both ways, plus the bit tricks behind IP masks, ASCII, bitwise operators and two's complement. Practice here, then run the drill in the arcade.
simple // the idea in plain words

Computers store everything as bits: a bit is a 0 or a 1. A byte is 8 bits, so one byte holds 256 values (0-255). A number system (a base) is just a way to write a number using a fixed set of digits. Same quantity, different spelling.
 | Name | Base | Digits | Example for 202
 | Binary | 2 | 0 1 | 11001010
 | Octal | 8 | 0-7 | 312
 | Decimal | 10 | 0-9 | 202
 | Hexadecimal | 16 | 0-9 A-F | CA (written 0xCA)
Try it live: the converter and the drill are on arcade/bits. Type a number in any box and the others update.
Place value is the whole trick

In decimal each place is worth 10 times the one to its right: 1, 10, 100, 1000. In binary each place is worth 2 times the one to its right. Memorize the powers of two, because you will use them forever:
 | 2^7 | 2^6 | 2^5 | 2^4 | 2^3 | 2^2 | 2^1 | 2^0
 | 128 | 64 | 32 | 16 | 8 | 4 | 2 | 1
Bigger ones worth knowing: 2^8 = 256, 2^10 = 1024 (1 KiB), 2^16 = 65,536 (the number of ports), 2^20 = 1,048,576 (1 MiB), 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 (the number of IPv4 addresses).
Binary to decimal: add up the places that are 1

Write the value under the place-value row and add the columns with a 1.
128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1
 1 1 0 0 1 0 1 0
128 + 64 + 8 + 2 = 202. Another one: 00101101 = 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 45.
Decimal to binary: subtract the biggest place that fits

Convert 77. Walk down the row, and at each place ask "does it fit?" If yes write 1 and subtract, otherwise write 0.
128 fits in 77? No: 0
64 fits? Yes: 1, 77 - 64 = 13
32? No: 0. 16? No: 0
8? Yes: 1, 13 - 8 = 5
4? Yes: 1, 5 - 4 = 1
2? No: 0. 1? Yes: 1
Result: 01001101. Check: 64 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 77.

Hex has 16 digits: 0-9 then A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15. One hex digit is exactly 4 bits (a nibble), so a byte is always two hex digits. That is why hex is everywhere: MAC addresses, colors (#FF8800), memory dumps, hashes, IPv6.
 | Dec | Bin | Hex | | Dec | Bin | Hex
 | 0 | 0000 | 0 | | 8 | 1000 | 8
 | 1 | 0001 | 1 | | 9 | 1001 | 9
 | 2 | 0010 | 2 | | 10 | 1010 | A
 | 3 | 0011 | 3 | | 11 | 1011 | B
 | 4 | 0100 | 4 | | 12 | 1100 | C
 | 5 | 0101 | 5 | | 13 | 1101 | D
 | 6 | 0110 | 6 | | 14 | 1110 | E
 | 7 | 0111 | 7 | | 15 | 1111 | F
Binary to hex: group by four
Split the bits into groups of four from the right and swap each group for its hex digit. 1100 1010 is C and A, so 0xCA. Going back is the same table in reverse: 0x3F is 0011 1111.

1 byte = 8 bits. An IPv4 address is 4 bytes (32 bits). A MAC address is 6 bytes (48 bits). An IPv6 address is 16 bytes (128 bits).
Network speeds are in bits (1 Gbps = 1 gigabit per second). File sizes are in bytes. Divide by 8 to compare: 1 Gbps moves at most about 125 MB per second.

Hex place values are powers of 16: 1, 16, 256, 4096. So 0x2F = 2 x 16 + 15 = 47. And 0xC0 = 12 x 16 = 192 (which is why 192 is the first octet of 192.168.x.x).
Decimal to hex: divide by 16. The quotient is the first digit, the remainder is the second. 202 / 16 = 12 remainder 10, so C and A: 0xCA. For anything over 255, keep dividing the quotient by 16 and read the remainders from the last one back to the first.
Fast route for a byte: convert to binary first, then group in fours. 202 = 1100 1010 = CA. Most people find that more reliable than dividing.

Octal digits are 3 bits each. That is the whole reason chmod 754 works: each digit is a rwx triple.
 | Digit | Bits | Permission
 | 7 | 111 | rwx
 | 6 | 110 | rw-
 | 5 | 101 | r-x
 | 4 | 100 | r--
 | 0 | 000 | ---
So 754 = rwx r-x r--. chmod 600 on a private key = rw- for the owner and nothing for anyone else. Convert a decimal by dividing by 8, same as the hex method but with 8.
The doubling shortcut for binary to decimal
Read the bits left to right. Start at 0. For each bit, double the running total and add the bit. For 1101: 0 -> 1 -> 3 -> 6 -> 13. It needs no table and works on any length.

An IPv4 address is 32 bits written as 4 bytes in decimal, separated by dots. Convert each byte on its own.
11000000.10101000.00000001.00001010
 192 . 168 . 1 . 10
11000000 = 128 + 64 = 192. 10101000 = 128 + 32 + 8 = 168. So this is 192.168.1.10.
Subnet masks are runs of ones

A mask is some 1s followed by all 0s. Only nine byte values can appear in a mask octet. Memorize the pattern:
 | Ones in the octet | Binary | Decimal
 | 0 | 00000000 | 0
 | 1 | 10000000 | 128
 | 2 | 11000000 | 192
 | 3 | 11100000 | 224
 | 4 | 11110000 | 240
 | 5 | 11111000 | 248
 | 6 | 11111100 | 252
 | 7 | 11111110 | 254
 | 8 | 11111111 | 255
/22 is 22 ones: three full octets would be 24, so it is 8 + 8 + 6 = 255.255.252.0. The host bits are the zeros, and a subnet holds 2^(host bits) addresses. /22 has 10 host bits, so 1024 addresses and 1022 usable. Practice that in the subnet drill and in the subnetting guide.

ASCII maps characters to numbers 0-127, one byte each. The ones worth knowing:
 | Char | Dec | Hex | Binary
 | 0 | 48 | 0x30 | 00110000
 | A | 65 | 0x41 | 01000001
 | a | 97 | 0x61 | 01100001
 | space | 32 | 0x20 | 00100000
 | newline | 10 | 0x0A | 00001010
Digits start at 0x30, so '7' is 0x37. Upper and lower case differ by exactly 32 (one bit, 0x20): A is 0x41 and a is 0x61. That is why a hex dump of Hello reads 48 65 6c 6c 6f. Learn to spot readable text in a dump: bytes 20 to 7E are printable.

These work on each bit position independently.
 | Op | Rule | 1100 vs 1010
 | AND | 1 only if both are 1 | 1000
 | OR | 1 if either is 1 | 1110
 | XOR | 1 if they differ | 0110
 | NOT | flip every bit | NOT 1100 = 0011
Uses you will meet:
AND with a mask finds the network: 192.168.1.77 AND 255.255.255.0 = 192.168.1.0. This is how a router decides if a host is local.
OR sets bits (turn on a flag). AND with the inverse clears them.
XOR flips bits and is its own inverse: x XOR k XOR k = x. Malware and simple ciphers use a single-byte XOR key for exactly this reason, and it is trivial to brute force (only 256 keys).
Shifts: x << 1 doubles a number, x >> 1 halves it. 1 << 4 is 16.

172.16.37.200/21. The mask is 21 ones = 255.255.248.0. Only the third octet matters: 37 = 00100101, mask 248 = 11111000, AND = 00100000 = 32. Network 172.16.32.0. The host bits in that octet are the last 3, so the block runs 32 to 39 and the broadcast is 172.16.39.255.

A byte can hold 0-255 (unsigned) or -128 to 127 (signed). Computers store negatives in two's complement: the top bit counts as -128 instead of +128.
00000101 = 5
11111011 = -128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1 = -5
To negate: flip all the bits, then add 1. 5 = 00000101, flipped 11111010, plus 1 = 11111011 = -5. Do it again and you are back at 5.
 | Bits | Unsigned | Signed
 | 00000000 | 0 | 0
 | 01111111 | 127 | 127
 | 10000000 | 128 | -128
 | 11111111 | 255 | -1
Range for n bits: unsigned 0 to 2^n - 1, signed -2^(n-1) to 2^(n-1) - 1. For 16 bits that is 0-65535 or -32768 to 32767.
Why this matters for security: overflow

Add 1 to the largest value and it wraps. A signed byte at 127 plus 1 becomes -128. An unsigned byte at 255 plus 1 becomes 0. Integer overflow bugs happen when code multiplies or adds a length and the result wraps small, so a buffer is allocated too short and a copy then overruns it. Also a signed/unsigned mismatch: a length of -1 compares as "less than the max" as signed, then is treated as 4 billion once converted to unsigned. This is classic material for the binary exploitation guide.

A multi-byte value has to be laid out in memory in some byte order. Big-endian puts the most significant byte first (how network protocols do it, "network byte order"). Little-endian puts the least significant byte first (x86 and most ARM). The 32-bit value 0x0A0B0C0D in memory:
big-endian: 0A 0B 0C 0D
little-endian: 0D 0C 0B 0A
In a debugger or hex dump on x86, an address like 0x00401000 appears as 00 10 40 00. Reading it backwards is the first thing every reverse engineer learns.

$ echo -n "Hi!" | xxd
00000000: 4869 21 Hi!
Left: offset in hex. Middle: bytes in hex, pairs grouped. Right: ASCII view with . for non-printable. A file's first bytes are its magic number: 4D 5A ("MZ") is a Windows executable, 7F 45 4C 46 ("\x7fELF") is Linux, 50 4B ("PK") is a zip or Office file, 89 50 4E 47 is PNG, 25 50 44 46 ("%PDF") is a PDF. Forensics uses these to spot a renamed file.

Base64 packs 3 bytes (24 bits) into 4 characters of 6 bits each, using A-Z a-z 0-9 + /. It is an encoding for text-safe transport, not encryption. Output length is always a multiple of 4 (padding with =).
Hex encoding is 2 characters per byte, so it doubles the size.
URL encoding writes unsafe bytes as % plus hex: space is %20, < is %3C, ' is %27. You will see this in every web log attack.
IPv6 is 128 bits written as 8 groups of 4 hex digits. Leading zeros can drop and one run of zero groups can become ::, so 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001 is 2001:db8::1.
MAC addresses are 48 bits, 6 hex pairs. The first 3 bytes are the vendor (OUI).

$ echo $((2#11001010))
202
$ echo $((16#CA))
202
$ printf '%d\n' 0xCA
202
$ printf '%x\n' 202
ca
$ printf '%o\n' 202
312
$ echo "obase=2; 202" | bc
11001010
$ echo "ibase=2; 11001010" | bc
202
$ python3 -c 'print(bin(202), hex(202), oct(202))'
0b11001010 0xca 0o312
$ python3 -c 'print(int("11001010", 2), int("CA", 16))'
202 202
Careful with bc: set obase first when going out, and with ibase set, the next number you type is read in that base (so to change ibase back to 10 you must type ibase=A).
Byte tricks in Python: bytes.fromhex("48656c6c6f") gives b'Hello', "Hello".encode().hex() gives 48656c6c6f, ord("A") is 65, chr(65) is A, 0xC0A8010A & 0xFFFFFF00 is the network, x ^ 0x41 is a one-byte XOR, ~x & 0xFF is a byte NOT.

Scenario (fictional, training only): an analyst on your team left two notes. ~/notes/mask.txt has a subnet mask in binary. ~/notes/capture.hex has a short plaintext message pulled from a packet, written as hex bytes. The message ends with a code word you need.
Decode the hex into text with xxd -r -p ~/notes/capture.hex, read the message, and submit the code word it names.
Solve it in the sandbox. Type hint when stuck and submit <answer> when you have it.
