Two models for the same thing: how data gets from an app on one machine to an app on another. Know the layers, what each one carries, and which attacks and tools belong to which.
simple // the idea in plain words

The OSI model splits networking into 7 layers. Each layer only talks to the layer above and below it, and each adds its own header on the way down (encapsulation) and strips it on the way up.
 | # | Layer | Data unit | What it does | Examples
 | 7 | Application | data | what the user's program speaks | HTTP, DNS, SMTP, SSH
 | 6 | Presentation | data | encoding, compression, encryption | TLS, JPEG, ASCII
 | 5 | Session | data | start, hold and end a conversation | NetBIOS, RPC, sockets
 | 4 | Transport | segment / datagram | end-to-end delivery, ports | TCP, UDP
 | 3 | Network | packet | addressing and routing between networks | IP, ICMP, routers
 | 2 | Data link | frame | delivery on one local network, MAC addresses | Ethernet, Wi-Fi, switches, ARP
 | 1 | Physical | bits | signals on a wire or radio | cables, hubs, radio
Bottom-up mnemonic: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away. Top-down: All People Seem To Need Data Processing.
The real internet runs on TCP/IP, which has 4 layers: application (OSI 5-7), transport (4), internet (3), link (1-2). OSI is the vocabulary; TCP/IP is the reality. When someone says "layer 7 firewall" they mean the OSI numbering.

L1: cables, fiber, radio. Problems: unplugged, bad cable, interference. Attacks: wiretap, jamming.
L2: MAC addresses (48 bit, 3c:52:82:4e:19:a7), switches, VLANs, ARP. Attacks: ARP spoofing, MAC flooding, VLAN hopping, rogue access points.
L3: IP addresses and routing. Routers decide where a packet goes next. Attacks: IP spoofing, ICMP floods, route hijacking.
L4: ports and connection state. TCP is reliable and ordered; UDP is fast and unchecked. Attacks: SYN flood, port scans, session hijack.
L5-6: sessions and encryption. Attacks: session hijacking, SSL stripping, downgrade attacks.
L7: the protocol the user's app speaks. Attacks: SQL injection, XSS, DNS poisoning, phishing, malicious uploads.

A browser sends an HTTP request. TCP wraps it in a segment (adds source and destination ports, sequence numbers). IP wraps that in a packet (adds source and destination IP). Ethernet wraps that in a frame (adds source and destination MAC, plus a checksum). The wire carries bits. The receiver reverses it. Key detail: MAC addresses change at every hop, IP addresses stay the same end to end (ignoring NAT).

Hub L1, repeats everything to every port.
Switch L2, learns MACs and forwards frames only to the right port. A multilayer switch also routes.
Router L3, forwards between networks using a routing table.
Firewall L3/L4 (stateful) or L7 (application, next-gen, WAF).
Load balancer L4 or L7.
Tools that live at a layer

L1: cable tester, link lights.
L2: arp -a, ip neigh, switch CAM table.
L3: ping, traceroute / tracert, ip route, route print.
L4: ss -tuln, netstat -ano, nmap, nc.
L7: curl, dig, Wireshark display filters, browser dev tools.
$ ip a
$ ip route
$ ss -tuln
$ dig example.com
The TCP three-way handshake and teardown

SYN (client picks initial sequence number), SYN-ACK (server acknowledges and picks its own), ACK. Data is numbered per byte, ACKs confirm receipt, loss triggers retransmit. Teardown is FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK (or a hard RST). A closed port answers a SYN with RST; a filtered port (firewall drop) answers nothing, which is how scanners tell them apart.
Why the models matter for defense

Defense in depth maps to layers: port security and 802.1X (L2), ACLs and segmentation (L3), stateful firewall (L4), WAF and input validation (L7), TLS (L5-6).
Troubleshooting is bottom-up: link light, IP config, gateway ping, outside ping, DNS, then the app. Each step rules a layer in or out.
Detection cares where evidence lives: ARP anomalies in L2 captures, port scans in L4 flow data, injection in L7 web logs.

MTU is 1500 bytes on Ethernet; bigger packets get fragmented or dropped (watch for broken VPNs).
TTL counts down each hop; traceroute abuses it to map the path.
ICMP is how routers say "unreachable" or "time exceeded" (L3, carried in IP).
VLANs (802.1Q) split one switch into separate L2 networks; a router is needed to cross them.
IPv6 has no ARP (it uses Neighbor Discovery) and no broadcast.

ARP is usually filed at L2 (some say 2.5). Routers are L3, switches L2, but "Layer 3 switch" exists.
TLS spans L5-6 in OSI but is just "between TCP and HTTP" in TCP/IP.
Port numbers are L4, IP addresses L3, MAC addresses L2. Three addresses, three layers.

Open-source intelligence is collecting what is already public and turning it into something useful. It is a core recon skill for defenders and attackers, and the legal and ethical lines matter more than the tools.
simple // the idea in plain words

OSINT (open-source intelligence) means gathering information from sources anyone can legally access: websites, social media, search engines, public records, DNS, job postings, code repositories, news, satellite imagery. It is used by SOC and threat intel teams, fraud and investigations teams, journalists, penetration testers (as the first phase of an engagement) and, unfortunately, by criminals building a phishing or social engineering plan.
simple // the idea in plain words

Rules first. OSINT is only fine when (1) the information is genuinely public, (2) you have a legitimate purpose, and (3) you stay inside the law and the engagement rules. Only investigate a target you are authorized to assess (your own organization, a signed scope, a CTF or training scenario that says OSINT is the point). Never log in to, guess passwords for, or trick your way into anything. Never collect on private individuals out of curiosity, never stalk or harass, and never publish personal data you find. "It was public" does not make every use legal or ethical.
Passive vs active:
Passive: you never touch the target's systems. Search engines, archived pages, WHOIS, certificate transparency logs, social media posts. Leaves no trace on the target.
simple // the idea in plain words

Active: you interact with the target (port scans, directory brute forcing, visiting a login page). Can be logged and can be illegal without authorization.
The intelligence cycle gives OSINT structure: plan (what question, what scope), collect, process (clean and dedupe), analyze (what does it mean, how confident), report, and then refine the question.
What defenders look for about their own organization

Employee names, roles and email format (first.last@) that make phishing believable.
Exposed subdomains, forgotten test sites, open cloud storage, leaked credentials or API keys in public repos.
Job posts that reveal the tech stack ("experience with Palo Alto, Splunk, AD").
Photos that show badges, screens, whiteboards or office layout.
Lookalike domains and fake social accounts impersonating the brand.

Search operators (Google dorks): site:example.com filetype:pdf, intitle:"index of", inurl:login, quotes for exact match, - to exclude.
Domains: whois, dig, nslookup, certificate transparency search (crt.sh) for every certificate ever issued to a domain, which reveals subdomains. DNSdumpster and SecurityTrails for DNS history.
Archived pages: the Wayback Machine shows deleted pages and old staff lists.
Internet-wide search: Shodan and Censys index banners of exposed services (what is visible, without you scanning).
Email and breaches: Have I Been Pwned shows whether an address appeared in a known breach, using the check on your own or authorized addresses.
Code: public GitHub search for an organization's name plus words like password, api_key, secret.
People and social: LinkedIn, X, forums. Pivot on usernames across sites. For authorized assessments only.
Images: reverse image search (Google Lens, TinEye), EXIF metadata (camera, timestamps, sometimes GPS), shadows and landmarks for geolocation exercises.
Frameworks: Maltego (link analysis), SpiderFoot, theHarvester, Recon-ng, and the OSINT Framework web directory of sources.
$ whois example.com
$ dig example.com ANY +noall +answer
$ theHarvester -d example.com -b crtsh
$ exiftool photo.jpg

Keep notes with source, URL, date and time for every finding; pages change. Take screenshots or archive copies.
Rate reliability of the source and confidence in your conclusion. One post is a lead, not a fact.
Use a clean browser profile or VM and no personal accounts, so you don't tip off the target or leak your own identity.
Law and ethics in more detail

Authorization is the dividing line. Testing or probing systems you don't own without permission can violate computer misuse law (in the US the CFAA) even if all you did was request public URLs thousands of times.
Terms of service: scraping or creating fake accounts can break a site's rules and expose you to account bans or legal action.
Privacy law: personal data of EU residents falls under GDPR, and several US states have privacy laws. Collecting and storing personal data needs a lawful basis, minimization and secure storage. Check with legal or a supervisor before building a dossier on a person.
Pretexting and impersonation (pretending to be someone to extract information) is social engineering, not passive OSINT. It is allowed in a scoped red team exercise and nowhere else.
Minimize harm: redact personal data in reports, don't collect family members' details, stop when the question is answered, and report exposures (leaked keys, exposed databases) to the owner through proper channels instead of using them.
Doxxing, stalking and harassment are crimes in many places and end careers. A good rule: would you be comfortable explaining exactly what you did, and why, to the target and a judge?

It maps to reconnaissance (MITRE ATT&CK TA0043) and is the first stage of the cyber kill chain. Attackers use it to pick targets, craft spear phishing, find credentials and choose an entry point. Defenders reverse the view: attack surface management is continuous OSINT of your own estate, and threat intelligence is OSINT plus feeds about adversaries.

Lock down social profiles, don't post badges, screens or travel in real time.
Use role addresses on public pages (info@, security@), not named staff lists where possible.
Remove old subdomains and certificates, and set up monitoring for new certificates issued for your domain.
Add a security.txt so researchers know who to tell.
Run secret scanning on repositories and rotate any key that was ever committed, even briefly.

Corroborate with at least two independent sources; check dates, since old data gets recycled as new.
Watch for disinformation and planted breadcrumbs; a source that is too convenient may be bait.
Beware confirmation bias: look for evidence against your hypothesis too.
State your analysis in calibrated language ("likely", "almost certain") with the confidence level, and separate what you saw from what you infer.

The ports and protocols that show up in every exam, log and scan, grouped by job, with the secure replacement for each insecure one. DNS and DHCP get a closer look.
simple // the idea in plain words

A port is a number (0-65535) that picks which program on a host receives the traffic. An IP address finds the machine; the port finds the program. Well-known ports are 0-1023, registered 1024-49151, ephemeral 49152-65535 (the random source port your client uses).
 | Port | Protocol | Use | Note
 | 20/21 | FTP | file transfer | cleartext. Use SFTP or FTPS
 | 22 | SSH / SFTP / SCP | remote shell, secure copy | the secure default
 | 23 | Telnet | remote shell | cleartext, replace with SSH
 | 25 | SMTP | mail between servers | cleartext unless STARTTLS
 | 53 | DNS | names to IPs | UDP normally, TCP for big answers and zone transfers
 | 67/68 | DHCP | automatic IP config | UDP, server 67, client 68
 | 69 | TFTP | trivial file transfer | no authentication
 | 80 | HTTP | web | cleartext
 | 110 | POP3 | fetch mail | cleartext
 | 123 | NTP | time sync | UDP
 | 143 | IMAP | mail sync | cleartext
simple // the idea in plain words

| 161/162 | SNMP | device monitoring | v1/v2c cleartext, use v3
 | 389 | LDAP | directory lookups | cleartext
 | 443 | HTTPS | web over TLS | the secure default
 | 445 | SMB | Windows file shares | never expose to the internet
 | 465/587 | SMTPS / submission | send mail securely | clients submit on 587
 | 514 | Syslog | log forwarding | UDP, no delivery guarantee
 | 636 | LDAPS | LDAP over TLS | secure
 | 993/995 | IMAPS / POP3S | mail over TLS | secure
 | 1433 | MS SQL | database | 
 | 3306 | MySQL | database | 
 | 3389 | RDP | Windows remote desktop | frequent ransomware entry point
 | 5432 | PostgreSQL | database | 
Pattern: the secure version is usually the same protocol wrapped in TLS on a different port (HTTP 80 to HTTPS 443, LDAP 389 to LDAPS 636, IMAP 143 to IMAPS 993).

TCP: connection first (handshake), ordered, retransmits loss, slower. Web, mail, SSH, databases.
UDP: no connection, no guarantee, low overhead. DNS queries, DHCP, NTP, VoIP, streaming, syslog.

You type example.com; your stub resolver asks a recursive resolver (ISP, 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8, or the corporate DNS server), which walks the tree: root servers, then .com servers, then the domain's authoritative server, and caches the answer for the record's TTL.
Record types:
A name to IPv4, AAAA name to IPv6
CNAME alias to another name
MX mail servers (with priority)
NS authoritative servers for the zone
TXT free text, used for SPF, DKIM, DMARC and domain verification
PTR reverse lookup, IP to name
SOA zone metadata, SRV service locations (AD uses these heavily)
$ dig example.com A
$ dig example.com MX +short
$ dig -x 8.8.8.8
$ nslookup example.com

The DORA exchange, all broadcast at first: Discover (client shouts), Offer (server proposes an address), Request (client accepts), Acknowledge (server confirms the lease). The lease also carries the subnet mask, default gateway, DNS servers and lease time. Renewal starts at 50% of the lease. Servers can hand out reservations (same IP for a given MAC) so servers and printers stay put.
APIPA: no DHCP answer means a Windows host self-assigns 169.254.x.x. Seeing this means DHCP is unreachable.
DHCP relay (IP helper) forwards broadcasts across routers so one server can serve many VLANs.

ARP: IP to MAC on a local network (L2/3). ICMP: ping and error messages. NAT/PAT: rewrite private addresses to a public one.
Kerberos 88 and LDAP 389: Active Directory authentication and lookups. RADIUS 1812: network login (Wi-Fi, VPN). TACACS+ 49: admin login to network gear.
IPsec (IKE 500/4500) and OpenVPN (1194) and WireGuard (51820): VPNs.

Cache poisoning: an attacker gets a resolver to store a forged answer. Defenses: random source ports and query IDs, DNSSEC (signed records).
Zone transfer (AXFR): copies a whole zone. Should be limited to secondary servers; an open AXFR hands an attacker the entire host list.
DNS tunneling: data smuggled in long subdomain names or TXT answers. Look for very long or high-entropy query names and one host sending huge volumes of queries.
DNS hijacking: changing a domain's registrar records or a router's DNS setting. Defenses: registrar lock, MFA, monitor records.
Typosquatting and lookalike domains: paypa1.com. Defense: user training, email filtering, DNS filtering.
DNS over HTTPS/TLS (DoH, DoT) hides queries from the local network, which protects privacy but also blinds a corporate DNS filter.

Rogue DHCP server hands out a malicious gateway or DNS. Defense: DHCP snooping on the switch (only trusted ports may answer).
DHCP starvation: flood Discovers to exhaust the pool. Defense: port security, rate limits.
Reading logs: a lease log ties an IP and time to a MAC, which is often the only way to map an alert's IP to a real device.

$ ss -tulnp # Linux: listening TCP/UDP with process
$ netstat -ano # Windows: all connections with PID
$ nmap -sV -p- 10.0.0.5
Anything listening that you can't explain is a finding. States to know: LISTEN, ESTABLISHED, TIME_WAIT, SYN_SENT (many in a row means outbound scanning or a blocked destination), SYN_RECV (many means a SYN flood).

open: service answered. closed: host answered with RST, nothing listening. filtered: no answer, a firewall is dropping.
The most common internet-facing risks: 3389 RDP, 445 SMB, 23 Telnet, 21 FTP, 1433/3306 databases, 161 SNMP with the default public community.

Nearly every web app keeps its data in a relational database. Learn tables, keys, joins, indexes and transactions, how the app talks to the database, and how to keep that conversation safe.
simple // the idea in plain words

A relational database stores data in tables. A table is like a spreadsheet: each row is one record (one customer, one order) and each column is one field (name, email, total). Software that manages them is a DBMS: PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle, SQLite.
Two kinds of keys tie the tables together:
Primary key: a column that uniquely identifies each row (customers.id).
Foreign key: a column that points at another table's primary key (orders.customer_id points at customers.id). That is how "this order belongs to that customer" is stored once, instead of copying the customer's details into every order.
customers orders
id | name | email id | customer_id | total
1 | alice | a@x.example 5001 | 1 | 40
2 | bob | b@x.example 5002 | 2 | 15
You talk to the database in SQL. The four basic moves are CRUD:
 | Action | SQL
 | Create | INSERT INTO customers (name) VALUES ('carol');
simple // the idea in plain words
How the web app uses it

The app server holds a connection to the database (usually pooled) and sends it SQL on behalf of each request: login looks up a user, a cart page reads cart rows, checkout inserts an order. The database is almost never exposed to the internet; only the app server can reach it, on a private network and a specific port (3306 MySQL, 5432 PostgreSQL, 1433 SQL Server, 1521 Oracle, 27017 MongoDB).
The app connects as a database user. That user should have only the rights it needs (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE on its own tables), never DROP, never admin. If an attacker finds a flaw in the app, the damage is capped by what that account can do.

A join combines rows from two tables on matching keys.
 | Join | Returns
 | INNER JOIN | rows with a match in both tables
 | LEFT JOIN | every row from the left table, with NULLs where nothing matches
 | RIGHT JOIN / FULL JOIN | the mirror image / both sides
SELECT c.name, o.id, o.total
FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.total > 20;
A LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL finds orphans: rows with no partner, a quick data-integrity check.

COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX with GROUP BY to summarize, HAVING to filter groups, ORDER BY ... DESC and LIMIT to rank. Example: SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 5;

Index: a side structure (usually a B-tree) that makes lookups on a column fast, like a book index. Costs space and slows writes. Primary keys are indexed automatically; index columns you search and join on. EXPLAIN shows whether a query used one. (See Big-O for why.)
Normalization: store each fact once. Split repeated data into its own table and link by key. Fewer update mistakes, more joins.
Transaction: a group of statements that succeed or fail together (BEGIN; ...; COMMIT; or ROLLBACK;). Moving money is two updates that must both happen.
ACID: Atomic (all or nothing), Consistent (rules always hold), Isolated (concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-done work), Durable (committed means saved even after a crash).
Constraints enforce the rules in the database itself: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK.

Relational: fixed schema, joins, strong consistency. NoSQL (MongoDB documents, Redis key-value, Cassandra wide-column, Neo4j graph): flexible shape or extreme scale, fewer guarantees. Both can be misconfigured and injected; MongoDB databases left open with no password are a repeat headline.

Parameterized queries (prepared statements) keep SQL code and user data apart. The query text is fixed with placeholders (WHERE email = ?), the values travel separately, so input can never become commands. This is *the* defense against SQL injection; escaping strings by hand and blocklisting characters are not.
Least privilege per application and per role; separate read-only accounts for reporting. No shared admin account in app configs.
Network: private subnet, firewall to the app server only, no public listener. Check with nmap from outside, and look for default ports in Shodan results for your own range.
Authentication: no default or empty passwords, secrets in a vault not in the repo, rotate. Enforce TLS between app and database.
Passwords in the table: never plaintext. Store a slow salted hash (argon2id, bcrypt, scrypt). See CIA and crypto.

Encryption at rest (disk or column level) and in backups. Sensitive fields (card numbers, ids) should be minimized or tokenized.
Auditing and monitoring: enable query/audit logs, alert on mass SELECT, schema changes, new admin users, and logins from odd hosts. Slow-query logs double as an anomaly signal.
Backups: 3-2-1, tested restores, and protected from the app account so ransomware can't delete them.
Data minimization and retention: data you don't keep can't leak. Delete test data copied from production.

sqlite> .tables
sqlite> .schema orders
mysql> SHOW TABLES; DESCRIBE orders;
psql> \dt \d orders
Look for: columns holding credentials or tokens, tables with personal data, missing foreign keys, nullable columns that shouldn't be, and who has which rights (SHOW GRANTS;).

Databases keep evidence: login tables, audit tables, transaction logs, binlog/WAL. Rows deleted by an attacker may still be in logs or backups. Capture before you repair, and note timestamps and the DB timezone.

Scenario (fictional, training only): the Shopwell test database shop.db has customers and orders. After a cleanup script ran, QA suspects some orders now point at customers that no longer exist (orphans), which breaks the "my orders" page.
Open it with sqlite3 shop.db ".schema" and look at the keys. Then find the order id whose customer_id has no matching row in customers. Submit that number, e.g. submit 5000.
Solve it in the sandbox. Type hint when stuck and submit <answer> when you have it.

The common web vulnerability classes at concept level: what each one is, why it happens, how defenders spot it, and the fix. Studied for defense and for practice on systems you are authorized to test.
simple // the idea in plain words

Rules first. Everything here is for understanding, defending and practicing on systems you own, a signed scope, or intentionally vulnerable training apps (OWASP Juice Shop, DVWA, WebGoat, PortSwigger Web Security Academy, TryHackMe rooms). Testing a real site without permission is illegal in most places (in the US, the CFAA), even if you "only looked". Labs on this site use fictional data and simulated systems.
Almost every web vulnerability comes from one mistake: the application trusts input or a request it should have checked. The OWASP Top 10 is the standard ranked list of the most common classes. The ones to know:
 | Class | One-line idea | Core fix
 | Broken access control (incl. IDOR) | you can reach things that aren't yours by changing an id or URL | server checks ownership/role on every request
simple // the idea in plain words

| Injection (SQL, OS command, LDAP) | input is treated as code by an interpreter | parameterized queries, no shell-outs, input validation
 | XSS (cross-site scripting) | input ends up in a page as script that runs in other users' browsers | output encoding, CSP, HttpOnly cookies
 | CSRF (cross-site request forgery) | another site makes your logged-in browser send a request | anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies
 | Broken authentication / sessions | weak passwords, no lockout, guessable or stolen sessions | MFA, rate limits, good session handling
 | Security misconfiguration | defaults, debug pages, open storage, verbose errors | hardening baselines, remove what you don't use
 | Vulnerable and outdated components | a library or CMS with a known CVE | inventory, patching, dependency scanning
simple // the idea in plain words

| SSRF (server-side request forgery) | you make the *server* fetch a URL it shouldn't (internal services, cloud metadata) | allow-list destinations, block internal ranges
 | Cryptographic failures | plaintext transport/storage, weak hashing | TLS everywhere, strong password hashing
 | Logging and monitoring failures | nobody noticed | log security events, alert, practice response
Ground rule that fixes a large share of these: validate on the server, authorize on the server, encode on output, and keep secrets out of the client. See how web apps work.
Injection (SQL injection as the model case)

Vulnerable code builds a query by gluing text together:
query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "' AND pass = '" + pw + "'"
If name contains SQL syntax (a quote and a comment marker, the classic textbook example), the input changes the *structure* of the query, for example turning the password check into a condition that is always true. The result is login bypass, data theft, or modification. Secure version:
cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ? AND pass_hash = ?", (name, hash))
Placeholders send the query and values separately, so the database never parses the input as SQL. Same idea for OS command injection (don't build shell strings from input; call APIs with argument lists) and NoSQL/LDAP injection. Detection: errors containing SQL fragments, requests with quotes, UNION, --, SLEEP( in parameters, and responses far larger than normal.

The app echoes user input into a page without encoding. Reflected (in a link or search box), stored (saved, e.g. a comment, hits everyone who views it), DOM-based (client-side JS writes unsafe data into the page). Impact: script runs as the victim on your site, so it can read page data, act as them, or steal a session cookie that isn't HttpOnly. Fixes: contextual output encoding (HTML, attribute, JS, URL), frameworks that auto-escape (React, templates), Content-Security-Policy, sanitizing rich text with a vetted library.

Your browser attaches your cookies to any request to the site, including ones triggered by a hostile page. Example: a hidden form that posts "change email" to your bank while you're logged in. Fixes: a per-session anti-CSRF token the attacker can't know, SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies, checking Origin/Referer, requiring re-auth for sensitive actions, and never changing state with GET.

Changing /orders/1002 or ?user_id=7 returns someone else's data because the server only checks "logged in". Also: forced browsing to /admin, privilege flags the client can set, missing function-level checks, directory listing. Fix: deny by default, one central authorization layer, check ownership on every object. See APIs, REST and JSON.

A feature that fetches a URL for you (image import, webhook, PDF render) can be pointed at http://localhost, internal admin panels, or the cloud metadata service (169.254.169.254), which can hand out credentials. Fixes: allow-list hosts, resolve and block private/loopback/link-local addresses, enforce IMDSv2 on cloud hosts, egress filtering.

Unrestricted upload: a server-side script uploaded as an "image" and then executed. Check type by content, rename files, store outside the web root, serve from a separate domain, never execute uploads.
Insecure deserialization: untrusted serialized objects rebuilt by the server can run code. Don't deserialize untrusted data; use plain JSON with validation.
Open redirect: ?next= sends users anywhere, which makes phishing links look legitimate. Allow-list redirect targets.

| Control | Stops | Limit
 | Parameterized queries, ORM used correctly | SQL injection | raw-SQL escapes in the ORM still bite
 | Output encoding + CSP | XSS | CSP needs tuning, encoding must match context
 | Authz middleware, deny by default | broken access control | logic flaws need tests
 | SameSite + CSRF tokens | CSRF | token must be validated, not just present
 | WAF | known patterns, virtual patch while you fix | bypassable, noisy, not a fix
 | Rate limits, lockout, MFA | brute force, credential stuffing | needs monitoring
 | SAST / DAST / dependency scan in CI | many bugs before release | false positives, blind to logic
 | Pen test / bug bounty | what automation misses | point in time

Threat model a feature before building it (what can go wrong, who attacks it). Use framework defaults instead of rolling your own auth or crypto. Code review for authorization checks. Keep dependencies and base images updated. Write abuse-case tests (user A requests user B's object) next to your normal tests. Treat the OWASP Cheat Sheet Series and ASVS as your checklist.

Web access logs (combined format) and WAF logs are the sensor. Hunting patterns:
Many 404s for odd paths from one IP: scanning (/.env, /wp-admin, /phpmyadmin).
Requests with ', %27, UNION, SELECT, <script, ../, ${jndi: in parameters: probing for injection, XSS, traversal.
A run of 500s on one parameter, then a 200 with a huge bytes value: an injection that worked.
Sequential id access with many 200s from one account: IDOR sweep.
Same account from several countries or user agents in a short time: session theft.
Map findings to MITRE ATT&CK (T1190 exploit public-facing application) and escalate per your IR process (incident response, log analysis, Security Onion / SIEM).

Run an intentionally vulnerable app in your own lab (Docker on the homelab, isolated from your real network). Walk the OWASP list: find one instance, explain why it happens, write the fix, and write the detection (a Sigma or WAF rule). That loop (break, fix, detect) is what interviewers want to hear. For bounty programs, read the scope and rules of engagement first and stay inside them.

Scenario (fictional, training only): your SOC watches the web server of Shopwell, a made-up store. The WAF flagged a burst of strange requests overnight. ~/web/access.log is the combined-format access log (fictional addresses from documentation ranges).
One IP sent SQL injection-style input (quotes and UNION SELECT in the id parameter) and then got a 200 response with an unusually large size, which suggests it worked. Find that IP. Submit the IP address.
Solve it in the sandbox. Type hint when stuck and submit <answer> when you have it.

How software teams decide what to build and how they work: requirements, user stories, Scrum and Kanban, estimation, code review and technical debt.
CS240: software engineering · course page with quizzes and exam
simple // the idea in plain words

Writing code is the easy part. The hard parts are knowing what to build and keeping a team working in step. A software development life cycle (SDLC) is the sequence of activities: requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, maintenance.
Two ways to run it:
Waterfall: finish each phase completely before the next. Good when requirements are fixed and mistakes are expensive to fix later (medical devices, avionics). Poor when the customer learns what they want only by seeing the software.
Agile: work in short cycles, show working software often, change direction when you learn something. Most modern teams are some flavor of agile.
simple // the idea in plain words

The Agile Manifesto values: individuals and interactions over process, working software over documentation, customer collaboration over contracts, responding to change over following a plan. The right-hand things still matter, the left-hand things matter more.
Vocabulary you will hear every day:
User story: a small piece of value from a user's view: "As a student, I want to reset my password so that I can log in when I forget it."
Backlog: the ordered to-do list of stories.
Sprint: a fixed time box (1-4 weeks) in which the team finishes a chosen set of stories.
Stand-up: a 15-minute daily sync: what I did, what I will do, what blocks me.
Definition of done: the shared checklist a story must meet (code reviewed, tests pass, deployed, documented).

Functional: what the system does ("a user can reset a password by email").
Non-functional (quality attributes): how well it does it: performance, security, availability, usability, maintainability. These drive architecture and are forgotten most often.
Acceptance criteria make a story testable. Given/When/Then style: *Given* a registered user, *When* they request a reset, *Then* an email with a single-use link valid for 30 minutes is sent.
Good requirements are specific, testable and traceable. "The page should be fast" is not; "95% of requests complete in under 300 ms" is.
Use cases, prototypes and talking to real users find requirements that nobody wrote down.

Roles: product owner (decides priority and value), scrum master (removes obstacles, coaches the process), developers. Events: sprint planning, daily stand-up, sprint review (demo to stakeholders), retrospective (what do we improve?). Artifacts: product backlog, sprint backlog, the increment. Scrum is a framework, not a bag of ceremonies: the point is the feedback loops.

Visualize work as cards on a board (To do, Doing, Review, Done), and set WIP (work in progress) limits per column so the team finishes things before starting new ones. Measure cycle time. Fits support and operations work where tasks arrive continuously. Many teams mix: "scrumban".

Teams use story points (relative size; Fibonacci 1, 2, 3, 5, 8) or t-shirt sizes, discuss differences in planning poker, then track velocity (points finished per sprint) to forecast. Estimates are about uncertainty, not promises. Break big stories down; if it cannot be estimated, run a time-boxed spike to learn first.

A second pair of eyes on every change. Review for correctness, tests, readability, security (input validation, auth checks, secrets), and design. Keep PRs small (under about 400 lines). Be kind and specific: comment on the code, not the person; separate "must fix" from "nit". Reviews spread knowledge and are one of the cheapest defect-finding methods known.

Shortcuts that make the next change slower, like a loan: sometimes worth taking, but it accrues interest. Track it visibly, pay it down continuously (the "boy scout rule": leave the code a little cleaner), and tie big payoffs to risk or delivery speed when arguing for time. Dead code, no tests, out-of-date dependencies and missing documentation all count.
Estimating honestly and planning with uncertainty

The cone of uncertainty: early estimates can be off by a factor of 4 either way. Reduce risk by building the scariest part first, using ranges ("3 to 6 weeks"), and re-forecasting from real throughput rather than guesses. Beware Brooks' law: adding people to a late project makes it later, because onboarding and communication grow faster than output. Hofstadter's law: it always takes longer than you expect, even when you account for that.
Working agreements that keep teams fast

Small batch sizes, thin vertical slices (UI to database) that can be released, not horizontal layers.
Trunk-based development and CI so integration is never a big-bang event (CI/CD chapter).
Pairing and mob programming for hard or risky work and onboarding.
Blameless postmortems: after an outage ask how the system allowed the failure, not who to blame. Write down timeline, impact, causes, and tracked actions.
Architecture decision records (ADRs): short documents capturing a decision, its context and trade-offs, so the reasoning survives staff turnover.
Write documentation where people look: README with how to run/test, runbooks for on-call, API specs (OpenAPI).

Add abuse cases and threat modeling (STRIDE) to design discussions: for each feature, how could someone misuse it?
Security acceptance criteria in stories ("password reset tokens are single-use").
Include security in the definition of done: dependency scan clean, no secrets, review by someone who knows the area.
A security champion inside each team connects developers with the security group.
See the secure SDLC chapter.

Velocity, burn-down charts and lines of code are easy to game and bad as targets (Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target it stops being a good measure). Prefer outcome measures: lead time, change failure rate, customer satisfaction, incidents.
Team and career skills this builds

Writing clear tickets and PR descriptions, estimating, breaking down ambiguous work, saying "I don't know yet, here is how I will find out", and communicating risk early. Interviewers ask behavioral questions about these; prepare a short story for a disagreement in code review, a deadline slip and a bug you introduced.

Waterfall versus agile: when would you choose each?
Write a user story and acceptance criteria for "forgot password".
What does a good PR look like? What do you look for as a reviewer?
Scrum versus Kanban in one minute.

How to prove what an algorithm costs and that it is correct: asymptotic notation, recurrences and the master theorem, amortized analysis, loop invariants, and NP-hardness at a glance.
CS201: data structures and algorithms in depth · course page with quizzes and exam
simple // the idea in plain words

Algorithm analysis answers two questions: is it correct and how does the work grow as the input grows. You do not time it on your laptop; you count steps as a function of input size *n*, so the answer holds on any machine.
The notations:
O(f): grows no faster than f (an upper bound). "Linear search is O(n)."
Ω(f): grows at least as fast as f (a lower bound). "Comparison sorting is Ω(n log n)."
Θ(f): both, a tight bound. "Merge sort is Θ(n log n)."
Constants and lower-order terms drop out: 3n² + 10n + 7 is Θ(n²).
Common growth rates from best to worst: 1, log n, √n, n, n log n, n², n³, 2ⁿ, n!. See ~/bigo for a visual of how fast they explode.
Count loops:
One loop over n items: O(n).
Loop inside a loop over the same n: O(n²).
A loop that halves (or doubles) its counter: O(log n).
Recursion that splits the problem in half and does linear work per level: O(n log n).
Always say which case you mean: best, average or worst. Quicksort is O(n log n) on average and O(n²) in the worst case. Also state space used, not only time.

f(n) is O(g(n)) if there exist constants c > 0 and n₀ such that f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀. To show 3n² + 10n + 7 is O(n²): for n ≥ 1, 10n ≤ 10n² and 7 ≤ 7n², so f(n) ≤ 20n². Pick c = 20 and n₀ = 1. Done.
Other useful facts: log_a n and log_b n differ only by a constant, so O(log n) needs no base. Polynomials of higher degree dominate. Exponentials beat any polynomial. n! beats 2ⁿ.

for i in range(n): # n times
 for j in range(i): # 0, 1, ... n-1 times
 work() # total n(n-1)/2 = Θ(n²)
i = 1
while i < n: # runs log₂ n times
 i *= 2
Nested loops are not always n²: if the inner loop runs i times the sum is 0+1+...+(n−1). If the inner loop is O(log n) the total is n log n.

Divide-and-conquer algorithms have running times like T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n): a subproblems each of size n/b, plus f(n) work to split and combine.
Merge sort: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n → Θ(n log n).
Binary search: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 → Θ(log n).
Naive Fibonacci: T(n) = T(n−1) + T(n−2) → Θ(φⁿ), exponential.
Master theorem (compare f(n) with n^(log_b a)):
If f(n) is polynomially smaller: T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a)). Example: T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n² → Θ(n³).
If f(n) is about equal: T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) · log n). Example: merge sort.
If f(n) is polynomially larger (and regular): T(n) = Θ(f(n)). Example: T(n) = T(n/2) + n → Θ(n).
You can always fall back on a recursion tree: draw the levels, add up the work per level, multiply by the number of levels.

Some operations are usually cheap but occasionally expensive. Amortized cost averages over a worst-case *sequence*, no probability involved. A dynamic array that doubles when full: pushes cost 1, except the push that copies n items. Total for n pushes ≤ 3n, so each push is amortized O(1). Methods: aggregate (total ÷ n), accounting (charge each cheap op extra "credit" to pay for the rare expensive one) and potential function.

To prove an iterative algorithm correct show three things about a property that holds at the top of every iteration:
Initialization: true before the first iteration.
Maintenance: if true before an iteration, still true after.
Termination: when the loop stops, the invariant gives the answer you wanted.
For recursion use induction: prove the base case, assume the recursive calls on smaller inputs are correct, prove the whole call is.

Guess T(n) ≤ c·n·log n for T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n. Assume it holds for n/2: T(n) ≤ 2·c(n/2)log(n/2) + n = c·n·log n − c·n + n ≤ c·n·log n whenever c ≥ 1. Fix the base case with a suitable n₀. The guess is proven; never "prove" by only checking small inputs.

Comparison sorting: Ω(n log n) from the decision-tree argument (n! leaves need height log₂(n!)).
Searching an unsorted list: Ω(n); you may have to look at every item.
Adversary arguments: pretend an adversary answers every query so as to force the most work.
Matching an upper bound and a lower bound proves an algorithm optimal for that model.
P, NP and NP-complete in practice

P: solvable in polynomial time (sorting, shortest path, MST).
NP: a proposed answer can be checked in polynomial time (a sudoku solution, a satisfying assignment, a Hamiltonian path).
NP-complete: the hardest problems in NP; if any one has a fast algorithm, all do. SAT, 3-coloring, subset sum, traveling salesman (decision form), clique, vertex cover. Knowing a problem is NP-complete tells you to stop looking for an exact fast algorithm and use heuristics, approximations, small-input DP or SAT solvers.
Proving a new problem NP-hard: reduce a known NP-hard problem to it in polynomial time.
P vs NP is unsolved. Modern cryptography assumes certain problems (factoring, discrete log) are hard on average, which is not the same as NP-complete.

Randomized algorithms: expected time (randomized quicksort is O(n log n) expected for every input) vs always-correct Las Vegas vs sometimes-wrong Monte Carlo (Miller-Rabin primality test).
Smoothed and average-case analysis: why simplex and quicksort work well in practice.
Cache and I/O models: an O(n) pass over an array beats an O(n) pointer chase by 10× or more because of memory locality. Constants matter once complexity ties.
Space-time trade-offs: hash tables, memoization and lookup tables trade memory for speed.

ReDoS (regular expressions with exponential backtracking), hash flooding, quicksort with a predictable pivot, zip bombs and XML entity expansion all abuse the *gap between average and worst case*. When you review code that handles untrusted input, ask what the worst-case input costs, not the typical one.

State the time and space complexity of every solution you give, unprompted, with the case you mean.
Solve T(n) = 3T(n/3) + n² with the master theorem. (n² dominates: Θ(n²).)
Why is building a heap O(n) and not O(n log n)? (Most nodes are near the bottom and sift down only a few levels.)
Amortized vs average: what is the difference? (Amortized is a guarantee over any sequence; average assumes a distribution.)

How real systems are structured (layers, monolith vs microservices, APIs, queues, caches), and how to build security into every phase of the software life cycle.
CS240: software engineering · course page with quizzes and exam
simple // the idea in plain words

Software architecture is the big-picture structure: the major parts, what each is responsible for, and how they talk. Decisions here are the expensive ones to change later.
The most common starting point is layers: a presentation layer (UI or API), a business logic layer (the rules), and a data layer (database). Each layer talks only to the one below it, which keeps responsibilities separate and testable.
Two overall shapes:
Monolith: the whole application is one deployable program. Simple to build, test and run; one deploy; function calls between parts. It is the right default for small teams.
simple // the idea in plain words

Microservices: many small independently deployable services, each owning its data and talking over the network (HTTP/REST, gRPC, message queues). Teams can ship independently and scale parts separately, but you pay with distributed-systems problems: network failures, versioned APIs, tracing across services and operational overhead.
Start with a well-structured monolith and split a service out only when there is a clear reason.
Building blocks you will meet: a load balancer spreading traffic over servers, a cache (Redis) for fast repeated reads, a database (relational or NoSQL), a message queue (RabbitMQ, SQS, Kafka) for work done later, a CDN for static files, and monitoring to see all of it.

Ask which of these matter most: performance, scalability, availability, security, maintainability, cost. They conflict: caching speeds reads but risks stale data; more replicas add availability but make consistency harder.

Services meet at an interface. Design it for the callers: stable resource names, versioning (/v1/), consistent errors and status codes, pagination, idempotency keys for payments, rate limits, and authentication on every call. Document with OpenAPI and test the contract. See REST and Spring Boot and APIs and JSON.

Vertical: a bigger machine. Easy, hits a ceiling.
Horizontal: more machines behind a load balancer. Needs stateless servers (no session kept in memory; store it in the database or a shared cache) so any server can handle any request.
Databases scale with read replicas, caching, sharding (split rows across servers) and indexes.
Queues smooth spikes: the web request enqueues a job and returns; workers process at their own pace.

Timeouts on every network call, retries with exponential backoff and jitter (only for idempotent operations), circuit breakers (stop calling a failing dependency), bulkheads (isolate resources), graceful degradation, health checks, and redundancy across zones. Assume everything fails; design for it.

A single relational database gives you ACID transactions. Across services you usually get eventual consistency: updates propagate with a delay. The CAP theorem says that during a network partition a distributed store must choose between consistency and availability. Patterns: sagas (a sequence of local transactions with compensating undo steps), the outbox pattern, and idempotent consumers.

Security belongs in every phase, not just at the end:
Requirements: security and privacy requirements, compliance (PCI, HIPAA, GDPR).
Design: threat modeling (STRIDE: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege), secure design principles.
Implementation: secure coding standards, code review, SAST, secret management.
Testing: unit tests for abuse cases, fuzzing, DAST, dependency scanning, penetration test.
Deployment: hardened configs, least-privilege identities, logging and alerting turned on.
Maintenance: patch management, vulnerability disclosure policy, incident response, end-of-life plans.
Frameworks: OWASP SAMM, BSIMM, NIST SSDF (SP 800-218), Microsoft SDL.

Know these cold (also Security+ material): least privilege, defense in depth, fail securely (deny by default, do not leak details in errors), separation of duties, complete mediation (check authorization on every access), economy of mechanism (keep it simple), open design (security does not depend on secrecy of the design), psychological acceptability (secure paths must be usable), and secure defaults.

Draw a data flow diagram: external entities, processes, data stores, data flows, and trust boundaries (where privilege or ownership changes). For each element and each boundary crossing, walk through STRIDE and list threats, then rate (DREAD or a simple likelihood × impact), choose mitigations (validation, authentication, encryption, rate limiting, logging) and write tests for them. Example: login form → API → user database. Spoofing: credential stuffing → rate limiting, MFA. Tampering: modified JWT → verify signature, pin algorithm. Information disclosure: verbose errors → generic message plus server log. Do this in design review, when changes are cheap.

Missing authorization on internal endpoints ("it is only called from the front end"), trusting the client, one shared database credential with full rights, secrets in config files in the repository, flat networks where one compromised service reaches everything, no audit logging, unauthenticated admin panels, sensitive data stored forever. Zero trust answers with: authenticate and authorize every request, between services too, using short-lived identity (mutual TLS, workload identity).

Three signals: logs (events), metrics (numbers over time) and traces (one request's path through many services). Add correlation IDs and structured JSON logs. Define SLIs/SLOs (service level indicators and objectives, such as 99.9% of requests under 300 ms) and alert on symptoms users feel. Security needs the same data: audit logs feed the SIEM and incident response.
The C4 model gives four zoom levels: system context, containers, components, code. Pair diagrams with ADRs (agile chapter) so people know both the structure and why. Keep them in the repository.

Refactor toward a design instead of rewriting: the strangler fig pattern routes traffic to new components one slice at a time while the old system shrinks. Modularize the monolith (clear module boundaries, no cross-module database reads) so a later split is possible. Rewrites usually take longer than planned and lose hard-won behavior.

Monolith or microservices for a three-person team? Defend your answer.

Git workflows, continuous integration and delivery, a real GitHub Actions pipeline, deployment strategies, and securing the pipeline itself.
CS240: software engineering · course page with quizzes and exam
simple // the idea in plain words

CI/CD is the habit of automatically building and testing every change, then shipping it with a button (or no button at all).
Continuous integration (CI): every push triggers a build and the test suite on a clean machine. Broken code is caught in minutes while the change is still fresh.
Continuous delivery: every passing change is automatically packaged and ready to release at any moment; a human approves the release.
Continuous deployment: every passing change goes straight to production with no human step.
The pipeline is a series of stages, and a failure stops everything after it:
commit → build → unit tests → security scan → package → deploy to staging → integration tests → deploy to production
Why bother: small frequent releases are safer than rare giant ones, humans stop doing repetitive manual deploys, and the pipeline is a written, repeatable record of how software gets built.
Everything starts with git. The basic team routine: create a branch, commit, push, open a pull request (PR), get a code review, wait for CI to go green, merge. Protected branches stop anyone from pushing straight to main. See the git guide.
$ git log --oneline

GitHub flow: short-lived feature branches off main, merged by PR. Simple, fits continuous delivery.
Trunk-based development: everyone merges to main at least daily, unfinished work hidden behind feature flags. Best for CI.
Git flow: long-lived develop, release and hotfix branches. Heavy; suits versioned products shipped on a schedule.
Merge strategies: merge commit (keeps history), squash (one clean commit per PR), rebase (linear history). Never rewrite history others already pulled.

name: ci
on:
 pull_request:
 push:
 branches: [main]
jobs:
 test:
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest
 steps:
 - uses: actions/checkout@v4
 - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
 with: { python-version: "3.12" }
 - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
 - run: pytest --maxfail=1
 scan:
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest
 steps:
 - uses: actions/checkout@v4
 - run: pip install bandit && bandit -r src
 deploy:
 needs: [test, scan] # only after both pass
 if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest
 steps:
 - uses: actions/checkout@v4
 - run: ./deploy.sh
 env:
 TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}
Concepts: a workflow is triggered by events; it has jobs that run on runners; jobs have steps; needs: orders jobs; secrets are injected, never written in the file; caching dependencies and matrix builds (several Python versions) speed things up. Other tools use the same ideas: GitLab CI, Jenkins, CircleCI, Azure DevOps.

Build once, promote the same artifact (a container image or package) through dev, staging and production, so what you tested is what ships. Configuration comes from environment variables, not baked into the artifact. Infrastructure as code (Terraform, CloudFormation) makes environments reproducible.

Rolling: replace instances a few at a time.
Blue/green: run the new version beside the old and flip traffic over; instant rollback by flipping back.
Canary: send 1-5% of traffic to the new version, watch error rate and latency, then widen.
Feature flags: ship code dark, turn it on per user or percentage; separates deploy from release.
Always have a rollback plan and watch metrics after a deploy (error rate, latency, saturation).

A Dockerfile describes an image (base OS, dependencies, your code). CI builds the image, scans it, pushes it to a registry, and the platform (Kubernetes, ECS, Cloud Run) runs it. Pin base image versions, use small images, and do not run as root.

Shift security checks left, to where fixing is cheap:
Secret scanning (gitleaks, GitHub push protection): block committed keys.
SAST (CodeQL, Semgrep): static analysis of source on every PR.
SCA / dependency scanning (Dependabot, Renovate, npm audit, OSV): known-vulnerable libraries, plus an SBOM (CycloneDX, SPDX) listing every component.
Container and IaC scanning (Trivy, Checkov): vulnerable images, open S3 buckets, 0.0.0.0/0 security groups.
DAST (OWASP ZAP) against a running staging copy.
Policy as code (OPA) to enforce rules automatically; signed artifacts (Sigstore cosign) and provenance (SLSA levels) so production only runs what your pipeline built.
The pipeline is an attack target

It holds credentials and can deploy to production, so it is a high-value prize.
Pin actions to a commit SHA, not a floating tag. The 2025 compromise of a popular GitHub Action leaked secrets from thousands of repos.
Least privilege tokens: set permissions: to read-only by default; use short-lived OIDC tokens to the cloud instead of long-lived keys.
Treat PRs from forks as untrusted: pull_request_target with a checkout of untrusted code is a known path to secret theft.
Script injection: run: echo ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }} lets a PR title run shell commands; pass values through env vars.
Protect branches (required reviews, required status checks, signed commits), separate build and deploy credentials, and log who deployed what.
Supply chain: typosquatted packages, dependency confusion, compromised maintainers (event-stream, xz). Use lockfiles, hash pinning, private registries and review dependency bumps.

Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service. Elite teams deploy many times per day with low failure rates; speed and stability improve together. Optimize the pipeline's feedback time first: if CI takes 40 minutes, people stop running it.

Use versioned migrations (Flyway, Alembic, Rails migrations). Make changes backward compatible in steps (expand/contract): add the new column, deploy code that writes both, backfill, switch reads, then drop the old column. Never ship a code change and an incompatible schema change in one step.

Solve problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems and remembering the answers: memoization, tabulation, the classic DP problems, plus greedy algorithms and backtracking.
CS201: data structures and algorithms in depth · course page with quizzes and exam
simple // the idea in plain words

Dynamic programming (DP) is a trick for problems where the same smaller question gets asked again and again. Instead of recomputing, you store each answer the first time and reuse it.
The standard example is Fibonacci. The naive recursion fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) recomputes fib(3) thousands of times and takes exponential time (about 1.6ⁿ steps). Remember each result and it drops to n steps.
from functools import lru_cache
@lru_cache(None)
def fib(n):
 return n if n < 2 else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
DP works when two things are true:
Overlapping subproblems: the same sub-question repeats.
Optimal substructure: the best answer to the big problem is built from best answers to smaller ones.
Two styles:
Top-down (memoization): write the recursion, cache the results.
Bottom-up (tabulation): fill a table from the smallest case up, in the right order.
Two relatives you should be able to tell apart from DP:
Greedy: always take the locally best choice and never look back. Fast, but only correct for some problems.
Backtracking: try a choice, recurse, undo it if it fails. Used for puzzles (sudoku, N-queens, permutations).
Watch a DP table fill cell by cell in the visualizer.

State: what do the parameters of a subproblem mean? (dp[i] = best answer using the first i items.)
Transition: how does a state follow from smaller ones?
Base cases: the smallest states you can answer directly.
Order: smaller states must be ready first.
Answer: which state holds the final result?

dp[i][j] = LCS length of the first i characters of A and first j of B. If A[i-1] == B[j-1] then dp[i-1][j-1] + 1, otherwise max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). O(len(A) × len(B)). The same table, with different costs, is edit distance (Levenshtein): the fewest inserts, deletes and replaces to turn one string into another. It powers spell check, diff tools and fuzzy matching of file names or malware families.

Choose items with weights and values to maximize value without exceeding capacity W. dp[w] = best value with capacity w; for each item, loop w from W down to the item's weight and set dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - wt] + val). O(n × W). (Note: W is a number, not the input size, so this is "pseudo-polynomial".)

Longest increasing subsequence (O(n²) or O(n log n) with binary search), climbing stairs, house robber, grid paths, partition into equal sums, matrix chain multiplication, longest palindromic substring.

Interval scheduling: sort by end time, take every interval that starts after the last chosen one ends.
Huffman coding: repeatedly merge the two least frequent symbols with a heap. Used in compression.
Dijkstra, Prim, Kruskal: greedy graph algorithms (graphs chapter).
A greedy choice must be proven safe (an "exchange argument": any optimal solution can be changed to include the greedy choice without getting worse). If you cannot prove it, test against DP on small inputs.

def subsets(nums):
 out, path = [], []
 def go(i):
 if i == len(nums): out.append(path[:]); return
 go(i + 1) # skip nums[i]
 path.append(nums[i]); go(i + 1); path.pop() # take it, then undo
 go(0)
 return out
Prune early (stop as soon as a partial answer cannot work) or it explodes: subsets are 2ⁿ, permutations n!.

Top-down only computes the states it needs and is easy to write, but it can hit the recursion limit (Python default is about 1000 frames) and has call overhead. Bottom-up avoids recursion and lets you keep only the last row or two: LCS can drop from O(mn) to O(min(m, n)) space. If you need the actual solution rather than just its score, store a parent pointer or walk the table backwards.

Phrases: "number of ways", "minimum/maximum cost", "is it possible", "longest/shortest ... subsequence", and a decision at each step where later choices depend on a small summary of earlier ones. If the state needs the whole history (not a small summary), DP will not be polynomial.

1-D: position or amount (dp[i]).
2-D: two sequences or two ranges (dp[i][j]), or position + remaining budget.
Bitmask: which items are used, for small n ≤ 20 (traveling salesman in O(n² 2ⁿ) instead of n!).
Interval DP: dp[l][r], as in matrix chain and optimal BSTs.
Tree DP: states at each node combine children's states.

Counting states × cost per transition gives the running time. Knapsack is O(nW), which is exponential in the number of bits of W, so it is pseudo-polynomial, and the general problem is NP-hard. DP is a way to be polynomial in the *values*, not a way around hardness.

Sequence alignment (Smith-Waterman) compares malware samples and binaries; edit distance clusters typosquatted domains and phishing URLs; Viterbi decoding (DP over a graph) drives speech recognition and some network anomaly models; dependency solvers and package managers use backtracking with pruning.

Climbing stairs, house robber, coin change, LCS, edit distance, LIS, 0/1 knapsack: know the state and transition of each from memory.
When does greedy work and when does it need DP? (Greedy-choice property vs overlapping subproblems.)
Reduce space: coin change is already O(amount); LCS only needs two rows.

Model networks, dependencies and attack paths as graphs, then run BFS, DFS, topological sort, Dijkstra, union-find and minimum spanning trees on them.
CS201: data structures and algorithms in depth · course page with quizzes and exam
simple // the idea in plain words

A graph is dots and lines: vertices (nodes) joined by edges. Computer networks, social networks, road maps, build dependencies and Active Directory permissions are all graphs. Edges can be directed (one-way, like a hyperlink or "can log in to") or undirected (two-way, like a cable), and can carry a weight (distance, latency, cost).
Two ways to store a graph:
Adjacency list: for each vertex, a list of its neighbors. Memory O(V + E). The default choice.
Adjacency matrix: a V×V grid with 1 where an edge exists. Memory O(V²), but "is there an edge A to B?" is O(1). Good for dense graphs.
Two basic ways to explore:
BFS (breadth-first search) uses a queue and visits everything 1 hop away, then 2 hops, and so on. It finds the shortest path when edges are unweighted.
DFS (depth-first search) uses a stack (or recursion) and goes as deep as it can before backing up. It finds connected components, detects cycles and orders tasks.
Both take O(V + E). Run both on the same graph in the visualizer and compare the order the nodes light up.
In security: BloodHound turns Active Directory into a graph and finds the shortest path from a normal user to Domain Admin. Lateral movement, attack trees and network segmentation reviews are graph problems.

A DAG (directed acyclic graph) can be laid out in an order where every edge points forward. That is the order to compile files, run build steps or take courses with prerequisites. Kahn's algorithm: count each node's in-edges, queue the nodes with zero, repeatedly remove one and decrement its neighbors. If you cannot remove all nodes, there is a cycle (circular dependency). DFS can do it too: output nodes in reverse finishing order.

Tracks which items are in the same group. find(x) returns the group's representative, union(a, b) merges groups. With path compression and union by rank both operations run in nearly O(1) (inverse Ackermann). Use it for connected components, detecting cycles while adding edges, and Kruskal's algorithm.

A spanning tree connects every vertex with V−1 edges and no cycles. The minimum one has the smallest total weight (cheapest cabling plan). Kruskal: sort edges, add each edge that does not form a cycle (check with union-find). Prim: grow one tree, always adding the cheapest edge leaving it (heap). Both O(E log V).

| Question | Algorithm
 | Fewest hops, unweighted | BFS
 | Cheapest path, weights ≥ 0 | Dijkstra
 | Weights may be negative | Bellman-Ford
 | Is it connected / how many groups | DFS or union-find
 | Order tasks with dependencies | Topological sort
 | Cheapest way to connect everything | Kruskal / Prim

If a later edge were negative, a node popped from the heap as "finished" could still be improved through a path found later. The proof of correctness assumes that any unvisited path to the node costs at least as much as the best frontier candidate, and negative weights break that. Use Bellman-Ford, or reweight with Johnson's algorithm for all-pairs.

Floyd-Warshall: three nested loops over (k, i, j) give all-pairs shortest paths in O(V³). Short and handy for small V.
Max-flow / min-cut (Ford-Fulkerson, Edmonds-Karp, Dinic): the most data you can push through a network, and the cheapest set of edges whose removal disconnects source from sink. A min-cut is literally the weakest set of links in a network.
Strongly connected components (Tarjan, Kosaraju): groups of nodes that can all reach each other in a directed graph. Collapsing them gives a DAG.
Bipartite matching: assign workers to tasks. Checking bipartiteness is a BFS 2-coloring.

Attack paths: nodes are users, groups, hosts; edges are "member of", "admin on", "has session on". BFS gives the shortest route to Domain Admin, and defenders break the shortest paths first.
Network segmentation: min-cut shows which firewall rules actually separate two zones.
Dependency graphs: a vulnerable library deep in a transitive dependency tree is a reachability question (software supply chain).
Malware/function call graphs and control-flow graphs: reverse engineering tools draw them and find loops with DFS back-edges.
Threat intel graphs: IPs, domains, hashes and actors linked by observed relationships; connected components cluster related campaigns.

Adjacency matrix BFS is O(V²), not O(V + E).
Recursive DFS on a path-shaped graph with 10⁶ nodes overflows the stack; use an explicit stack.
The shortest path problem is easy; the longest simple path and the traveling salesman problem are NP-hard. Heuristics and approximations take over there.

Number of islands in a grid: DFS/BFS or union-find, O(rows × cols).
Course schedule: is there a cycle in the prerequisite graph?
Word ladder: BFS where nodes are words and edges differ by one letter.
Clone a graph, detect a cycle in a directed vs undirected graph, find the shortest path in a weighted graph.

How hash tables get O(1) lookups, what happens when keys collide, why load factor matters, and how hashing shows up in Bloom filters, caches and denial-of-service attacks.
CS201: data structures and algorithms in depth · course page with quizzes and exam
simple // the idea in plain words

A hash table (dictionary, map, set) stores key/value pairs and finds a key in about one step, no matter how many items it holds. It is the most used data structure in everyday code: Python dict and set, Java HashMap, JavaScript Map and objects.
How it works:
A hash function turns the key into a big integer. Same key always gives the same number.
That number modulo the table size picks a bucket (an array slot).
Store or look up the item in that bucket.
Two different keys can land in the same bucket. That is a collision, and every hash table needs a plan for it. The two plans:
Chaining: each bucket holds a small list of the items that landed there.
Open addressing: if the bucket is taken, probe other slots (the next one, then the next, ...) until you find a free one.
Hash tables give O(1) average insert, lookup and delete. They do not keep keys in order, so "give me the smallest key" is O(n). Use the visualizer to insert keys and watch collisions form.
$ python3 -c "print(hash('abc') % 8, hash('abd') % 8)"
(Python randomizes string hashes per run, so the numbers change each time. That is on purpose, see the complex tier.)

Load factor α = items ÷ buckets. With chaining the average chain length is α, so lookups cost O(1 + α). When α passes a threshold (0.75 is common) the table doubles and rehashes every key into the new array. One insert might cost O(n), but doubling makes the amortized cost per insert O(1).

All items live in the array itself. Linear probing tries slot h, h+1, h+2, ... It is cache friendly but suffers clustering: long runs of filled slots make later probes longer. Quadratic probing and double hashing spread probes out. Deletes need a tombstone marker, otherwise you break the probe chain for keys stored after the deleted slot. Keep α under about 0.5 to 0.7 or probing gets slow.
What makes a good hash function

Deterministic: same key, same hash.
Uniform: spreads keys evenly across buckets.
Fast for table use.
Keys used in a table must be immutable (or hash must not change). That is why Python lists cannot be dict keys but tuples can.
If you override __eq__ you must keep __hash__ consistent: equal objects must have equal hashes.

Membership checks (x in seen), de-duplication, counting words (Counter), two-sum (store target - x), caching (functools.lru_cache), and joining two datasets by key. Replacing a nested loop with a set lookup is the single most common interview speed-up: O(n²) becomes O(n).

If every key lands in one bucket, the table is a linked list and every operation is O(n). An attacker who knows your hash function can craft keys that all collide: hash flooding, a denial-of-service attack found against web frameworks in 2011. The fix is a keyed hash with a random per-process secret (SipHash in Python, Rust, Ruby), so the attacker cannot predict buckets. Some languages also convert long chains into balanced trees (Java 8 HashMap).

Hash tables use fast non-cryptographic hashes (SipHash, MurmurHash, FNV, xxHash). Cryptographic hashes (SHA-256, BLAKE2/3) add three guarantees: preimage resistance (cannot find an input for a hash), second-preimage resistance, and collision resistance. They are much slower. Never use MD5 or SHA-1 where collision resistance matters, and never use a plain fast hash to store passwords (use bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2).

A Bloom filter answers "have I seen this?" using a bit array and k hash functions. Insert sets k bits; a query checks them. It can say "definitely not present" or "probably present" (false positives, never false negatives), in far less memory than storing the keys. Used for malicious-URL lists, "is this password in a breach?" pre-checks and database lookups that avoid disk reads. False-positive rate is about (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k for m bits and n items.

When a cache or database is spread over many servers, hash(key) % servers reshuffles nearly every key when you add a server. Consistent hashing places servers and keys on a ring; a key belongs to the next server clockwise, so adding a server moves only about 1/N of the keys. Used by Cassandra, DynamoDB and CDNs.

For a fixed key set (reserved words, protocol names) perfect hashing gives O(1) with zero collisions. When you need ordered keys or prefix search, use a balanced tree or a trie instead. Hash tables also sit behind the file-integrity checks (hashing files with sha256sum) you already know from forensics: same idea, a fixed-size fingerprint of arbitrary data.

SOLID principles, the design patterns that actually show up (factory, builder, singleton, adapter, decorator, strategy, observer), UML basics, and when not to use a pattern.
CS240: software engineering · course page with quizzes and exam
simple // the idea in plain words

A design pattern is a named, reusable solution to a problem that keeps appearing in object-oriented code. They come from the 1994 "Gang of Four" book. Knowing the names lets you talk about design in one word ("use a strategy there") and recognize the structure when you read other people's code, such as Spring, Java's standard library or a plugin system.
Patterns come in three families:
Creational (how objects get made): Factory, Builder, Singleton.
Structural (how objects fit together): Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy.
Behavioral (how objects talk): Strategy, Observer, Command, Iterator, State.
Before the patterns, learn the guide rails. The SOLID principles:
Single responsibility: a class has one reason to change.
Open/closed: add new behavior by adding code, not editing working code.
Liskov substitution: a subclass must work anywhere its parent works.
simple // the idea in plain words

Interface segregation: many small interfaces beat one giant one.
Dependency inversion: depend on abstractions (interfaces), not concrete classes.
Two shorthand rules: favor composition over inheritance (have an object, don't extend a class unless it really *is* one), and program to an interface.
Patterns are tools, not goals. Using five patterns where a function would do is a bug of its own. See the OOP basics in the Java OOP guide.
Factory: hide which class gets created
A function or method returns the right implementation: Parser.for_file("a.json") returns JsonParser. Callers depend on the interface, and adding a format changes one place.
Builder: construct complex objects step by step
Useful when a constructor would take ten parameters. HttpRequest.builder().url(u).header(k, v).timeout(5).build(). The result can be immutable and validated once in build().
Makes sense for a config or logger; but it is global state in disguise, hard to test and hostile to concurrency. Prefer passing one instance in (dependency injection).

Adapter: wrap an incompatible interface to look like the one you expect (a wrapper around a third-party SDK so you can swap vendors).
Decorator: wrap an object to add behavior while keeping the same interface (a logging or caching layer, Python @decorator, Java BufferedReader around FileReader).
Facade: a simple front over a messy subsystem.
Proxy: a stand-in that controls access (lazy loading, access checks, remote calls).

Instead of a class creating its own database connection, it receives one in its constructor. Tests pass in a fake; production passes in the real one. Frameworks (Spring, ASP.NET, Angular) automate this with an IoC container.
UML at the level you need

Class diagram: boxes with name, fields, methods; arrows for inheritance (hollow triangle), implementation (dashed), association and composition (diamond).
Sequence diagram: lifelines across the top, messages down the page; shows who calls whom in a request.
Use case diagram and state diagram for requirements and lifecycles.
Sketch the small diagram that answers the question, not the whole system. Tools: draw.io, PlantUML, Mermaid (renders in GitHub markdown).

If Square extends Rectangle and setting width also changes height, code written for rectangles breaks. A subclass must keep the parent's promises: accept at least what the parent accepts, return at least what the parent guarantees, throw no new surprises. When inheritance forces NotImplementedError, the hierarchy is wrong.

High-level policy (business rules) should not import low-level detail (SQL, HTTP). Both depend on an interface owned by the policy side. This is the heart of hexagonal / clean architecture: the domain sits in the center; databases, web frameworks and message queues plug in at the edges. It makes the core testable without a database and lets you replace infrastructure.
Command, State, Visitor, Iterator, Template Method

Command: turn a request into an object (undo/redo, job queues, macro recording).
State: an object changes behavior with its internal state; replaces giant switch blocks (order: new, paid, shipped).
Visitor: add operations to a class hierarchy without editing it (compilers walk syntax trees).
Iterator: walk a collection without exposing its internals (for x in obj).
Template Method: a base class fixes the steps, subclasses fill in some.
Chain of Responsibility: pass a request along handlers until one handles it (middleware, servlet filters, logging).

God object, shotgun surgery (one change touches twenty files), feature envy, primitive obsession, deep inheritance trees, copy-paste duplication, premature abstraction ("we might need it"), the big ball of mud. Refactoring catalog (extract method, replace conditional with polymorphism, introduce parameter object) is the cure, backed by tests.

Input validation at a boundary (facade/adapter) so untrusted data never reaches core logic.
Least privilege by splitting interfaces (ISP): a component that only reads should only get a read interface.
Secure defaults with the builder: unsafe options need explicit flags.
Singletons with mutable shared state are a source of race conditions and TOCTOU bugs.
Deserialization of untrusted objects (a "factory" that instantiates any class named in the data) is a classic remote code execution bug in Java and Python.

Explain SOLID with one example for each letter.
When is a strategy better than an if/else chain, and when is it overkill?
Why do people call singletons an anti-pattern? How do you test code that uses one?
Design a parking lot, a rate limiter or a notification system: start with requirements, nouns become classes, then show which pattern you used and why.
