Know how the six classic sorts work, what each costs, which are stable, and why nothing that compares can beat n log n. Then count comparisons in real code.
CS201: data structures and algorithms in depth · course page with quizzes and exam
simple // the idea in plain words

Sorting puts items in order so you can search them fast (binary search), merge them, spot duplicates and group them. You almost always call the built-in sorted() or Arrays.sort(). You learn the algorithms because interviews ask about them and because the *ideas* (divide and conquer, invariants, trade-offs) show up everywhere.
The three simple sorts, all O(n²) in the worst case:
Selection sort: find the smallest item, put it first, repeat on the rest. Always about n²/2 comparisons, even on sorted input.
Insertion sort: grow a sorted prefix. Take the next item and slide it left until it fits, like sorting playing cards in your hand. Fast on nearly-sorted data (O(n)).
Bubble sort: swap neighbors that are out of order, repeatedly. Easy to teach, rarely worth using.
The three fast sorts, O(n log n):
simple // the idea in plain words

Merge sort: split in half, sort each half, merge the two sorted halves. Predictable and stable, needs O(n) extra space.
Quicksort: pick a pivot, put smaller items left and larger right, recurse on both sides. Fastest in practice on arrays, but a bad pivot choice gives O(n²).
Heapsort: build a max-heap, then repeatedly remove the largest. In place, no bad case, not stable.
Try them in the algorithm visualizer: the bars show every compare and swap, and the counter shows why O(n²) hurts.
$ python3 -c "print(sorted([5,2,9,1], reverse=True))"

def insertion_sort(a):
 for i in range(1, len(a)):
 key = a[i]
 j = i - 1
 while j >= 0 and a[j] > key: # shift bigger items right
 a[j + 1] = a[j]
 j -= 1
 a[j + 1] = key
Loop invariant: before each pass, a[0:i] is sorted. Each pass keeps it true while extending it by one. When i reaches n, the whole array is sorted. Naming the invariant is how you prove a loop correct.

def merge_sort(a):
 if len(a) <= 1: return a
 mid = len(a) // 2
 left, right = merge_sort(a[:mid]), merge_sort(a[mid:])
 out, i, j = [], 0, 0
 while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
 if left[i] <= right[j]: # <= keeps equal items in order: stable
 out.append(left[i]); i += 1
 else:
 out.append(right[j]); j += 1
 return out + left[i:] + right[j:]
There are log₂ n levels of splitting, and each level merges n items in total, so the work is n log n in every case. Cost: O(n) extra memory.

def quicksort(a, lo=0, hi=None):
 if hi is None: hi = len(a) - 1
 if lo >= hi: return
 pivot = a[(lo + hi) // 2]
 i, j = lo, hi
 while i <= j:
 while a[i] < pivot: i += 1
 while a[j] > pivot: j -= 1
 if i <= j:
 a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]; i += 1; j -= 1
 quicksort(a, lo, j); quicksort(a, i, hi)
Average O(n log n). The worst case (always picking the smallest or largest as pivot, like "first element" on already-sorted data) is O(n²) and recursion depth n. Fixes: random pivot, median-of-three, and recursing on the smaller side first so the stack stays O(log n). Introsort (used by C++ std::sort) switches to heapsort when recursion gets too deep.

A binary heap is an array where the children of index i are at 2i+1 and 2i+2 and every parent is at least as big as its children (max-heap). Building the heap takes O(n); each of the n removals costs O(log n). In place, O(1) extra space, O(n log n) always, but poor cache behavior and not stable.

A sort is stable if equal keys keep their original order. It matters when you sort by two keys: sort by date, then (stable) by name, and the dates stay ordered within each name. Stable: insertion, merge, bubble, Timsort, counting. Not stable: selection, quicksort, heapsort.

| Sort | Best | Average | Worst | Space | Stable
 | Selection | n² | n² | n² | 1 | no
 | Insertion | n | n² | n² | 1 | yes
 | Merge | n log n | n log n | n log n | n | yes
 | Quick | n log n | n log n | n² | log n | no
 | Heap | n log n | n log n | n log n | 1 | no
 | Counting | n + k | n + k | n + k | n + k | yes
Why n log n is the floor

A comparison sort decides the order using only "is a < b?" questions. There are n! possible orderings, and each yes/no answer at best halves the possibilities, so you need at least log₂(n!) questions. By Stirling's approximation, log₂(n!) is about n log₂ n. No comparison sort can beat Ω(n log n) in the worst case.

Counting sort: for integer keys in 0..k, count how many of each, then write them out. O(n + k).
Radix sort: sort by the last digit, then the next, using a stable counting sort at each digit. O(d·(n + k)) for d digits. It sorts fixed-width IP addresses, timestamps and strings fast.
Bucket sort: spread items into buckets by value range, sort each bucket. Great when values are uniform.
These only work when keys have a known, bounded form.

Timsort (Python, Java objects): finds natural runs in the data, extends short runs with insertion sort, then merges with rules that keep it stable. O(n) on already-sorted input, O(n log n) worst case.
Introsort (C++ std::sort): quicksort that falls back to heapsort at depth 2·log n and to insertion sort for tiny ranges.
External sort: when data does not fit in RAM, sort chunks, write them out, then k-way merge. This is how databases and sort(1) handle huge files.
Sorting is also a security topic: an attacker who controls input can trigger quicksort's O(n²) case if the pivot is predictable (algorithmic complexity DoS).

To find the k-th smallest item you do not need a full sort. Partition like quicksort, then recurse only into the side that contains position k. Average O(n), worst O(n²). The median-of-medians variant guarantees O(n).

Which sorts are stable, and why does it matter?
Why is quicksort faster than merge sort in practice despite the same average? (In place, cache friendly, small constants.)
Sort a list of 1 million 16-bit integers fast. (Counting sort, k = 65,536.)
What is the best sort for a nearly-sorted list? (Insertion sort or Timsort.)

Then look at the insertion sort number next to it: that gap is what O(n²) versus O(n log n) means at n = 200.

Unit, integration and end-to-end tests, test-driven development, mocks, coverage, property and fuzz testing, and how to find a bug with a boundary test.
CS240: software engineering · course page with quizzes and exam
simple // the idea in plain words

Testing means running your code against examples where you already know the right answer, automatically, so you find out something broke in seconds instead of in production. A test suite is the safety net that lets you change code without fear.
The levels (the test pyramid):
Unit tests: one function or class in isolation. Hundreds of them, each runs in milliseconds.
Integration tests: several parts together, such as your code with a real database or an API call. Dozens.
End-to-end (E2E) tests: drive the whole app like a user, through a browser or a real HTTP client. A handful, because they are slow and flaky.
Many cheap tests at the bottom, few expensive ones at the top.
What a unit test looks like (Python pytest):
def add_tax(price, rate):
 return round(price * (1 + rate), 2)
def test_add_tax():
 assert add_tax(100, 0.08) == 108.0
def test_zero_price():
 assert add_tax(0, 0.08) == 0
Every test follows arrange, act, assert: set up the input, call the code, check the result.
Where bugs hide: boundaries. If a rule says "free shipping at 50 dollars or more", test 49.99, 50 and 50.01. Off-by-one errors (< vs <=) are the most common bug in the world.
$ python3 -c "print(round(100*(1+0.08),2))"

A loop: red (write a failing test for the next small behavior), green (write the least code that passes), refactor (clean up with the tests as a safety net). It forces testable design and gives you a regression suite for free. It is a habit, not a religion: use it where the rule is clear.

Fast, isolated, repeatable, self-checking: no ordering between tests, no reliance on the clock, network or a shared database state.
Tests one behavior, with a name that says which (test_expired_token_is_rejected).
Fails for exactly one reason, and the failure message explains it.
Tests behavior through the public interface, not private details, so a refactor does not break it.
Flaky tests (pass and fail randomly) are worse than none: people stop trusting red builds. Fix or delete them.

When the real dependency is slow, random or dangerous (network, database, clock, payment API), swap in a stand-in:
Stub: returns canned answers.
Fake: a working lightweight version (in-memory database).
Mock: also records calls so you can assert "sent exactly one email".
from unittest.mock import Mock
def test_alert_sent():
 mailer = Mock()
 notify(mailer, "disk full")
 mailer.send.assert_called_once_with("ops@example.com", "disk full")
Over-mocking makes tests pass while the real thing is broken. Mock the boundary of your system, not your own internals.

Line/branch coverage says which code ran during tests. 100% does not mean correct (it ran, but was it asserted?). Low coverage in a security-critical path, such as authentication, is a red flag. Use it to find untested code, not as a score. Mutation testing goes further: it changes your code (flips < to <=) and checks that a test fails; surviving mutants reveal weak tests.
Python pytest/unittest, Java JUnit/Mockito, JavaScript Jest/Vitest, browser E2E with Playwright/Cypress, API tests with Postman/curl. Run them with one command in CI (next chapter).

Instead of hand-picked examples, state a property that must hold for all inputs and let a library generate hundreds of cases (Python hypothesis, JS fast-check, Haskell QuickCheck).
from hypothesis import given, strategies as st
@given(st.lists(st.integers()))
def test_sort_properties(xs):
 ys = sorted(xs)
 assert len(ys) == len(xs)
 assert all(a <= b for a, b in zip(ys, ys[1:]))
Good properties: round trips (decode(encode(x)) == x), idempotence (sort(sort(x)) == sort(x)), invariants, comparison to a slow but obviously correct version. The library shrinks a failing input to the smallest example.
Fuzzing is the security cousin: feed huge numbers of malformed or random inputs into a parser and watch for crashes, hangs and memory errors. Coverage-guided fuzzers (AFL++, libFuzzer, Jazzer, Go's built-in fuzzing) mutate inputs that reach new code paths. Most memory-safety CVEs in parsers were found this way. Run a fuzzer in CI on every code path that handles untrusted data.

Time and randomness: inject a clock and a seeded random generator; never call time.now() deep inside logic.
Databases: run migrations against a throwaway real database in a container (Testcontainers) rather than mocking SQL.
Concurrency: tests can pass 999 times and fail once; use deterministic schedulers, thread sanitizers and stress runs.
Legacy code with no tests: first write characterization tests that record what the code does today, then refactor.
Contract tests (Pact) check that two services agree on an API shape without a full integration environment.
Snapshot tests store output and diff it; easy to write, easy to approve blindly.

SAST (static analysis such as CodeQL, Semgrep, Bandit), DAST (scan the running app, OWASP ZAP), dependency scanning (Dependabot, pip-audit, npm audit), secret scanning (gitleaks) and container scanning (Trivy). They catch categories of bugs unit tests do not think of. Treat findings like failing tests: triage, fix or document the exception.
When a bug is reported: first write a failing test that reproduces it, then fix it. The test stays forever and the same bug cannot return unnoticed. Do this for every security fix too.

Explain the test pyramid and why E2E-heavy suites become slow and flaky.
What is the difference between a mock and a stub?
How would you test a function that sends an email or reads the clock?
Someone says "we have 90% coverage, so we are safe". Respond.

Binary search trees, why balance matters, heaps and priority queues, tries, and the four traversals, with the cost of every operation.
CS201: data structures and algorithms in depth · course page with quizzes and exam
simple // the idea in plain words

A tree is data arranged as a root with child nodes below it, no loops. Folders on a disk, the HTML page you are reading and a company org chart are all trees. A binary tree gives each node at most two children, called left and right.
A binary search tree (BST) adds one rule: everything in a node's left subtree is smaller, everything in the right subtree is larger. To find a value, start at the root and go left or right, throwing away half the tree each step. If the tree is balanced this takes O(log n): a million items need about 20 steps.
Four ways to walk a tree (traverse it):
In-order (left, node, right): visits a BST in sorted order.
Pre-order (node, left, right): copy a tree or print a folder structure.
Post-order (left, right, node): delete a tree, or compute sizes from the bottom up.
Level-order (row by row, using a queue): the BFS of trees.
A heap is a different tree: the parent is always smaller (min-heap) or larger (max-heap) than its children, so the smallest item is always at the top. It powers priority queues: "give me the most urgent job next".
Insert numbers into the BST and heap tabs of the visualizer and watch the shape change.

AVL tree: after each insert/delete, every node's two subtree heights differ by at most 1. Violations are fixed with rotations (single or double, left or right). Strictly balanced, so lookups are fastest.
Red-black tree: a looser color-based balance, fewer rotations on updates. Used in Java TreeMap, C++ std::map and the Linux scheduler.
B-tree / B+ tree: nodes hold many keys and have many children, so the tree is very shallow. Built for disk: each node is one disk page. This is what database indexes and file systems use.
All guarantee O(log n) search, insert and delete.

Stored in a plain array: node i has children 2i+1 and 2i+2 and parent (i-1)//2.
push: append at the end, sift up while smaller than the parent. O(log n).
pop min: swap the root with the last item, remove it, sift down. O(log n).
peek the min: O(1). heapify an existing array: O(n).
import heapq
h = []
for x in [5, 1, 8, 3]: heapq.heappush(h, x)
heapq.heappop(h) # 1
heapq.nsmallest(2, [5,1,8,3]) # [1, 3]
Use heaps for the top-k items, merging k sorted lists, scheduling, and Dijkstra's shortest path.

A trie (prefix tree) has one edge per character; a path from the root spells a word. Lookup and insert cost O(length of the word), independent of how many words are stored. Perfect for autocomplete, dictionary checks, IP routing tables (longest-prefix match) and matching many malware or IDS signature strings (Aho-Corasick builds on a trie).

| Structure | Search | Insert | Delete | Notes
 | Unbalanced BST | O(h) | O(h) | O(h) | h from log n to n
 | AVL / red-black | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(log n) | ordered, range queries
 | Binary heap | O(n) | O(log n) | O(log n) | min/max in O(1)
 | Trie | O(L) | O(L) | O(L) | L = key length

A perfect binary tree of height h has 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes, so n nodes need height at least log₂(n+1) − 1. An AVL tree of height h has at least F(h+3) − 1 nodes (Fibonacci), which grows like φ^h with φ ≈ 1.618, so h ≤ 1.44·log₂ n. That is the proof that AVL operations are O(log n) even in the worst case.

A right rotation at node y with left child x makes x the parent, moves x's old right child to become y's left child, and keeps the BST order intact. Four imbalance cases: left-left (one right rotation), right-right (one left rotation), left-right (left then right) and right-left (right then left). Each rotation is O(1), and an insert needs at most two, so insert stays O(log n).

Segment tree / Fenwick tree: range sums or minimums with updates in O(log n).
Skip list: a probabilistic layered linked list with O(log n) expected operations. Redis uses it for sorted sets.
Merkle tree: each parent is the hash of its children. Proves a file chunk belongs to a set with O(log n) hashes. Git, Bitcoin, certificate transparency and BitTorrent use it.
Treap, splay tree, LSM tree: randomization, self-adjusting, and write-optimized storage (RocksDB, Cassandra).

Deep trees overflow the call stack, so interviews ask for iterative versions: in-order uses an explicit stack (go left pushing nodes, pop, visit, go right); level-order uses a queue. Morris traversal does in-order in O(1) space by temporarily threading pointers.

Validate a BST: pass min/max bounds down; do not only compare a node with its children.
Lowest common ancestor of two nodes in a BST: walk down until the two values split.
Why do databases use B+ trees instead of binary trees? (Fewer disk reads: high fan-out means 3-4 levels for millions of rows.)
Top-k frequent items: count with a hash map, then keep a size-k heap.

bst.py inserts the numbers in keys.txt into a plain, unbalanced BST. Finish height() (the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path), then run it. The keys arrive in sorted order, so the tree is far taller than a balanced one would be.
Submit the height the script prints, e.g. submit 7.

How the chatbot on this site works: search first, then optionally a small model running on your own machine. Why it can still be wrong.
simple // the idea in plain words

The chatbot at ~/ai/chat does not call any server. Everything runs in your browser tab.
It has two modes:
Search mode (default). Your question is matched against the text of this site: the guides, the Security+ notes, the glossary, the cheatsheets and the AI chapters. You get the best-matching passages back, each with a link to the page it came from. Nothing is generated, so nothing is invented. If the site doesn't cover it, it says so.
Local model mode (optional). You can download a small language model into your browser. It then writes an answer in sentences, using the passages from search mode as its source material. It is slower, needs a recent Chrome or Edge with WebGPU, and is much weaker than the big hosted chatbots.
simple // the idea in plain words

Why not just plug in a famous model? A website can't hold a secret. Anything in the page's JavaScript is visible to every visitor, so an API key placed there would be copied and used on someone else's bill within hours. A hosted model needs a small server in the middle that holds the key. This site is static files, so it has no middle.
Rules for any chatbot, including this one:
It can be wrong, and it sounds sure either way. Check anything that matters against the cited page or official docs.
Citations are the point. An answer with no source you can open is a guess.
Never paste secrets into a chat box, local or hosted.

A language model only knows what was in its training data, and it can't look things up. RAG fixes that in three steps:
Retrieve. Search your own documents for passages relevant to the question.
Augment. Paste those passages into the prompt: "Answer using only this text. Cite it."
Generate. The model writes the answer from the pasted text instead of from memory.
question -> search the site index -> top 4 passages
 -> prompt = rules + passages + question
 -> model writes the answer, citing [1] [2]

At build time a script reads every built page, splits it into chunks at each heading, and writes one JSON index. In the browser the chat loads that file and scores each chunk with BM25, a classic ranking formula:
words that are rare across the site count more than common ones ("kerberos" beats "the")
a word that repeats in a chunk helps, with diminishing returns
short chunks are not punished or favored unfairly (length normalization)
matches in a chunk's title get a boost
That is keyword search, not meaning search. It finds "kerberos" when you type "kerberos". It can miss "how do tickets work in AD" if those words never appear together. Embedding-based search fixes that at the cost of a model and more data.
What a small local model is and isn't

The optional model is a few hundred million to about 1.5 billion parameters, quantized (weights stored in 4 bits instead of 16 or 32) so it fits in GPU memory. It runs through WebGPU, the browser's access to your graphics card. The weights are downloaded once and cached by the browser. They are not sent anywhere, and neither is your question.
Expect: fine at rephrasing the retrieved passages, poor at multi-step reasoning, prone to confident mistakes. Frontier models are hundreds of times larger.
Search mode: runs in your browser, no setup, never invents facts, no prose of its own (it quotes the site).
Local model: runs on your GPU, 200 MB to 1.5 GB download, sometimes invents facts, basic prose.
Hosted model (API): runs in a data center, needs a server to hold the key, sometimes invents facts but less often, best prose.

A language model predicts a plausible next token. Plausible is not the same as true. When retrieval returns nothing useful, a model still produces fluent text, and that text is a hallucination. RAG reduces this but doesn't remove it:
retrieval can return the wrong passage, and the model faithfully summarizes it
the model can ignore the passage and answer from memory
the model can blend two passages into a claim neither makes
Mitigations used here and in real products: instruct the model to answer only from the context and say "not covered" otherwise, number the sources so claims can be traced, show the sources next to the answer, and keep the generated text visibly separate from the quoted text.

Prompt injection. Retrieved text goes into the prompt, so the model can't tell your instructions from instructions hidden in a document. A RAG system that indexes untrusted content (web pages, tickets, email) can be steered by that content. This site only indexes its own pages, which is why a local model here is low risk. See attacking AI.
Data leakage. A RAG index returns whatever it holds, to anyone who can ask. Per-user access control has to happen at retrieval time, not in the prompt.
Key exposure. Client-side API keys are public keys. The standard fix is a thin proxy that holds the key, authenticates the caller, rate limits, and logs. Without those limits, an exposed proxy is an open bill.
Supply chain. The local mode loads a JavaScript library from a CDN and weights from a model host. Pin versions, and know that you are running third-party code and data. Model files can be tampered with the same way packages can.
Tuning knobs in a RAG system

Chunk size. Too small loses context, too large dilutes the match. Splitting at headings, as done here, keeps each chunk about one idea.
Top-k. More passages give more coverage and more distraction. Small models do worse with long prompts, so this site passes four.
Hybrid search. Combine keyword scores (BM25) with embedding similarity. Keyword search nails exact terms like port numbers and CVE ids, embeddings catch paraphrases.
Evaluation. Keep a list of questions with known source pages and measure how often the right page lands in the top results. Without that, "it seems better" is the only evidence.

What AI changes for attackers, what it does not change, and how to adjust your defenses accordingly.
simple // the idea in plain words

AI gives attackers the same thing it gives everyone else: speed, scale and polish. It makes existing attacks cheaper rather than inventing a new kind of hack.
Better phishing. Typos and awkward grammar used to be a giveaway. Now a message in clean, natural language in any language costs nothing to produce, and can be tailored to a target from public information.
Voice and video fakes (deepfakes). A few seconds of audio can be enough to clone a voice. Fraud calls "from the CEO" and fake video meetings have been used to move real money.
Faster recon. Summarizing a target's public footprint (job posts, social profiles, leaked data) takes minutes.
Coding help. Assistants speed up writing scripts and tweaking existing malware. Mainstream models refuse some requests, but criminal-marketed tools and jailbreaks exist.
Vulnerability research. Models and agents are getting better at spotting bugs in code, which helps defenders and attackers alike.
Stop relying on "it looks wrong" as your main defense. Rely on process: verify requests out-of-band, use phishing-resistant MFA, and require approval steps that a convincing message cannot skip.

Barrier to entry dropped for low-skill actors. Cost per attempt dropped for everyone.
Personalization at scale. Spear phishing used to need human research per target. Now it can be generated per row of a spreadsheet.
Multilingual reach. The "bad translation" tell is gone.
Social engineering across channels. Email plus a cloned voice call plus a fake video call in a single story.
Adaptive tooling. Malware that asks a model to rewrite itself is possible in principle and has been shown in research, though most real-world attacks still rely on old, boring techniques that work.

Initial access is still dominated by stolen credentials, phishing, exposed services and unpatched software.
Attackers still need infrastructure, a way to get paid and a way to stay undetected, and defenders still see the artifacts.
Basic hygiene (MFA, patching, least privilege, backups, logging) blocks most of it, with or without AI.

Out-of-band verification for money and access. Hang up and call back on a known number. Use a pre-agreed code word for high-risk approvals.
Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2 or passkeys) so a perfect fake login page captures nothing reusable.
Update awareness training. Teach "verify the request" rather than "spot the errors".
Email authentication and filtering: SPF, DKIM and DMARC, plus link and attachment sandboxing.
Limit what a public footprint reveals: org charts, employee emails, voice samples.
Watch for AI-assisted scraping and credential stuffing with rate limits and bot detection.

AI companies and security vendors now publish reports on how their tools are misused (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Microsoft have each published such reports). These are valuable primary sources, with a caveat: each vendor sees only its own platform and has reasons to emphasize some findings. Read for the concrete behaviors (what task was automated, which stage of the kill chain) and discount the headlines. A good question for any claim: what was automated, what still needed a human, and what was the success rate?

Recon: OSINT summarization, target profiling
Weaponization: phishing lures, scripts and malware tweaks, exploit adaptation from public advisories
Delivery: mass personalization, voice/video impersonation
Exploitation: automated vulnerability triage and proof-of-concept drafting; the shrinking window between a patch being published and exploit code appearing is the thing to watch
Actions on objectives: summarizing stolen data to find the valuable parts faster
Each stage maps back to a defensive control and a log source. That is how to answer "what do we do about AI attackers": nothing new at the principle level, but faster patching, tighter identity controls and better detection coverage, because the time you have is shrinking.

Lure content is less detectable by grammar, so key on infrastructure and behavior: new domains, mismatched Reply-To, authentication failures, odd sending patterns, link destinations
Voice and video: procedural controls beat detection tools, which are unreliable and in an arms race
Credential theft: impossible-travel, new device, token anomalies and conditional access policies
Automation at the target: unusually regular timing, high request rates, uniform user agents
Ethics and boundaries for a learner

Practice on systems you own or have written permission to test (your homelab, CTF platforms, intentionally vulnerable VMs). Using AI to attack anyone else is the same crime as doing it by hand, and the provider logs can be subpoenaed.

Where AI genuinely helps a SOC today, where it fails, and how to put it in a workflow without trusting it blindly.
simple // the idea in plain words
Defenders drown in volume: millions of log lines, hundreds of alerts, too few analysts. AI helps by doing the reading and sorting so humans can do the deciding.

Filtering the obvious: spam, known-bad file families and routine alerts get classified automatically
Summarizing: turn an alert, a ticket thread or a 40-page incident into five lines
Translating: plain English into a SIEM query (KQL, SPL, SQL), or an unfamiliar log format into an explanation
Drafting: incident reports, detection rule first drafts, shift handoff notes
Prioritizing: rank vulnerabilities by how likely they are to be exploited (the EPSS score from FIRST does this with a statistical model)

Knowing your environment. It has not seen your network
Admitting what it left out. A summary can omit the one detail that matters
Being consistent. Same input, different output
Rule of thumb: AI proposes, a human or a deterministic check disposes. The lab below shows why.

Detect: ML classifiers on email, endpoint and network data; anomaly detection on logins and data transfer (UEBA); LLM-assisted rule writing from a description of the behavior
Triage: auto-enrich an alert (who is this user, is this IP known, what else did this host do), then summarize with a verdict and the evidence behind it
Investigate: natural-language search over logs, "what did this account touch in the last 24h", timeline building
Respond: suggested playbook steps; automated, pre-approved low-risk actions such as disabling a compromised token
Learn: postmortem drafts, detection-gap analysis, training scenarios
A sane workflow for AI-assisted triage

Collect the raw evidence with normal tools. Do not let the model fetch it from memory
Give the model the evidence and a narrow question ("list every distinct source IP in this log and what each did")
Make it quote: ask for log line numbers or exact strings with every claim
Spot-check the claims against the raw data. Check what the summary omits, not just what it says
The analyst writes the verdict. The model's text is a draft

Omission. A fluent summary that is accurate in every sentence and still misses a source, a host or a time window
Invented specifics. IPs, CVE numbers and hostnames that look right and are not
False confidence. "No evidence of compromise" when it simply was not shown the evidence
Data leakage. Pasting customer logs, credentials or incident details into a tool your company has not approved
Alert fatigue, moved. If it raises 100 new "AI findings" a day, you replaced one noise source with another

Put the LLM where errors are cheap. Enrichment, summarization and query drafting are recoverable. Autonomous containment (isolating a production server) is not. Use tiers: suggest, then approve, then auto-execute only for low-impact, reversible actions with a rollback.
Constrain output. Ask for JSON with required fields (verdict, evidence[], confidence, unknowns[]), validate against a schema, and reject anything that does not parse. An explicit unknowns field helps counter omission.
Ground it. RAG over your runbooks, asset inventory and detection catalog, so answers come from your sources and cite them.
Log everything. Store the prompt, retrieved context, model version and output for each decision. You need that for audit, debugging and tuning. Models change, and a silent upgrade can change behavior.

Evaluate before trusting. Build a test set of past incidents with known answers, run the pipeline, and measure precision, recall, and the specific misses. Re-run after any model, prompt or data change. Track operational metrics (mean time to triage, escalation rate, analyst override rate) and not just model scores.
Protect the pipeline itself. The agent reads attacker-controlled text (email bodies, log fields, filenames, web pages). Anything the attacker can write into a log can try to instruct your tools. Strip or fence untrusted fields, minimize tool permissions, and never give a triage agent credentials it does not need.

LLMs are decent at drafting a Sigma rule or a KQL query from a description of attacker behavior and at mapping it to MITRE ATT&CK. They are not a substitute for testing: run every generated rule against known-good and known-bad data, check the false-positive rate, and read the logic line by line. The same applies to AI-written SOAR playbooks and scripts.
Metrics that show whether it helps

Time to first triage, percent of alerts closed correctly without escalation, analyst overrides of the AI's verdict, and missed-detection reviews. If overrides are high, the tool is creating work. If nobody ever overrides, nobody is checking.

The auto-triage assistant attached a summary. It reads well, and its verdict is "single source, contained, low risk". Your job is to check it against the raw vpn_auth.log.
Compare the summary's claims with the log. The summary is missing one external IP address that was involved in a successful login. Resolve the ticket with that IP address.
This one is a ticket in the queue. Open the attachments, investigate in the console under the ticket, then resolve it with your answer. Hints cost 15 points, wrong answers 5.

Where this is likely headed in security, what is hype, and how to position yourself. Opinion and trend, clearly labeled.
simple // the idea in plain words

Nobody knows exactly where this goes, and anyone who sounds certain is selling something. What can be said with reasonable confidence is where the pressure is building:
Attacks get faster and cheaper. More attempts, better lures, shorter time between a bug being public and someone exploiting it.
Defense gets more automated. Routine triage, enrichment and reporting move to machines. Humans move toward judgment, investigation and engineering.
AI systems become targets. Every company deploying assistants and agents creates a new thing to secure.
Identity and trust get harder. If voice, video and writing can be faked, "does this look real" stops being a security control.
Rules arrive. Governments and standards bodies are writing AI requirements. The EU AI Act entered into force in August 2024 with obligations phasing in over several years, and NIST has published an AI Risk Management Framework.
Treat everything on this page as a forecast as of November 2026, not a fact. The reading list on the news page is how you keep it current.

Agentic security tools. AI that does multi-step work: investigates an alert, runs queries, drafts the containment ticket. The open question is how much autonomy organizations will accept and how they will audit it.
Automated vulnerability discovery and repair. DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge (finals in August 2025) was built to test systems that find and patch bugs in open-source code with no human help. Expect the discovery side to speed up, which makes fast patching and good software supply-chain hygiene more important, not less.
Non-human identities. Agents need credentials. API keys, service accounts and tokens for AI systems are a growing attack surface and a growing audit problem.
Provenance and authentication. Efforts like content credentials (C2PA) try to prove where media came from. Treat as helpful, partial, and easy to strip.
Regulation and liability. Expect more requirements on logging, testing and disclosure for AI systems, and more questions about who is responsible when an agent causes a breach.
Small and local models. Models that run on your own hardware reduce the "where did my data go" problem, a big deal for sensitive incident data.
Fundamentals (identity, patching, segmentation, logging, backups, people and process) keep paying off. Attackers keep choosing the cheapest path. Tools change faster than principles.
Scenarios for the next few years, with signposts

Defender-favoring: automation closes the gap on triage and patching faster than attackers scale. Signposts: falling mean time to detect/patch in published industry reports, more fixes landing before exploitation.
Attacker-favoring: cheap exploit generation outpaces patch deployment, especially for under-resourced organizations. Signposts: shrinking time-to-exploit after disclosure, more mass exploitation of freshly published bugs.
Mixed (my base case): both sides speed up, advantage depends on organization maturity, and the gap between well-run and poorly-run shops widens.
I mark the last one as my judgment and not a finding. Check it against data as it arrives.

Detection engineering and data skills: writing and testing detections, SQL and Python for log analysis. Someone has to build and evaluate the pipelines AI plugs into
Verification mindset: auditing AI output, building evaluation sets, knowing when a result is untrustworthy
Identity and cloud security: where the new attack surface is
AI security itself: red-teaming LLM apps, threat modeling agents, governance. A young specialization with demand and few experienced people
Communication: explaining risk to non-technical decision makers. Not automated away easily

Entry-level triage work is the most exposed to automation, which means early-career people should aim to build skills the automation cannot replace sooner: investigation, scripting, and showing evidence of hands-on work (homelabs, write-ups, CTFs). Employers that hire for this will increasingly ask how you use AI responsibly. Having a clear answer is a differentiator, and the next chapter is meant to give you one.

From a 1956 summer workshop to chatbots in the SOC: the short version of how we got here, and why it keeps happening in waves.
simple // the idea in plain words

AI is not new. The term was coined in 1956 and the field has gone through boom, bust, boom cycles ever since. Each boom promised more than the hardware and data of the day could deliver, so funding collapsed, and each comeback happened because something concrete changed: more computing power, more data, or a better method.
The idea that matters for security: AI has been in defensive tools for decades (spam filters, antivirus classifiers, anomaly detection). What changed recently is that general-purpose language models became cheap and easy for everyone to use, attackers and defenders alike.

1950 Alan Turing publishes "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" and proposes what became the Turing test
1956 The Dartmouth workshop. The phrase "artificial intelligence" is coined for it
1958 Frank Rosenblatt demonstrates the perceptron, an early learning machine
1966 ELIZA, a chatbot that pattern-matches your sentences back at you
1970s First "AI winter": results fall short of promises and funding dries up
1980s Expert systems (hand-written if/then rules) go commercial. The second bust follows in the late 80s and early 90s
1997 IBM Deep Blue beats world chess champion Garry Kasparov
2012 AlexNet wins the ImageNet image contest by a wide margin and deep learning takes over
2016 AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol at Go
2017 The transformer architecture is published ("Attention Is All You Need")
2022 ChatGPT launches in November and language models go mainstream
Pattern worth remembering: every wave starts with a demo that looks like magic and ends with people learning exactly where it breaks. Security work lives in the "where it breaks" part.
Four eras, and why each ended

Symbolic AI (1950s-80s). Humans wrote the rules. Works on narrow, well-defined problems (expert systems for diagnosis and configuration). Breaks when the world is messier than the rule list, and rules do not scale to maintain.
Statistical machine learning (1990s-2000s). Instead of writing rules, show the machine labeled examples and let it fit a model. This is where spam filtering (naive Bayes classifiers became popular around 2002) and early ML malware classification come from. It needs hand-picked features, which takes expert effort.
Deep learning (2012 onward). Neural networks learn their own features from raw data, given enough data and GPUs. Image recognition, speech and translation jump forward. For security: much better malware and phishing classifiers, and also adversarial examples (tiny input tweaks that fool a model), described in research from 2013 and 2014.
Foundation models and LLMs (2018 onward). One model, trained on a huge amount of text and code, can be steered by plain-language instructions to do many tasks. This is the first era where a non-expert can use the technology without building anything.
The security timeline runs in parallel

1987 Dorothy Denning's intrusion-detection model: learn what normal activity looks like and flag deviations. The basis of anomaly detection ever since
Early 2000s Bayesian spam filtering becomes standard
2010s Machine-learning endpoint products, behavior analytics (UEBA) and "anomaly" network tools reach the market
2016 DARPA Cyber Grand Challenge: machines find, patch and exploit bugs in a live competition, no humans driving
2016 Microsoft's Tay chatbot is manipulated into abusive output within a day of launch, an early public lesson in adversarial users
2019 A widely reported voice-clone fraud against a UK energy firm; deepfake-enabled fraud has since grown (a Hong Kong finance worker was reported to have paid out around US$25 million in 2024 after a deepfake video call)
2023 Security vendors announce LLM assistants for analysts; "criminal LLM" tools such as WormGPT are advertised on forums
2024-2025 Researchers show AI agents finding real vulnerabilities in real software (Google's Big Sleep reported an exploitable bug in SQLite in late 2024), and DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge finals run at DEF CON in August 2025

Neural networks are old. Backpropagation (popularized in 1986) is what trains them. What was missing was compute (GPUs), data (the web), and an architecture that parallelizes. The transformer (2017) replaced sequential processing with attention, which trains efficiently across thousands of chips. Scaling the same recipe (more parameters, more data, more compute) kept producing new abilities, and the 2020 scaling-law results formalized the trend. That is the real story behind the jump from GPT-style research models to usable assistants: a lot of engineering on top of an old idea.
Lessons the security field already paid for

Detection ML has always fought concept drift. Models trained on yesterday's traffic degrade as behavior changes, so they need retraining, monitoring and a baseline to compare against.
Anomalous is not malicious. Early anomaly detectors drowned analysts in false positives, which is a big reason behavior analytics took years to become useful. Expect the same failure mode from any AI that raises alerts.
Anything that learns can be taught wrong. Spammers poisoned and evaded Bayesian filters (random words appended to messages). The modern version is data poisoning and prompt injection.
Automation shifts work, it does not delete it. The Cyber Grand Challenge machines were impressive on a small contrived OS, and human experts still found the real-world case far messier. Treat "AI solves X" claims the same way: ask what the test environment looked like.

Turing 1950; Denning 1987; the transformer paper (2017); the NIST adversarial machine learning taxonomy (NIST AI 100-2). Links live on the news and sources page.

How to get the most out of AI as a learner and on the job without trusting it where you shouldn't.
simple // the idea in plain words
Treat an AI assistant like a fast, well-read, overconfident intern: great at first drafts, explanations and busywork, wrong often enough that you check everything that matters.

Try first, then ask. Struggle with the problem for a few minutes, then ask for a hint, not the answer. Understanding comes from the struggle.
Ask it to explain, then quiz you. "Explain TCP three-way handshake like I know subnetting but not sockets. Then ask me 5 questions, one at a time."
Verify against real docs. Official documentation, RFCs and the vendor's reference are the source of truth.
Write your own notes afterwards. If you can't explain it without the chat open, you haven't learned it.
Check the exam rules. For certifications like Security+, use AI to study, never during an exam.

Use only approved tools, and never paste credentials, customer data or private incident details into one that isn't.
You own the output. If AI wrote it and it's wrong, it's still your name on it.
Keep a human in the loop for anything that changes a system.

Role: You are helping a SOC analyst triage a VPN alert.
Context: <paste only the relevant log lines / ticket text>
Task: List every distinct source IP and what each one did.
Format: Table: ip | actions | first_seen | last_seen. Quote the log line number for each row.
Constraints: Use only the text above. If something isn't in it, write "not in data".
Check: After the table, list anything you are unsure about.
The parts that do the most work: give the evidence, constrain to it, demand quotes, and ask for unknowns.

Decompose. Break big tasks into steps and check each. One huge prompt hides errors.
Ask it to argue the other side. "What evidence would show this is benign?" counters the model's tendency to agree with you.
Generate, then test. Detection rules, scripts and regexes: run them on sample data before trusting them. Do it in a VM or lab, not on production.
Don't ask leading questions. "Is this malware?" invites "yes". Ask "what behaviors does this show, and which are consistent with legitimate software?"
Use it to understand, not to skip. Paste an unfamiliar command or log line and ask what each part does, then confirm in the man page.

Great: explaining concepts and unfamiliar output, drafting reports and emails, boilerplate scripts, regex, converting formats, brainstorming test cases, study quizzes
Good with review: query writing (KQL, SPL, SQL), detection rule drafts, code review, summaries of long text
Poor: exact facts without sources (CVE specifics, version numbers), anything requiring your private environment, final verdicts on incidents, legal or compliance sign-off

A verification checklist you apply to every AI output that matters: Are the entities complete (IPs, users, hosts)? Do quoted lines exist in the source? Are identifiers real (look them up)? What did it leave out? Would I bet my reputation on this?
A prompt library of tested prompts for recurring tasks, versioned like code, each with a sample input and the output you expect.
A small evaluation set. For a task you do often (say, triaging phishing reports), keep ten past cases with known answers and run prompt changes against them. This is how professionals tell "feels better" from "is better".
Log what you used it for, in a work journal. It makes audits, handoffs and your own learning easier.

Know your organization's policy before you paste anything. Classify data first. Strip or pseudonymize identifiers when possible (swap real usernames and IPs for placeholders). Prefer enterprise tools with contractual data protections and a retention policy over consumer apps. For sensitive material, local models are an option.

Start read-only. Grant one capability at a time. Require approval for each side-effecting action until you have measured reliability. Review the action log, not just the final answer. Remember the triad from the previous chapter: untrusted input, sensitive access and an outbound channel should not all exist in one agent.

If a tool does your thinking, you stop building the skill. Alternate: do the task by hand sometimes, then compare with the AI's approach. For learners, a rule: no AI for the first pass on a lab you are trying to learn from. Use it for review and for what to study next. Interviewers can tell the difference between someone who can explain the answer and someone who pasted it.
In interviews and on a resume

Be specific: "used an LLM to draft Sigma rules, then validated against a test log set and tuned for false positives" says more than "familiar with AI tools". Show the verification step. It is the part employers worry about.

How AI systems get attacked: prompt injection, data poisoning, leaks and agent abuse, and how to build so one bad document cannot hijack your tools.
simple // the idea in plain words
AI systems are software with a new kind of weakness: they follow instructions written in ordinary language, and they cannot reliably tell whose instructions they are.

Prompt injection. Hidden or planted text tells the model to do something other than what the user asked. "Ignore previous instructions" is the cartoon version. The realistic version is a web page, email or PDF that contains instructions meant for an AI assistant that reads it.
Jailbreaks. Tricking a model into ignoring its safety rules.
Data poisoning. Corrupting the data a model learns from or retrieves from, so it behaves badly later.
Data leakage. Getting a model to reveal secrets from its prompt, its documents or its training data.
Excessive agency. The model is given more power than it needs (send email, run commands, read files), so a successful injection has real consequences.
The dangerous combination is an assistant that reads untrusted content, has access to something sensitive, and can send data out. Remove any one of the three and most of the damage goes away.
The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025 edition)

LLM01 Prompt injection (direct, and indirect through content the model reads)
LLM02 Sensitive information disclosure
LLM03 Supply chain (models, datasets, plugins)
LLM04 Data and model poisoning
LLM05 Improper output handling (model output used unchecked in a shell, SQL query or web page)
LLM06 Excessive agency
LLM07 System prompt leakage
LLM08 Vector and embedding weaknesses (RAG stores)
LLM09 Misinformation
LLM10 Unbounded consumption (cost and denial of service)

Direct: the user types the attack. Mostly a problem for policy bypass. Indirect: the attacker never talks to the model; they plant text where it will be read: a web page, a shared document, an email, a code comment, an issue ticket, even a filename. Hidden formatting (white text, HTML comments, tiny fonts) hides it from humans and not from the model. The indirect case is what threatens real deployments.

Evasion / adversarial examples: small input changes that flip a classifier's decision (malware tweaked to look benign)
Model extraction and membership inference: probing a model to copy it or learn whether a record was in its training data
Supply chain: poisoned model files (some formats can execute code when loaded), malicious packages and plugins

Least privilege for every tool an agent can call
Human approval for anything with side effects: sending, deleting, paying, running
Break the triad: if it reads untrusted content, do not also give it unrestricted outbound channels and secrets
Treat model output as untrusted input to whatever consumes it
Egress controls and logging so exfiltration attempts are visible
Keep secrets out of prompts; keep them in systems the model cannot read
Why filters are not a fix

Input filters and "ignore malicious instructions" system prompts raise the cost of an attack and can catch known patterns, but language is open-ended and the same intent can be phrased endlessly. Treat prompt injection like XSS in the early years: it must be handled by architecture, with detection as a bonus. Design as if the model is already compromised and ask what it could reach.

Privilege separation: one component reads untrusted content and can only return structured data (no tools). A separate component with tools only sees that sanitized output.
Allow-lists for destinations, domains and file paths, enforced outside the model
Confirmation with context: show the human exactly what will be sent and where, not the model's description of it
Capability scoping per task, short-lived credentials, read-only by default
Rendering controls: block automatic image or link loading from model output, a common exfiltration channel (data encoded into a URL)
Red-team continuously: replay known injection corpora against your own app after each change

MITRE ATLAS: ATT&CK-style matrix of tactics and techniques against AI systems
NIST AI 100-2: taxonomy of adversarial machine learning attacks and mitigations
NIST AI Risk Management Framework: governance-level guidance
OWASP GenAI Security Project: the LLM Top 10 and related guidance
Links on the news and sources page.

Standards for connecting models to tools (such as the Model Context Protocol) expand the attack surface: every tool description and tool result is more text the model might obey. Review third-party tool servers like you would any dependency, and watch for tools whose descriptions or outputs contain instructions.

Your company runs an AI assistant that reads the finance inbox and summarizes invoices. This morning it also emailed some data somewhere nobody expected.
Investigate in ~/agent: the assistant's run.log, the document it was summarizing in ~/inbox, and config.txt. Find the document text that hijacked the assistant, and work out where the data was sent.
Submit the email address the stolen data went to.
Solve it in the sandbox. Type hint when stuck and submit <answer> when you have it.

What a language model actually is, in three depths, and why knowing it makes you better at both using and securing AI.
simple // the idea in plain words

A large language model (LLM) is a program trained on a huge amount of text and code to do one thing: predict what comes next. Given "The capital of France is", the likeliest next word is "Paris". Do that one word at a time and you get sentences, essays, code and conversations.
Three consequences you can already use:
It does not look things up. It produces what is statistically likely given everything it has seen. Often that equals the truth. Sometimes it is a confident, fluent mistake (a "hallucination").
It only knows what it was trained on, plus what you give it. Paste the log into the conversation and it can reason about that log. Without it, it can only guess.
It follows the text in front of it. Instructions, documents and your question all arrive as one stream of text. It cannot reliably tell "my boss told me this" from "the web page I'm reading told me this". That single fact is the root of prompt injection.
Three kinds of AI you will meet in security

Classifiers. Look at an input, output a label or score: spam or not, malware or benign, risky login or normal. Narrow, fast, measurable.
Anomaly detectors. Learn "normal" and flag outliers. Good at finding the unknown, noisy by nature.
Generative models (LLMs). Produce text, code and summaries. Flexible, easy to use, and the least predictable of the three.

Tokens. Text is cut into pieces (words or parts of words) and turned into numbers. Models have a context window: a limit on how many tokens they can consider at once. Anything outside it does not exist for the model.
Embeddings. Each token becomes a vector of numbers. Similar meanings end up near each other, which is what makes semantic search work.
Transformer layers. Stacked layers use attention to decide which earlier tokens matter for the next one. That is how it connects "it" back to the right noun.
Output. The model assigns a probability to every possible next token, and one is picked. Temperature controls how adventurous the pick is. Low is repeatable, high is varied.

Pretraining: learn to predict the next token across a very large text and code corpus. This is where the broad knowledge and the biases come from.
Fine-tuning and preference tuning: further training on curated examples and human or automated feedback, so the model follows instructions and avoids harmful output.
Deployment: wrapped with a system prompt, safety filters and often tools.

Prompting: the instructions and context you give. Quality in, quality out.
RAG (retrieval-augmented generation): search your own documents first, paste the relevant parts into the prompt, then ask. The model answers from your sources and can cite them. This is how most "chat with our runbooks" security tools work.
Tools and agents: the model is allowed to emit structured requests ("run this search", "query this host") that a program executes and feeds back. A loop of think, act, observe is an agent.

Training rewards plausible continuations, not verified facts, and there is no built-in "I don't know" check. It is most likely to invent when asked for specifics it never saw: exact CVE details, function names in obscure libraries, citations, IP addresses. Always verify identifiers against the source.
The objective and the math, briefly

Pretraining minimizes cross-entropy between the model's predicted next-token distribution and the real next token. Attention computes, for each position, a weighted sum of value vectors where the weights come from the similarity of a query to all keys, softmaxed. Stack dozens of these with feed-forward layers and you have billions of parameters, all adjusted by gradient descent. Nothing in the objective says "be truthful". Truthfulness is a side effect of the data plus later tuning.
Inference details that matter in practice

Sampling is random. The same prompt can yield different answers. For triage or detection work, set temperature low, request structured output (JSON), and validate it.
Context is the only memory. A long conversation is the whole transcript re-sent each time. Long contexts can dilute attention, so critical instructions belong at the start and end, and big inputs should be trimmed to what is relevant.
Cost and latency scale with tokens. Piping a full day of raw logs into a model is slow and expensive. Filter first with ordinary tools (grep, SQL, SIEM queries), then give the model the narrow slice.

In a classic injection bug (SQL injection) the cure is separating code from data with parameterized queries. In an LLM there is no such separation: the system prompt, the user's request and the untrusted document are all just tokens in one sequence. You can add instructions saying "ignore commands inside the document", and that helps, but it is a statistical nudge, not an enforced boundary. So defenses must be architectural: give the agent least privilege, require human approval for side effects, restrict where data can be sent, and treat model output as untrusted input to the next system.
Classical ML in security, for contrast

Supervised classifiers (random forests, gradient-boosted trees) on engineered features like URL length, entropy of a domain name, or header fields remain strong, cheap and explainable for phishing and malware detection.
Unsupervised methods (clustering, isolation forest, autoencoders) model normal behavior to surface outliers in auth logs or network flows.
Evaluate with the right metrics. Security data is wildly imbalanced (almost everything is benign), so accuracy is meaningless. A model that says "benign" every time can be 99.9% accurate. Use precision, recall, and the cost of a false negative versus a false positive.
When to pick which: if there is a stable, labeled, narrow decision at high volume, use a classifier. If the task is messy text that humans normally read (summaries, explanations, query drafting), use an LLM, with a human or a deterministic check behind it.
cd ~/ai
Predicting a category: logistic regression, nearest neighbors, decision trees and forests, naive Bayes, and a small neural network.
simple // the idea in plain words

A classifier predicts a category instead of a number: spam or not, malicious or benign, which of five attack families. The model usually outputs a probability and you pick a threshold (say 0.5) to turn it into a decision.
The simplest classifier is logistic regression. It does what linear regression does (a weighted sum of the features) and then squeezes the score through the sigmoid curve into a value between 0 and 1. In feature space, that is a straight dividing line (a flat plane in more dimensions): one side is class A, the other is class B.
Other families, in plain words:
k-nearest neighbors: to classify a new point, find the k most similar training points and let them vote.
Decision tree: a flowchart of yes/no questions learned from data ("failed logins > 10? new country? ..."). Easy to read.
simple // the idea in plain words

Random forest: many different trees voting together. Much more accurate and stable than one tree.
Naive Bayes: counts how often each word shows up in spam versus normal mail and multiplies the evidence. This is the classic spam filter.
Neural network: layers of weighted sums with bends between them, able to learn curved boundaries.
Try them on the ML playground: a straight-line model cannot separate two rings of points, a small network can.
Pick the simplest model that works. A readable tree or a logistic regression you can explain beats a mysterious one that scores 0.5 percent higher.

p = sigmoid(w . x + b) with sigmoid(z) = 1 / (1 + e^-z). It is trained by gradient descent on cross-entropy loss, which punishes confident wrong answers heavily. The weights are interpretable: a positive weight on "failed_logins" means more failures raise the odds of the malicious class. It is a fine, fast baseline, and often the right answer.

A tree picks, at each step, the question that best separates the classes (measured by Gini impurity or entropy) and recurses. Left alone it grows until it memorizes the data, so limit depth or leaf size. A random forest trains many trees on random subsets of rows and features and averages them, which cuts variance. Gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM) builds trees one after another, each fixing the previous errors, and is often the top performer on tabular security data. Neither needs feature scaling.

k-NN needs no training but stores everything and is slow at prediction time; it also requires scaled features. Naive Bayes assumes features are independent given the class (naive, but it works for text) and is quick, tiny and handles little data well.

One hidden layer: h = tanh(W1 x + b1), then p = sigmoid(W2 h + b2). Training uses backpropagation to get the gradient for every weight, then gradient descent. More hidden units means a more flexible boundary and more risk of overfitting. For images, audio and text, specialized networks (convolutional, transformer) learn their own features from raw input; for rows of tabular logs, trees often win.

Models need numbers. Typical features: URL length, count of digits and special characters, entropy of a domain name (random-looking domains from malware have high entropy), hour of day, bytes in versus out, ratio of failed to total logins, days since the account was created. Text becomes numbers with bag-of-words, TF-IDF or embeddings. Good features matter more than the choice of algorithm.

Small tabular data and a need to explain decisions: logistic regression or a shallow tree.
Larger tabular data, accuracy first: gradient-boosted trees.
Text, images, raw bytes, sequences: neural networks, or reuse a pretrained model and fine-tune it.
No labels at all: see unsupervised below.

Without labels you can still find structure. k-means groups points around k centers; isolation forest isolates points that are easy to split off, so outliers score high; autoencoders learn to reconstruct normal data and flag what they reconstruct badly; PCA shrinks dimensions. These power anomaly detection. The catch: "unusual" is not the same as "malicious", so expect many false positives and plan the triage workflow before the model.

Attacks are rare: maybe 0.1 percent of events. A model that says "benign" every time is 99.9 percent accurate and useless. Options: class weights, over- or under-sampling (only on the training split), better metrics (next chapter), and choosing the threshold on purpose.

A probability of 0.9 should be right about 90 percent of the time; many models are not calibrated, so check with a reliability plot and recalibrate (Platt scaling, isotonic regression) if you rely on the number. The threshold is a business decision: a missed breach and a false alarm cost different amounts.

Evasion: tweak malware or a phishing page slightly so it crosses the boundary (adversarial examples). Attackers do this by padding files, renaming strings or adding benign content.
Poisoning: slip mislabeled or crafted samples into the training data.
Model theft / extraction and membership inference: probe the model to copy it or learn whether a record was in training.
Drift: attacker and normal behavior change, and the model silently decays. Monitor input distributions and retrain on a schedule.
The chapter attacking AI covers these in more detail.

Judging a model honestly: the confusion matrix, precision and recall, thresholds, ROC curves, the base-rate trap and data leakage.
simple // the idea in plain words

You trained a classifier. Is it good? "It's 99 percent accurate" is almost never the right answer to give.
Count every prediction in one of four boxes (the confusion matrix), taking "malicious" as the thing we look for:
True positive (TP): said malicious, was malicious. Caught.
False positive (FP): said malicious, was fine. A false alarm.
False negative (FN): said fine, was malicious. A miss.
True negative (TN): said fine, was fine.
Two numbers matter most:
Precision = TP / (TP + FP): when the model raises an alarm, how often is it right?
Recall = TP / (TP + FN): of all the real attacks, what share did it catch?
Accuracy = (TP + TN) / everything. When attacks are rare it hides the truth: a model that never alerts is 99.9 percent accurate and catches nothing.
Ask two questions of every detector. How many real attacks does it miss? How many alerts does an analyst have to waste time on?

F1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall), a single score that is low if either is low. A model gives scores, and you choose the threshold: lower it and you catch more attacks (recall up) but raise more false alarms (precision down). Raise it and the reverse. There is no free setting; pick it from the cost of a miss versus the cost of an alert. In a SOC, alert fatigue is a real cost, because ignored alerts are how breaches slip through.

Sweep the threshold from 0 to 1 and plot true positive rate (recall) against false positive rate (FP / (FP + TN)). That is the ROC curve. The area under it (AUC) is the chance that a random malicious example scores higher than a random benign one: 0.5 is a coin flip, 1.0 is perfect. For very rare positives, a precision-recall curve is more informative than ROC because ROC's false positive rate looks tiny when negatives are huge.

Suppose 1 in 1,000 events is malicious, and your model has 99 percent recall and a 1 percent false positive rate. Out of 100,000 events: 100 attacks (99 caught), 99,900 benign (999 false alarms). Of 1,098 alerts only 99 are real, so precision is about 9 percent. Great-sounding rates can still bury analysts. Always compute precision at the real-world base rate.

Hold out a test set you do not touch while tuning.
Cross-validation (k folds) gives a steadier estimate on small data.
For logs or incidents, split by time. For users or hosts, keep all of one entity in the same split.
Duplicates between train and test (the same malware family, near-identical phishing emails) inflate scores. Group by family or campaign.

Leakage is when information from the answer slips into the features or from the test set into training. Typical causes: a feature computed after the event (a "blocked" flag), scaling or imputing on the whole dataset before splitting, tuning on the test set repeatedly, the same sample in both splits, and labels derived from the same rule the model then re-learns. If a result looks too good, assume leakage first.
Offline metrics are not production metrics

Drift: input data shifts (new software, new attacker tools, a company reorg) and the score drops without any code change. Monitor feature distributions and the alert-to-confirmed ratio, and set retraining triggers.
Label delay and bias: you only learn the truth for alerts someone investigated, so the labels you collect are biased toward what the old system flagged.
Feedback loops: if analysts only review what the model flagged, the model never sees its misses.
Adversarial pressure: your test set does not include an attacker who is trying to beat you. Keep a red-team set and re-score on it.

For numeric predictions: MAE (mean absolute error, in the units of the target, robust to outliers), RMSE (punishes big errors), R squared (the share of variance explained, can be misleading out of sample). Always compare to a dumb baseline such as predicting the mean, yesterday's value, or "benign".

State the data window, the split method, the base rate, the metrics at the chosen threshold with confidence intervals if you can (bootstrapping works), and the baseline you beat. Include failure cases you looked at by hand. A model card (what it is for, what data, known limits) is the short document that lets someone else trust or reject your work.

A teammate trained a phishing-email classifier and says it is "good enough: 85 percent accurate". You are given its predictions on a labeled test set in ~/model/predictions.csv (columns: actual, predicted).
Work out the model's recall on the phish class, as a whole-number percent (for example 60). That is the share of real phishing emails it actually caught.
Solve it in the sandbox. Type hint when stuck and submit <answer> when you have it.

The linear algebra and slope you need for machine learning, as a short refresher with Python: vectors, dot products, matrices and gradients.
simple // the idea in plain words

You do not need a math degree to follow machine learning. You need four ideas, and you can run all of them in Python.
A vector is a list of numbers. A login attempt could be [hour, failed_count, new_country] = [3, 12, 1]. Each position is a feature. Two vectors of the same length can be added or scaled position by position.
The dot product multiplies matching positions and adds: [1,2,3] . [4,5,6] = 1*4 + 2*5 + 3*6 = 32. In ML this means "weigh each feature and add up the evidence". A weight vector w says how much each feature matters, and w . x is the score.
A matrix is a grid of numbers. Rows can be examples and columns features. Multiplying a matrix by a vector does one dot product per row, so you score *all* your examples in one step. Neural networks are mostly big matrix multiplications.
simple // the idea in plain words

A slope tells you which way is downhill. Training a model means minimizing an error number. If you know the slope of the error at your current settings, you nudge the settings the opposite way. Repeat. That is gradient descent, and all of modern ML rests on it.
import numpy as np
w = np.array([0.5, 2.0, -1.0]) # weights
x = np.array([3, 12, 1]) # one login attempt
print(w @ x) # dot product = the score: 24.5
Vector = features. Dot product = weighted evidence. Matrix = many dot products at once. Slope = which way to adjust.

The length (norm) of a vector is the square root of the sum of squares. The distance between two points is the length of their difference. Nearest-neighbor methods use exactly this. Features on very different scales (a count in the thousands next to a flag of 0/1) distort distance, so we scale features first, for example subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation.
Cosine similarity is the dot product of two vectors divided by both lengths. It measures the angle, not the size, and is how text and embeddings are compared: a value near 1 means "pointing the same way". The chat search on this site uses a text-ranking relative of this idea.

Shapes matter. An (m, n) matrix times an (n, k) matrix gives an (m, k) matrix. The inner sizes must match. A dataset X with 1000 examples and 3 features has shape (1000, 3); weights w of shape (3,) give predictions X @ w of shape (1000,). Transpose (X.T) swaps rows and columns. The identity matrix I leaves vectors unchanged. Most "shape mismatch" errors in ML code are this rule being broken.

The derivative of a function at a point is its slope there. For f(x) = x^2 the slope is 2x: at x = 3 it is 6 (going up to the right), so to decrease f you move left. With many inputs, the gradient is the vector of slopes, one per input. It points uphill; you step the opposite way:
new_w = w - learning_rate * gradient
The learning rate is the step size. Too big and you overshoot and diverge; too small and training crawls.

If the output depends on g, which depends on x, the slopes multiply: d f(g(x)) / dx = f'(g(x)) * g'(x). Backpropagation is just this rule applied layer by layer, working backward from the error to every weight.
What to understand, not just compute

Linear means "weighted sum". A linear model draws a straight line (a flat plane in more dimensions) through feature space. Stacking linear layers alone gives another linear model; the nonlinearity between layers (ReLU, tanh) is what lets networks bend the boundary.
Loss surfaces: for linear regression with squared error the surface is a single bowl (convex), so gradient descent reaches the one minimum. For neural networks the surface is bumpy; you find a *good* point, not a guaranteed best, and different random starts give different models.
Stochastic / mini-batch gradient descent estimates the gradient from a small batch of examples. It is noisier but much cheaper per step, and the noise often helps. One pass over the data is an epoch.
Dimensions: with many features, points are far apart and distance gets less meaningful (the "curse of dimensionality"), and the risk of fitting noise rises. This is why feature choice and regularization matter.
Eigenvectors / PCA: the directions along which data varies most; PCA keeps the top few to shrink dimensions or visualize. You will meet it in anomaly detection write-ups. Know what it is for before you know how to derive it.

Compute the dot product of [2, 0, 1] and [1, 5, 3] by hand, then with NumPy. (5)
What is the shape of A @ B if A is (4, 3) and B is (3, 2)? What if B is (2, 3)? ((4,2); error)
For f(x) = (x - 4)^2, start at x = 0 with learning rate 0.1 and do three gradient steps by hand. The gradient is 2(x - 4). (0 -> 0.8 -> 1.44 -> 1.952)

Free, high-quality material: Khan Academy linear algebra, 3Blue1Brown's "Essence of linear algebra" videos, and the NumPy quickstart. Check the AI reading list for dated links. This chapter is a refresher; if a term here feels new, spend an evening with those videos before the next chapter.

Fitting a line to data: linear regression, the loss, gradient descent, overfitting and why you hold out a test set.
simple // the idea in plain words

Machine learning replaces hand-written rules with a model fitted to examples. The simplest supervised kind is regression: predict a number from other numbers.
Example: you have 50 past incidents with (number of affected hosts, hours to contain). Plot them and draw the straight line that passes closest to all the points. Now for a new incident with 30 hosts you can read off an estimate. That line is a linear regression model: hours = w * hosts + b. The slope w and intercept b are the parameters the machine learned.
How does it find the best line? It needs a number that says how wrong a line is. For each example take the gap between the prediction and the real value, square it, and average them. That is the mean squared error (MSE), the loss. Training means changing w and b to make the loss small.
The three words to keep: features (inputs), labels (the right answers), model (the formula with adjustable numbers). Learning from labeled examples is supervised learning.
A model never "understands" anything. It finds numbers that make a loss small on the data you gave it. Everything else follows from that sentence.

Start with any w and b (for example 0). Compute the loss, then the slope of the loss for each parameter, then take a small step downhill:
for epoch in range(1000):
 pred = w * X + b
 err = pred - y
 w -= lr * (2 * (err * X).mean())
 b -= lr * (2 * err.mean())
The learning rate lr sets the step. If the loss goes up or turns into nan, it is too large. For plain linear regression there is also a direct formula (the normal equation) that jumps to the answer, and scikit-learn's LinearRegression uses linear algebra for that. Gradient descent matters because it works for models that have no formula, including neural networks. Play with this on the ML playground.

With several features the model is a dot product: y = w . x + b. The same code works with X as a matrix and w as a vector (see the math refresher). Scale your features (mean 0, spread 1), or gradient descent zigzags because one feature's units dwarf the others.

If you check the model on the same data it learned from, you only learn how well it memorized. So split the data:
Train (about 70 to 80 percent): fit the parameters.
Validation: compare model choices and settings.
Test: touch once at the end for an honest score.
Time-ordered data (logs, incidents) must be split by time (train on the past, test on the future), not shuffled, or you leak the future into training.

A line too simple for the data underfits (high error everywhere). A model with too many knobs (a degree-15 polynomial, a huge tree) can pass through every training point and overfit: low training error, high test error, because it learned the noise. The fix menu: more data, fewer or simpler features, regularization (penalize large weights so the model stays simple), early stopping, and cross-validation to measure honestly.

Ridge (L2) adds lambda * sum(w^2) to the loss, which shrinks weights toward zero and is stable when features are correlated. Lasso (L1) adds lambda * sum(|w|) and tends to push some weights exactly to zero, acting as feature selection. lambda is a hyperparameter: you set it, you do not learn it, and you tune it on the validation set.
Bias, variance, and the honest error

Expected test error splits into bias (the model family is too simple, systematic miss), variance (the fit changes wildly with different training samples) and irreducible noise (no model removes it). More complexity lowers bias and raises variance, which is the shape behind the overfitting curve. Learning curves (error versus training-set size) tell you whether more data will help: if train and validation error have converged high, you need a better model, not more data.

Residual plots: if the errors show a pattern instead of noise, the model is missing structure (a curve, an interaction).
Outliers pull a squared-error fit hard; consider robust losses or inspect those rows.
Leakage: a feature that secretly contains the answer (the ticket's "resolved_at" used to predict resolution time) gives a gorgeous test score and a useless model. Ask of each feature: *will I know this at prediction time?*
Extrapolation: a model fitted on 5 to 50 hosts says nothing reliable about 5,000.
Correlation is not cause: regression finds association in the data you have.

Forecasting capacity and log volume, estimating time-to-contain, scoring risk, baselining normal traffic per host so that big deviations stand out. For anomalies, a regression baseline plus a threshold on the residual is a cheap first detector.
