Message-based vectors: email, SMS (smishing), instant messaging. Also image-based and file-based (malicious attachments).
Voice calls (vishing), removable devices (USB drops), vulnerable software (client-based vs agentless), unsupported systems.
Unsecure networks: wireless, wired, Bluetooth. Open service ports, default credentials, supply chain (MSPs, vendors, suppliers).
Human vectors: phishing, vishing, smishing, misinformation/disinformation, impersonation, business email compromise, pretexting, watering hole, brand impersonation, typosquatting.

A threat vector is the path an attacker uses to get in. The attack surface is every place a vector could exist. This objective splits into technical vectors (software, networks, devices) and human vectors (social engineering).

| Vector | What it means | Key defenses
 | Message-based | Email, SMS, instant messages, collaboration chat carry links, attachments and scams. Email is the biggest one | Spam and attachment filtering, link rewriting, DMARC/DKIM/SPF, user awareness
 | Image-based | Malicious code or links hidden in image files (SVG with scripts, steganography) | Content inspection, don't auto-render untrusted images
 | File-based | Documents, PDFs, archives, macros, executables | Sandboxing, disable macros, attachment scanning, application control
 | Voice call | Vishing, spoofed caller ID, deepfake voice | Call-back verification, policy, awareness
 | Removable device | USB drives dropped in a parking lot, malicious cables, autorun malware | Disable USB ports or autorun, USB data blockers, endpoint control

| Vulnerable software | Unpatched code. Client-based (agent installed) or agentless (scanned remotely) | Patching, vulnerability scanning
 | Unsupported systems and applications | No vendor patches (end of life). Becomes a permanent hole | Replace, isolate, compensating controls
 | Unsecure network | Wireless (open Wi-Fi, weak WPA, rogue AP), wired (unprotected ports), Bluetooth (bluejacking, bluesnarfing) | Encryption, 802.1X, NAC, disable unused ports
 | Open service ports | Every listening port is an entry point | Close unused ports, host firewall, scan regularly
 | Default credentials | admin/admin on routers, cameras, IoT | Change at install, password policy
 | Supply chain | Attack through a trusted vendor, MSP or supplier | Vendor assessment, contracts, monitoring

Supply chain pieces to recognize: a managed service provider (MSP) has remote access to many customers, so compromising one MSP can reach all of them. A vendor supplies hardware or software. A supplier provides parts and components. Tainted hardware, counterfeit parts and poisoned updates are all supply chain attacks.

Social engineering manipulates people rather than systems. Attackers rely on psychological levers: authority, urgency, scarcity, social proof, familiarity/liking, trust, fear and consensus.
#### Phishing family
Phishing: fraudulent email pretending to be a trusted sender, tricking you into clicking, opening or entering credentials. Clues: wrong or look-alike domain, mismatched link text, generic greeting, urgency, bad grammar (though modern ones are polished), unexpected attachment.
Spear phishing: aimed at a specific person or group with personal details.
Whaling: spear phishing aimed at senior executives.
Vishing: voice phishing by phone, often with spoofed caller ID.
Smishing: phishing by SMS text message.
Pharming: redirects victims to a fake site by corrupting DNS or the hosts file.

Typosquatting (URL hijacking): registers a mistyped domain (exampel.com) to catch typos. Related: brand impersonation (a site or email using a company's branding).
Business email compromise (BEC): a spoofed or hijacked executive or vendor email asks staff to wire money or change payment details. Defended with out-of-band verification.
#### Impersonation and pretexting
Impersonation: pretending to be someone else (IT support, auditor, delivery person, executive).
Pretexting: an invented scenario that justifies the request ("I'm from payroll and need to confirm your bank details").
Identity fraud: using someone's stolen identity for gain.
Eliciting information: casual conversation that draws out details without the target noticing.
Defense: policies for verifying identity, call-back procedures, escalation, and a culture where people can say "let me verify that".
#### Watering hole attack

The attacker compromises a website that the target group already visits (an industry forum, a supplier portal) and waits. Visitors get infected with no click on a bad link. Defense: patching, web filtering, browser isolation, endpoint protection, monitoring for odd behavior after visiting trusted sites. This is also why you can't rely on "only visit trusted sites".
#### Other social engineering
Misinformation / disinformation: false information, spread by mistake or on purpose, to influence behavior or reputation.
Dumpster diving: reading discarded paper for data. Shred documents.
Shoulder surfing: watching a screen or keypad. Privacy screens, awareness of surroundings.
Tailgating / piggybacking: following someone through a secured door. Access control vestibules, badge checks.
Baiting: leaving something tempting (infected USB drive) for a victim to pick up.

Quid pro quo: offering a service or benefit in return for information or access.
Influence campaigns: coordinated misinformation (often state-backed) to shape opinion.
Hoax: a false warning (a fake virus alert) to cause panic or unneeded actions.

Vectors, with the lesson's examples
A threat vector (attack vector) is how an attacker gets in. Attackers hunt for unknown vectors as well as known ones.
Messaging: email links and attachments, SMS texts, and instant or direct messages that let the attacker talk to you one on one. Typical lures are fake invoices for services never rendered and cryptocurrency scams (steal a wallet or sell coin that does not exist). A fake "USPS package suspended, incorrect address" text from an odd sender is the standard example. Report junk instead of clicking.

Images: SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) is an XML file, not just a picture, so it can carry HTML or JavaScript. A few lines of XML can draw a triangle and also run a script (a cross-site scripting demo). Browsers usually block XSS, but a browser bug or a non-XSS script can slip through. Input validation on SVG helps, and some browsers let you disable image types.
Files: executables run in memory, but also PDFs (text, images and scripting in one container), compressed archives (zip, rar hide one bad file among thousands), and Office files with macros that can gather data and send it out. Browser extensions and add-ins can themselves be malicious.
Voice: vishing, spam over IP (automated VoIP spam), war dialing (hunting for unpublished numbers), and DoS through messaging systems.

Removable media: a $10 USB drive can bypass millions in firewalls and IPS, especially against an air-gapped network. Drop drives in the parking lot and wait. A modified USB can present itself as a keyboard and type commands on its own. It also makes it easy to copy large amounts of data out.
Vulnerable software: keep updating (monthly Microsoft updates plus every other product). Agentless web-based systems have a central server: infect it and every client that logs in gets a fresh infected instance.
Unsupported systems: no patches = large risk. The classic case is an old OS on an old PC under a desk that IT does not even know exists. Fix by keeping an up-to-date inventory and scanning the network regularly.

Unsecure networks: use WPA3 instead of WEP, WPA or WPA2, scan for open or rogue wireless access points, and turn on 802.1X for wired and wireless. Bluetooth can be used for recon or exploited via weak implementations.
Open ports: a web server uses TCP 80 and 443. Each new service needs its own port, so more services means more exposure and more misconfiguration chances. Use port-based or application-aware firewalls to expose only the one service needed.
Default credentials: admin/admin on routers and access points. Many devices now force a change at first login. Sites such as routerpasswords.com list defaults for thousands of devices, so attackers can look them up.

Supply chain: tampering can happen at manufacturing (maker unaware) or afterward by a third party. An MSP is a high-value target. The Target 2013 breach came through an HVAC contractor network, then to the point-of-sale systems to steal card numbers. Counterfeit hardware: fake Cisco Catalyst switches in 2020, spotted because they could not update software properly.
Phishing details
Phishing is social engineering through mail, text or other channels to make you give up private data. Check where links really point, and watch for off fonts and spacing, a deadline ("you will be blocked"), and a sender whose domain does not fit the service (an iCloud sender for a Rackspace notice).
Best practice: never click a link in an email. A fake login page can closely copy the real one, sometimes even reusing the same email image.

Stolen email access is powerful: send mail as you, search for financial info, and use password reset on other sites (the reset goes to the attacker-controlled mailbox).
Typosquatting example from the lesson: professormessor.com instead of professormesser.com. Pretexting is outright lying with a made-up story (a "Visa" call about a failed electric bill payment). Vishing spoofs caller ID. Smishing is SMS phishing. Other scams to know: fake check scam, phone verification code scam.
Impersonation details
Scam call samples: a "Microsoft Windows" urgent checkup, a "US Treasury enforcement action", a "0% rate for your excellent payment history". Impersonation is pretending to be someone you are not, to build trust: claim to be the help desk, a VP of finance or manufacturing (rank), or bury you in technical jargon.

Goal is eliciting information through a story, never a direct request for your bank number.
Identity fraud: open credit cards in your name mailed to their address (shows up as nonpayment on your credit report), open bank accounts in your name to stash money and take loans, or tax fraud by filing your return first and collecting your refund.
Prevention: do not volunteer information, remember help desks never need your password, never give personal data (address, SSN, birthday) by phone or email, and verify by calling a public number yourself. Verification should be normal procedure in your organization.
Watering hole details

When employees will not plug in parking-lot USBs or click email links, the attacker poisons a site you will visit later (a local sandwich shop's ordering site). It needs research on which third-party sites staff use plus a vulnerability on that site, or emailing attachments to that third party to get into their network and then yours.
January 2017 example: the Polish Financial Supervision Authority, the Mexican National Banking and Securities Commission and a state-owned bank in Uruguay had malicious JavaScript added, served only to IP addresses of particular financial organizations; everyone else saw a normal site. The outcome was never made public. Symantec antivirus did detect and block the code on visitors who had it.

Defense is defense in depth: antivirus, firewall and IPS stacked (that is why firewalls and IPS ship together). The firewall may pass the traffic, but the IPS recognizes the malicious content.
Misinformation and brand impersonation
Misinformation and disinformation are factually incorrect, not just opinion, usually meant to divide or confuse groups. Influence campaigns are often run by nation states on social media or even in ads, to persuade or to distract from damaging truths.
Steps: create many fake accounts, post content from one, amplify with likes, shares and follows, the platform's algorithm shows it to real users, who share it, and eventually mass media reports on it.

Brand impersonation: build hundreds or thousands of sites using a famous brand (Coca-Cola, McDonald's), get them indexed by Google, and search results redirect victims to a "you won" or "download this software" page that delivers adware, tracking or data exfiltration.

Spear phishing = targeted. Whaling = targeted at executives. Vishing = voice. Smishing = SMS.
Watering hole hits a site the *targets use*, not the targets directly.
Typosquatting = a deliberately mistyped domain. Pharming = DNS redirect with a correct URL typed.
Tailgating can be unknowing (someone follows you through); piggybacking often has the authorized person's consent. The exam usually treats them together.
Default credentials and open ports are configuration vectors, not software bugs.
The attack surface shrinks when you remove unused services, ports, accounts and software.

Application: memory injection, buffer overflow, race conditions (TOCTOU), malicious updates.
Web: SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS). OS-based, hardware (firmware, end-of-life, legacy).
Virtualization: VM escape, resource reuse. Cloud-specific, supply chain (service/hardware/software providers).
Cryptographic weaknesses, misconfiguration, mobile (sideloading, jailbreaking), zero-day.
A vulnerability is a weakness an attacker can exploit. Objective 2.3 lists the families you must recognize in a scenario. For each one, learn what it is, how it shows up, and the mitigation.

Memory injection: malicious code is placed into a running process's memory (often by a malicious DLL or code injection into a trusted process), so it runs with that process's privileges and hides inside a legitimate name. Mitigation: endpoint protection, memory protections, application control, patching.
Buffer overflow: the program writes more data into a fixed-size buffer than it can hold, spilling into adjacent memory. The attacker can crash the program or overwrite a return address to run their own code. Mitigations: input validation and bounds checking, safe languages, ASLR (random memory layout), DEP/NX (data pages can't execute), stack canaries, patching. Seen as a crash or unexpected behavior after oversized input.

Race condition: the outcome depends on timing between operations. The classic is time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU): the program checks a condition, then acts on it, and an attacker changes the state in between. Related: time-of-use errors and file/temp-file races. Mitigation: atomic operations, locks, minimize the gap, secure coding.
Malicious update: an attacker poisons a software update channel or fake update prompt to deliver malware (this is also a supply chain risk). Mitigation: update only from the vendor, verify digital signatures and hashes, use trusted repositories, test updates, application control.

SQL injection (SQLi): user input is placed into a SQL statement, letting the attacker change the query (for example ' OR 1=1 --). Impact: read, change or delete data, bypass login. Mitigations: parameterized queries / prepared statements, input validation, stored procedures, least-privilege database accounts, web application firewall. Don't rely on blocklists of bad characters.
Cross-site scripting (XSS): the attacker gets script to run in another user's browser in the context of a trusted site.
 | Type | How it works
 | Reflected (non-persistent) | Script is in a crafted link; the server echoes it back immediately in the response. Needs the victim to click
 | Stored (persistent) | Script is saved on the server (comment, profile) and runs for every visitor. Highest impact
 | DOM-based | The client-side JavaScript itself writes untrusted data into the page; the server may never see it

Impact: steal session cookies, redirect users, act as the user. Mitigations: output encoding, input validation, Content Security Policy, HttpOnly cookies, frameworks that escape by default. Contrast with CSRF, which makes a logged-in browser send an unintended request (see 2.4).

Unpatched flaws, privilege escalation bugs, insecure default settings, unneeded services, outdated or end-of-life OS versions. Mitigation: patch management, hardening baselines, remove unused components, endpoint protection, vulnerability scanning.

Firmware flaws (BIOS/UEFI, network device firmware, printers): hard to patch and invisible to most tools.
End-of-life hardware that no longer receives updates.
Legacy devices that can't support modern security.
Speculative execution CPU flaws (Meltdown, Spectre) that let one process read another's data.
Mitigations: firmware updates, retire unsupported hardware, secure boot, supply chain verification, isolation.

VM escape: code running in a guest breaks out to the hypervisor or other VMs. Rare but severe, because the hypervisor controls everything.
VM sprawl: unmanaged, forgotten virtual machines that never get patched or monitored.
Resource reuse: memory or storage from one VM leaking into another.
Mitigations: patch the hypervisor, limit who can manage it, inventory and decommission VMs, segment management networks, separate sensitive VMs.

Misconfigured storage buckets, overly broad IAM roles, exposed management consoles and APIs, weak keys, lack of logging, and misunderstanding the shared responsibility model (the provider secures the cloud itself; the customer secures their data, access and configuration). Mitigations: CSPM tools, least privilege IAM, encryption, MFA, logging, regular configuration review.

Compromise through a service provider, hardware provider or software provider: a tainted firmware, a backdoored library, a compromised MSP. Mitigations: vendor due diligence, software bills of materials, signed code, limit vendor access, monitor third-party connections, validate hardware sources.

Open permissions (world-readable files and shares), unsecured admin accounts, default accounts and passwords, open ports and unneeded services, insecure protocols (Telnet, FTP, HTTP), weak encryption settings, verbose error messages that leak details.
Mitigations: secure baselines and hardening guides, configuration management, change control, automated audits, vulnerability scans.

Jailbreaking / rooting removes OS protections and lets unsigned code run.
Sideloading installs apps outside the official store, skipping its review.
Outdated OS, malicious apps, unencrypted data, insecure Wi-Fi, lost devices.
Mitigations: MDM, app allow lists, enforce updates and encryption, block jailbroken devices.

A flaw unknown to the vendor (and so unpatched) that attackers are already exploiting or could. The vendor has had "zero days" to fix it. Mitigations: defense in depth, segmentation, EDR/behavior detection, rapid response, virtual patching (WAF/IPS rules), threat intelligence. Once a patch exists it is no longer a zero-day, only a known unpatched vulnerability.

Memory and buffer attacks
Nothing runs unless it is loaded from disk into memory. Malware can run as its own process or inject itself into an existing process between that process's start and end addresses. Benefits: it dodges tools looking for a malicious process and inherits that process's rights, which is a quick privilege escalation.
DLL injection: get a malicious DLL onto storage, then put its path into the target process. When the process reaches that reference it loads the DLL into memory and the malware runs.
Buffer overflow: writing more than the area expects (the developer should do bounds checking, for example only 8 bytes). Overflow is hard to exploit reliably because it can just crash the app, so attackers look for one that is repeatable and always gives an advantage.

Lesson example: variable A holds 8 bytes, variable B (2 bytes, value 1979) controls permissions, under 2000 means user and over 24,000 means admin. Typing the 9-character word "excessive" into A spills the ninth character e (hex 65) into B and changes it to 25,856, so the attacker is admin without credentials.
Race conditions
Two events happen at nearly the same time and the application did not plan for it. TOCTOU (time of check to time of use): the app reads a value, something else changes it before the app uses it.
Bank example: two users each transfer $50 from account A to B, both starting at $100 each. Deposits update instantly but withdrawals are not shown immediately, so after both withdraw, user 2 still sees A with $50 when it really should be $0 and B ends up with $200.

Real cases: the Mars rover Spirit (2004) looped on reboots because of a file system error each boot, fixed by sending code to bypass it. Pwn2Own Vancouver 2023: a TOCTOU in the Tesla Model 3 infotainment system via Bluetooth gave root on that system and a $100,000 prize plus the car.
Updates and OS
Updates are effectively new installs, so they can carry malware. Best practices: backup first, use trusted sources, ideally download from the developer, and prefer digitally signed updates. A random "update Chrome" pop-up after clicking a search result is suspect, while one at browser launch is more trustworthy. Built-in app updaters verify signatures automatically.

That trust is not total: SolarWinds Orion (reported December 2020). Attackers got into the development system months before and their code was rolled into a normal, digitally signed update that auto-distributed to customers. Hundreds of large government agencies and companies were hit and attackers pivoted to other systems. Rare, but shows a trusted process distributing malware.

OS updates: operating systems are huge (Windows 11 has tens of millions of lines of code), so unknown vulnerabilities exist. Microsoft releases patches on Patch Tuesday, the second Tuesday of each month. May 2023 had almost 50 patches (8 elevation of privilege, 4 security feature bypass, 12 remote code execution and others); April 2023 had almost 100. The Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) lists them. Once a flaw is public, attackers reverse engineer the patch, so patch fast. In large environments, test first, expect some patches to need a reboot, and keep a backup for rollback.
SQL injection
Code injection types include HTML, SQL and XML. SQL is the usual way apps talk to databases. Normal query: SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = 'Professor'. Injected: ... name = 'Professor' OR 1=1, which is always true and returns everything. If you ever see 1=1 in a request, think SQL injection.

It needs no extra software and no victim clicks, just typing into an existing input field. Impact: view, change or delete everything, or take the database down.
Demo: WebGoat (webgoat.org), an intentionally vulnerable app. Input of employee name Smith and a transaction authentication number; injecting ' or '1'='1 into the number field returned every record.
Cross-site scripting
Abbreviated XSS because CSS already means cascading style sheets. Named for early browser flaws where info from one site leaked to another. It abuses the browser's trust of websites, usually with JavaScript.

Reflected (non-persistent): attacker sends a link containing a script (email, text). The victim clicks, lands on a legitimate trusted site that echoes the script from the input (for example a search box), and the script quietly sends cookies and session IDs to the attacker, giving the same access as the victim. Demo: script pasted into a credit card number field showing an alert with the session ID cookie; a real attacker would silently send it.
Stored (persistent): the payload is saved on a site such as a social network post. Everyone viewing it runs the script, and it can even include code to re-share itself so it spreads.

Subaru (June 2017, researcher Aaron Guzman): the login token never expired and let you do any service request, and you could add your email to someone else's account to manage their car too. Combined with XSS, a stolen token would work forever. Reported by the researcher and fixed.
Defenses: do not click untrusted links (type trusted domains yourself), limit or disable JavaScript (limited protection, breaks sites), keep the browser patched, and developers must validate all inputs.
Hardware, firmware and EOL

Embedded devices (thermostats, HVAC controllers, time clocks, stoves, fridges, garage doors, door locks, IoT) run a hidden OS called firmware that only the manufacturer can update. Makers often do not prioritize security: Trane ComfortLink II thermostats were reported vulnerable in April 2014, first patch April 2015, another January 2016, while desktop OS vendors patch within about a month.
EOL (end of life): manufacturer announces it will stop selling the product, but support and patches may continue for a while. EOSL (end of service life): no more security patches (maybe paid premium support). EOSL is the date that matters most; replace gear once it hits it.

Legacy platforms (old OS, old application, old middleware) that are critical to the mission cannot be turned off easily. Compare the risk of keeping versus replacing, add mitigations such as extra firewall rules to limit who can reach it and extra IPS signatures for older OSes, and build a plan to replace it.
Virtualization
Cloud VMs get created and torn down constantly with varying CPUs, memory and storage, which makes posture management harder. Apply the same OS best practices to VMs. Virtual-specific issues include local privilege escalation, command injection and information disclosure.

VM escape: normally a VM cannot reach another VM on the same hypervisor, but flaws let an attacker hop between them, and a hypervisor may host tens or hundreds. March 2017 Pwn2Own: a bug in the Microsoft Edge JavaScript engine reached the Edge sandbox, then a Windows 10 kernel bug gave full guest control, then a VMware hardware-simulation bug let them hop to another VM. It was first demonstrated at the contest, so VMware had time to patch.
Resource reuse: the hypervisor can overcommit (three VMs with 2 GB each on a 4 GB host). With a hypervisor memory-management bug, one VM can write to a memory area another VM reads. Fix: update the hypervisor.
Cloud

Stats from the lesson: roughly 76% of organizations did not use MFA on the central cloud console, and up to 63% of code in the cloud was unpatched, some with CVSS 7 or higher. Public cloud means anyone can try to connect, so expect DoS/DDoS, authentication bypass from weak or misconfigured auth, directory traversal (moving around the web server folder structure) and remote code execution on unpatched systems. Examples: Log4j and Spring Cloud Function, easy to exploit and giving full control. Also XSS from missing input validation, out-of-bounds write (writing to memory you are not authorized to, causing RCE or a crash) and SQL injection against cloud-hosted databases.
Supply chain

The chain runs from raw materials through suppliers, manufacturers and distributors to customers; compromise at any point matters. Service providers (network, utilities, cleaning, payroll, accounting, cloud) can expose sensitive data, so contracts often include the right to audit and ongoing security audits.
Target, November 2013: over 40 million cards stolen. An HVAC firm in Pennsylvania got malware through an email, it was a Target supplier with access to Target's HVAC systems, and the HVAC and cash register networks were not segmented, so attackers reached every register. They stayed in for months. Lesson: non-IT providers count, and segmentation matters.

Hardware: treat new gear as untrusted out of the box. Use a short list of trusted vendors and procurement and implementation policies. July 2022: the DHS arrested the head of a reseller of counterfeit Cisco products (over a billion dollars, about 30 companies, selling since 2013, mostly made in China). Devices failed and some caught fire. Verify hardware before production.
Software: check digital signatures, think about auto-updates, and note that open source can also be changed maliciously. SolarWinds Orion: about 18,000 customers including Fortune 500 and US federal agencies; malicious code signed and shipped in March and June 2020, detected only in December 2020, reaching Microsoft, Cisco, Intel, the Pentagon, Homeland Security and Treasury.
Misconfigurations

Open data: attackers scan for unsecured cloud storage. June 2017: 14 million Verizon records sat in an open Amazon S3 bucket left by a third party; found by a researcher, not an attacker.
Unsecured admin accounts: Linux root, Windows Administrator (the superuser accounts). Weak passwords such as 123456, ninja and football are brute-forced. Best practice: disable direct root/administrator login, log in as a normal user and elevate with su/sudo or Windows Run as administrator, and keep admin accounts very few.
Insecure protocols: Telnet, FTP, SMTP and IMAP are cleartext. A Wireshark capture of HTTP shows browser version, referring URLs and cookies. Use SSH, SFTP, HTTPS and so on. The "wall of sheep" at DEFCON 22 displayed credentials captured from HTTP, IMAP and POP3.

Default credentials: the Mirai botnet tries 60+ default username/password pairs on IoT devices (cameras, routers, doorbells, garage openers). It is open source, so researchers and attackers both use it.
Open ports: each inbound service opens a port. Firewall rule sets are large and it is easy to accidentally expose something, so audit the rule base regularly.
Mobile
Small, always moving, always online, holding personal and corporate data. Rooting is Android and jailbreaking is iOS: replacing the OS with a third-party one, which defeats MDM controls. Sideloading is installing apps outside the approved store or company app library, easily done once rooted or jailbroken. Policies (AUP, employee handbook) forbid this and violations can lead to dismissal.
Zero-day

Researchers and attackers both hunt for flaws; attackers keep theirs secret, so the vendor has no idea and there is no patch. Exploiting an unpatched, unknown flaw is a zero-day attack. Track vulnerabilities at CVE (cve.mitre.org). Examples in the lesson: April 2023 Chrome zero-day (memory corruption and sandbox escape); May 2023 Microsoft patch for self-signed code running during the UEFI boot despite secure boot; May 2023 Apple iOS/iPadOS fixes for a sandbox escape, an information disclosure and arbitrary code execution, some already used in the wild.

| Scenario | Answer
 | Input like ' OR '1'='1 changes a login query | SQL injection
 | A comment box runs JavaScript for everyone who loads the page | Stored XSS
 | Oversized input crashes a program and runs shellcode | Buffer overflow
 | File permissions change between a check and the open | Race condition (TOCTOU)
 | Guest VM reads the host or other guests | VM escape
 | Phone has unsigned apps installed through a side channel | Sideloading / jailbreak
 | A vendor's patch was altered before download | Malicious update / supply chain
 | Flaw with no patch available being exploited | Zero-day
 | Forgotten test VMs that never get patched | VM sprawl

Malware: ransomware, trojan, worm (self-spreading), spyware, bloatware, virus, keylogger, logic bomb, rootkit.
Physical: brute force, RFID cloning. Network: DDoS (amplified, reflected), DNS attacks, wireless, on-path, credential replay, malicious code.
Application: injection, buffer overflow, replay, privilege escalation, forgery (CSRF/SSRF), directory traversal.
Crypto: downgrade, collision, birthday. Password: spraying (one password, many accounts) vs brute force.
Indicators: account lockout, concurrent session usage, blocked content, impossible travel, resource consumption/inaccessibility, out-of-cycle logging, missing logs, published/documented.
Objective 2.4 is a scenario objective: you are shown symptoms or logs and must name the attack or malware. Learn each item as what it does, how it looks, how to stop it.

Malware is software built to harm or take control of a system. Infection routes: email attachments, drive-by downloads, malicious updates, removable media, trojanized apps, exploited vulnerabilities.
 | Type | Defining behavior | Notes
 | Virus | Needs a host file and user action to spread | Attaches to programs or documents (macros). Can be fileless, living only in memory
 | Worm | Self-replicates across networks without user action | Exploits vulnerabilities, spreads fast, can overload networks (Slammer, WannaCry). Stop with patching, segmentation, firewalls
 | Trojan | Disguised as useful software | Often installs a backdoor. RAT (remote access trojan) gives remote control
 | Ransomware | Encrypts data and demands payment | Often exfiltrates first (double extortion). Defend with offline backups, patching, EDR, awareness

| Spyware | Secretly gathers information | Browser hijackers, adware, tracking cookies, keylogging
 | Bloatware | Preinstalled unwanted software | Wastes resources, expands attack surface; remove it
 | Keylogger | Records keystrokes | Captures passwords. Hardware or software
 | Rootkit | Hides deep in the OS or firmware | Gives persistent privileged access and hides processes. Often needs a reinstall or reflash. Boot-time scanning and secure boot help
 | Logic bomb | Triggers on a condition (date, event, a user being removed) | Common insider tool. Detect with code review and file integrity monitoring
 | Botnet / bot | Compromised hosts controlled remotely | Used for DDoS, spam, credential stuffing. Controlled via command and control (C2)

| Fileless malware | Runs in memory using built-in tools (PowerShell, WMI) | Leaves little on disk, so signature AV misses it. Use behavior detection (EDR)
 | Cryptojacking | Uses your CPU/GPU to mine cryptocurrency | Symptom: slow systems, high CPU and power
Signs of ransomware: files renamed/encrypted, a ransom note, backups deleted or encrypted. Signs of a worm: unusual network traffic and many hosts failing at once. Signs of rootkit: security tools disabled, strange behavior that scans can't find.

Brute force (physical): forcing locks, doors or enclosures.
RFID cloning: copying the data from an access card or fob to make a duplicate. Defend with encrypted/mutual-auth cards and shielded wallets.
Environmental attacks: heat, cooling failure, power loss, water, fire against infrastructure.
Skimming: a device on a card reader steals card data.
Malicious USB cables and devices that inject keystrokes.

#### Denial of service
DoS: one source overwhelms a service. DDoS: many sources (usually a botnet). Impact is on availability.
Amplified: a small request produces a large reply (DNS, NTP). Reflected: spoofed source address sends the replies to the victim. Combined: reflection + amplification.
Application-layer attacks target a web app (HTTP floods, Slowloris). Operational technology (OT) DoS can affect physical processes.
Mitigation: upstream DDoS scrubbing/CDN, rate limiting, redundancy, anycast, ISP help, WAF.
#### DNS attacks
DNS poisoning / cache poisoning: false records get cached so users are sent to the attacker's address.
Domain hijacking: attacker takes over the domain registration or registrar account.
URL redirection and DNS tunneling (data hidden in DNS queries to exfiltrate or run C2).
Domain reputation matters: monitoring newly registered, look-alike domains.

Mitigation: DNSSEC (signed records), registrar lock and MFA, restrict zone transfers, DNS filtering and logging.
#### Wireless attacks
Rogue access point: unauthorized AP plugged into the network.
Evil twin: rogue AP imitating a legitimate SSID so users connect to it (often paired with a captive portal). Defense: 802.1X/WPA3-Enterprise with certificate validation, VPN on public Wi-Fi.
Deauthentication: forged frames disconnect clients (used to force reconnects/capture handshakes). 802.11w (management frame protection) mitigates it.
Jamming: radio noise blocks the signal.
WPS PIN attacks, Bluetooth attacks (bluejacking sends unwanted messages, bluesnarfing steals data), NFC relay and war driving.
#### On-path and replay

On-path (formerly man-in-the-middle): attacker sits between two parties, reading or altering traffic. ARP poisoning is a common local technique. SSL stripping downgrades HTTPS to HTTP. Defense: encryption (TLS), HSTS, certificate validation, Dynamic ARP Inspection.
Browser on-path (man-in-the-browser): malware in the browser alters transactions.
Replay attack: capture a valid message (authentication token, session) and resend it. Defense: timestamps, nonces, one-time session tokens, sequence numbers, MFA. Pass-the-hash replays a captured hash instead of a password.
Session hijacking: stealing a session ID/cookie to impersonate a logged-in user.

Injection: SQL, command, LDAP, XML. Untrusted input is interpreted as commands. Fix: validation, parameterization, least privilege.
Buffer overflow: too much data overwrites memory (see 2.3).
Privilege escalation: gaining more rights. Vertical (user to admin) or horizontal (to another user's data).
Forgery: CSRF (a logged-in browser sends an unintended request; defended with anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies) and SSRF (the server is tricked into making requests to internal systems or cloud metadata).
Directory traversal: ../../ sequences read files outside the web root. Fix: canonicalize and validate paths.
Replay, race conditions and cross-site scripting also appear here.
API attacks and XML external entity (XXE) may appear in scenarios.

Downgrade attack: force the use of a weaker protocol or cipher (forcing TLS 1.0, export ciphers). Disable old versions.
Collision attack: find two inputs with the same hash (breaks MD5/SHA-1 signatures).
Birthday attack: exploits the math of collisions; needs far fewer tries than brute force. Use longer hashes.
Key-related: weak keys, key reuse, stolen keys, brute force against short keys.
Side-channel attacks (timing, power) leak keys from the way hardware behaves.

| Attack | Method | Defense
 | Online brute force | Try many passwords against a live login | Account lockout, rate limiting, MFA
 | Offline brute force | Crack a stolen hash with no lockout | Strong passwords, slow salted hashes, key stretching
 | Dictionary | Try common words and variants | Password blocklists, length
 | Password spraying | A few common passwords across many accounts (avoids lockout) | MFA, monitor many failures across users
 | Credential stuffing | Reuse breached username/password pairs on other sites | Unique passwords, MFA, breach checking
 | Rainbow table | Precomputed hash-to-password lookup | Salting
 | Hybrid | Dictionary plus mutations (Password1!) | Long passphrases

An IOC is evidence that a system is or was compromised. Look for:
Account lockout or administrative disable that nobody requested. Attackers may lock an account to trigger a help-desk password reset they can social-engineer.
Concurrent session usage: one account active in two places at once.
Blocked content: AV or update sites suddenly unreachable because malware blocks security tools.
Impossible travel: logins from distant places within a time too short to travel (Omaha and Sydney minutes apart).
Resource consumption: CPU, bandwidth or disk use spikes, especially unusual traffic at 3 a.m. (data exfiltration).
Resource inaccessibility: a server crashes after exploitation attempts, data suddenly encrypted, or an account locked from brute force.
Out-of-cycle logging: events at times they should not happen (patches installing at an odd hour, transfers at 3 a.m.).
Missing logs: attackers delete logs, so alert when expected logs stop.
Published or documented: your private data appears publicly or on leak sites, often tied to ransomware extortion.

Malware overview
Malware types work together: a worm exploits a known vulnerability, drops a backdoor, the attacker connects and installs more. Infection ways: an email click, a pop-up, a drive-by download (downloads with no click, rare), or a worm using a known vulnerability. Data is valuable (personal archives, planning documents, employee and financial data), either to steal or to hold for ransom.
Ransomware is a business model: encrypt everything in your personal folders but leave the OS working so you can read the ransom note, then demand cryptocurrency for the key. Defenses: offline backups (so the ransomware cannot find and encrypt them), OS and app patches, and up-to-date antimalware signatures. Backups plus updates are the two basics.
Viruses and worms

A virus needs a human to start it (click a link or run an executable), then spreads through the file system or network shares. Some sit quietly. Types: program viruses, boot sector viruses (run at boot), script viruses, macro viruses (Office) and fileless viruses.
Fileless: never writes malicious code to disk, so signature-based AV that watches disk writes misses it. Typical chain: user clicks a malicious link, the site exploits a flaw (Flash, Java, a known Windows bug), the code launches PowerShell, downloads more scripts and runs them in memory, exfiltrates data, and adds an autostart entry in the Windows registry to survive reboot.

Worms self-replicate without user action, spread at network speed, and can strike any time. Stop them with network firewalls, personal firewalls and IPS that have the right signatures. Example: WannaCry used EternalBlue (an SMB v1 flaw) to infect a vulnerable system, install a backdoor, pull ransomware, and keep scanning for more victims.
Spyware, keyloggers and bloatware
Spyware watches everything: ads, stolen info, affiliate fraud, browsing habits. It arrives via peer-to-peer software, fake security software or email links, often installs a keylogger, and is hard to uninstall. Use anti-malware (the lesson names Malwarebytes), research what you install, and keep a known good backup.

Bloatware is manufacturer-installed (paid) software: takes space, runs at startup, and can have vulnerabilities on a brand-new device. Remove via the OS app list, the app's own uninstaller, or as a last resort third-party uninstaller software.
Keyloggers capture keystrokes (URLs, passwords, card numbers), but also the clipboard, screenshots, chats and search queries, and they send the log to the attacker about once a day. Typing is not encrypted, so encryption elsewhere does not help. The lesson's demo tool is DarkComet, a RAT with a keylogger that even recorded the delete key.
Logic bombs and rootkits

Logic bomb: waits for a date/time or event (a particular user logging in). Usually custom-made, so no antivirus signature exists. South Korea, March 20, 2013 at 2:00 PM: a Trojan delivered by email to banks and broadcasters (March 19) wiped storage and the master boot record, so machines and the bank's ATMs rebooted with the message "Boot device not found." Defense: limit and monitor changes to core OS files, and enforce least privilege so nobody casually has admin rights.
Rootkit: "root" is from the Unix superuser. It hides in the kernel, so it is part of the OS, does not show in process lists and evades normal AV. Not every rootkit is in the kernel; those running as ordinary processes can still be caught. Use standalone removal tools after infection. Secure boot (UEFI) checks the OS signature and kernel before booting so the rootkit cannot load.
Physical

Whoever physically touches a computer can bypass the OS, and "door locks only keep out honest people". Brute force a door or window. RFID cloning: cloners cost under $50, copy a badge in seconds, and can even work by brushing someone on a train. MFA (PIN, biometrics) beats a cloned badge.
Environmental: cut power (possible from outside the building), attack the HVAC control system so equipment overheats and shuts down, or trigger the fire suppression system to cause denial of service.
Denial of service
Motives: competitive advantage, a smokescreen for another attack, or simple vulnerabilities. Easy methods include pulling power. Self-inflicted DoS examples: a network loop from plugging two switches together twice with no spanning tree, saturating a small DSL line downloading a big Linux ISO, and a water line over a data center ceiling breaking.

DDoS uses botnets under one command. The Zeus botnet reached over 3.6 million computers. It is an asymmetric threat: the attacker with few resources defeats a larger target.
Amplification uses services where a small request gets a big answer (NTP, DNS, ICMP). The lesson's example: a dig ANY isc.org query of about 15 characters returned about 1,300 characters, roughly 86x. Attack flow: the botnet's command and control tells bots to query open DNS resolvers with the source address spoofed to the victim, so the large responses hit the victim web server.
DNS attacks

DNS maps names to IPs. Methods to redirect: edit the client's hosts file (needs local access and usually elevated rights; the file is checked before DNS), on-path interception of DNS queries, or modify the DNS server itself (attacker at 100.100.100.100 changes the record so user 2 gets the attacker's IP). Servers are usually well protected.
Domain hijacking: take over the registration through brute force, social engineering, or leaked credentials, then change the DNS settings. October 22, 2016: 36 domains of a Brazilian bank (over 5 million customers, about $27 billion in assets) were altered for about six hours, so the attackers effectively became the bank's IP address and could collect credentials.

URL hijacking / typosquatting / brandjacking: look-alike domains for ad revenue, to sell back to the owner, to redirect to a competitor, to phish logins, or to drop ransomware or botnet code. Variants: misspell a letter (messor), drop a letter, add a letter (messers), or use a different top-level domain (.org).
Wireless
Deauthentication: management frames in older 802.11 are sent in the clear and unauthenticated, so an attacker can forge them. Lesson demo: find the AP BSSID and the victim's MAC with airodump-ng (monitor interface wlan0mon), then aireplay-ng -0 to send deauth frames; the victim keeps dropping. Fix: the 802.11w / 802.11ac-and-newer updates encrypt management frames like disassociate, authenticate and channel switch announcements. Beacons, probes, authentication and association still must be in the clear.

RF jamming lowers the signal-to-noise ratio. Everyday jammers: microwave ovens and fluorescent lights on 2.4 GHz. Deliberate jam signals can be constant, random data, many legitimate frames, random-time, or reactive (only when someone transmits). The attacker must be nearby, so hunt it with a directional antenna ("fox hunt") and an attenuator to triangulate.
On-path
Also called man-in-the-middle; invisible to both sides; can read and modify. ARP poisoning works on the local subnet because ARP has no authentication: the attacker sends an unsolicited ARP reply claiming to be 192.168.1.1 with the attacker's MAC; the victim's ARP cache updates (the same trick on the router), and traffic flows through the attacker. Normal ARP: broadcast asking who has the IP, reply with the MAC, cache it for some minutes.

On-path browser (man-in-the-browser): a Trojan on the victim's device acts as a proxy, so it sees data even if the network traffic is encrypted, waits for a banking login, grabs credentials and starts hidden sessions to move money.
Replay
The attacker needs something to replay and gets it via a physical network tap, ARP poisoning, or malware. Replay is not itself on-path, though on-path is often used to collect the data.
Pass the hash: capture the username and hashed password during authentication, replay it to the server. Counter: encryption, plus salting so each authentication uses a different salt and hash, with the server refusing to accept the same hash twice.

Cookies are not executable, but hold session IDs and tracking data. Session hijacking / sidejacking: steal the session ID after the victim logs in, and the server treats you as the logged-in user. Collected via packet capture (Wireshark, Kismet), XSS, or header tampering with tools like Tamper, Firesheep and Scapy, plus browser cookie editors. Fix: encrypt end to end with HTTPS (browser extensions can force HTTPS), or at least a VPN to a concentrator.
Malicious code in the news

Scripts, macros, executables and Trojans together require layered defense: anti-malware, firewall, patching, and user training. WannaCry: SMBv1 vulnerability allowing arbitrary code execution, then ransomware. British Airways: 22 lines of malicious JavaScript on the checkout pages (XSS-style), about 380,000 victims' cards at risk. Estonian Central Health Database: SQL injection exposed health records of the whole country.
Application attacks
Injection types: SQL, HTML, XML, LDAP. Buffer overflows usually just crash the app unless repeatable. Privilege escalation: vertical to admin or horizontal (user A gets user B's access). Mitigations: patch, update AV signatures, data execution prevention (DEP), and ASLR (randomized memory locations). Example: CVE-2023-29336, Win32k elevation of privilege (May 2023) giving SYSTEM, the highest Windows privilege.

Cross-site request forgery (CSRF, "sea surf", one-click attack, session riding): pages load content from many servers (client side HTML/JavaScript and server side code like PHP). The attacker abuses the server's trust of your authenticated browser, such as a bank transfer link sent by email, or posting on your Facebook. Defense: a cryptographic anti-forgery token per request.
Directory traversal: a web server misconfiguration or software bug lets requests reach outside the web root. A log line with ../../windows/system.ini is the tell, and ../ moves up one directory.
Cryptographic attacks
Attackers go after the implementation, not the algorithm, because public algorithms have withstood scrutiny.

Birthday attack: among 23 people there is about a 50% chance two share a birthday; at 30 people about 70%. Applied to hashes, finding any two inputs with the same hash is far easier than matching a specific hash. Counter: larger hash output.
MD5 was published April 1992, collisions found in 1996, and in December 2008 researchers made a forged CA-signed certificate that validated via MD5, so the industry moved off MD5.
Downgrade / SSL stripping: on-path attacker strips HTTPS. The victim's first request is HTTP, the attacker proxies it and opens its own HTTPS session to the server, then sends everything to the victim in HTTP. The victim's username and password are readable, and the attacker relays them over HTTPS. Everything after is in the clear between victim and attacker. Defense: HSTS and HTTPS-only.
Password attacks

Never store plaintext. Store hashes (fixed-length output, different inputs give very different hashes, no way back). A one-character change (123456 vs 1234567) yields completely different SHA-256 hashes.
Spraying: try the few most common passwords (123456, 123456789, qwerty, password, 1234567) against each account, about 3 attempts, then move to the next so no lockout or alarm fires.
Brute force: try every combination (aaaaa, aaaab, ...) and compare hashes to the stolen hash. Online is slow and triggers lockout. In practice the attacker downloads the credential file and brute forces offline with unlimited time, limited only by computing power and hash strength and password length.
Indicators of compromise

An IOC is evidence you are highly confident means compromise: large unusual traffic, changed file hashes, traffic from unexpected countries, changed DNS records, odd login patterns, files read far more than normal.
Account lockout you did not cause (or an administrative disable nobody ordered). The attacker may do it on purpose to call the help desk and get a password reset, so use strong reset procedures.
Concurrent session usage: one account in two places (but legit multi-device use and service logins exist; check login reports, like Gmail's activity list).
Blocked content: malware disables AV updates, so failure to reach security sites or patches is an IOC.
Impossible travel: login from Omaha, Nebraska and minutes later from Australia. Check authentication logs.

Resource consumption: unusual traffic at 3:00 AM from file transfer or exfiltration, visible in firewall flow logs. Some breaches were noticed only by one small transfer at an odd time.
Resource inaccessibility: crashed server (from exploitation attempts), network disruption used as a diversion, data encrypted, or an account locked by brute force.
Out-of-cycle logging: events outside the expected schedule (patches installing off the regular patch time, firewall logs showing transfers at odd hours).
Missing logs: attackers delete logs, so alert when expected log data disappears.
Published/documented: data appears on the internet, often because ransomware gangs steal data first (double extortion) and then leak it if you do not pay. Researchers then trace the source and notify the owner.

Virus needs user action; worm spreads on its own.
Spraying = one password across many accounts; brute force = many passwords on one account.
Evil twin imitates a known network; rogue AP is any unauthorized AP.
Replay resends valid captured data; on-path intercepts live.
Rainbow tables are defeated by salts.
Logic bomb waits for a trigger; backdoor gives hidden access.

2.5 Explain the purpose of mitigation techniques used to secure the enterprise

watched the videos
 read the notes
 wrote my own notes
 flashcards mastered

Segmentation, access control (ACLs, permissions), application allow lists, isolation, patching, encryption, monitoring.
Least privilege; configuration enforcement; decommissioning.
Hardening: install endpoint protection, host-based firewall, HIPS, disable ports/protocols, change default passwords, remove unnecessary software.
Mitigation techniques are the practical ways to shrink risk. The exam wants you to match a problem to the control that actually fixes it.

Segmentation: splitting the network into separate zones (VLANs, subnets, firewalls) so an intruder in one area can't move freely. Limits lateral movement and contains incidents. Examples: separate guest Wi-Fi, a DMZ for public servers, isolated OT/IoT networks.
Access control list (ACL): rules on a router, firewall or file system that allow or deny based on source, destination, port, user. Network ACLs filter traffic; file system ACLs control who can read/write files.
Permissions: least privilege on files, folders, databases and cloud resources.
Application allow list (whitelist): only approved programs may run. Strongest application control, but takes maintenance. A deny list (blocklist) blocks known bad software and misses new threats.
Isolation: a compromised or untrusted system is cut off from the network (quarantine VLAN, network access control).
Decommissioning: remove unused systems, accounts and services, and securely wipe data.

Patching: apply vendor fixes promptly, after testing. Emergency patching for actively exploited flaws.
Encryption: protects data at rest, in transit and in use.
Monitoring: logging, SIEM, alerts, and review to detect problems early.
Least privilege: only the access needed for the job, for the time needed.
Configuration enforcement: automated checks that systems keep their secure baseline (group policy, configuration management, compliance scanning).
Decommissioning and hardening (below) reduce the attack surface.
Defense in depth: layers so one failure doesn't expose everything.

Hardening means removing or locking down everything that isn't required.
 | Technique | What to do
 | Encryption | Full-disk encryption on endpoints, TLS everywhere
 | Endpoint protection | Antivirus/anti-malware, EDR for behavior detection, host-based firewall, HIDS/HIPS
 | Host-based firewall | Allow only the ports and apps a system needs
 | Disable ports and protocols | Turn off unused ports (physical switch ports and listening services) and insecure protocols (Telnet, FTP, SMBv1)
 | Default password changes | Change vendor defaults on routers, cameras, databases, admin consoles
 | Remove unnecessary software | Fewer programs, fewer vulnerabilities
 | Patching | Operating system, applications, firmware
 | Secure baselines / configuration standards | Documented, approved settings applied consistently
 | Account controls | Remove unused accounts, restrict admin, MFA, password policy
 | Network access control (NAC) | Check device health/identity before network access
 | Mobile device hardening | MDM, screen lock, remote wipe, update enforcement

Segmentation reasons
Segment physically (separate devices), logically (VLANs on switches), or virtually (cloud and VM architectures). Reasons: performance (a dedicated subnet for a high-bandwidth app), security (users talk to an application server, only the application server talks to the database server, enforced by a firewall or ACL), and mandates (PCI DSS may require card data kept completely separate from the rest of the network).
ACL criteria: source IP, destination IP, port numbers, time of day, or user. Example rules from the lesson: Bob can read files on a resource, Fred can access the network, James can reach 192.168.1.0/24 only on TCP 80, 443 and 8088. Operating system file and folder permissions and group membership are ACLs too. Take care not to write an ACL that locks you out of managing the device.

Application allow/deny lists: allow list means nothing runs unless approved (restricted); deny list means everything runs except named items. Antivirus is a deny list. Windows rules can identify an application by hash (a change in the file breaks the match), by digital signature/certificate (allow anything signed by Microsoft, Adobe or Google and block unsigned), by path (only run from a specific directory), or by network zone (private vs public).
Mitigation details
Patching also improves stability. Home OSes patch themselves; large organizations test first then push, with emergency patches when attackers are actively exploiting a hole.
Encryption limits what an attacker can take: EFS for files and folders, FDE for devices that leave the building (BitLocker on Windows, FileVault on macOS), and application-level encryption so data stays protected regardless of the file system.

Monitoring comes from switches, routers, sensors, firewalls, IPS and OS authentication logs, and a SIEM consolidates them for reports.
Least privilege: ideally nobody runs as admin; elevate temporarily and drop back. This limits an attack to what that one user can see.
Configuration enforcement / posture assessment at login checks OS version and patches, EDR version and signatures, local firewall and EDR turned on, and a device certificate. A failing device goes to quarantine or a private VLAN to fix itself, then retries.
Decommissioning: remove or wipe storage (SSD, hard drive, USB) before retiring equipment. Reuse the drive internally after formatting, or destroy it if sensitive data may remain.
Hardening details

OS hardening: apply monthly security updates, set a password policy (the lesson's example: at least 8 characters with upper, lower, numbers and special characters), keep accounts to least privilege, limit which IP address range can reach the server, run antivirus, anti-malware or endpoint detection, and encrypt (EFS for files, FDE, VPN and HTTPS for traffic).
Endpoint hardening: attacks can be inbound, and an infected device can be a launch point against others. Different platforms (desktop, laptop, tablet, phone) need different tools, layered as defense in depth.

EDR: over a million malware variants appear daily, so signatures alone do not scale. EDR adds behavioral analysis, machine learning, process monitoring, root-cause analysis, and automatic response (isolate the system, quarantine the threat, roll back to a previous config) through an API, reporting to a central console without waiting for a ticket.
Host-based firewall: software firewall on the OS, controls inbound and outbound by process, sees traffic before/after encryption, can block unknown processes until approved, and is centrally manageable.
HIPS: usually built into EDR or anti-malware. It uses signatures, heuristics and behavior. Because it runs on the OS it can detect a buffer overflow, a registry change, or modified files in the core Windows folder and then alert and block.

Open ports: close as many as possible, using the host or a firewall (a next-generation firewall can control the service, not only the port number). Installers sometimes ask to open ports 0 to 65535 just so the vendor avoids support calls; that is not actually needed. Check with Nmap.
Default passwords: change them on routers, switches, firewalls, access points and application consoles, even when the device does not prompt you. Add MFA or centralized authentication where possible.
Remove unused software: every app has its own update process and its own bugs, so the easiest fix is to delete what you do not use.

| Problem | Best-fit mitigation
 | Infection spreads between departments | Segmentation
 | Legacy system can't be patched | Isolation / ACL (a compensating control)
 | Unknown program ran on a server | Application allow list
 | New server still has admin/admin | Change default credentials, secure baseline
 | Telnet service found running | Disable it, use SSH
 | Unused switch ports are active | Disable unused ports
 | Stolen laptop | Full-disk encryption
 | Brute-force against a login | Lockout, rate limiting, MFA
 | Zero-day with no patch | Segmentation, EDR, virtual patching, monitoring

Allow list beats deny list for application control.
Segmentation limits spread; it does not remove the vulnerability.
Isolation is a containment action; patching is the real fix.
If the question says "least effort and still effective", look for disabling unused services, changing defaults and patching.

3.1 Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models

watched the videos
 read the notes
 wrote my own notes
 flashcards mastered

Cloud: responsibility matrix (shared responsibility), hybrid, third-party vendors. IaC, serverless, microservices.
Network infrastructure: physical isolation (air-gapped), logical segmentation, SDN.
On-premises, centralized vs decentralized, containerization, virtualization, IoT, ICS/SCADA, RTOS, embedded systems, high availability.
Considerations: availability, resilience, cost, responsiveness, scalability, ease of deployment, risk transference, ease of recovery, patch availability, inability to patch, power, compute.

Objective 3.1 compares architecture models and the security trade-offs of each. The pattern is the same everywhere: what does this model give you, what does it cost you, and who is responsible for securing which part.

Service models (what you rent):
 | Model | You get | Customer secures | Provider secures
 | IaaS (infrastructure) | Virtual machines, storage, networks | OS, apps, data, configuration, access | Hardware, hypervisor, facility
 | PaaS (platform) | A runtime to deploy code | App code, data, access | OS, runtime, infrastructure
 | SaaS (software) | A finished application | Data, user access, configuration | Everything else
The shared responsibility model: the provider is responsible for security *of* the cloud, the customer for security *in* the cloud. The more managed the service, the more the provider handles, but the customer always keeps responsibility for their data and who can access it.

Deployment models: public (shared provider infrastructure), private (dedicated to one organization), community (shared by organizations with common needs), hybrid (mix of cloud and on-prem or multiple clouds). Multi-cloud uses more than one provider (resilience, avoids lock-in, more to manage).
Other cloud concepts:
Third-party vendors add supply chain risk and need contracts, assessments and monitoring.
Infrastructure as code (IaC): define servers and networks in versioned code so builds are repeatable and reviewable. Misconfigurations can be copied everywhere, so scan templates.
Serverless / function as a service: you run code without managing servers. The provider handles scaling and patching; you still secure code, permissions and data.

Microservices: an application split into small independent services that communicate by API. Easier to scale and update, but more network connections and APIs to secure.
Software-defined networking (SDN): separates the control plane from data forwarding so networks are configured centrally by software. SD-WAN does the same for wide area links.
On-premises: you run everything. Maximum control, maximum responsibility and capital cost.
Centralized vs decentralized: central control is easier to manage and secure; decentralized spreads risk but is harder to manage consistently.

Physical isolation / air gap: no network connection to anything else. Used for the most sensitive systems (classified networks, ICS). Data moves only by controlled removable media, which is itself a risk.
Logical segmentation: VLANs, subnets, firewalls and access control lists separate traffic on shared hardware.
Network layers matter when choosing devices: switches (layer 2), routers (layer 3), firewalls (3 to 7).
Software-defined networking (above) and zero trust (1.2) both reduce implicit trust.

Virtualization: multiple VMs on one host. Isolation is strong but not perfect (VM escape, sprawl, see 2.3).
Containerization (Docker, Kubernetes): packages an app with its dependencies, sharing the host OS kernel. Lighter than VMs, weaker isolation, so secure the images, the registry and the orchestrator.
Internet of Things (IoT): smart devices, cameras, sensors. Often weak default credentials, little patching, long life. Segment on their own VLAN.
Industrial control systems (ICS) / SCADA: supervisory control of industrial processes. Availability and safety come first; systems are old and patching is difficult. Isolate from IT networks. PLCs (programmable logic controllers) run physical equipment.
Real-time operating systems (RTOS): strict timing, minimal features, used in embedded devices. Security patches are rare.
Embedded systems: dedicated hardware/software inside a device (appliances, vehicles, medical devices). Hard to update and monitor.
High availability (HA): redundancy so a failure does not interrupt service (clusters, load balancers, redundant power and links).

When picking an architecture, weigh:
 | Consideration | Question
 | Availability | How much downtime is acceptable?
 | Resilience | Can it keep working, or recover quickly, after failure?
 | Cost | Capital vs operating expense; security tools; staff
 | Responsiveness | Latency and performance for users
 | Scalability | Can it grow (or shrink) with demand? Cloud scales elastically
 | Ease of deployment | How fast and consistent is setup? IaC helps
 | Risk transference | Can risk be moved to a provider or insurer? (Not responsibility)
 | Ease of recovery | How quickly can it be restored?
 | Patch availability | Will the vendor release fixes?
 | Inability to patch | Common for ICS, IoT, embedded: needs isolation and compensating controls
 | Power and compute | Resource needs, especially for low-power or edge devices

Cloud responsibility and hybrid
Providers publish a responsibility matrix for SaaS, PaaS, IaaS and on-premises; each provider's differs and a contract can modify it. Example from the lesson: the OS is the provider's job for SaaS and PaaS and the customer's for IaaS and on-prem, but accounts and identities are always the customer's responsibility.
Hybrid here means using multiple clouds across different providers (the lesson's framing). Costs: providers do not talk to each other, so authentication, server and firewall settings must be configured separately and kept matching; logs use different formats and terminology; and data moving between clouds crosses the public internet, so protect it in transit.

Third parties on top of the cloud (for example a third-party firewall in front of your app) need a vendor risk management policy, a shared incident response process with all parties, and continuous monitoring of security and availability.
Infrastructure as code: describe hosts, web servers and database servers as code, tweak the code, and rebuild a perfect instance on any provider at any time.
Serverless: the app is broken into individual functions; each runs only when needed, in whatever OS fits, is built in real time and removed when not needed (saves money), and most security work sits in the cloud.

Monolithic vs microservices: a monolith is one executable (UI, login, business logic) installed locally and needing change control to update. With microservices, the client talks to an API gateway, which routes to the right service. Benefits: scalability (add copies of the busy service), resilience (losing one service does not kill the app), and tailored security per service (authentication service vs database-writing service).
Network infrastructure
Air gap: physical isolation, such as web servers in one rack and databases in another, or an MSP putting each customer on its own switch. It does not scale (100 customers = 100 switches), so VLANs give the same separation on shared switches. VLANs cannot talk to each other directly.

SDN planes: the data plane (forwarding, NAT, encryption, trunking), the control plane (routing tables, dynamic routing, session and address tables), and the management plane (SSH, SNMP, API configuration). Splitting these into software lets cloud builders add devices on demand. Example: load balancer to web servers A and B plus a database server, then click to insert a firewall between the internet and load balancer and another between web servers and database.
Other infrastructure
On-prem vs cloud: cloud security is centralized with no hardware or data center to staff, and the provider handles it. On-prem gives full control and local security but you pay for staff, equipment, purchase time and configuration. Attackers do not care where it is.

Centralized management: one console for consolidated alerts, log analysis and global patching, but it is a single point of failure, and needs more storage and CPU as the organization grows.
Virtualization: infrastructure, then hypervisor, then separate VMs each with a guest OS and apps. Inefficient when every guest is the same OS. Containers share one host OS and put only the app and dependencies in a container, managed by container software such as Docker. Containers are isolated from each other, easy to swap, and designed for one host OS (Windows containers vs Linux containers).
IoT: home (garage openers, video doorbells, smartwatches) and workplace (air quality, temperature, lighting). Makers are good at thermostats, not security, and one exploited device can expose the network.

SCADA / ICS: networks large machinery (manufacturing, power generation, refineries) from a central control room, and must be completely segmented from outside.
RTOS: Windows and Linux are non-deterministic; deterministic real-time systems (cars with anti-lock brakes, military, manufacturing) let one task take priority. They are self-contained and hard to access.
Embedded system: purpose-built hardware and software for one task (traffic lights, watches, medical monitors).
HA vs redundant: redundant means a spare exists (maybe in a closet needing to be racked and configured). High availability keeps running through a failure, for example a firewall pair in active/passive (failover) or active/active (both working, no visible failure). More HA means more cost (second firewall, network, power), so it is a business decision.
Infrastructure considerations

Availability is measured as uptime percent (for example 99.999%), and in security means available to the *right people*. Resilience measure: MTTR (mean time to repair). First find the root cause; hardware needs replacing, software needs a patch, redundant parts need replacing.
Cost includes install cost (varies by platform), maintenance (vendor or internal), replacement, plus accounting aspects: depreciation (capital expense), operational costs and tax implications.
Responsiveness: users notice delay; measure across a transaction's steps. Elasticity: expand and contract capacity with demand (quarter end, time of day). Building the largest version costs money, so start at the current load and scale, sometimes automatically. Extend security monitoring as it scales.

An application instance has many parts (web server, database, caching server, firewall). Orchestration automates building the whole stack on demand. Deployment still needs project planning: where, who, resources, budget, change control.
Risk transference: cybersecurity insurance (for example for ransomware) can cover outages, financial loss and legal costs. It does not prevent the attack.
Ease of recovery: reload an OS from media (about an hour) vs restore from an image backup (about 10 minutes) after malware. Plan the fastest recovery.
Patch availability: patch before production, test monthly patches, deploy fast. Inability to patch is common for embedded systems such as HVAC controls and time clocks with no connectivity; add a firewall in front as another layer.

Power: have a licensed electrician review usage; data centers differ from offices; use a UPS or generator for backup. Compute: the cloud "compute engine" does the processing and can scale across many processors.

You can transfer risk (insurance, outsourcing), but you can never transfer accountability for your data.
Air-gapped means no network connection at all; a segmented VLAN is not an air gap.
Containers share a kernel; VMs have their own. VMs are more isolated.
When a device cannot be patched, think segmentation and access control, not "patch harder".
SaaS leaves the customer the *least* security work, but never zero.
