3.2 Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure

watched the videos
 read the notes
 wrote my own notes
 flashcards mastered

Infrastructure: device placement, security zones, attack surface, connectivity, failure modes (fail-open vs fail-closed).
Device attributes: active vs passive, inline vs tap/monitor.
Devices: jump server, proxy server, IPS/IDS, load balancer, sensors, port security (802.1X, EAP), firewalls (WAF, UTM, NGFW, layer 4/7).
Secure communication: VPN, remote access, tunneling (TLS, IPsec), SD-WAN, SASE.
Objective 3.2 is about where security devices go, how they behave when they fail, and how traffic gets protected as it moves.

Security zones group systems by trust: internet (untrusted), a DMZ / screened subnet for public-facing servers, internal (trusted), and often a management network and a guest network. Rules between zones control what can talk to what.
Attack surface shrinks when you minimize exposed services and reduce connectivity between zones.
Device attributes:
 | Attribute | Option A | Option B
 | Active vs passive | Active: can block or change traffic | Passive: only observes and alerts
 | Inline vs tap/monitor | Inline: traffic flows *through* the device (can block). A failure may drop traffic | Tap / SPAN port: a copy of traffic goes to the device. No effect on flow, cannot block directly
 | Failure mode | Fail-open: on failure, traffic is allowed (keeps availability, loses security) | Fail-closed: on failure, traffic is blocked (keeps security, loses availability)
Choose by what matters more. A safety door fails open so people can escape. A firewall protecting sensitive data usually fails closed.

IDS (intrusion detection system): detects and alerts; passive. IPS (intrusion prevention system): detects and blocks; inline.
Detection methods: signature-based (known patterns, fast and accurate for known threats, misses new ones), anomaly/behavior-based (learns normal and flags deviations, catches unknown but more false positives), heuristic.
Network-based (NIDS/NIPS) watch network traffic. Host-based (HIDS/HIPS) run on a single system and see local activity (files, processes, logs).
Tune rules to reduce false positives (alert on benign) and false negatives (miss a real attack).

Jump server (jump box / bastion host): a hardened intermediate host used to reach devices in a secure zone. Admins log into it first, which gives one monitored, controlled entry point.
Proxy server: sits between users and the internet. Forward proxy filters and caches outbound web requests (content filtering, logging, anonymity). Reverse proxy sits in front of servers (hides them, load balances, terminates TLS).
Load balancer: spreads traffic across servers for availability and scale; health-checks servers; can offload TLS.
Sensors and collectors: devices that gather logs and network data for the SIEM.
Web application firewall (WAF): layer 7 filter for web apps (SQLi, XSS).
UTM (unified threat management): firewall, IPS, antivirus, filtering and VPN in one appliance.
NGFW (next-generation firewall): application-aware, user-aware, with deep packet inspection and integrated IPS.

Port security on a switch limits MAC addresses per port, shuts ports that violate the rule, and disables unused ports.
802.1X is port-based network access control. A device must authenticate before the switch port or wireless association allows traffic. Three roles: supplicant (client), authenticator (switch/AP), authentication server (usually RADIUS). It uses EAP methods (EAP-TLS with certificates is strongest).
Network access control (NAC) adds posture checks (patched? antivirus running?) and can quarantine noncompliant devices.
Loop protection (STP, BPDU guard), DHCP snooping (blocks rogue DHCP servers), dynamic ARP inspection (blocks ARP spoofing), MAC filtering (weak, easy to spoof).

| Type | Works at | What it does
 | Packet filter / stateless | Layer 3-4 | Allows or denies by IP, port, protocol; no memory of connections
 | Stateful | Layer 3-4 | Tracks connection state, so return traffic of an allowed session is permitted
 | Proxy / application firewall | Layer 7 | Terminates and re-creates the connection, can inspect content of specific protocols
 | Next-generation firewall | Layers 3-7 | Application identification, user identity, IPS, TLS inspection, threat feeds
 | WAF | Layer 7 (HTTP) | Protects web apps
 | Host-based | On the endpoint | Per-host rules
Rules are processed top to bottom; the first match wins. End with an implicit deny: anything not explicitly allowed is blocked. Place specific rules before general ones.
Network vs host firewall, hardware vs software, appliance vs virtual vs cloud are all deployment variants.

VPN: encrypted tunnel over an untrusted network. Remote-access VPN (client to network) and site-to-site (network to network).
IPsec: layer 3. AH gives integrity/authentication only; ESP gives encryption plus integrity. Transport mode protects the payload (host to host); tunnel mode wraps the whole original packet (gateway to gateway). IKE negotiates keys.
TLS secures applications (HTTPS, email, VPN). SSL VPNs use TLS, work through firewalls on 443.
Split tunnel sends only corporate traffic through the VPN; full tunnel sends everything (more control, more load).
Always-on VPN reconnects automatically.
SD-WAN: software-defined routing over multiple links (MPLS, broadband, LTE) with central policy.
SASE (secure access service edge): delivers networking and security (SWG, CASB, ZTNA, firewall-as-a-service) from the cloud, so remote users and branches get consistent security.
Secure Shell (SSH) for remote administration; RDP carries risk if exposed to the internet.
Tunneling protocols encapsulate one protocol inside another (GRE, L2TP).

Zones and attack surface
A security zone is a logical grouping by use or access type, not an IP range. Simple model: trusted/internal vs untrusted/external. Finer zones named things like inside, internet, servers, databases and screened. Rules then read clearly: trusted to untrusted allowed, untrusted to screened allowed, and untrusted straight to trusted usually blocked (only in special cases). Lesson diagram: internet, firewall, router, then internal mail, database and directory servers; a better design adds a screened zone.
Other devices that help the design: honeypots, jump servers, network sensors, load balancers.

Ways in (like a house with doors, windows and a basement): application code, open server ports, the authentication process, and human error (one mistaken firewall rule). All of them together are the attack surface; minimize it by auditing code, blocking ports and monitoring traffic in real time.
Connectivity: secure network drops and cabling (physical and logical protection), because a tap can see all traffic, so add application-level encryption. Use IPsec tunnels site to site and a VPN concentrator for remote users.
IPS
An IPS watches live traffic and blocks known exploits, buffer overflows and SQL injection. An IDS only alerts.

Inline devices can fail (power loss, hardware, software bug). Fail-open keeps traffic flowing with no security checking. Fail-closed cuts the link. Most networks prefer fail-open but check the documentation for your device. Failure mode only matters when the device is inline/active.
Layout example: internet, firewall, IPS, core switch. Active monitoring (inline) is the default config for IPS and can remove malicious traffic before it reaches the switch. Reasons to avoid it: fear of causing downtime or of blocking legitimate traffic.
Passive monitoring: a port mirror / SPAN (Switch Port Analyzer) or a physical network tap sends a copy of the traffic to the IPS. It cannot cause an outage but cannot block in real time, so it behaves like an IDS.
Appliances in detail

Jump server: a hardened device inside the network reachable from outside. Admins connect to it, then SSH onward (two-step). It must be tightly secured because compromising it gives access to everything behind it.
Proxy: makes requests for users, can evaluate responses, cache (saving bandwidth), URL filter and content scan. Explicit proxy must be configured in the app or OS; transparent proxy is invisible to users. NAT is a simple form of proxy. An application proxy understands one protocol (HTTP proxy), and some handle several (HTTP, HTTPS, FTP).
Forward (internal) proxy: users go to the internal proxy, which fetches from the internet and inspects the reply. Reverse proxy: sits in front of your web server for inbound traffic, drops malicious requests, and caches identical requests to speed responses and reduce server load.

Open proxy: available to anyone, used to bypass controls. Unknown owner may inject ads or malicious code, so many organizations block them.
Load balancer distributes load across a web server or database farm and gives fault tolerance (convergence is fast and mostly unnoticed). Active/active uses every server; active/passive keeps standby servers that take over (server A and B active, C and D standby; a failure promotes a standby). Extra features: TCP offloading (one persistent TCP session instead of one per user), SSL/TLS offloading (decrypt at the balancer using purpose-built hardware, send clear traffic to the servers, re-encrypt responses), caching, prioritization, and content switching (send certain request types to specific servers).

Sensors and collectors: switches, routers, firewalls, IPS, authentication logs and web server logs generate stats; standalone sensors collect traffic stats too. A collector is the central database, which may be a vendor console or a SIEM that consolidates, correlates and compares data (example report: failed authentications and port scans).
Port security and 802.1X
EAP is a framework used by many wired and wireless vendors. 802.1X (port-based NAC) is the common integration: you cannot use a switch port until you authenticate. Back ends include RADIUS, LDAP, TACACS+, Kerberos (for example an Active Directory database through Kerberos or LDAP).

Three parts: supplicant (client), authenticator (switch or AP), authentication server. Flow: the supplicant connects with no access, the authenticator sends an EAP request, the supplicant sends an EAP response with its identity, the authenticator forwards that to the authentication server, which asks for more details (credentials), the supplicant provides them, the authenticator relays them, and the server replies with success so the authenticator opens access.
Firewalls in detail
Traditional network firewalls decide by Layer 4 (TCP/UDP port). NGFW works at Layer 7. Firewalls can also be Layer 3 devices (routing, NAT, routing protocols) at the edge, and include a VPN.

UTM (also called web security gateway or all-in-one security appliance): URL filtering, content inspection, malware blocking, spam filtering, CSU/DSU, routing and switching, firewall, IDS/IPS, bandwidth shaping (QoS) and VPN concentrator. Drawbacks: many only work at layer 4, and turning on many features slows the device.
NGFW (also called application layer gateway, stateful multilayer inspection, deep packet inspection): full packet decode, identifies who, where, and the application. Example: allow Microsoft SQL Server regardless of port, allow viewing but not posting to Twitter, restrict YouTube, even if ports are similar. Includes a vulnerability list (acts like an IPS) and URL categories (block "gambling") or individual URLs (espn.com, yahoo.com).

WAF: analyzes input to web apps over HTTP/HTTPS, blocks SQL injection, usually used with an NGFW, and is required by PCI DSS for card applications. A sample log shows time, date, ID, URL (index.cgi), service IP and port, client IP and country, and the attack name "SQL Injection in Parameter," blocked by a standard policy.
Secure communication in detail
A VPN concentrator is the endpoint for encrypted connections; today often inside an NGFW, or software, with client software often built into the OS.
IPsec packet structure: the original IP header and data are encrypted and wrapped with an IPsec header and trailer, then a new IP header points to the concentrator. The far end strips the outer layers and decrypts.

SSL/TLS VPN runs over TCP 443, passes through most firewalls, and is used for remote access from a single device. It can use normal credentials (not forced to use certificates or shared passwords, though it can), can be browser-based with no client install, and can be always on. IPsec site-to-site VPN uses firewalls as endpoints, so devices need no extra software.
SD-WAN was built for cloud access: instead of every site hauling traffic to a central data center and then out to the cloud (extra hops), the WAN adapts to reach cloud apps directly. SASE is described as the next generation of VPN: security services live in the cloud near the services, and SASE clients on every device (office, home, mobile) connect securely. Organizations often combine remote-access SSL VPNs, IPsec site-to-site VPNs, SD-WAN for connectivity and SASE for security.

Inline = can block; tap/passive = can only alert.
Fail-open favors availability; fail-closed favors security.
IDS doesn't block; IPS does.
802.1X authenticates devices at the port; a firewall doesn't.
ESP encrypts; AH doesn't.
A jump server reduces exposure by giving admins a single controlled path.

3.3 Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data

watched the videos
 read the notes
 wrote my own notes
 flashcards mastered

Data types: regulated, trade secret, intellectual property, legal, financial, human/non-human readable.
Classifications: sensitive, confidential, public, restricted, private, critical.
Data states: at rest, in transit, in use. Data sovereignty and geolocation.
Methods: geographic restrictions, encryption, hashing, masking, tokenization, obfuscation, segmentation, permission restrictions.
Data protection starts with knowing what data you have, how sensitive it is, where it lives, and what state it is in. Only then can you choose the right control.

Regulated data: controlled by law or industry rules, so mishandling brings fines. Examples: health records (HIPAA), payment cards (PCI DSS), personal data of EU residents (GDPR), financial data.
Trade secrets: information that gives a business an edge and is protected by secrecy (recipes, formulas, source code).
Intellectual property (IP): patents, copyrights, trademarks, designs.
Legal information: contracts, case files, discovery.
Financial information: accounts, statements, payment data.
Human-readable data is directly understood by people (text, documents). Non-human-readable needs software to interpret (binary files, encoded or encrypted data, databases).

Classification labels data by sensitivity so the right protection applies. The scheme depends on the organization.
 | Common labels | Meaning
 | Public | Safe to release; no harm
 | Private / internal | For internal use; low impact if leaked
 | Sensitive | Needs protection; loss would hurt
 | Confidential | Limited access; significant harm if exposed
 | Restricted | Tightest control; severe harm
 | Critical | Essential to operations; availability matters most
Government labels you may see: Unclassified, Confidential, Secret, Top Secret.
Roles: the data owner decides classification and access (accountable). The data steward manages quality and metadata. The data custodian (usually IT) implements technical protection. The data controller decides why and how personal data is processed; the data processor processes it on the controller's behalf. A data protection officer (DPO) oversees privacy compliance.

| State | Where it is | Typical protection
 | At rest | Stored on disk, database, backup, USB | Full-disk/file/database encryption, access control, secure storage
 | In transit (in motion) | Moving across a network | TLS, IPsec/VPN, SSH, secure protocols
 | In use | Being processed in memory/CPU | Secure enclaves, memory protection, access controls, limiting exposure on screen
A complete data protection plan covers all three.

Data sovereignty: data is subject to the laws of the country where it is stored. Cloud region choices can affect compliance.
Geolocation / geographic restrictions: limit where data can be stored or accessed from (block access from certain countries, keep EU data in the EU).
Privacy regulations (GDPR, CCPA) add requirements around consent, retention and breach notification.

Geographic restrictions: control by location (above).
Encryption: converts data so only key holders can read it (at rest, in transit).
Hashing: one-way fingerprint for integrity and password storage.
Masking: hides part of a value while keeping format (XXX-XX-1234). Often used in test and support views.
Tokenization: swaps sensitive data for a token; the real value sits in a secure vault.
Obfuscation: makes data hard to understand (not strong security by itself).
Segmentation: separate networks or databases for sensitive data so access is restricted.
Permission restrictions: least privilege, role-based access, need to know.
Data loss prevention (DLP): policies and tools that detect and block sensitive data leaving (email, USB, cloud uploads).
Rights management / classification labels that travel with the file.
Retention and disposal: keep only what is needed, then destroy it securely (shredding, degaussing, wiping).

Types and classes
Regulated data has rules set by a third party (card data under PCI standards) or by government law, which can dictate how long data is kept. Trade secrets are known only to the organization. Intellectual property is often visible but protected by copyright and trademark law. Legal records (court records, judge and attorney names) are often public, but parts hold private PII and live in separate systems. Financial data covers both company books and personal bank details.
Human-readable (documents, spreadsheets) vs non-human-readable (encoded data, barcodes, images) vs mixed (a barcode with its digits printed underneath).
Sensitivity differs: a license plate lookup is mild, medical history never accessible. Match controls: specific permissions, a stricter viewing process, or a restricted network area.

Proprietary data is unique to the organization. PII: name, date of birth, mother's maiden name, biometrics, address. PHI: health status, healthcare records, even healthcare payments.
Classification example set: sensitive (IP, PII, PHI), confidential (more sensitive, extra access), public/unclassified (government), private/classified/restricted (extra rights, maybe an NDA), and critical (must always be available, so plan uptime).
States of data
At rest counts as at rest even if it is not encrypted. Add FDE, database or file/folder encryption, plus user and group permissions.
In transit (in motion): protect with a firewall or IPS (allow known good, block unusual) and with encryption such as TLS or a site-to-site IPsec VPN.

In use: data in RAM or the CPU is usually decrypted since it must be processed, so attackers target it. Target, November 2013: code on every point-of-sale terminal pulled 110 million card records from terminal memory, even though Target encrypted data in transit and at rest.
Data sovereignty: data stored in a country follows that country's laws and court orders. GDPR (EU) requires data on EU citizens to be stored in the EU. Check rules for each geography you operate in.
Geolocation uses GPS, 802.11 (matching visible SSIDs against wireless databases) and mobile provider data. Streaming services blocking foreign content is the everyday example. You can grant more data access when the user is inside the corporate building.
Protecting data details

Geographic restrictions use IP subnet (good for known internal subnets, poor for mobile devices), GPS, and wireless data. Geofencing applies policy based on location (for example, only accessible inside corporate facilities).
Data lives on devices, on networks and in CPU/memory, and each location can be attacked, so protect all of them.
Encryption turns plaintext into ciphertext and needs the right implementation and key to decrypt. Confusion is the property that the ciphertext looks very different from the plaintext (PGP "Hello, world" demo).

Hashing: message digest or fingerprint, cannot rebuild the data. Used for passwords, for download checks (Linux ISO hash next to the file), and with public key crypto in digital signatures. A collision is two inputs with the same hash, and algorithms with this problem were dropped. SHA-256: 256 bits, 64 hex characters; changing a period to an exclamation mark changes the entire hash.
Obfuscation: developers obfuscate code to protect it (the code still works the same), and attackers use it to hide malicious scripts. Example: one line of PHP echo "Hello, world" turned into a longer valid PHP script that outputs the same.

Masking hides part of data such as card numbers on receipts (last four shown); can shuffle, encrypt, or use asterisks. Tokenization replaces data with a one-time token (phone or smartwatch payment); no encryption or hashing needed and no way to derive the card number from the token. Flow: register the card on the phone, the token service server returns tokens, NFC sends a token at the store, and the store checks it with the token server.
Segmentation: one big database means one breach exposes everything. Split data into separate databases with security matched to sensitivity (a name list needs less than health or financial data).
Permission restrictions begin with secure authentication (password policy, extra factors) and continue with groups and file permissions after login.

Masking hides *display*; tokenization replaces *storage*; encryption is reversible with a key.
Owner decides classification; custodian implements controls.
In use data is the hardest to protect because it must be decrypted to be processed.
Regulated data = legal requirement; classification = your own scheme. Both can apply.
DLP is a detective *and* preventive technology for data leaving the organization.

3.4 Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture

watched the videos
 read the notes
 wrote my own notes
 flashcards mastered

High availability: load balancing vs clustering. Site considerations: hot (ready now), warm (some gear), cold (empty space), geographic dispersion.
Platform diversity, multi-cloud. Continuity of operations, capacity planning (people, technology, infrastructure).
Testing: tabletop exercises, failover, simulation, parallel processing.
Backups: onsite/offsite, frequency, encryption, snapshots, recovery, replication, journaling.
Power: generators, UPS.
Resilience is the ability to keep working through failures and to recover quickly when something does break. This objective is about availability, one third of the CIA triad.

Load balancing: spreads work across multiple servers. Adds capacity and survives a server failure. Can be active/active.
Clustering: servers work together as one system. Active/passive: a standby takes over on failure. Active/active: all nodes serve traffic.
Redundancy at every layer: power supplies, NICs, disks (RAID), switches, internet links, data centers.
Multi-cloud and geographic dispersion protect against a regional outage or provider problem.

| Site | State | Recovery time | Cost
 | Hot site | Fully equipped, data replicated, running | Minutes to hours | Highest
 | Warm site | Equipment ready, data restored when needed | Hours to days | Medium
 | Cold site | Empty space with power and connectivity | Days to weeks | Lowest
Geographic dispersion: put sites far enough apart that one disaster doesn't hit both.
Platform diversity: using different operating systems, vendors or technologies so a single flaw can't take down everything.
Continuity of operations planning (COOP): how critical functions continue during a crisis.

Make sure you have enough of what the business needs. Plan for:
People: staff to run operations (including during an incident).
Technology: servers, storage, bandwidth, licenses.
Infrastructure: space, power, cooling, network.
Under-capacity creates outages; elastic cloud capacity can scale to match demand.

You don't know a plan works until you test it.
Tabletop exercise: a discussion-based walkthrough of a scenario. Cheap, low risk, finds gaps in plans and communication.
Failover test: actually switch to the backup system or site to confirm it works.
Simulation: a realistic drill that mimics an incident with participants acting it out.
Parallel processing: run the recovery system alongside production to compare results without switching traffic.
Record results, fix gaps, retest. Update the plan after every test and every real event.

Types: full (everything; slowest to take, fastest to restore), incremental (changes since the last backup of any type; fast to take, slowest to restore because you need the full plus every increment), differential (changes since the last *full*; restore needs the full plus the latest differential).
Snapshots: point-in-time state of a VM or volume. Quick to take and revert, but usually on the same storage, so they are not a backup by themselves.
Replication: copying data to another location continuously or on a schedule (synchronous for no data loss, asynchronous for distance).
Journaling: records changes so state can be rebuilt after a failure.
Onsite vs offsite: onsite restores faster; offsite (or cloud, or tape vaulted) survives a disaster at the main site. Follow the 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 media types, 1 offsite (modern advice adds 1 offline/immutable).

Immutable and offline backups resist ransomware that encrypts or deletes reachable backups.
Encryption protects backups at rest and in transit; they hold all your data.
Frequency is set by the RPO (recovery point objective): how much data you can afford to lose.
Retention sets how long backups are kept; disposal must be secure.
Test restores regularly. An untested backup is a hope, not a control.

Uninterruptible power supply (UPS): battery that bridges brief outages and allows safe shutdown; also conditions power (surges, sags).
Generator: longer-term power, takes time to start, so it pairs with a UPS. Needs fuel and testing.
Dual power supplies and separate circuits/feeds for critical equipment.
Managed PDUs monitor and control power at the rack.

| Metric | Meaning
 | RTO (recovery time objective) | Maximum acceptable time to restore a service
 | RPO (recovery point objective) | Maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time
 | MTTR (mean time to repair) | Average time to fix a failure
 | MTBF (mean time between failures) | Average time a repairable system runs between failures

High availability and sites
Redundant parts (spare in a box that you must rack and configure) is not HA. HA means the second system is already running beside the first and takes over load, at the cost of extra systems, better power and higher-quality components.
Server cluster: several servers act as one (users see a single server), and members know about each other. Nodes can be added or removed in real time, usually with identical operating systems, and clustering is turned on in the OS. Nodes use shared storage rather than local disks to stay in sync.
Load balancing differs: the servers do not know about each other, the central balancer decides who gets what, and servers can run different operating systems. It removes a failed server automatically and you can add capacity by adding servers.

Site resiliency: a recovery site allocated ahead of time, with data synced, used for hours or weeks, then you move back. Hot site = exact replica of the data center (hardware bought twice, apps updated, data constantly synchronized). Cold site = empty building with power and lighting; you bring data, equipment and people. Warm site = in the middle: some equipment and some data, you add the rest.
Geographic dispersion: a recovery site far away survives hurricanes or floods that would hit one down the street, but a farther site makes it harder to move equipment and staff (especially after a natural disaster) and to move back later.

Platform diversity: vulnerabilities are usually OS-specific, so mix Linux and Windows in the data center and macOS and Windows on clients. Multi-cloud: AWS, Azure and Google Cloud have separate processes, so an outage or security concern at one provider need not affect another.
COOP (continuity of operations planning): when technology is unavailable, use non-technical fallbacks: manual signed transactions, paper receipts, phoning in a card for approval. Design these beforehand.
Capacity planning
Too little supply gives slowdowns and outages; too much wastes money. Plan people (call center staff are hard to ramp up or down; hiring and training takes time and money), technology (choose things that scale, such as load-balanced web servers, multiple SQL servers, or splitting databases across servers), and infrastructure.

The cloud makes deployment easy (no hardware to buy, rack and test): click to create an instance, ramp up in busy periods, then rightsize when demand drops. More cloud resources means higher bills.
Recovery testing
Run recovery tests on a regular schedule with a specific scope and time window that does not affect production, then evaluate and update the plan. Full tests are expensive, so use a tabletop exercise (talk through the steps around a table with other departments) to find logistics gaps.
Failover test: ideally automatic and invisible to users. Needs redundant switches, firewalls and routers (many have failover built in). Example design: two ISPs, two routers, redundant firewalls, multiple switches, multiple server links, and load balancers.

Simulations: phishing simulation (can the systems detect it, who clicked, who needs more training), password reset process tests, data exfiltration tests.
Parallel processing: spread transactions across multiple cores or computers for efficiency, and if one processor is lost the rest absorb the load.
Backups in detail
Decide: how much data, the backup type, media (tape, disk, cloud), where to store it (on site, off site, cloud), the software, and the schedule (full daily, or daily changes with a weekly full).
On-site: same location, no WAN needed, immediately available, cheaper. Off-site: transfer or ship media elsewhere, reachable from a new data center after a disaster. Many organizations use both (on-site for fast restores, off-site for long term).

Frequency depends on data volume and how often it changes. Multiple backup sets: for example about 30 daily, 4 weekly and 12 monthly copies.
Encrypt backups, especially in the cloud. Story: tapes stolen from an employee's car during an errand on the way to the storage facility. Keep the recovery keys safe so you can restore.
Snapshots: one click for a VM or cloud system, similar to an incremental backup (changes only). Lesson example: a 1 TB VM with 100 GB used; Monday snapshot captures all 100 GB; Tuesday has 40 GB changed; Wednesday grows to 120 GB with 20 GB new. Take one daily and before big changes, and revert in a few clicks.
Test your restores regularly by simulating a disaster or restoring one database, then confirm applications can use the data (that is the second half of the test).

Replication: copy one source to one or many sites in near real time (seconds or minutes); the copy is used for backup storage, a replicated infrastructure or a hot site disaster recovery.
Journaling: write to a journal on the drive first, then copy to the final location. A power loss during the journal write loses only the journal; a loss between journal and database is repaired from the journal on startup. After success, clear the journal.
Power in detail

Power outages can last minutes, hours or days. A UPS covers blackouts, brownouts (low voltage) and surges (excess voltage). Types: offline/standby (runs on mains, switches to battery on failure; low end), line-interactive (can raise voltage during brownouts), and online/double-conversion (always runs from the battery, no switching). Size the batteries for the time you need. Many have signaling to shut systems down gracefully before the battery empties, plus outlet counts and surge suppression for Ethernet and phone lines.
Generator: long-term power while there is fuel; may power a whole building or marked outlets only. There is a start-up ramp of about a minute, so use both: UPS covers the gap until the generator takes over.

Hot > warm > cold in speed and cost.
Differential needs the last full + latest differential; incremental needs the last full + all increments.
Snapshots and replication are not substitutes for backups (replication copies corruption and deletions too).
RPO drives backup frequency; RTO drives how fast the recovery solution must be.
A tabletop is discussion only; a failover really switches systems.
4.1 Given a scenario, apply common security techniques to computing resources

watched the videos
 read the notes
 wrote my own notes
 flashcards mastered

Secure baselines: establish, deploy, maintain. Hardening targets: mobile, workstations, switches, routers, cloud, servers, ICS/SCADA, embedded, RTOS, IoT.
Wireless: site surveys and heat maps; WPA3, RADIUS, AAA. Cryptographic protocols and authentication protocols.
Application security: input validation, secure cookies, static code analysis, code signing. Sandboxing. Monitoring.
Mobile solutions: MDM; deployment models BYOD, COPE, CYOD; connection methods cellular, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth.

Objective 4.1 is about configuring things securely from the start and keeping them that way. It covers baselines, hardening for each kind of device, wireless and mobile security, and application security.

A secure baseline is the documented, approved set of security settings for a type of system (a Windows workstation, a Linux web server, a switch). It follows three steps:
Establish: define the baseline from vendor guidance, CIS benchmarks, STIGs or your own policy.
Deploy: apply it consistently (group policy, configuration management, golden images, automation).
Maintain: monitor for drift, update the baseline for new threats and patches, and re-apply it.
Baselines make systems consistent, make audits easier, and give you a known-good reference to detect unauthorized change.

For every device class, the same ideas apply: remove what you don't need, change defaults, patch, restrict access, log. The exam tests what is *special* about each class.
 | Target | Hardening focus
 | Workstations | Patching, endpoint protection/EDR, host firewall, full-disk encryption, least privilege, remove bloatware, disable unneeded services
 | Servers | Minimal installed roles, remove unneeded services/accounts, restrict admin access, patching, logging, secure remote admin
 | Switches and routers | Change default credentials, disable unused ports, use SSH not Telnet, secure management access (dedicated VLAN), update firmware, port security, disable unused services
 | Cloud infrastructure | Least privilege IAM, MFA, private storage by default, encryption, security groups, logging, scan IaC templates

| Mobile devices | MDM policy, screen lock, encryption, patching, app control, remote wipe
 | ICS/SCADA | Isolate from IT networks, strict access control, monitor, compensating controls because patching is hard and availability/safety come first
 | Embedded systems and RTOS | Limited patch options, so isolate, restrict network exposure, vendor lifecycle awareness
 | IoT | Change default passwords, separate VLAN, disable unneeded features, firmware updates
Hardening also includes: encryption, minimal software, secure configuration, disable unused ports and protocols, restrict admin rights, enable logging.

Site survey: measure signal and interference to plan access point placement.
Heat map: visual map of coverage strength and dead zones.
Channel selection to avoid overlap and interference, AP placement (not near external walls so the signal doesn't leak far outside), power levels.
Plan for capacity and for connecting wired backhaul.

Mobile device management (MDM) enforces policy on phones and tablets: require a PIN, encryption, remote wipe, app allow lists, geofencing, block jailbroken devices, push updates and certificates. Mobile application management (MAM) controls just the apps/data, which suits personal devices. Unified endpoint management (UEM) covers all endpoint types.
Deployment models:
 | Model | Who owns the device | Trade-off
 | BYOD (bring your own device) | Employee | Cheapest; hardest to control, privacy and data separation issues
 | COPE (corporate-owned, personally enabled) | Company | More control, personal use allowed
 | CYOD (choose your own device) | Company | Employee picks from an approved list
 | Corporate-owned | Company | Maximum control
Connection methods: cellular, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth (pairing risks, bluejacking/bluesnarfing), NFC, USB. Containerization / work profiles separate work data from personal data. Geofencing restricts features by location. Remote wipe erases a lost device.

WPA3 (current): uses SAE (simultaneous authentication of equals) instead of PSK handshake, protecting against offline password guessing, and adds forward secrecy and stronger encryption. WPA2 uses AES-CCMP; WPA TKIP; WEP is broken.
Personal vs Enterprise: Personal uses a shared password. Enterprise uses 802.1X with a RADIUS server so each user authenticates individually (different credentials, revocable per user).
Authentication protocols (EAP family): EAP-TLS (certificates on both sides, strongest), PEAP (TLS tunnel protecting a password exchange), EAP-TTLS, EAP-FAST.
Captive portals for guest access. Guest networks should be separate from the internal network.
Open networks have no encryption; WPA3 OWE (enhanced open) encrypts without a password.
Disable WPS, change default SSID/password, hide nothing in the name of security (hiding SSID is weak).
Rogue AP and evil twin detection through WIDS/WIPS.

Input validation: check all input for type, length, range and format, on the server side. Prevents injection and overflows.
Secure cookies: set Secure (HTTPS only), HttpOnly (not readable by scripts), SameSite (limits cross-site sending).
Static application security testing (SAST): analyze source code without running it. Dynamic testing (DAST): test the running app. Code review, fuzzing (random/malformed input).
Code signing: digitally sign code so users can verify the publisher and that it wasn't altered.
Sandboxing: run code in an isolated environment so damage is contained.
Software composition / package monitoring: track third-party libraries for known vulnerabilities.
Secrets management: no passwords or keys in code or repos.
Secure development lifecycle: security built into each phase.

Baselines
A baseline covers firewall settings, patch levels, the underlying OS, file permissions and application configuration. Each time an application instance is deployed, its baseline goes with it, and you keep checking that settings still hold; if not, make a plan to correct it quickly.
Sources: the application developer, the OS manufacturer (Microsoft), and appliance makers. Windows 10 has over 3,000 group policy settings (only a subset matter for security). Microsoft publishes baselines for Windows and Windows Server and the Security Compliance Toolkit (SCT) to deploy them.
Deploy through a central console, Active Directory group policy, or an MDM for mobile; automate it for hundreds or thousands of devices. Updates are needed for new vulnerabilities, app updates, or a new OS. Two vendors' baselines can conflict, so choose the better one. Test before deploying and audit afterward.

Hardening targets (lesson specifics)
Default configs are rarely secure. Look for manufacturer hardening guides, otherwise ask the vendor or look for third-party guides.
Mobile: patches (often security fixes), segment company data from personal data, manage with an MDM.
Workstations (Windows, macOS, Linux): patches for the OS, apps and firmware; vendors bundle monthly so you can test once. Remove unused software.
Network infrastructure: switches, routers and firewalls run embedded OSes, so change default credentials, use local or central authentication, and check the manufacturer for rare updates, treating a security release as a significant event.
Cloud management workstation: has broad access to cloud systems so it must be secure. Use least privilege for cloud apps and devices, install EDR, back up (ideally to a different cloud provider).

Servers: security patches and service packs, minimum password length and complexity, least privilege, disable unused accounts, limit which devices can reach the server (policy or firewall), plus EDR, antivirus or anti-malware.
SCADA/ICS: distributed control with real-time monitoring and control, often on an isolated, air-gapped network with no internet access.
Embedded (smartwatches, TVs, appliances): hard to upgrade and patches are rare, so install them as soon as they appear, and consider a separate network with a firewall.
RTOS: deterministic (processes have expected time frames) for industrial, military and automotive. Isolate, run minimum services, and add a separate firewall or host-based security if it must talk to the network.
IoT: makers are not security experts, so prioritize patches and segment IoT devices on their own network.
Wireless and mobile

Site survey: learn which access points are nearby (yours and others), the spectrum in use and the best channels, then repeat periodically because neighbors change. A heat map shows coverage (red/yellow strong, blue weak). Tools: built-in OS utilities, NetSpot, and survey tools listing SSIDs, BSSID, channel and band. A spectrum analyzer shows every signal on a frequency, including non-Wi-Fi devices.

MDM capabilities: push policies and required apps, disable the camera at headquarters and re-enable it outside, create a business partition separate from personal data, force screen locks and PIN/password. BYOD (also "bring your own technology") needs modern devices that can be managed, privacy for the user, and a process for when the phone is sold or traded in. COPE: company buys it, personal use allowed, with corporate data partitioned so one partition can be wiped. CYOD: user chooses from corporate-owned options.
Cellular (4G/5G, divided into cells): worry about traffic monitoring and location tracking; keep devices patched. Wi-Fi: use VPN or other encryption on untrusted networks (coffee shop, hotel), because attackers nearby can do on-path or interference attacks. Bluetooth is a PAN; use the formal pairing process and do not auto-connect to unknown devices.

Wireless security settings
Wireless is over the air, so encrypt and authenticate. A message integrity check (MIC) ensures frames arrive unchanged.
WPA2 problem: the four-way handshake carries a hash tied to the pre-shared key. Capture it, then brute force it offline with GPU or cloud cracking in days.
WPA3: GCMP (Galois Counter Mode Protocol) provides confidentiality plus integrity through a Galois message authentication code. The handshake is replaced by SAE (simultaneous authentication of equals), based on Diffie-Hellman, with mutual authentication and session keys created on each end rather than sent across. Each user gets a different session key even with the same PSK. Also known as the dragonfly handshake.
Network modes: open/none, WPA3-Personal (PSK), and WPA3-Enterprise (802.1X) tied to RADIUS, LDAP or TACACS+.

AAA: identification (username), then authentication, authorization (what you can access) and accounting (login time, data sent and received, logout). RADIUS (remote authentication dial-in user service) is widely supported for routers, switches, servers and VPNs. A central AAA server lets you disable one account when someone leaves.
802.1X (NAC) works on wired and wireless. EAP is the flexible framework inside it. Roles: supplicant, authenticator, authentication server. Flow: authenticator blocks and asks for identity, supplicant sends an EAP response with its name, authenticator asks the server whether to continue, supplicant gives credentials, server validates and allows.
Application security

Input validation: check every field against the expected format (a ZIP code has a set length and character set, and formats differ by country) and prompt for correction. Fuzzing automates random input to see how the app behaves.
Cookies are data files, not executables, but hold useful info. Secure cookies have an attribute requiring HTTPS. Anything in a cookie can be read, so never store sensitive data in one.
SAST (static application security testing): analyzers find buffer overflows and injections in code, but miss problems like how cryptography is implemented, and produce false positives to triage. Example output: filetest.c line 32 using gets with no overflow check, recommend fgets.

Code signing answers whether the code changed and whether it truly came from that developer. A CA signs the developer's key, the developer signs code, and the OS checks during install and warns if validation fails.
Sandboxing: the app only reaches the data it needs. Development sandboxes keep a new app away from production; VMs are isolated; mobile OS sandboxes mean a browser cannot reach your camera roll.
Monitoring: built-in logging reveals SQL injection attempts, unusual file transfers or rising client access.

EAP-TLS is strongest because it needs certificates on client and server.
WPA3-Personal protects against offline dictionary attacks via SAE.
BYOD = employee owns; COPE = company owns, personal use allowed.
Baselines: establish → deploy → maintain.
SAST examines code; DAST tests running software.

Group Policy hands-on lab
Windows admin / PowerShell hands-on lab

Acquisition/procurement, assignment/accounting (ownership, classification), monitoring/asset tracking (inventory, enumeration).
Disposal/decommissioning: sanitization, destruction, certification, data retention.
You cannot protect what you don't know you have. Asset management covers the whole life of hardware, software and data, from buying through disposal.

| Stage | What happens | Security concern
 | Acquisition / procurement | Requesting, approving and buying | Buy from trusted sources to avoid counterfeit or tampered products; define security requirements; vendor due diligence
 | Assignment / accounting | Give it an owner and record it | Ownership and classification of each asset; someone is accountable for it
 | Monitoring / asset tracking | Keep the inventory accurate | Know what exists, where, its patch level and its status
 | Disposal / decommissioning | Retire it safely | Data must be removed or destroyed; keep records

Inventory: a list of all assets with details (type, owner, location, serial number, OS version, software, classification, purchase and warranty dates). An asset you don't know about is an asset you can't patch.
Enumeration: discovering what is on the network, with scanning and network access control, so unknown devices (shadow IT) show up.
Tracking tools: barcode or RFID tags, asset management software, configuration management database (CMDB), mobile device management.
Track software licenses and approved software lists too.
Every asset has a business owner who decides how it's used and what protection it needs, and is classified (public, private, confidential, restricted) so controls match its value (see 3.3).

When hardware or media is retired, data may still be recoverable. Pick the method based on data sensitivity and whether the device will be reused.
 | Method | What it does | Reusable afterward?
 | Sanitization (wiping) | Overwrites data (secure erase, multiple-pass, cryptographic erase) so it can't be recovered. Follows NIST SP 800-88 | Yes
 | Cryptographic erase | Destroy the encryption key so encrypted data is unreadable | Yes
 | Degaussing | Strong magnetic field scrambles data on magnetic media (HDD, tape) | HDD no longer works; no effect on SSD
 | Physical destruction | Shredding, pulverizing, drilling, incineration, disintegrating | No
 | Certificate of destruction | A vendor's written proof of destruction | n/a
Retention: keep data only as long as policy or law requires, then dispose of it. Over-retention increases breach impact; under-retention can break legal requirements.
Legal hold: when litigation is possible, relevant data must be preserved and *not* disposed.
Media types: SSDs and flash need different methods than magnetic disks (degaussing doesn't work on SSD). Paper needs shredding or pulping.
Document the disposal: who, what, when, how, and keep the certificate.

Procurement and tracking
Procurement flow: the end user states a need, works with IT and purchasing, budget and approvals (IT, purchasing, management), negotiation of price, license terms and contract details, then delivery and an invoice. Invoice terms may be pay in full immediately or net 30 or 60 days.
Tangible items go into a central asset tracking system for their whole life cycle. Ownership: a laptop is recorded under the user's name, so IT knows who to visit for updates.
Record the type (laptop, desktop, mobile) and whether it is hardware or software, because that drives tax treatment. Hardware is a capital expenditure with depreciation; software generally does not depreciate and is an operating expense.

Uses: inventory (laptops, routers, cables), help desk tickets pre-filled with make and model, enumeration (a desktop is one asset, or its CPU, memory, drives and peripherals), and an asset tag or barcode that also deters loss or theft.
Sanitization and destruction in detail
Choose by plan: disposing or recycling means delete everything; reusing internally may only need removal of sensitive files. Secure delete utilities make data unrecoverable so the same drive can be reused.
Physical destruction: shredder or industrial pulverizer, or a drill or hammer for a few drives (holes in platters). Degauss with a strong electromagnetic field (renders a hard drive unusable). Incinerate for certainty.
For hundreds or thousands of drives, hire a destruction service and get a certificate of destruction.
Data retention

Retention covers original data, copies and backups. Laws may require keeping email or financial records for set years. Write policies and procedures for it. It is also good practice: tie to backup policy for accidental deletions and for disaster recovery. Different data types need different retention lengths.

Degaussing only works on magnetic media.
Sanitization lets you reuse the device; destruction does not.
Cryptographic erase is the fast option for encrypted drives.
Every asset needs an owner and a classification.
Don't dispose of data under legal hold.

4.3 Explain various activities associated with vulnerability management

watched the videos
 read the notes
 wrote my own notes
 flashcards mastered

Identification: vulnerability scans, application security (static/dynamic analysis, package monitoring), threat feeds (OSINT, proprietary, ISAC, dark web), penetration testing, bug bounty, system/process audits.
Analysis: confirmation (false positive/negative), prioritize, CVSS, CVE, classification, exposure factor, environmental variables, impact, risk tolerance.
Response: patching, insurance, segmentation, compensating controls, exceptions and exemptions.
Validation: rescanning, audit, verification. Reporting.
Vulnerability management is a repeating cycle: find weaknesses, analyze which matter, fix or mitigate them, verify the fix, and report.

Vulnerability scanning: automated tools probe systems for known weaknesses (missing patches, misconfigurations, open ports, default credentials). Scan types:
Credentialed (authenticated) scans log in and see much more (installed software, local settings). Fewer false positives.
Non-credentialed scans see only what an outsider sees.
Intrusive scans actively test and can disrupt systems; non-intrusive scans avoid that.
Agent-based vs agentless; internal vs external; compliance scans against a standard.
Use the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) list and the NVD; scanners rely on updated signature feeds.
Application security testing: static analysis (SAST) of source code, dynamic analysis (DAST) of the running app, fuzzing, package monitoring for vulnerable libraries.

Penetration testing: authorized attackers try to exploit weaknesses to prove real impact. Unlike a scan, it exploits. Types:
Known environment (white box): full information. Partially known (gray). Unknown environment (black box): tester starts like an outsider.
Rules of engagement define scope, timing and limits; get written authorization.
Reconnaissance can be passive (OSINT, no direct contact) or active (probing the target).
Phases: planning, discovery/recon, attack/exploitation (including lateral movement, privilege escalation, persistence, pivoting), cleanup, reporting.
Responsible disclosure and bug bounty: a program that invites researchers to report flaws privately for recognition or payment.
System and process audit: checking configuration and procedures against policy.

Threat feeds supply indicators and context so you know what to look for.
Open-source intelligence (OSINT): public sources (news, social media, vulnerability databases, public repositories, government bulletins).
Proprietary / third-party (commercial) feeds: paid, curated, often more timely.
Information-sharing organizations: ISACs and ISAOs where members share threats in an industry.
Dark web monitoring: leaked credentials and chatter about your organization.
Standards STIX (format) and TAXII (transport) automate sharing; indicators of compromise are the unit of exchange.
Also used for: threat maps, vulnerability databases, public/private information sharing, and tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) analysis.

Confirm the finding: a false positive is reported but not real; a false negative is a real flaw the scan missed (dangerous). Verify with logs, config checks or manual testing.
Prioritize and classify by severity and context:
CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System): 0 to 10 base score (Low 0.1-3.9, Medium 4.0-6.9, High 7.0-8.9, Critical 9.0-10.0), plus temporal and environmental adjustments.
Exposure factor and environmental variables (is it internet-facing? what data is on it?).
Industry/organizational impact (regulations, business criticality).
Risk tolerance (how much exposure the business accepts).
Whether an exploit exists or is being used in the wild raises priority.
Treat zero-days, legacy systems and unpatchable devices as special cases.

Patching: apply vendor fixes; test first, schedule through change management.
Insurance: transfer part of the financial risk (does not fix the flaw).
Segmentation: isolate the vulnerable system.
Compensating controls: alternative protection when you can't fix (WAF rule, firewall block, extra monitoring).
Exceptions and exemptions: formally accepted when remediation isn't possible or practical, with documented justification, approval and review date. This is risk acceptance.
Configuration changes and removing the vulnerable software.

Rescanning after the fix to confirm it's gone.
Verification: confirm the system still works and the fix held.
Audit the process; maintain evidence.
Reporting: communicate findings, risk, status and trends to technical staff and management. Include severity, affected assets, owner, due date and the plan.

Scanning
A vulnerability scan checks whether an attack is possible and does not attack (otherwise it is a pen test). A port scan is the simplest example: open ports are not necessarily vulnerable but show where an attacker could look. Scan from outside, and also from inside to cover insider threats.
Reports are huge and not always accurate, so review for false positives. Severity levels: critical, high, medium, low, informational. Sample findings: an OpenSSH/OpenSSL random number generator weakness (weak SSH host keys, critical) and unsupported Unix OS detection (a system you did not know was still running and cannot be patched). Verify findings, then run confirmed ones through change control to patch.

SAST reviews source for buffer overflows and injections but misses implementation problems like authentication and cryptography. Sample output: test.c line 73, SetSecurityDescriptorDacl, never create a NULL ACL.
Fuzzing / dynamic analysis (also fault injection, robustness testing) feeds random input and watches for crashes, server errors or exceptions. The first fuzzer came from a 1988 University of Wisconsin class project led by Professor Barton Miller. It is automated with hundreds or thousands of iterations. A free tool is CERT's Basic Fuzzing Framework (BFF).
Package monitoring: verify packages came from the manufacturer, not a third party, and test unknown packages in a lab environment before production.
Threat intelligence
Know the threats and the threat actors (hacker groups, their tools). Use it to choose tools and training, and share across research and IT teams.

OSINT sources: hacking-group discussion groups, social media, researchers, government hearings and reports, and public commercial data like financial reports. Commercial/third-party services see many organizations at once, spot trends and alert early.
Cyber Threat Alliance (CTA): members submit threat data in a standard format, the alliance validates and scores each submission for severity, and members use it. The dark web (an overlay network on the internet that needs special software) shows hacking groups, tools and techniques, and stores selling stolen data such as credit cards. Monitor it for your organization's name.
Penetration testing
Pen tests are actual exploits and may be required at regular intervals. NIST SP 800-115 is the technical guide to security testing and assessment.

Rules of engagement: when testing is allowed, test types (on-site physical breach, internal or external), hours (for example after 6 PM only), in-scope IP ranges, out-of-scope systems, emergency contacts, and how to handle sensitive data found. Exploits can crash systems (a buffer overflow for privilege escalation), so protect critical production systems.
Techniques per system: password brute force, social engineering (can be by phone), database injection, buffer overflow.
After the first access: lateral movement, persistence (a backdoor, a new account, changing passwords, since the original hole might be patched), pivoting (use the compromised host as a relay/proxy to reach other internal systems).

Responsible disclosure and bug bounty: a researcher reports to the developer, who fixes, tests and publishes a patch; only afterward is the issue published in the CVE list, often weeks or months later. Bounties are funded by the developer.
Analyzing
False positive: report says it exists but it does not. Low/informational findings that are real are not false positives. False negative: real flaw the scanner missed, which is worse. Update scanner signatures before scanning to reduce both; ask the vendor for updated signatures if needed.
CVSS scores 0 to 10 (10 most critical) and appears in multiple versions (CVSS 2.0, 3.x). The NVD (nvd.nist.gov) syncs with the CVE list (cve.mitre.org). Vendors keep their own databases (Microsoft security bulletins). Scanners usually give the CVE; some findings are generic with no CVE, so research or verify.

Scanners also cover applications (CVE-2020-1889, WhatsApp desktop bypass), web applications (CVE-2020-24981, UCMS 1.4.8 access control), and network devices (CVE-2020-2579, D-Link).
Exposure factor is a percentage: a flaw that disables a service half the time is 50%; one with no patch on a public web server that fully disables the service is 100%. Combine with CVSS to prioritize.
Environmental variables: public cloud versus isolated lab. Industry impact: Tallahassee Memorial Health, February 2023, ransomware closed the hospital for two weeks (ER diversions, surgeries canceled); March 2019 DDoS on Salt Lake City and LA County power generators. Consider user numbers and type, internal vs external, whether the app is critical or revenue-generating, and exploit ease.

Risk tolerance decides patch order and how much testing is acceptable before deploying. A widely affecting, easily exploited flaw means low tolerance and rushed testing.
Remediation details
Patches arrive on a schedule (weekly/monthly) or out of cycle for severe flaws or zero-days.
Cyber insurance pays after events (revenue loss, data recovery, phishing losses, lawsuits) but excludes things like intentional acts and some fund transfers. Ransomware has increased uptake.
Segmentation: VLANs or separate switches (air gap: customer A and B on different switches). Different VLANs only talk through a router. NGFWs show application-level flows between segments (spotting SSH leaving a server).

When you cannot patch: disable the vulnerable service, revoke access to the app, use the edge firewall policy, router ACLs, or a software firewall on the server. Patching is best; these are compensating controls.
Exceptions/exemptions are decided by a security or change committee, not one person. Example: a flaw exploitable only locally on a server inside a data center may be reasonable to leave unpatched until the conflict is resolved.
Validation: scan after patching to confirm the fix and find missed systems; audit samples manually; use reporting (total vulnerabilities, patched vs unpatched, new threats over time, patch errors, exceptions and exemptions, systems left to patch).

Credentialed scans give more accurate results than non-credentialed.
A vulnerability scan finds weaknesses; a penetration test exploits them.
False negative (missed vulnerability) is more dangerous than a false positive.
CVE identifies a specific flaw; CVSS rates how severe it is.
Cyber insurance transfers financial risk; it doesn't remediate.
Always rescan to validate after remediation.

Monitor systems, applications and infrastructure. Activities: log aggregation, alerting, scanning, reporting, archiving, alert response (quarantine, alert tuning).
Tools: SCAP, benchmarks, agents/agentless, SIEM, antivirus, DLP, SNMP traps, NetFlow, vulnerability scanners.
Monitoring turns raw activity into alerts people can act on. This objective covers what to monitor, how logs are gathered and analyzed, and the tools that make it practical.

Systems and computing resources: logins and where from, service activity, backups, installed software and versions, patch status.
Applications: availability, errors, unusual usage, performance.
Infrastructure: firewalls, IPS, VPN connections (employees vs vendors vs guests), switches and routers, cloud services.
Network traffic: volume and destinations. A large unexplained transfer can mean data exfiltration.
Monitoring is a detective control. Real-time monitoring also supports reaction (quarantine, disable an account).

| Activity | What it is
 | Log aggregation | Collect logs from many systems into one place, normalize formats (usually a SIEM)
 | Scanning | Regularly inventory devices and check versions, drivers, patches and vulnerabilities
 | Reporting | Build reports from the stored data: compliance, patch status, OS versions, trends, "how many systems are affected by today's new CVE?" (including forward-looking views like end-of-life dates)
 | Archiving | Retain logs for investigations, legal and regulatory needs. Attackers can sit undetected for months, so long retention matters
 | Alerting | Notify people when something actionable happens (spike in authentication failures, large transfer, new admin account)
 | Response / quarantine | Isolate the affected system to prevent further spread
 | Alert tuning | Adjust thresholds and rules to cut noise

False positive: alert fires but nothing is wrong. Too many cause alert fatigue, and analysts start ignoring them.
False negative: a real attack produces no alert. The dangerous one.
Alert tuning is the continuous balance between the two. Set thresholds, whitelist known-good activity, add context, and review rules regularly.
Alerts can be e-mailed, texted, paged, or sent to a SOC (security operations center) dashboard or ticketing system.

SIEM (security information and event management): central log collection plus correlation, alerting, dashboards and reporting. Pulls from firewalls, servers, endpoints, IDS/IPS, applications. Correlates events across sources (e.g. failed VPN logins followed by a success from a new country). Supports forensic search and compliance reports.
SOAR (security orchestration, automation and response): automates response with playbooks (disable account, block IP, open a ticket). See 4.7.
SCAP (Security Content Automation Protocol): NIST standards that give tools a common language for vulnerabilities and configuration so scanners, patch systems and reporting tools can interoperate. Components include CVE, CVSS, OVAL and XCCDF checklists for compliance.
Benchmarks and baselines: CIS benchmarks, vendor guides and DISA STIGs are used to measure configuration against a standard.

Agents and agentless monitoring: software on the host vs remote polling (SNMP, WMI, API).
NetFlow / sFlow / IPFIX: summaries of network conversations (who talked to whom, how much). Good for spotting exfiltration and scanning without capturing content.
Antivirus / EDR / XDR: endpoint telemetry; DLP for data leaving; vulnerability scanners (Nessus, OpenVAS); protocol analyzers (Wireshark).
SNMP (versions 1/2 use cleartext community strings; SNMPv3 adds authentication and encryption) for device status; SNMP traps push alerts.
Syslog for log forwarding.

What gets monitored and why
Monitor authentications (logins from where, such as lots of logins from a country with no employees), services (type and amount of activity, backup completion, software versions to decide patching), applications (availability), and traffic volume (a sudden spike above the norm may mean exfiltration). Stay in contact with software vendors so you hear about security issues.
Infrastructure examples: VPN users broken down into employees, vendors and guests; firewall and IPS spikes in attacks as a warning. Roll everything into dashboards for a glance at posture.
A SIEM consolidates logs from firewalls, switches, servers and routers (different formats) into one database, allowing correlation (VPN authentication, then what was accessed), reports on application access, and data-transfer baselines with alerts when exceeded.
Scanning and reporting

Devices constantly move (laptops, phones, tablets), so continuously scan for OS versions, driver versions, installed apps and log anomalies, and store results in a database for later reports. Make reports actionable: not just how many devices are compliant, but which are not and what is needed.
When a new vulnerability drops, the database lets you instantly report how many systems are affected. Ad hoc "what if" reports: for example how many systems will be exposed when an OS reaches end of life in six months.
Archiving
An IBM security report from 2022 said it takes about nine months on average to identify and contain a breach, so keep long-term logs and backups. Some laws require collecting data for a set period.
Alerts

Examples of alert triggers: more authentication errors (password spraying or brute force), or a large data transfer from the data center to an internet site. Deliver by SMS, email, or to a separate SOC alert group, not only a screen or morning report.
Common reaction: quarantine the system so the attacker cannot reach others. Accuracy is a balancing act: false positives are inaccurate alerts, false negatives are events never logged or alerted. Tuning takes time, after which alerts reflect what is really happening.
Tools in detail
SCAP (maintained by NIST, scap.nist.gov): a common language so a next-gen firewall, IPS and vulnerability scanner all call the same vulnerability the same thing. This lets tools automate the chain: scanner finds it, management system pushes the patch, no human needed.

Benchmarks: the Center for Internet Security (CIS) has a library (cissecurity.org). Example: a mobile benchmark disables screenshots and screen recording, blocks voice calls while locked, and forces encrypted backups.
Agent vs agentless compliance checks: checks run at connection or login. An agent is installed beforehand, always on, but needs ongoing updates of code and rules. Agentless runs on demand (for example at VPN login), executes in memory, verifies compliance and removes itself; no maintenance, but it only runs when triggered so must be run regularly.
SIEM also supports correlation across VPN logins, application server activity and firewall blocks, plus forensic reports of what happened before an event.

Antivirus vs anti-malware: the terms are effectively interchangeable today. DLP looks for and blocks sensitive data (Social Security numbers, medical info, card data) in real time; can run on endpoints or in cloud systems.
SNMP: built into most devices. Metrics live in the MIB (Management Information Base) identified by OIDs (numeric object identifiers). Polling uses UDP 161: the management station asks a router how many bytes crossed an interface, waits (5 or 10 minutes), asks again, and graphs the changes. SNMP traps are proactive alerts from the agent to the station on UDP 162; example: send a trap when CRC errors rise by 5, and the station then fires alerts, SMS or automation.

NetFlow: standard for traffic flow and application-use statistics. A probe (in a switch/router software or external, fed by a SPAN port or tap) sends metrics to a collector that shows top 10 conversations, top 10 endpoints, and traffic events.
Vulnerability scanner: minimally invasive, no exploits, includes port scans and discovery of active hosts across an IP range. Scan internally, and also from outside to see what an attacker would see. Verify results because not everything is accurate. Sample critical finding: a server random-number-generator flaw allowing remote shell, and an unsupported Unix OS.

Collect logs and scan results.
SIEM normalizes, correlates and stores.
Rules and thresholds raise alerts.
Analysts investigate, tune rules, escalate to incident response.
Reports show trends and compliance.

SIEM = collection + correlation + alerting. SOAR = automated response.
SCAP standardizes vulnerability/config data between tools; it isn't a scanner.
False negatives are a bigger risk than false positives, but too many false positives cause alert fatigue.
NetFlow shows traffic metadata, not packet contents.
SNMPv3 is the secure version.

4.5 Given a scenario, modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security

watched the videos
 read the notes
