Firewall: rules, access lists, ports/protocols, screened subnets. IDS/IPS: trends, signatures.
Web filter: agent-based, centralized proxy, URL scanning, content categorization, block rules, reputation.
OS security: Group Policy, SELinux. Secure protocols, DNS filtering, email security (DMARC, DKIM, SPF, gateway).
File integrity monitoring, DLP, NAC, EDR/XDR, user behavior analytics.
Objective 4.5 is "modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security": which tool fits which problem, and how you tune it. Expect scenario questions that ask what to change.

Rules use source, destination, port, protocol, and action. Evaluated top to bottom, first match wins, with an implicit deny at the end. Place specific rules first; remove stale rules.
Access control list (ACL) is the rule set. Screened subnet (DMZ) hosts public services between two firewalls/interfaces.
Ports and protocols: allow only what's needed (443, 22, 53...); block risky ones (Telnet, SMBv1, RDP from the internet).
Types: stateless, stateful, next-generation (NGFW) with application awareness, user identity and TLS inspection, UTM, WAF, host-based.
Inbound vs outbound rules: egress filtering stops malware from calling out and data leaving.
Logging firewall decisions feeds the SIEM.

Agent-based: software on the endpoint enforces policy anywhere (good for roaming laptops).
Centralized proxy / secure web gateway (SWG): all web traffic passes through one place for filtering, malware scanning and logging.
URL scanning / categories: allow or block by site category (gambling, adult, malware).
Content categorization, block rules, reputation scores for domains, and DNS filtering that refuses to resolve known-bad domains.
TLS inspection lets the filter see inside HTTPS but requires certificates and has privacy implications.

Group Policy (Windows domain): centrally enforce settings such as password rules, disabled services, firewall settings and application restrictions across thousands of computers.
SELinux (and AppArmor): Linux mandatory access control that limits what a process can do even if compromised.
Patching, local firewall, least privilege, secure boot, disabling legacy protocols.

Use encrypted versions and retire cleartext ones:
 | Insecure | Secure replacement | Port change
 | Telnet (23) | SSH (22) | 
 | HTTP (80) | HTTPS (443) | 
 | FTP (21) | SFTP (22, over SSH) or FTPS (990) | 
 | POP3 (110) / IMAP (143) | POP3S (995) / IMAPS (993) | 
 | SMTP (25) | SMTP with TLS (587 submission / 465) | 
 | LDAP (389) | LDAPS (636) | 
 | SNMP v1/v2 | SNMPv3 | 
 | Syslog (514) | Syslog over TLS | 
 | VoIP RTP | SRTP | 
Choose the protocol when the question mentions confidentiality, plus port knowledge when asked which port to open or close. Also use DNSSEC, NTP with authentication, and TLS 1.2+.

SPF (Sender Policy Framework): a DNS record listing the mail servers allowed to send for a domain.
DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail): the sending server signs messages; receivers verify with a DNS public key. Proves the message came from the domain and wasn't altered.
DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance): tells receivers what to do when SPF/DKIM fail (none, quarantine, reject) and sends reports back. Builds on SPF and DKIM.
Gateways: spam filters, attachment sandboxing, link rewriting, anti-phishing, DLP, encryption (S/MIME, PGP, TLS).
Mailbox protections: MFA, disable legacy protocols, external sender banners, user reporting button.

Log sources: operating systems, firewalls, IPS, applications, network devices, cloud, endpoints.
SIEM correlation and dashboards; NetFlow; packet captures; DLP alerts.
Tune rules and thresholds to cut false positives; add new detections as threats change.
Archive and protect log integrity (send off-host, restrict deletion).

Antivirus/anti-malware: signature-based detection of known threats.
EDR (endpoint detection and response): continuous behavior monitoring, investigation and response on endpoints. XDR extends across endpoints, network, cloud and email.
Host-based firewall and HIPS.
Application allow list and device control (block USB storage).
DLP agents, full-disk encryption, patch management, mobile device management.
Configuration enforcement and compliance checks.
Network access control (NAC) and posture assessment before connecting.

Firewalls
A network firewall sits inline and can also be a VPN endpoint (site-to-site or remote access) and a layer 3 router/NAT device at the ingress/egress point. NGFW (also application layer gateway, stateful multilayer inspection, deep packet inspection) classifies each application, which takes more analysis than ports.
Same service, two views. Traditional: web = TCP 80/443, SSH = TCP 22, RDP = TCP 3389, DNS = UDP 53, NTP = UDP 123. NGFW recognizes the application itself (while still allowing port matching). NGFW rule fields: name, source and destination zone, IPs, services (ports), user, application, web category and URL list.
Rule order: top to bottom, first match wins, specific rules high and broad ones low, and an implicit deny at the end. The rule base is an ACL.

Lesson rule table example: accept inbound TCP 22 (SSH), 80 (HTTP), 443 (HTTPS), 3389 (RDP), UDP 53 (DNS), UDP 123 (NTP), and deny ICMP (ping), followed by implicit deny.
Screened subnet: a third firewall interface for services that must be reachable from the internet; internet traffic goes to the screened subnet and back out, and cannot reach the internal network with confidential data.
IPS rules: usually inside the NGFW, with signatures (the lesson shows one for the Conficker worm), and can also detect anomalies such as generic database injection with no specific signature. Thousands of signatures can be grouped (block every database-injection rule). Customize to balance security against false positives. Sample rules: malware names with ports, and an FTP login worm.
Web filtering

A content filter (URL filter, website category filter) controls the data in and out and is like parental controls at home. Some block known-bad sites (malware, viruses). URL lists have allow lists and block lists; URLs are grouped into categories (auction, hacking, malware, travel, recreation and 50+ more such as adult, educational, gambling, government, home and garden). Example policy: educational allowed; home and garden allowed but logged or alerted; gambling blocked.
Standalone URL filters are now commonly built into NGFWs, but that assumes users are behind the firewall. Agent-based filters on the device work anywhere and are centrally managed, but the agents and category lists need regular updates.

Proxy: requests on the user's behalf, then inspects the response; can cache, perform access control (by username/password or IP), URL filter and malware check. Explicit proxy needs client config; transparent proxy does not. A forward (internal) proxy serves internal users, with the organization controlling its configuration.
Reputation filtering: levels such as trustworthy, low risk, medium risk, suspicious, high risk; usually automated by scanning sites, with manual override allowed. Block high-risk, allow trustworthy.
DNS filtering: the DNS server will not return the IP of known-bad domains (updated by real-time threat intelligence, commercial or public lists). Users get a default IP or none. It also breaks malware calling its command and control server by name.
Operating system security

Active Directory: central, redundant database of computers, devices, users, file shares, printers and security groups. Single source of authentication and permissions, assignable to users or groups. Group policy (Group Policy Management Editor) overlays settings: login scripts, QoS-type network configuration, security parameters for users and devices.
Linux default is discretionary access control (DAC) where users set permissions; high-security environments use mandatory access control (MAC) with a central administrator. SELinux (open source, installable on many distributions) supports least privilege so a breach or malicious code has limited scope.
Secure protocols

Telnet, FTP, SMTP and IMAP are cleartext. Use packet capture to see: headers visible, payload should be encrypted. DEFCON's wall of sheep shows people sending IMAP, HTTP and POP3 insecurely. Replace Telnet with SSH, HTTP with HTTPS, IMAP with IMAPS, FTP with SFTP. If you cannot use a secure protocol, better not to use the app.
Port 80 usually means HTTP and 443 HTTPS, but a port number does not guarantee encryption; check server settings and confirm with a packet capture. Network-level options: WPA3 on wireless, or a VPN (encrypted tunnel to a concentrator, though it needs client software and your own concentrator or a third-party service).
Email security
Email protocols have little built-in checking, so spoofing is common. The mail gateway (on-premises in a screened subnet, or cloud-based) decides inbox, spam or discard.

SPF: a TXT record in DNS listing servers authorized to send for the domain (example: mailgun.org). DKIM: the sending mail server signs messages in transit; the signature is in the headers and receivers verify with the public key in a DNS TXT record. Note: this is not a signature the user adds to a message.
DMARC: a TXT record (DMARC1) saying what to do when SPF/DKIM fail: accept (none), spam folder/quarantine, or reject, and where to send compliance reports. The reports show how many messages validated and how many were spoofed.
Monitoring data
File integrity monitoring (FIM) watches files that should not change. Windows SFC (System File Checker) checks critical OS files on demand and replaces bad ones. Linux Tripwire gives real-time monitoring. A host-based IPS can do FIM too.

DLP deployment types: endpoint DLP watches data in use; network DLP (inside an NGFW or standalone appliance) watches data in motion; server-resident DLP covers data at rest; cloud DLP blocks sensitive uploads and malware to cloud apps.
USB blocking: November 2008, the US Department of Defense had the agent.btz worm spread via a USB drive, so USB storage was banned/blocked by local DLP agents until restrictions lifted in February 2010.
Email DLP: inbound (suspicious keywords, spoofed or imposter mail, quarantine) and outbound (fake wire transfer emails, W-2 data with Social Security numbers). Boeing, November 2016: an employee emailed a seemingly blank spreadsheet to a spouse with hidden fields holding data for 36,000 employees; email DLP would have stopped it.
Endpoint security

Endpoints (desktops, laptops, phones, tablets) need defense in depth. The edge firewall rules are fairly static. Access control rules can use user or group, location, data location and application, and can change with posture.
Posture assessment at connect or login: is the device trusted (a company certificate), is antivirus installed, running and updated, are required apps present and current, is there full disk encryption. Agent types: persistent agent (always installed, can run any time, needs updates), dissolvable agent (runs at login then removes itself), and agentless NAC (integrated with Active Directory, only runs at login and logoff). Failing devices can be quarantined on their own VLAN with remediation instructions, then reassessed.

More than a million malware variants a day makes signatures alone inadequate. EDR adds behavior analysis, machine learning, process monitoring and root-cause analysis and can automatically isolate, quarantine and roll back. XDR adds data from many systems and the network, correlates it, reduces false positives and speeds investigation. Data sources include user behavior analytics which builds baselines of normal users, devices, traffic and repositories, then flags abnormal events using rules, pattern matching or statistics.

SPF = who may send; DKIM = signature that proves authenticity/integrity; DMARC = policy plus reporting. 
Implicit deny is the last rule in a firewall.
EDR watches behavior and can respond; plain antivirus relies on signatures.
SFTP runs over SSH (port 22); FTPS runs FTP over TLS (990/989).
SELinux is mandatory access control on Linux; Group Policy manages Windows settings.

Provisioning/de-provisioning, permission assignments, identity proofing, federation, SSO (LDAP, OAuth, SAML), interoperability, attestation.
Access models: mandatory, discretionary, role-based, rule-based, attribute-based, time-of-day restrictions, least privilege.
MFA: something you know, have, are, somewhere you are. Hard/soft tokens, security keys, biometrics.
Password concepts: length, complexity, reuse, expiration, age; password managers; passwordless.
Privileged access management: just-in-time permissions, password vaulting, ephemeral credentials.
Identity and access management (IAM) decides who gets in, what they can do, and how that is kept under control. Expect scenario questions that ask for the best model or factor.

Provisioning: creating accounts and assigning access when someone joins. De-provisioning: removing access promptly when they leave or change role. Delays here are a leading cause of insider and former-employee incidents.
Permission assignments and implications: least privilege, need to know. Over-permission accumulates ("permission creep") when people change roles; review periodically.
Identity proofing: verifying a person is who they claim before issuing credentials (documents, in-person checks, knowledge checks).
Federation: trust between organizations so one login works across them. The identity provider (IdP) authenticates; the service provider (SP) relies on it.
Single sign-on (SSO): authenticate once, access many systems. Convenient, but a compromised SSO account exposes many systems, so protect it with MFA.
Standards:
LDAP: directory access protocol (Active Directory speaks it).

SAML (Security Assertions Markup Language): XML-based federation and SSO, common in enterprise and between organizations.
OAuth: authorization framework letting an app act on your behalf with limited scope, without your password ("allow this app to read my calendar").
OpenID Connect (OIDC): identity layer built on OAuth for authentication.
Kerberos: ticket-based authentication in Active Directory. Uses a key distribution center and timestamps (clocks must be in sync).
RADIUS/TACACS+: centralized AAA for network access (TACACS+ encrypts the whole payload and separates authentication, authorization and accounting).
Interoperability, attestation (proving a device or software is in a known good state).

Password vaulting / privileged access management (PAM): store admin credentials in a vault, check them out for a limited time, record sessions, and rotate secrets. Just-in-time (JIT) permissions grant elevated access only when needed.

| Model | Who decides | Description
 | Mandatory (MAC) | The system/administrator, using labels | Subjects and objects have labels (e.g. Secret, Top Secret); users can't override. Very strict, used in military
 | Discretionary (DAC) | The owner of the resource | Owner sets who can access (Windows file sharing). Flexible but easy to misconfigure
 | Role-based (RBAC) | The role | Permissions attached to job roles; users get roles. Scales well
 | Rule-based | A set of rules | Access governed by rules such as time of day or source IP, same for everyone
 | Attribute-based (ABAC) | Attributes | Decisions use attributes of the user, resource, action and environment (department, clearance, location, time)
 | Time-of-day restrictions | Time | Access limited to specific hours
 | Least privilege | Principle | Only the minimum access needed
Quick tell: "labels/clearance" → MAC. "Owner decides" → DAC. "Job function/group" → RBAC. "Attributes/context" → ABAC. "Rules/ACL with conditions" → rule-based.

Factors are different categories of proof. Two passwords are not two factors.
 | Factor | Examples
 | Something you know | Password, PIN, security answer
 | Something you have | Smart card, hardware token, phone app, security key (FIDO2)
 | Something you are | Fingerprint, face, iris, voice
 | Somewhere you are | Location, IP, geofence
 | Something you do | Behavior: gait, typing rhythm
OTP types: HOTP (counter-based), TOTP (time-based, 30-second codes in authenticator apps). Push notifications and SMS codes are weaker (SIM swapping, push fatigue); FIDO2/WebAuthn security keys and passkeys resist phishing.
Biometrics are measured by FAR (false acceptance: an impostor gets in), FRR (false rejection: a legitimate user is locked out), and the CER/EER (crossover error rate where they are equal; lower is better). Biometrics are convenient but cannot be changed if stolen.
Authentication, authorization and accounting all remain separate steps.

Modern guidance (NIST SP 800-63B): length over complexity, allow long passphrases, check against breached/common password lists, no forced periodic changes without evidence of compromise, don't use security questions or hints.
Rules you still see: minimum length, complexity, history (no reuse), maximum/minimum age, lockout after failed attempts, expiration.
Password managers generate and store unique passwords per site.
Passwordless options: passkeys, security keys, biometrics plus device.
Stored passwords must be salted and hashed with a slow algorithm.
Account types: user, privileged (admin; use separate accounts and PAM), service (non-interactive; rotate credentials, restrict logon), guest, shared (avoid; breaks accountability).
Account policies: expiration for contractors, disable on termination, location and time restrictions, impossible travel detection.

IAM lifecycle
IAM covers employees, vendors, contractors and customers, and data on devices, in a data center or in the cloud. It starts when a user needs access and ends when access is removed (onboarding, changes after a promotion or move, offboarding). It tracks name, attributes, group permissions and application access, and logs and monitors access (often required by regulation).
Provisioning and deprovisioning give the right permissions and limit ongoing access (never admin by default). Users get permissions through groups (a new hire joins the email group). Documents a user creates are private to them by default, and users have limited access to the core operating system, which also limits malware.

Identity proofing: resolution (verify they are who they say), extra validation (something only they know, security answers), and attestation through government documents such as a passport or driver's license, in-person meeting, or automated checks using credit report questions about past addresses or assets.
SSO and standards in detail
Authentication flow: client to a central point (VPN concentrator, Active Directory) with a username and password, an authentication server validates and approves. SSO: log in once and reach resources (printers, shares) for a time window, such as 24 hours before re-authenticating. Your authorization process must support it.

LDAP: access to large directories; based on the X.500 specification from the ITU (ancestor: DAP over OSI). Names are distinguished names of attribute=value pairs (CN = common name); objects form a directory information tree with containers for country, organization, organizational units and leaf objects.
SAML: authenticate to a third-party database instead of keeping your own. Not designed for mobile devices. Flow with three parties: client (browser), resource server, and an authorization/identity server. The client requests a URL, the resource server sends an encrypted SAML request that redirects to the authorization server, the user logs in, the server issues a SAML token, and the client presents the token to the resource server.

OAuth: authorization framework built by large companies for mobile and multi-device use. It is paired with OpenID for authentication. Example: Zapier asks for permission to view, edit, create and delete in your Google Drive, and your Allow click creates the link.
Federation: network access without a local authentication database, such as signing in with Twitter, Facebook or LinkedIn. The site must have a relationship set up with those providers.
Interoperability drives selection: a new VPN concentrator that supports LDAP fits an existing Active Directory; an OAuth app needs authentication via an API that feeds OAuth.
Access control in detail
Policy is defined, then IT turns it into OS-level rights. Least privilege is the baseline for any model and limits damage from malware running as that user.

MAC: labels on resources (confidential, secret, top secret); the administrator decides who gets what (a shipping clerk might get confidential, a senior manager top secret).
DAC: the data creator controls access and permission levels (read-only vs modify). Flexible but less secure because every user must choose correctly.
RBAC: administrator makes groups (manager, director, team lead, project manager), assigns rights to the group, and adds users to groups. In Windows these are groups (for example a shipping and receiving group, and a managers group that can also view shipping logs).
Rule-based: system-enforced rules created by the administrator and attached to objects; users cannot change them. Examples: data in a lab accessible only 9 AM to 5 PM, or a web form only usable with the Chrome browser.

ABAC: next-generation model combining many criteria such as source IP, time of day, action (read or write), and relationship to the data.
Time-of-day restrictions work across models; include the user's time zone for global companies. Examples: training room network off midnight to 6 AM, conference room access limited after 8 PM, R&D databases only 8 AM to 6 PM.
MFA details

Factors: something you know (password, PIN, an unlock pattern), something you have (smart card plus PIN, USB security key with your certificate, hardware token showing numbers also computed by the server, software token on your phone, SMS code), something you are (biometrics store a mathematical representation, not a picture; hard to change; combine with other factors since biometrics can be bypassed), and somewhere you are (a login from another country 10 minutes after you were elsewhere is refused; IP address is imperfect and harder with IPv6; combine with GPS).
Password security details
Entropy means unpredictability: avoid single words, mix upper and lower case, numbers and special characters. Minimum 8 characters, rising over time; phrases give longer passwords.

Password age and expiration (30, 60, 90 days; 15 or 7 for critical systems), reminders before expiry, and history to block reuse.
Use a different password per account; a password manager stores them in an encrypted database protected by extra credentials or MFA, ships in many operating systems, has enterprise versions, gives a health summary (compromised or weak passwords) and generates random passwords.
Passwordless: face unlock on a phone, a Windows PIN. Usually initially set up with a password or another factor.
Just-in-time permissions: a technician requests access from a central clearinghouse or password vault under pre-set policy; the vault creates ephemeral credentials from the primary ones (primary credentials never shown) and deletes them after the session. If an attacker breaches an ordinary account, they do not have admin access.

OAuth = authorization; OIDC = authentication layer on top; SAML = XML federation/SSO.
FAR lets the wrong person in; FRR keeps the right person out.
A password plus a PIN is one factor (both something you know).
Kerberos needs synchronized clocks.
RBAC is the best fit for large, role-structured organizations.
MAC is the strictest; DAC is the most flexible.

Use cases: user provisioning, resource provisioning, guard rails, security groups, ticket creation, escalation, enabling/disabling services, CI testing, integrations/APIs.
Benefits: efficiency, enforcing baselines, standard infrastructure, scaling, employee retention, reaction time, workforce multiplier.
Considerations: complexity, cost, single point of failure, technical debt, ongoing supportability.
Automation and orchestration let a small team handle a large environment consistently and quickly. The exam wants the use cases, the benefits and the risks.

User and resource provisioning: create accounts, assign groups, build servers and cloud resources from templates, with the same security settings every time.
Guard rails and security groups: automatically enforce limits on what can be created or changed.
Ticket creation and workflow routing from alerts.
Escalation: route unresolved or severe issues to the right team.
Enabling/disabling services and access: for example disable a compromised account or block an IP on a firewall immediately.
Continuous integration and testing (CI/CD): run security tests every time code changes.
Integrations and APIs: connect security tools so they share data and trigger each other.
Incident response playbooks: automated steps for common incidents.

| Benefit | Why it matters
 | Efficiency / time saved | Routine work done in seconds
 | Enforcing baselines | Every system built and checked the same way
 | Standard infrastructure configurations | Fewer one-off, forgotten settings
 | Scaling in a secure manner | Handle growth without hiring in proportion
 | Employee retention | Less repetitive work, more interesting work
 | Reaction time | Machine-speed response to threats
 | Workforce multiplier | One analyst handles what many would

Complexity: automation needs design, testing and documentation.
Cost: tools and skills to build and maintain.
Single point of failure: a broken or compromised automation system can affect everything at once.
Technical debt: scripts and workflows nobody maintains.
Ongoing supportability: someone must own and update the automation as systems change.
Mistakes at scale: a bad rule applied automatically hits thousands of systems instantly. Test in a safe environment and use change control.
Secrets: automation accounts and API keys are powerful and must be protected.

Benefits in the lesson's words: scripts fix problems without a middle-of-the-night call, can resolve some problems before anyone notices, run at machine speed without typos, and free staff for more interesting work. Examples: a script that waits for a patch to land in a folder and deploys it everywhere; a script that builds a default router configuration; a script that creates firewall rules when a new remote-site firewall is deployed. When scaling a cloud application, scripts should add firewalls and other security devices, not only servers and databases.
Reacting fast: monitor disk space and clear temporary files when it gets low, running 24/7. Onboarding script: creates the account, assigns groups, home directory, nearby printer and email. Offboarding automation also applies.

Guardrails: automated verification of what a human types. Example: a technician tries to delete a folder but picks a far larger path; the guardrail blocks anything that would delete critical files.
Security groups: automatic add/remove, plus alerts (be told immediately if someone joins the administrator group). Ticket creation: turn an email to the help desk into a ticket and assign it. Escalation: if the script cannot fix a problem, it pages the on-call technician.
Enable/disable services on a timer, push code updates continuously, and talk to APIs on cloud platforms, firewalls and other devices so you can control them programmatically.

Concerns: scripts are complex and need much testing against other systems; someone must write them (time and cost); a script is a single point of failure; technical debt grows when a script hides a deeper problem instead of fixing the root cause; and someone must support scripts as the OS or scripting language changes.

Scripting (PowerShell, Python, Bash) for custom tasks.
Infrastructure as code (Terraform, Ansible, CloudFormation): declare desired state; the tool makes it so.
SOAR platforms: orchestrate tools and run playbooks and runbooks.
APIs connect systems; webhooks trigger actions.
Orchestration coordinates many automated tasks into one workflow; automation performs a single task.

Automation = a single task done by machine. Orchestration = coordinating many automated tasks.
A big automation benefit is consistency (enforcing baselines), not just speed.
Risks include single point of failure and technical debt.

Process: preparation, detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned.
Training and testing: tabletop exercise, simulation.
Root cause analysis, threat hunting.
Digital forensics: legal hold, chain of custody, acquisition, reporting, preservation, e-discovery.
Incident response (IR) is the structured way a team handles a security event. The exam expects the phases in order, the planning activities, and the basics of digital forensics.

| Phase | What happens
 | 1. Preparation | Plan, train, equip. Everything that has to exist before an incident
 | 2. Detection and analysis | Notice something, confirm it is an incident, scope and prioritize it
 | 3. Containment | Stop the spread: isolate hosts, disable accounts, block traffic
 | 4. Eradication | Remove the cause: malware, backdoors, malicious accounts, close the vulnerability
 | 5. Recovery | Restore systems from known-good sources and return to normal operations, with monitoring
 | 6. Lessons learned | Post-incident review to improve the process
Memory aid: Prepare, Detect/analyze, Contain, Eradicate, Recover, Lessons learned.
Many questions ask "what is the next step?" Contain before eradicating. Preserve evidence before wiping.

Incident response plan with defined roles, authority and escalation. Playbooks and runbooks for common incident types.
Contact list and communication plan: who to inform (management, legal, HR, PR, law enforcement, customers, regulators), with out-of-band channels because email may be compromised.
Incident response team: IR manager, security analysts, IT/system owners, legal, HR, communications.
Go bag / jump kit: laptops, forensic software, write blockers, cables, blank media, documentation, a camera.
Known-good images and backups to rebuild from.
Training and exercises before the incident; you cannot learn during one.
Monitoring and detection tools in place: SIEM, EDR, IDS/IPS, logging.

Sources: IPS/IDS alerts, antivirus, SIEM correlation, log anomalies (unexpected admin changes, new accounts), network traffic spikes, user reports, threat intelligence.
Triage: determine whether it's a real incident versus a normal event, then prioritize by impact on the business.
Sandbox analysis of suspicious files shows what they do safely.
Document everything with timestamps from the start.
Root cause analysis (RCA) identifies how it happened so the same hole is closed.

Containment: isolate or quarantine affected systems, disable compromised accounts, block malicious IPs. Short-term (stop the bleeding) and long-term (clean network). Weigh evidence preservation against speed.
Eradication: remove malware, patch the exploited vulnerability, reset credentials, rebuild from known-good images where trust is lost.
Recovery: restore from clean backups, re-enable services in stages, monitor closely for reinfection, verify integrity.
Reconstitution returns systems to normal operation.

A meeting with everyone involved: what happened, the timeline, how well the plan and tools worked, what indicators were missed, and what to change. Feed the results back into the plan, monitoring and training. Produce a report.

Tabletop exercise: discussion of a scenario around a table. Low cost, no systems touched.
Walkthrough: step through the plan to verify accuracy.
Simulation: a more realistic drill, possibly with technical injects.
Full test / functional exercise: the team performs real actions.
Root cause analysis and threat hunting (proactively searching for undetected compromise) support the process.
Stakeholder management: keep leaders, legal and communications informed; retention and escalation rules; notification requirements for regulators and affected people.

Forensics collects and analyzes evidence in a way that holds up in court and in internal investigations.
Legal hold: a legal instruction to preserve relevant data (electronically stored information, ESI). Disposal is suspended.
Chain of custody: documented record of who handled the evidence, when, where and why, from collection to presentation. Gaps can make evidence inadmissible. Use hashes and signed logs to prove it wasn't altered.
Acquisition: copy evidence without changing it. Use a write blocker on disks and work on forensic images (bit-for-bit copies), not the original. Hash original and copy and compare.

Order of volatility: collect the most volatile data first, as it disappears fastest: 1. CPU registers and cache 2. RAM, routing/ARP tables, process table 3. Temporary files and swap 4. Disk 5. Remote logs and monitoring data 6. Physical configuration, topology 7. Archival media and backups
Sources: disk, memory, firmware, network traffic, logs, snapshots of VMs, mobile devices, cloud. Live acquisition may be needed for encrypted systems (a powered-off system loses the keys).
Preservation: keep original data pristine; analyze copies; store securely.
Reporting: summary, acquisition details, findings, methods, and conclusions that a third party can reproduce.
E-discovery: collecting, preparing, reviewing and producing electronic documents for legal proceedings.
Admissibility: evidence must be authentic, complete and properly handled.

Timeline analysis, time offsets (note clock differences), and data carving (recover files from raw disk).
Provenance shows where evidence came from; hashes show it's unchanged.

Process and preparation
Example incidents: a user clicks an attachment and malware runs; a DDoS from botnets overwhelms the WAN link; stolen data held for ransom; or software that lets outsiders in. The NIST guide is SP 800-61 Revision 2, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide (the lesson's phases: preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity).
Preparation items: an up-to-date communication/contact list; an incident go bag (laptops with specialized software, removable media, forensic software, a digital imaging system for photos and video); documentation and network diagrams; security baselines and file hashes of critical files; known-good OS and application images; and policies and procedures everyone follows.

Detection is hard because attacks arrive constantly and most are automated scripts. Sources: web server logs (a vulnerability scan shows up), a patch calendar (watch for attacks on unpatched systems), occasional direct contact from attackers, IPS alerts (buffer overflow attempt), antivirus reports, configuration changes made by an attacker, and a large traffic increase (exfiltration). Stop an attack quickly rather than watching it.
Sandbox analysis shows what malware changes in the OS, but malware may detect a VM with limited connectivity and delete itself or behave differently.
Recovery means removing bad software and replacing it with known good: remove the malware or reimage, disable breached or attacker-created accounts, fix the original vulnerability, restore from known-good backups or reinstall from original media, then lock things down.

Post-incident meeting as soon as possible while memories are fresh: what happened, the timeline, how well the plan worked, whether indicators were missed (if so change monitoring), and what to change next time. Planning and training must occur before an incident (no on-the-job training). Large organizations with multiple IR teams may find it expensive, but it saves money after a big incident.
Exercises and analysis
Test with test systems, limited time, and evaluate afterwards. Full-scale disaster events cost time, money and people, so start with a tabletop: sit around a table for a few hours, walk through one scenario (what first, what second) and watch how other departments respond at the same time.

Simulation examples: phishing emails (see who clicks), calling the help desk to see if someone changes a password, or sending data out to see if monitoring catches it. A third-party phishing simulation also tests mail filters and anti-phishing systems, and users who click get more training.
Root cause analysis: one incident has many small events (breach a vulnerability, move data, plant malware). Use logs and attacker artifacts to rebuild how they got in. There may be multiple root causes, and user mistakes (social engineering) are part of it.
Threat hunting: find the vulnerability before attackers do, for example adjusting firewall rules, tracking newly announced vulnerabilities, and checking installed systems are patched. Automated tools can stop some attacks without you watching.
Forensics in detail

Collection details are mostly beyond the exam, but RFC 3227 covers guidelines for evidence collection and archiving. Evidence may be used in legal proceedings years later, so take extensive notes.
Legal hold: a lawyer or legal entity sends a document describing data that must be preserved; it goes to the data custodian, who evaluates it. Data is collected into a separate ESI (electronically stored information) repository, which may require converting (for example a proprietary email format to text). You must keep it safe for the court.
Chain of custody: keep data pristine, and track every person who accesses it. Physical analogy: evidence in a sealed bag, with each access recorded on the bag. Digital version uses hashes and digital signatures. Every piece of data from every source needs its own chain of custody.

Sources: disk or memory, firmware, file system, other systems, servers, network devices, firewall logs, a VM snapshot, and easily overlooked places like log files, the recycle bin, temporary storage, browser bookmarks and saved logins.
Documentation/report: a summary of the event, detailed steps from source to acquired data and the integrity checks, an analysis (factual description of structure and use), and a conclusion.
Preservation: work on copies so the original is untouched (and mobile devices can be remotely wiped, so copy them). Prefer live collection, especially for systems with encryption that locks when powered off.

E-discovery: collecting, preparing, reviewing, interpreting and producing electronic documents. It is about acquisition, with no analysis required. Often paired with forensics: you create a drive image, then the forensics team determines whether deleted data exists and recovers it.

Contain before eradicate. Don't wipe a system before capturing evidence unless policy says otherwise.
Chain of custody is about *handling*; hashing proves *integrity*; both are needed.
Capture memory first (most volatile).
A tabletop is discussion only.
Lessons learned happens *after* recovery.
Legal hold stops routine deletion.

Log data: firewall, application, endpoint, OS-specific security logs, IPS/IDS, network logs, metadata.
Data sources: vulnerability scans, automated reports, dashboards, packet captures.
When something goes wrong, data sources tell the story. Objective 4.9 asks which log or data source answers a given question, and how to use it.

Logs are time-ordered records of events. A good investigation correlates several sources by timestamp, so time synchronization (NTP) matters.
 | Source | What it records | Typical use
 | Firewall logs | Allowed/denied connections: IPs, ports, protocols, bytes | Find scans, blocked attacks, exfiltration, command-and-control traffic
 | Application logs | Application events and errors | Trace what a user or attacker did inside an app; find failed logins, crashes
 | Endpoint logs | OS and security events on hosts (Windows Security log, auditd, EDR) | Logons, process creation, file and registry changes, privilege use
 | OS-specific security logs | Authentication, account changes, policy changes | Account lockouts, privilege escalation, new accounts
 | IPS/IDS logs | Signature matches and alerts | What attack patterns were seen and from where

| Network logs | Switch, router, DNS, DHCP, proxy, VPN, wireless controller | Who had which IP, which domains were looked up, who connected remotely
 | Metadata | Data about data: email headers, file properties (author, timestamps), EXIF, mobile call/location records, web request headers | Who created/sent something, when, from where
Related sources:
Vulnerability scan output shows weaknesses present at scan time.
Automated reports from SIEM and dashboards summarize activity and trends.
Packet captures (full content) vs NetFlow (conversation summaries).
Web server and DNS logs: attack patterns (scans, SQLi attempts), suspicious domains.
Authentication logs (RADIUS, Active Directory, SSO, VPN): who logged in, from where, success or failure.
Cloud audit logs (API calls, console activity).
Mobile logs and location data.
Database logs for queries and access.
Syslog consolidates logs from network devices and Linux/Unix.

Aggregate logs in a SIEM so you can search across sources and see an end-to-end timeline.
Correlate: link events from different systems (a DHCP lease, a firewall log and an endpoint log tell one story).
Normalize formats and time zones.
Protect integrity: send logs to a central write-once store so attackers can't delete them. Missing logs are an indicator of compromise.
Retention must meet investigation and regulatory needs.
Packet captures and dashboards help visualize patterns and trends.

| Question | Best source
 | Which IPs connected to the internal server and were blocked? | Firewall log
 | Which user installed a program on a workstation? | Endpoint / OS security log
 | What domain did a host resolve before it got infected? | DNS log
 | Who had IP 10.1.2.3 at 02:10? | DHCP log
 | Which account logged in over VPN from a foreign country? | VPN / authentication log
 | Who really sent this email and from what server? | Email header metadata
 | What did the web application do when it crashed? | Application log
 | Which known attack signature was matched? | IPS/IDS log
 | What weaknesses exist on this server? | Vulnerability scan
 | What exactly was in the traffic? | Packet capture

Firewall log fields: timestamp, source IP (and on some NGFWs the receiving MAC), destination IP, port, application, and the disposition (allowed or blocked). An NGFW adds application and URL-category visibility plus anomaly hints. DNS sinkhole hits in the logs can point to an infected internal host.
Application logs: Windows Event Viewer's Application section; on Linux and macOS look under /var/log. Everything usually rolls up into the SIEM, where it can be filtered several ways.
Endpoint logs: logon and logoff, system events, running processes, device management events (password changes, lockouts) and directory service activity.
OS security logs catch brute force attempts, changes to critical system files and authentication events. One odd entry, such as a service disabled that an admin would not normally disable, can raise an alert and stop an attack early.

Send only what matters to the SIEM: collecting everything is costly, so forward the data useful for security decisions.
IPS/IDS functions now usually live inside the NGFW. A Snort-style entry shows timestamp, alert class (for example a possible DoS via SYN flood), priority, and source and destination IP and port.
Network device logs (switches, routers, access points, VPN concentrators) show routing table changes, failed authentication to the device and attacks. Example: a switch logs a TCP SYN attack on a port and auto-blocks the SYN traffic for 60 seconds.
Metadata: email headers (sending servers, SPF and signature details), photo EXIF (device and GPS coordinates), browser data (OS, browser type, IP), and document properties (author, title, contact details).

Vulnerability scan logs reveal hosts with no firewall, antivirus or anti-spyware, open shares needing no credentials, guest accounts left on, unsupported operating systems and world-readable NFS shares. Update the scanner's signatures first so it knows current vulnerabilities.
Automated reports are only useful if someone reads them; on terabytes of data, narrow reports run faster. A dashboard is a live at-a-glance view (active firewall rules, warnings, users and devices) for the SOC screen and generally avoids long-term data because that takes too long to compile.
Packet captures: Wireshark on wired or wireless networks, and some switches, routers and firewalls can capture themselves. The top pane lists each packet (for example an HTTP GET); the detail pane breaks one frame into Ethernet, IPv4, TCP and HTTP layers.

Metadata is data about data; it can prove who and when without revealing content.
A packet capture shows content; NetFlow shows only who talked to whom.
Firewall logs won't show what happened inside an encrypted session or inside the host; use endpoint logs.
Accurate time across devices is what makes correlation possible.

5.1 Summarize elements of effective security governance

watched the videos
 read the notes
 wrote my own notes
 flashcards mastered

Guidelines, policies (AUP, information security, business continuity, disaster recovery, incident response, SDLC, change management).
Standards (password, access control, physical, encryption) and procedures (change management, onboarding/offboarding, playbooks).
External considerations: regulatory, legal, industry, local/regional/national/global.
Monitoring and revision; governance structures (boards, committees, government entities, centralized/decentralized).
Roles: owners, controllers, processors, custodians/stewards.

Governance is how an organization sets, communicates and enforces security expectations. This objective is a hierarchy: policies say *what* and *why*, standards say *how much*, procedures say *how exactly*.

| Document | Purpose | Detail level | Example
 | Policy | High-level statement of management intent and rules; approved by leadership | Broad, rarely changes | "All laptops must use full-disk encryption"
 | Standard | Specific, measurable requirement that implements a policy | Mandatory specifics | "AES-256, managed through BitLocker with TPM"
 | Procedure | Step-by-step instructions to carry out a task | Detailed, changes often | "How to enable BitLocker and escrow the recovery key"
 | Guideline | Recommended practice, not mandatory | Advice | "Prefer passphrases of 4+ words"
Order from top to bottom: policy → standard → procedure. Policies are the *why*, procedures the *how*.

Acceptable use policy (AUP): what users may and may not do with company systems and data.
Information security policies: overall program rules.
Business continuity and disaster recovery: how operations continue and recover.
Incident response policy and plan.
Software development life cycle (SDLC) policy: security built into development.
Change management policy (see 1.3).
Access control / identity policies, password policy, data classification and handling, remote access/BYOD, clean desk, retention and privacy.

Specify what must be used or achieved:
Password standards (length, complexity, history, lockout).
Access control standards (who can approve, how long reviews take).
Physical security standards.
Encryption standards (algorithms, key lengths).
Based on frameworks and regulations: NIST, ISO/IEC 27001, CIS Controls, PCI DSS.

Documented, repeatable steps so everyone does it the same way:
Onboarding and offboarding (provision accounts, collect devices, disable access).
Playbooks for incident types.
Change management procedure and approval flow.
Patching, backup and restore, account recovery.
Procedures must be tested and kept current.

Governance is shaped by outside forces:
Regulatory: laws and rules that apply to your industry or location (HIPAA, GDPR, PCI DSS, GLBA, SOX).
Legal: contracts, liability, litigation, data protection.
Industry requirements and standards.
Local, regional, national and global differences, such as data residency.
Policies must be reviewed regularly, especially after incidents, audits, regulatory changes or business changes. Track exceptions and keep approval records.

Boards and committees: oversight and strategy (a security steering committee or board).
Government entities and regulators.
Centralized vs decentralized governance.
Data roles and responsibilities (from 3.3 and here):
 | Role | Responsibility
 | Data owner | Senior person accountable for a dataset; decides classification and who can access it
 | Data steward | Manages data quality, labels and metadata
 | Data custodian / processor (technical) | Implements storage, backup, access controls
 | Data controller | Decides why and how personal data is processed
 | Data processor | Handles personal data on the controller's behalf
 | Data protection officer (DPO) | Advises on and monitors privacy compliance
 | Data subject | The individual the data is about

Policies state what to do and why; the technical controls from 1.1 are how they are enforced. Policies also answer scenario questions (virus found, home VPN access, vulnerability exploited) and list roles and responsibilities. They are only documents: the organization must enforce them. An AUP also protects the company legally if someone is dismissed for breaking it.
Business continuity example: when card processing is down, retail staff take manual transactions and phone the card company to approve. It must be planned and tested before the event. A disaster recovery plan is continuity for widespread or long outages (natural, technical or human-caused) and covers an alternate location, data recovery, application restoration and staff availability there.

Incident roles: incident response team, IT security management, compliance officers, technical staff and users who saw the event. NIST SP 800-61 Rev 2 lifecycle: preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication and recovery, post-incident activity.
SDLC: Waterfall is linear (requirements, development, testing, deployment, maintenance); Agile cycles design, develop, test, deploy and review constantly.
Change management records frequency, duration, install process and a fallback procedure. Steps: scope (one server or many, one file or an OS), risk, formal plan, approval, backup plan, then documentation. A change control board approves and schedules.

Standards come from ISO and NIST or are written in house. Password standards cover complexity, resets, change frequency, storage and approved managers; a standard may forbid local accounts on network gear and require LDAP to Active Directory. Access standards may require MAC instead of DAC, sign-off or training before access, and removal on a security issue, expiry, departure or contract end. Physical standards cover badges, electronic locks, biometrics, motion detection and visitor escorts, differing for employee, contractor and guest. Encryption standards fix the hash or algorithm per data state (use, transit, rest).

Procedures: onboarding gives the handbook and AUP sign-off, accounts, permissions and devices. Offboarding decides what happens to hardware and data; disable rather than delete the account because deleting can lose decryption keys. Playbooks (breach investigation, ransomware recovery) can be automated in a SOAR platform so staff focus on harder work. Revisit playbooks when new tech or emerging threats appear.
Governance structure: a board sets broad objectives; committees of subject matter experts do the work and report back for approval. Government bodies add legal, administrative and political concerns and often hold open meetings. Centralized means one group decides; decentralized lets those doing the work decide.

Regulation and legal: SOX (2002, public company finances), HIPAA (health data storage, transfer and disclosure). Teams need a process to report illegal activity, respond to a legal hold, and meet breach disclosure deadlines that vary by region. Some countries require citizens' data to stay in-country. Industries differ: power generation is often air-gapped, healthcare needs heavy encryption with wide access. Scope grows from local to national (defense) to global companies facing many differing laws.
Data roles: the owner is a senior person (the VP of sales for customer data, the treasurer for finances) ultimately responsible. The controller decides how data is used (a payroll department) and the processor acts on those instructions (the payroll company). The custodian/steward keeps data accurate, private and compliant, assigns sensitivity labels and ties them to access control.

A policy is mandatory and high-level; a guideline is optional advice.
Procedures are the most detailed and change most often.
The data owner is accountable; the custodian implements.
Regulatory vs legal: regulations from agencies; legal covers contracts and court obligations. Questions often just want "external considerations".

study --objective 5.2
SY0-701domain 5.0 · Security Program Management & Oversight5.2
5.2 Explain elements of the risk management process

watched the videos
 read the notes
 wrote my own notes
 flashcards mastered

Risk identification, assessment (ad hoc, recurring, one-time, continuous), analysis: qualitative vs quantitative.
SLE = asset value x exposure factor. ALE = SLE x ARO.
Risk register: key risk indicators, risk owners, thresholds. Risk tolerance, appetite (expansionary, conservative, neutral).
Strategies: transfer, accept (exemption, exception), avoid, mitigate.
Business impact analysis: RTO, RPO, MTTR, MTBF.
Risk management is about deciding which risks to treat, how, and in what order. The exam mixes definitions, formulas and strategies.

Risk = likelihood × impact: the chance that a threat exploits a vulnerability and the harm that follows.
Risk assessment identifies and evaluates risks. Risk register lists identified risks, owners, ratings, and treatment. Risk owner is the person accountable for a specific risk. Risk tolerance / appetite is how much risk the organization will accept. Risk threshold is the line that triggers action.
Inherent risk is before controls; residual risk is what is left after controls; control risk is the chance controls fail.
Risk reporting communicates risks to leadership. Risk indicators (KRIs) warn that risk is rising.
Risk posture is the overall state of risk. Risk appetite types: expansionary (accepts more), conservative (accepts little), neutral.

| Type | When
 | Ad hoc | One-off, as needed
 | Recurring | On a schedule (annual)
 | One-time | For a specific project or change
 | Continuous | Ongoing monitoring

Qualitative: ranks risk with descriptive scales (low, medium, high) using judgment and risk matrices/heat maps. Quick, subjective.
Quantitative: uses numbers and money.
Quantitative formulas (memorize):
 | Term | Meaning | Formula
 | AV | Asset value | 
 | EF | Exposure factor: percent of the asset lost in one event | 
 | SLE | Single loss expectancy: cost of one event | SLE = AV × EF
 | ARO | Annualized rate of occurrence: how many times per year | 
 | ALE | Annualized loss expectancy: expected yearly loss | ALE = SLE × ARO
Example: a server worth $100,000 would lose 50% of its value in a flood (EF 0.5): SLE = $50,000. Floods are expected once every 10 years (ARO 0.1): ALE = $5,000. A mitigation costing more than $5,000 per year is not cost-effective for this risk.
Other terms: probability, likelihood, impact, exposure factor. Vulnerability and threat feed the likelihood.

| Strategy | Meaning | Example
 | Avoid | Stop the risky activity | Don't launch the risky service
 | Mitigate | Reduce likelihood or impact with controls | Patch, segment, train
 | Transfer | Shift financial impact to another party | Cyber insurance, outsourcing
 | Accept | Live with it | Exception/exemption with documented approval; risk acceptance
 | Share (sometimes listed) | Spread between parties | Joint ventures
Exemptions/exceptions are formal acceptance with documentation and expiry.
You can transfer financial loss, but not accountability.
Controls should cost less than the risk they reduce.
A register lists each risk, description, owner, likelihood, impact, rating, controls, and status. It's reviewed regularly and drives treatment plans and reporting to executives.

The BIA identifies critical functions, the systems they depend on, and what happens when they are unavailable. It produces the recovery metrics:
 | Metric | Meaning
 | RTO | Recovery time objective: maximum tolerable downtime before the function must be restored
 | RPO | Recovery point objective: maximum tolerable data loss, as time since last good copy
 | MTTR | Mean time to repair: average time to fix
 | MTBF | Mean time between failures: reliability of repairable systems
 | MTTF | Mean time to failure (non-repairable items)
 | Recovery site / mission-essential functions / identification of critical systems / single points of failure | What to protect first, what has no redundancy
BIA feeds business continuity and disaster recovery planning.

Assessment timing: one-time assessments tie to a project (an acquisition, new equipment or software). Ad hoc ones answer a specific question, for example the CEO hears of an attack type at a conference and a temporary committee studies only that, then disbands. Recurring ones run every quarter, six months or year, often internally; PCI DSS requires an annual one for card-holding firms. Continuous assessment is built into change control, where each change gets a risk step.
Qualitative example (traffic-light grid scoring impact, ARO, cost of controls, overall risk): legacy Windows clients (medium impact, high ARO, medium cost) rate high overall; untrained staff (low impact, medium ARO, low cost) rate medium; devices with no antivirus (medium impact, high ARO, medium cost) rate very high.

Asset value is not just replacement cost; it can include lost sales and fines. EF is 0.25 for a quarter lost and 1.0 for total loss. Laptop example: AV $1,000, EF 1.0, so SLE $1,000; seven stolen per year gives ALE $7,000. The data on the laptop may be worth more than the laptop, which is why qualitative analysis is still needed.
Impact categories: life first (people cannot be replaced), then property, safety and finance.
Likelihood is qualitative (rare, possible, almost certain); probability is quantitative and based on history or expectation. The terms are often used interchangeably.

Appetite vs tolerance: appetite is how much risk the organization is willing to take, and its qualitative stance is the risk appetite posture (conservative, neutral, expansionary). Tolerance is the wider band around it. Speed-limit analogy: the limit is the appetite; police not ticketing until well over it is the tolerance, which tightens in bad weather.
Risk register: each line has a key risk indicator (for example purpose not well defined, deliverables incomplete, schedule unclear), an owner, and a threshold, balancing money spent against what the risk would cost.

Strategies: transfer (cyber insurance), accept (the most common), exemption (a policy cannot be followed: a manufacturing machine running unpatchable Windows is exempted if kept off the network), exception (policy says patch within three days, but the patch crashes a critical app so the deadline is extended), avoid (remove the risk entirely), mitigate (a next-generation firewall for internet exposure). Risk reporting lists critical and emerging risks for management purchase decisions and is constantly updated.

BIA metrics: RTO is time until operational (for example both the database and web server running). RPO is the data that must be restored before you count as operational (for example the last 12 months of customer data). MTTR covers diagnosing, getting, installing and configuring replacement gear; a two-hour third-party replacement contract or on-site spares lower it. MTBF is estimated time between outages, from the manufacturer or history; roughly total uptime divided by number of breakdowns.

SLE × ARO = ALE; AV × EF = SLE.
Insurance = transfer. Policy exception = accept. Firewall rule = mitigate. Shutting the service = avoid.
Residual risk remains after controls; you accept it or add more controls.
RPO is about data loss; RTO is about time to restore service.
Qualitative uses categories; quantitative uses numbers.

5.3 Explain the processes associated with third-party risk assessment and management

watched the videos
 read the notes
 wrote my own notes
 flashcards mastered

Vendor assessment: penetration testing, right-to-audit clause, evidence of internal audits, independent assessments, supply chain analysis.
Vendor selection: due diligence, conflict of interest. Monitoring and questionnaires, rules of engagement.
Agreements: SLA, MOA, MOU, MSA, WO/SOW, NDA, BPA.
You inherit the risks of everyone you do business with. This objective covers how to assess vendors and the agreements that bind them.

Vendor assessment: judge suppliers before and during the relationship.
Penetration testing (with permission) and right-to-audit clauses allow verification.
Evidence of internal audits and independent assessments (SOC 2 reports, ISO 27001 certification).
Supply chain analysis: who are *their* suppliers? (fourth parties)
Vendor questionnaires about security practices, incident history and controls.
Vendor selection: due diligence (investigate before signing), conflict of interest check.
Vendor monitoring: continuous review of performance, security posture and incidents. Reassess periodically.
Vendor viability, financial stability, and geographic location (laws and data sovereignty).
Questionnaires, rules of engagement for tests, and right to audit are standard.
Offboarding / termination: return or destroy data, revoke access, confirm deletion.

| Agreement | Purpose | Key features
 | SLA (service level agreement) | Defines the level of service a provider will deliver | Measurable targets such as 99.9% uptime, response times, penalties
 | MOA (memorandum of agreement) | Formal agreement on how parties will work together | Stronger than an MOU; sets responsibilities
 | MOU (memorandum of understanding) | Statement of shared intent | Generally non-binding; informal
 | MSA (master service agreement) | Umbrella contract with standing terms | Later work orders reference it, speeding up new projects
 | WO / SOW (work order / statement of work) | Defines a specific project | Scope, deliverables, deadlines, acceptance criteria, cost
 | NDA (non-disclosure agreement) | Keeps information confidential | Legal consequences for sharing; mutual or one-way
 | BPA (business partners agreement) | Sets how partners operate together | Profit/loss sharing, responsibilities, exit
Contracts often add security requirements, breach notification timelines, audit rights, data handling and termination clauses.

Why assess vendors: a payroll provider holds a great deal of your data, so put the risk assessment terms in the contract, with penalties for breach.
Penetration testing a vendor: similar to a vulnerability scan but actively exploits. It can be required at standard intervals and run by a specialist third party. The rules of engagement state the test type (on-site physical, internal, or across the internet), dates and hours (business or after hours), IP ranges, emergency contacts, handling of sensitive data found, and which devices are in scope and out of scope.
Right to audit clause: audits happen regularly, can set how they run, and are often performed by an outside party who is not part of the contract. Audit focus: access management, offboarding, password handling and storage, VPN access controls. Repeat audits over a long relationship.

Supply chain analysis follows the chain from raw materials to final product: how the product reaches the customer, how groups coordinate, how security is handled between the two technical teams, and changes to business process. SolarWinds: malware slipped into its product code and shipped with a valid digital signature between March and June 2020, announced December 2020; of roughly 300,000 customers, at least 18,000 installed it.
Independent assessments give an outside view built on experience across many organizations.
Due diligence means verifying claims (revenue, customer count) and can include background checks and interviews. Conflict of interest examples: the vendor also serves your biggest competitor, employs an executive's relative, or offers gifts for signing.

Monitoring after signing: financial health checks, IT security reviews, news and social media. Someone in the company owns each vendor relationship, and monitoring should be both quantitative and qualitative. Questionnaires ask about the vendor's due diligence, conflict handling, disaster recovery and data storage/protection; answers feed an ongoing vendor risk analysis.
SLA example for an ISP: no more than four hours unscheduled downtime, technician dispatch, spare equipment kept on site.
MOU: broad goals, may include confidentiality, informal and unsigned in spirit. MOA: a step above, more detail on the relationship, may hold some binding language, but is not a contract and is generally not legally enforceable.

MSA is a legal contract with terms (service, billing, payment) that later work orders / SOWs build on. A SOW lists scope, location, deliverables schedule and expectations, and settles disputes over what was or was not covered.
NDA forms: unilateral (one party bound), bilateral/mutual (both), multilateral (more than two). It is a formal signed contract, signed before sharing the protected information.
BPA: financial details, ownership stake, who makes business decisions, and what happens when finances go wrong or a disaster closes the business.

SLA is about *service levels*; SOW is about *project scope*; MSA is the *master* terms.
MOU is informal and non-binding; MOA is more detailed but still generally not an enforceable contract; MSA and NDA are legal contracts.
NDA protects confidentiality.
Third-party risk includes fourth parties (your vendor's vendors).
You can outsource work, not accountability.

watched the videos

Compliance reporting (internal, external). Consequences of non-compliance: fines, sanctions, reputational damage, loss of license, contractual impacts.
Compliance monitoring: due diligence/care, attestation and acknowledgement, internal/external, automation.
Privacy: legal implications, data subject, controller vs processor, ownership, data inventory and retention, right to be forgotten.
Compliance means following the laws, regulations and standards that apply to you, and being able to prove it. Failing has consequences.

Internal compliance reporting: for management, audit committees, and governance. External reporting: to regulators, auditors, customers.
Compliance monitoring: continuous checks that controls operate as required. Includes due diligence / due care (research before acting; acting responsibly), attestation and acknowledgement (people or systems formally confirm compliance), and automation (compliance scanning, evidence collection).

Fines and sanctions from regulators.
Reputational damage and loss of customers.
Loss of license to operate.
Contractual impacts (lost business, penalties).
Criminal liability in serious cases.

| Item | Focus
 | GDPR | EU/EEA personal data. Rights to access and erasure, consent, breach notification within 72 hours, large fines
 | HIPAA | US health information (PHI)
 | PCI DSS | Card payment data; required by card brands for merchants and processors
 | SOX | US public company financial reporting integrity
 | GLBA | US financial institutions' customer data
 | FERPA | US student education records
 | CCPA/CPRA | California consumer privacy
 | ISO/IEC 27001 / 27002 | Information security management system and controls
 | NIST CSF, SP 800-53, SP 800-171 | US frameworks and controls
 | CIS Controls / Benchmarks | Prioritized security practices
 | SOC 2 | Audit report on service providers' security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy
 | Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) | Cloud-specific controls

Legal implications: local, regional, national and global laws apply, depending on where the data subjects live.
Data subject rights: access, correction, deletion, portability, objection.
Controller decides purpose; processor acts on its behalf; data protection officer oversees compliance.
Right to be forgotten, consent, data minimization, retention limits, breach notification.
Data inventory and retention policies determine what you hold and how long.
Privacy impact assessment evaluates risks of a project that handles personal data.
Sovereignty and cross-border transfer rules.

Compliance means meeting standards set by law or by agreement with a third party. Penalties include fines, job loss and even prison. A central compliance officer (CCO) makes sure the organization follows state, local, federal and other requirements and reports the status. External requirements need periodic reports; wrong or missed reports bring penalties or sanctions.
Laws named: SOX (Public Company Accounting Reform and Investor Protection Act, 2002), HIPAA (medical privacy in the US) and GLBA (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, 1999; the privacy notices from your bank).

HIPAA penalty tiers (as given in the lesson): up to $50,000 and/or one year for a basic violation; up to $100,000 and/or five years if done under false pretenses; up to $250,000 and/or ten years if the intent is commercial advantage, personal gain or malicious harm; civil fines of $100 per violation capped at $25,000 for identical violations. Exact figures are not what the exam tests; know that penalties scale with intent.
Reputational damage example: Uber was breached in October 2016 (25.6 million names, emails and phone numbers), disclosed it only in November 2017 after allegedly paying the hackers $100,000 under an NDA, paid $148 million in 2018, and its former security chief got three years' probation and a $50,000 fine in May 2023. Disclosing on time would have kept it compliant.

Other consequences: loss of a license needed to sell the product, sanctions that stop others buying from you, and contractual breach, which two private parties can often settle without legal proceedings.
Due care is what you do internally; due diligence is what you do with third parties. The responsible executive signs the attestation and acknowledgment that compliance is in good standing. Large firms automate monitoring with tools that collect data from people, third parties and other departments and compile reports.

Privacy starts locally (property, vehicle and medical licensing records), then national (HIPAA), then multinational (GDPR for everyone living in the EU). Protected data includes name, address, photo, email, bank details, social posts, genetic makeup and location. The right to be forgotten lets a data subject demand removal; a data subject is any identified or identifiable natural person, so effectively all of us. GDPR frames privacy from the individual's perspective rather than the company's.
Payroll example: the payroll department is the controller (decides pay and timing) and the outside payroll company is the processor; an NDA keeps the exchanged data private. A processor can be internal or a third party.

Data inventory: a list of all data held, with owner, update frequency and format. Know the uses (collaboration, IT security, data quality checks) and check that any sharing with outsiders fits privacy law.

GDPR covers EU residents' data wherever the company is.
PCI DSS is an industry standard, not a law; HIPAA is law.
Due diligence = investigate before; due care = act reasonably after.
Attestation is a formal confirmation of compliance.
Compliance is not the same as security, but it sets a minimum.

5.5 Explain types and purposes of audits and assessments

watched the videos
 read the notes
 wrote my own notes
 flashcards mastered

Attestation; internal (compliance, audit committee, self-assessments) and external (regulatory, examinations, assessment, independent third-party audit).
Penetration testing: physical, offensive, defensive, integrated; known, partially known, unknown environment; reconnaissance (passive, active).
Audits and assessments check that controls exist, work, and follow the rules. They differ by who does them and what question they answer.
Formal statement by a responsible party (or an auditor) that the requirements are met. For example, a SOC 2 report is an auditor's attestation about a provider's controls.

| | Internal | External
 | Who | Your own staff or internal audit team | Independent third party
 | Purpose | Self-assessment, readiness, ongoing improvement, audit committee reporting | Independent assurance for regulators, customers, partners; required certifications
 | Bias | Closer knowledge, less independence | Independent, more credible, costs more
Internal audits include compliance checks, audit committee reporting, and self-assessments.
External audits include regulatory examinations (government or industry regulators), examinations by independent auditors, and independent third-party audits (ISO, SOC 2, PCI QSA assessments).
Assessment is a broader evaluation of security posture; audit compares to a defined standard and gives a conclusion.

An authorized simulated attack that tries to exploit weaknesses (see 4.3).
Environment (what the tester knows):
Known environment (white box): full knowledge and access.
Partially known (gray box): some information.
Unknown environment (black box): no insider information.
Test type / what's tested: physical, offensive, defensive, and integrated testing.
Reconnaissance: passive (public sources) and active (touches the target).
Teams: red team (attackers), blue team (defenders), purple team (red and blue work together to improve defenses), and white team (referees/coordinators).
Rules of engagement, scope, authorization and reporting are essential. Findings are ranked and tracked to remediation.

Audit purposes: examine infrastructure, software, devices on the network, and policies and procedures against modern threats. It can find vulnerabilities before attackers do. Attestation is an opinion on the truth of the audit results: audit first, then attest.
Internal audits answer compliance questions. An audit committee manages risk oversight and starts and stops internal audits. They usually begin with self-assessments, which the committee compiles into a compliance picture.
External audits are required by some regulations, which also set the type and frequency. Auditors work on site through your records and show where you stand today and where to improve.

Physical penetration testing: with physical access an attacker can alter the boot process, boot from other media or replace OS files, which is why servers sit in secured data centers. Testers try doors, windows, elevators and entering without a key.
Red team attacks and exploits; blue team spots attacks in real time and blocks them. Combined, the red team passes openings to blue for patching and better detection.
Environments: known (full disclosure), partially known (some information, to aim testers at certain systems), unknown (no information, also called a blind test).

Reconnaissance builds a network map, IP configuration, networks, remote site links, and finds security tools, servers and applications. Passive: social media, the corporate website, forums and Reddit, social engineering, dumpster diving, and talking to third parties. Active: ping and port scans, DNS queries to the corporate server, OS fingerprinting and version scans. Active recon is easily seen and leaves evidence in firewall logs.

Black box = tester knows nothing; white box = knows everything.
Passive recon = no direct contact with target systems.
Red attacks, blue defends, purple combines both, white oversees.
An audit compares against a standard; a penetration test attempts to break in.
External audits provide independence; internal audits provide readiness.
